Definition

Inflammation is the local physiological response of vascularised living tissue to injury, designed to deliver leucocytes and plasma proteins to the site so that the offending agent can be destroyed and the damaged tissue repaired. Once the trigger is contained, the inflammatory reaction must resolve, organise, or progress — these are the three principal outcomes.

Possible Outcomes

  1. Resolution — complete restoration of normal architecture. Requires minimal parenchymal necrosis, intact basement membrane, rapid clearance of debris and a regenerative capacity of the local cells (labile/stable cells). Classic example: lobar pneumonia — macrophages clear the exudate and alveoli re-aerate.
  2. Healing by scarring (organisation / repair) — when tissue destruction is substantial or parenchyma cannot regenerate (permanent cells like neurons, cardiac myocytes), granulation tissue replaces the defect, matures into a collagenous scar. Example: myocardial infarction → fibrous scar.
  3. Abscess formation — when pyogenic bacteria are enclosed by fibrin and neutrophils, liquefactive necrosis produces pus enclosed in a pyogenic membrane. Common in S. aureus infections of skin, brain, lung.
  4. Chronic inflammation — persistence of the offending agent (intracellular microbes like M. tuberculosis, foreign bodies, autoimmunity) shifts the response to lymphocytes, macrophages and plasma cells with simultaneous tissue destruction and repair.
  5. Fibrosis — prolonged chronic inflammation drives TGF-β-mediated fibroblast proliferation and collagen deposition, leading to organ dysfunction (e.g. lung fibrosis, cirrhosis).
  6. Spread — via lymphatics (lymphangitis, lymphadenitis), haematogenous (bacteraemia, septicaemia, pyaemia), or direct extension to adjacent structures (pleural empyema from pneumonia).
  7. Systemic effects — fever, leucocytosis, acute-phase response (CRP, ESR), and in severe cases septic shock with multi-organ dysfunction.
flowchart TD A[Acute Inflammation] --> B{Trigger cleared?} B -- Yes, minimal damage --> C[Resolution] B -- Yes, parenchyma destroyed --> D[Healing by Scarring] B -- No, pyogenic bacteria --> E[Abscess] B -- No, persistent agent --> F[Chronic Inflammation] F --> G[Fibrosis] A --> H[Lymphatic / Haematogenous Spread] A --> I[Systemic: Fever, Shock]

Clinical Pearl

Whether an inflammation resolves or scars depends chiefly on the regenerative capacity of the parenchymal cells (labile > stable > permanent) and the extent of basement membrane damage. A basally intact basement membrane permits complete regeneration; a destroyed one almost always heals with a scar.
q0_0_1_4:
Definition

Apoptosis (Kerr, Wyllie & Currie, 1972) is a form of programmed, energy-dependent, single-cell death characterised by cell shrinkage, chromatin condensation, membrane blebbing and formation of apoptotic bodies — without significant inflammation. It corresponds to the "falling of leaves" in Greek.

Pathogenesis

Apoptosis is executed through two converging pathways that activate a cascade of caspases (cysteine-aspartate proteases):

  • Extrinsic (death-receptor) pathway — FasL/Fas (CD95), TNF/TNFR1, TRAIL/DR4-5 receptor engagement recruits FADD/TRADD → activation of initiator caspase-8 → caspase-3.
  • Intrinsic (mitochondrial) pathway — DNA damage, growth-factor withdrawal, hypoxia, radiation activate pro-apoptotic Bcl-2 family members (Bax, Bak, Bid, Bad, PUMA, Noxa) which permeabilise the outer mitochondrial membrane → release of cytochrome-c into cytosol → Apaf-1 + cytochrome-c + procaspase-9 form the apoptosome → activates caspase-9 → caspase-3.

Both pathways converge on executioner caspase-3, which cleaves nuclear lamins, cytoskeleton, PARP-1 and ICAD (liberating DNase to fragment DNA into 180 bp multiples — "ladder pattern" on gel). Apoptotic bodies are then phagocytosed by neighbouring cells or macrophages through phosphatidylserine (flipped to outer leaflet), thrombospondin and vitronectin receptors — without an inflammatory response.

Regulation: anti-apoptotic Bcl-2, Bcl-xL, Mcl-1 oppose Bax/Bak. p53 induces apoptosis in damaged cells by upregulating Bax, PUMA, Noxa.

flowchart TD A[Death receptor ligand] --> B[Fas/TNFR] B --> C[Caspase-8] C --> D[Caspase-3] E[Stress: DNA damage, hypoxia, ROS] --> F[p53 / Bax, Bak] F --> G[Mitochondrial outer-membrane permeabilisation] G --> H[Cytochrome-c + Apaf-1] H --> I[Apoptosome → Caspase-9] I --> D D --> J[Chromatin condensation, DNA ladder, apoptotic bodies]

Two Differences — Necrosis vs Apoptosis

FeatureNecrosisApoptosis
Cell sizeEnlarged (swelling, oncosis)Shrunken
InflammationAlways presentAbsent
DNA breakdownRandom, diffuse (smear)Internucleosomal 180-bp ladder
ATP requirementNone (passive)Active, ATP-dependent

Clinical Pearl

Apoptosis is physiologically silent; necrosis is always noisy. Excessive apoptosis causes neurodegeneration (Alzheimer, Parkinson) and aplastic anaemia; deficient apoptosis drives autoimmunity (SLE) and cancer (follicular B-cell lymphoma due to Bcl-2 over-expression from t(14;18)).

Definition

Amyloidosis refers to a heterogeneous group of disorders characterised by extracellular deposition of insoluble, fibrillar β-pleated sheet proteinaceous material — amyloid — in various tissues.

Pathogenesis

Amyloid fibrils are 7.5–10 nm rigid, non-branching filaments. All amyloid share a common β-pleated sheet conformation confirmed by Congo-red apple-green birefringence under polarised light and a characteristic cross-β X-ray diffraction pattern. A glycoprotein called serum amyloid P (SAP) and glycosaminoglycans are universally associated and stabilise the fibrils, preventing their breakdown.

Fibrillogenesis involves: (1) overproduction of a precursor protein; (2) misfolding into β-sheets; (3) proteolytic cleavage where needed; (4) aggregation and tissue deposition. The most important precursors are:

  • AL (amyloid light chain) — monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains from plasma-cell dyscrasias (multiple myeloma, B-cell lymphoma, MGUS).
  • AA (amyloid-associated) — derived from serum amyloid A (SAA), an acute-phase reactant; chronic inflammation (TB, rheumatoid arthritis, IBD, bronchiectasis, leprosy).
  • ATTR (transthyretin) — familial (mutant TTR) and wild-type / senile systemic amyloidosis (cardiac).
  • Aβ2-microglobulin — dialysis-associated.
  • Aβ peptide — Alzheimer disease (cerebral, vascular).
  • Localised — endocrine (medullary thyroid CA — calcitonin), atrial amyloid (ANP), type-2 diabetes islet amyloid (amylin / IAPP).

Classification

TypePrecursorClinical Setting
Systemic AL (primary)Ig light chainMultiple myeloma, MGUS, B-cell lymphoma
Systemic AA (secondary)Serum amyloid AChronic inflammation: TB, RA, IBD, bronchiectasis, leprosy, osteomyelitis
Hereditary/familialMutant transthyretin, fibrinogen Aα, apolipoprotein A-I, lysozymeFamilial amyloid polyneuropathy, nephropathy
Dialysis-relatedβ2-microglobulinLong-term haemodialysis; carpal tunnel, arthropathy
Senile systemicWild-type TTRCardiac amyloidosis in elderly
Cerebral / ageingAβ peptideAlzheimer disease
Endocrine / localisedCalcitonin, amylin (IAPP), ANP, prolactinMedullary thyroid CA, type-2 diabetes, atrial amyloid

Diagnosis

  1. Tissue biopsy — abdominal subcutaneous fat pad aspiration is the gold standard for systemic amyloidosis (sensitivity ~80%, specificity 100%). Rectal, gingival, renal or bone-marrow biopsies are alternatives.
  2. Congo red stain — orange-pink under light, apple-green birefringence under polarised light; pathognomonic.
  3. Crystal violet — metachromatic rose-pink.
  4. Thioflavin T — yellow-green fluorescence under UV.
  5. Immunohistochemistry / immunofluorescence — anti-κ, λ, SAA, TTR antibodies classify the type.
  6. Electron microscopy — non-branching 7.5–10 nm rigid fibrils.
  7. Mass spectrometry (Laser Microdissection / Mass Spectrometry, LMD/MS) — modern gold standard for typing.
  8. SAP scintigraphy — images systemic amyloid load.
  9. Supportive workup — serum/urine electrophoresis & free light-chain assay (AL), ESR/CRP & SAA (AA), echocardiography & cardiac MRI (cardiac amyloid), TTR gene sequencing.

Clinical Pearl

Macroglossia + periorbital purpura + nephrotic-range proteinuria + restrictive cardiomyopathy = think AL amyloidosis. Always send serum free light chain ratio and urine for Bence-Jones protein. Fat-pad aspiration combined with Congo red gives the quickest diagnosis.

Definition

Thromboembolism is the dislodgement of a thrombus (or part of it) from its site of formation and its impaction in a downstream vessel. The dislodged fragment is an embolus. >99% of emboli are thromboembolic.

Pathogenesis

Thrombus formation is governed by Virchow's triad:

  1. Endothelial injury — exposes subendothelial collagen & tissue factor, disrupts antithrombotic properties of endothelium (dominant in cardiac and arterial thrombi).
  2. Abnormal blood flow — stasis (DVT, atrial fibrillation) and turbulence (aneurysms, bifurcations) prevent dilution of clotting factors and bring platelets into contact with endothelium.
  3. Hypercoagulability — primary (Factor V Leiden, prothrombin G20210A, antithrombin/protein C/S deficiency) and secondary (malignancy, pregnancy, OCPs, immobilisation, surgery, nephrotic syndrome, antiphospholipid syndrome).

Once formed, a thrombus may: (i) lyse, (ii) organise into a scar, (iii) recanalise, or (iv) embolise. Emboli fragment most readily when loosely attached to a vein wall or to a roughened aortic/atrial surface. DVT of the deep calf, popliteal, femoral or iliac veins is the source of pulmonary embolism; left atrial thrombi (in mitral stenosis / AF) and left ventricular mural thrombi (post-MI) embolise to the systemic circulation — brain, spleen, kidney, gut, limbs.

flowchart TD A[Virchow Triad: Injury, Stasis, Hypercoagulability] --> B[Thrombus formation] B --> C[Dislodgement] C --> D{Origin} D -- Venous --> E[Pulmonary embolism] D -- Left heart / arterial --> F[Systemic embolism: brain, spleen, kidney, gut, limbs] D -- Right heart --> E B --> G[Recanalisation / Organisation]

Types of Thromboembolism

  • Pulmonary thromboembolism — saddle PE (large), lobar, micro-embolic; 95% arise from DVT of lower limbs.
  • Systemic arterial embolism — mural thrombus (post-MI), atrial thrombus (AF, mitral stenosis), vegetations (endocarditis), aortic aneurysm.
  • Paradoxical embolism — venous thrombus crosses a patent foramen ovale or ASD to reach systemic circulation.
  • Septic embolism — infected thrombus → pyaemic abscesses (e.g. IE, Lemierre syndrome).
  • Fat embolism — long-bone fractures, liposuction; triad of respiratory distress, neurological symptoms, petechial rash at 24–72 h.
  • Amniotic fluid embolism — during labour; sudden dyspnoea, hypotension, DIC.
  • Air embolism — >100 mL needed; chest trauma, neurosurgery, decompression sickness ("caisson disease").

Laboratory Diagnosis

  • DVT — D-dimer (high NPV), compression ultrasonography (gold standard), venography (historical).
  • Pulmonary embolism — Wells score → D-dimer, CT pulmonary angiography (gold standard, filling defect), V/Q scan (if CTPA contraindicated), echocardiography (right heart strain — McConnell's sign), troponin/BNP.
  • Hypercoagulability workup — PT, aPTT, platelet count, fibrinogen, D-dimer, antithrombin, protein C & S, Factor V Leiden (APC resistance), prothrombin G20210A, lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin & anti-β2-GPI antibodies, homocysteine.
  • Arterial embolism — ECG (AF, MI), echocardiography (vegetations, mural thrombus, atrial thrombus), CT angiography, carotid Doppler.

Clinical Pearl

Sudden dyspnoea + pleuritic chest pain + tachycardia in a post-operative or bedridden patient = pulmonary embolism until proven otherwise. A normal D-dimer excludes PE in low-risk patients (Wells ≤4); confirm with CT pulmonary angiography. Anticoagulate early — heparin bridge to warfarin/DOAC.

Definition

Hemolytic Disease of the Newborn (HDN) — also called erythroblastosis fetalis — is a condition in which transplacental passage of maternal IgG antibodies against fetal red-cell antigens causes immune-mediated haemolysis of fetal erythrocytes, leading to fetal anaemia, jaundice and, in severe cases, hydrops fetalis or kernicterus.

Pathogenesis

Maternal IgG (the only immunoglobulin that crosses placenta) is raised against fetal RBC antigens inherited from the father but absent in the mother. Sensitisation occurs in a previous pregnancy, miscarriage, abortion or transfusion. Subsequent pregnancies with an antigen-positive fetus trigger an anamnestic IgG response; antibodies cross placenta, bind fetal RBCs and cause extravascular haemolysis via Fc-receptor macrophages in the fetal spleen and liver.

TypeAntibodySeverity
Rh (D) incompatibilityAnti-D IgGCommonest severe; usually 2nd+ pregnancy
ABO incompatibilityAnti-A / Anti-B (IgG)Mild; first pregnancy possible; group O mother + A/B infant
Minor antigensAnti-c, Anti-E, Anti-Kell, Anti-Duffy, Anti-KiddVariable; Kell causes severe anaemia by erythroid suppression

Laboratory Evaluation

  1. Antenatal — maternal
    • Blood group & Rh typing (every mother at booking).
    • Indirect antiglobulin / indirect Coombs test — screens maternal serum for IgG antibodies at 12, 28 weeks.
    • Anti-D titre — >1:16 is significant; serial doubling titres warrant fetal monitoring.
    • Cell-free fetal DNA (cffDNA) in maternal plasma — RhD genotype of fetus (non-invasive).
  2. Antenatal — fetal
    • Middle cerebral artery (MCA) peak systolic velocity Doppler — >1.5 MoM predicts moderate/severe anaemia.
    • Percutaneous umbilical blood sampling (PUBS) — direct fetal Hb, bilirubin, blood group, Coombs.
    • Amniocentesis — delta-OD450 of amniotic fluid (Liley chart, Queenan curve).
    • Serial ultrasound — hydrops (ascites, pleural effusion, skin oedema, polyhydramnios).
  3. Postnatal — neonatal
    • Cord blood: blood group, direct antiglobulin test (DAT / direct Coombs), Hb, bilirubin, reticulocyte count, peripheral smear (spherocytes, nucleated RBCs).
    • Serial serum bilirubin (every 4–6 h) — "rate of rise" drives phototherapy/exchange decision.
    • Kernicterus watch — lethargy, poor feeding, hypotonia, high-pitched cry, seizures.

Safety Precautions

  • Antenatal anti-D prophylaxis — Rh-negative mother receives 300 µg (1500 IU) anti-D immunoglobulin at 28 weeks, within 72 h of delivery, and after any sensitising event (abortion, APH, ectopic, trauma, amniocentesis, external cephalic version).
  • Confirm fetomaternal haemorrhage (FMH) by Kleihauer-Betke test or flow cytometry; give extra anti-D if large FMH.
  • Avoid unnecessary instrumentation and traumatic deliveries.
  • Handle fetal blood samples with universal precautions — risk of needle-stick, infection, bleeding.
  • Phototherapy — protect eyes with eye-pads, monitor temperature and hydration.
  • Exchange transfusion — use irradiated, CMV-negative, leucocyte-reduced, antigen-negative (O-negative or ABO/Rh-compatible) blood; aseptic technique; monitor Ca2+, glucose, pH, platelets.
  • Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) reduces exchange rate in severe HDN.
  • Breast-feeding is not contraindicated in ABO/Rh HDN — milk jaundice and breastfeeding jaundice are different entities.

Clinical Pearl

Anti-D prophylaxis at 28 weeks + within 72 h of delivery has reduced Rh-haemolytic disease of the newborn by >95%. The first pregnancy is usually the sensitising event — hence the rationale for routine antenatal prophylaxis even in primigravida.

Clinical Features

  • Craniofacial — flat facial profile, brachycephaly, upslanting palpebral fissures, epicanthal folds, Brushfield spots on iris, small nose, protruding tongue, small low-set ears, single transverse palmar crease (simian crease), clinodactyly of 5th finger, wide sandal gap.
  • Cardiac — congenital heart defects in ~40% — AV septal (endocardial cushion) defect, VSD, ASD, PDA, tetralogy of Fallot.
  • GI — duodenal atresia ("double-bubble" sign), Hirschsprung disease, imperforate anus.
  • CNS — intellectual disability (IQ 25–50), hypotonia in infancy, early-onset Alzheimer-type dementia by 4th–5th decade.
  • Endocrine — hypothyroidism, short stature, infertility (males almost always; females subfertile).
  • Hematologic — 10–20× increased risk of childhood leukaemia (ALL, AMKL).
  • Other — atlantoaxial instability, recurrent otitis media, conductive hearing loss, refractive errors.

Definition

Obesity is excessive adiposity with adverse health effects. WHO defines it as BMI ≥30 kg/m² (overweight: 25–29.9; central obesity in Asians: waist >90 cm men, >80 cm women).

Etiopathogenesis

  • Positive energy balance — caloric intake > expenditure (sedentary lifestyle, energy-dense diet).
  • Genetic — monogenic obesity (leptin, leptin-receptor, POMC, MC4R mutations); polygenic ("common obesity").
  • Neuroendocrine — hyperactivity of orexigenic NPY/AgRP neurons; hypoactivity of anorexigenic POMC/CART neurons; ghrelin ↑, leptin & insulin resistance.
  • Endocrine — hypothyroidism, Cushing syndrome, PCOS, growth hormone deficiency, hypogonadism.
  • Drugs — antipsychotics (olanzapine, clozapine), steroids, tricyclics, insulin, sulfonylureas, β-blockers, gabapentin, pizotifen.
  • Gut microbiome — increased Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratio enhances calorie harvest.
  • Early life — maternal obesity, gestational diabetes, low birth weight followed by rapid catch-up growth.
  • Psychosocial — stress (cortisol), sleep deprivation, depression.

Sequelae (Complications)

  1. Metabolic — insulin resistance, type-2 diabetes, metabolic syndrome, NAFLD / NASH, dyslipidaemia, gout, cholelithiasis.
  2. Cardiovascular — hypertension, atherosclerosis, coronary disease, heart failure, stroke, venous thromboembolism, varicose veins.
  3. Respiratory — obstructive sleep apnoea, obesity-hypoventilation syndrome (Pickwickian), asthma exacerbation.
  4. Musculoskeletal — osteoarthritis (knees, hips), gout, low back pain, disability.
  5. Endocrine / reproductive — PCOS, infertility, erectile dysfunction, pregnancy complications (pre-eclampsia, GDM).
  6. GI — GERD, gallstones, NAFLD, colorectal & pancreatic cancer.
  7. Oncologic — increased risk of breast, endometrial, colon, renal, oesophageal, pancreatic, liver cancers.
  8. Psychosocial — depression, anxiety, social stigma.
  9. Skin — acanthosis nigricans, intertrigo, striae, lymphoedema.

Clinical Pearl

Central (visceral) adiposity is more dangerous than subcutaneous — it releases free fatty acids & pro-inflammatory adipokines (TNF-α, IL-6, leptin, resistin) and reduces adiponectin, driving insulin resistance and atherogenesis. Waist circumference and waist-hip ratio are better predictors of metabolic risk than BMI alone.

Definition

Carcinogenesis is the multistep process by which normal cells are transformed into malignant cells through accumulation of genetic and epigenetic alterations in oncogenes, tumour-suppressor genes and DNA-repair genes — producing the hallmarks of cancer: self-sufficiency in growth signals, evasion of apoptosis, limitless replicative potential, sustained angiogenesis, tissue invasion & metastasis, and genomic instability.

Viral Carcinogenesis

Oncogenic viruses contribute to ~15–20% of human cancers globally. They act by integrating viral DNA into the host genome (or persisting as episomes), expressing viral oncoproteins that drive proliferation and disable tumour-suppressor pathways, or by inducing chronic inflammation and immunosuppression.

Virus (Family)CancerMechanism
HPV 16, 18 (Papova)Cervical, oropharyngeal, anal, penile SCCE6 binds & degrades p53; E7 inactivates Rb
HBV, HCV (Hepadna, Flavi)Hepatocellular carcinomaChronic inflammation → cirrhosis; HBx activates NF-κB, src; HCV core drives ROS, fibrosis
EBV (Herpes γ)Burkitt lymphoma, Hodgkin lymphoma, nasopharyngeal CA, post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorderLMP-1 mimics CD40 (B-cell proliferation); EBNA-2 drives c-MYC; "African Burkitt" has t(8;14)
HTLV-1 (Retro)Adult T-cell leukaemia / lymphomaTax protein activates NF-κB, IL-2R → autocrine T-cell proliferation
HHV-8 (KSHV)Kaposi sarcoma, primary effusion lymphoma, multicentric Castleman diseaseLatent nuclear antigen (LANA), viral cyclin, vGPCR drive angiogenesis
MCV (Polyoma)Merkel cell carcinomaTruncated large T antigen inactivates Rb

Mechanistically, viruses are directly transforming (HPV, EBV, HTLV-1) when they express oncoproteins in tumour cells, or indirectly carcinogenic (HIV — immunosuppression permits oncogenic viruses; HCV — chronic inflammation).

Clinical Pearl

Three vaccines already reduce viral cancer burden: HPV vaccine (cervical & oropharyngeal cancer), HBV vaccine (hepatocellular carcinoma), and HCV antiviral cure (DAAs). Prevention is currently the most powerful tool against virus-induced cancers.

Diagnostic Criteria for SLE

Two systems are widely used — the SLICC 2012 (Systemic Lupus International Collaborating Clinics) and the newer EULAR/ACR 2019. ANA is the entry criterion in both.

SLICC 2012 — ≥4 criteria (at least 1 clinical + 1 immunological)

Clinical (11):

  • Acute cutaneous lupus (malar rash, photosensitive, subacute cutaneous)
  • Chronic cutaneous lupus (discoid, panniculitis, lupus tumidus)
  • Nonscarring alopecia
  • Oral / nasal ulcers
  • Joint disease — synovitis involving ≥2 joints
  • Serositis — pleurisy or pericarditis
  • Renal — urine protein >500 mg/24 h or RBC casts
  • Neurologic — seizures, psychosis, mononeuritis, myelitis, peripheral neuropathy, acute confusional state
  • Haemolytic anaemia
  • Leukopenia (<4000) / lymphopenia (<1000)
  • Thrombocytopenia (<100,000)

Immunological (6): ANA above lab reference range; anti-dsDNA; anti-Sm; antiphospholipid antibodies (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, anti-β2-glycoprotein I); low complement (C3, C4, CH50); direct Coombs test (in absence of haemolytic anaemia).

EULAR/ACR 2019

ANA ≥1:80 (entry). Additive weighted score ≥10 from clinical domains (constitutional, haematologic, neuropsychiatric, mucocutaneous, serosal, musculoskeletal, renal) and immunological domains (SLE-specific antibodies, antiphospholipid, complement). Renal biopsy class III/IV/V lupus nephritis earns 8 & 10 points respectively. Sensitivity ~92%, specificity ~93%.

Clinical Pearl

ANA is the screening test; anti-dsDNA & anti-Sm are highly specific (>95%) and confirm SLE. Anti-dsDNA titres also track disease activity and correlate with lupus nephritis. Low complement (C3, C4) suggests active immune-complex disease.

Indications for CSF Examination

  • Suspected meningitis (pyogenic, tuberculous, viral, fungal) or encephalitis
  • Subarachnoid haemorrhage (if CT negative but clinical suspicion high — xanthochromia)
  • Demyelinating disorders — multiple sclerosis, Guillain-Barré, transverse myelitis (oligoclonal bands)
  • CNS syphilis, neuroborreliosis, neurocysticercosis, cryptococcal meningitis (HIV)
  • CNS malignancy — carcinomatous meningitis, leukaemia/lymphoma (cytology)
  • Demarcation of treatment response in tuberculous or pyogenic meningitis
  • Measurement of intracranial pressure (idiopathic intracranial hypertension, normal-pressure hydrocephalus)
  • Therapeutic — intrathecal methotrexate, baclofen pump

Contraindications

  • Raised intracranial pressure (esp. with posterior fossa lesion) — risk of tonsillar herniation; perform fundoscopy & CT/MRI first.
  • Bleeding diathesis — platelets <50,000, INR >1.5, on anticoagulants (correct first).
  • Local skin infection at the puncture site (cellulitis, abscess).
  • Suspected spinal cord compression / epidural abscess — image first.
  • Severe scoliosis / spina bifida — relative; image-guided approach.
  • Uncooperative / combative patient — sedation needed.
  • Cardiorespiratory compromise (cannot tolerate lateral decubitus posture).

Complications

  • Post-lumbar puncture headache — commonest (10–30%); due to CSF leak through dural puncture. Reduced by smaller needle (25 G), bevel parallel to dural fibres, hydration, supine rest 1–2 h; treat with caffeine, epidural blood patch if persistent.
  • Back pain at the puncture site — local trauma, transient.
  • Herniation — rare but fatal, in raised ICP.
  • Infection — iatrogenic meningitis, epidural abscess, discitis.
  • Bleeding — spinal epidural/subdural haematoma (especially coagulopathic).
  • Rare — 6th nerve palsy, intracranial subdural haematoma, pneumocoelous, neurogenic bladder.

Clinical Pearl

Always look at the fundus for papilloedema and obtain a CT/MRI brain in immunocompromised, focal neurology, seizures, altered sensorium or HIV-positive patients before lumbar puncture. Opening pressure, cell count, glucose, protein, gram stain, AFB, culture and viral PCR are the minimum dataset to interpret CSF.

Definition

Exfoliative cytology is the microscopic examination of cells that are spontaneously shed (desquamated) or mechanically scraped/brushed from body surfaces — used as a rapid, minimally invasive screening and diagnostic tool.

Sample Types

  • Naturally shed — sputum, urine, CSF, pleural, pericardial & peritoneal fluids, nipple discharge.
  • Scraped / brushed — Pap smear (cervix), buccal smear, lesion scrapings; brushings during endoscopy/bronchoscopy; cervical, oesophageal, gastric, biliary, bronchial brush cytology.
  • Fluid after centrifugation — body cavity effusions.

Procedure (Pap smear)

  1. Patient in lithotomy; speculum inserted without lubricant (saline only).
  2. Sample transformation zone with Ayre's spatula + endocervical brush (or liquid-based cytology with broom-type device).
  3. Smear on slide & fix immediately in 95% ethanol (conventional) OR rinse into liquid medium (ThinPrep, SurePath).
  4. Stain with Papanicolaou stain (haematoxylin, Orange G, EA polychrome); air dry & mount.
  5. Report using Bethesda system — NILM, ASC-US, ASC-H, LSIL, HSIL, SCC, AIS, glandular cell atypia.

Advantages

  • Simple, cheap, OPD-based, painless, repeatable.
  • High sensitivity for premalignant lesions (Pap smear has reduced cervical cancer mortality by >70%).
  • Liquid-based cytology improves sample quality & allows HPV DNA co-testing.

Limitations

  • Requires expert cytopathologist — inter-observer variability.
  • False negatives — poor sampling, inflammation, blood, scant dyskaryotic cells.
  • Cannot assess invasion depth — biopsy needed for confirmation.
  • Less sensitive for high post-menopausal squamocolumnar junction (use endocervical brush).

Clinical Pearl

The single most cost-effective cancer screening test ever devised is the cervical Pap smear. Combined with HPV DNA testing, sensitivity for high-grade CIN exceeds 95%. All women 21–65 years should be screened every 3 years (or every 5 years with HPV co-testing 30+).

Physical Examination of Urine

  1. Colour
    • Pale yellow — dilute (polyuria, diabetes insipidus)
    • Dark yellow — concentrated (dehydration, fever, jaundice first morning sample)
    • Red / brown — haematuria, haemoglobinuria, myoglobinuria, porphyria, beetroot, rifampicin, phenytoin
    • Black on standing — alkaptonuria, melanuria
    • Green-blue — pseudomonas, methylene blue, amitriptyline, propofol
    • Milky — chyluria, pyuria, phosphaturia
  2. Appearance / Transparency — clear (normal); cloudy (pyuria, phosphate crystals in alkaline urine, amorphous urates, chyluria, spermatozoa); frothy (proteinuria).
  3. Odour — aromatic (normal); ammoniacal (UTI, stale); faecal (colo-vesical fistula); fruity (ketones, DKA); mousy (phenylketonuria); cabbage/maple syrup (MSUD); sweaty feet (isovaleric acidaemia).
  4. Foam test — persistent yellowish foam = proteinuria; red foam = haematuria.
  5. Volume — 24-h urine 600–1800 mL. Polyuria >3 L/d; oliguria <400 mL/d; anuria <100 mL/d.
  6. Specific gravity — 1.003–1.030. Low (1.001–1.005) in diabetes insipidus, over-hydration. High (>1.025) in dehydration, glycosuria, proteinuria. Fixed at 1.010 in chronic renal failure.
  7. pH — 4.5–8.0 (average 6.0). Acidic in high-protein diet, DKA, lactic acidosis, diarrhoea, NH4Cl. Alkaline in vegetarian diet, UTI with urea-splitting organisms (Proteus, Klebsiella), vomiting, renal tubular acidosis, diuretics.
  8. Deposits — phosphates (white, alkaline), urates (pink, acidic), oxalates (envelope-shaped), blood clots, gravel.

Dark urine + tea-coloured froth + positive blood on dipstick but no RBCs on microscopy = haemoglobinuria / myoglobinuria (rhabdomyolysis, intravascular haemolysis). Always confirm with serum CK / LDH / haptoglobin and plasma-free haemoglobin.

Laboratory Investigations in Diabetes Mellitus

  1. Fasting plasma glucose (FPG) — ≥126 mg/dL after 8 h fast (normal <100; prediabetes 100–125).
  2. 2-h post-prandial / OGTT plasma glucose — ≥200 mg/dL after 75 g glucose load.
  3. Random plasma glucose — ≥200 mg/dL with classical symptoms (polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss) diagnostic.
  4. HbA1c (glycated haemoglobin) — ≥6.5% diagnostic; 5.7–6.4% prediabetes; reflects glycaemic control over preceding 8–12 weeks.
  5. Oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) — 75 g glucose; sample at 0, 30, 60, 90, 120 min; diagnose gestational DM (75 g, IADPSG criteria) and borderline diabetes.
  6. Urine glucose — appears when blood glucose exceeds renal threshold (~180 mg/dL).
  7. Urine & blood ketones — β-hydroxybutyrate (preferred), AcAc; diagnosing DKA.
  8. C-peptide — distinguishes type-1 (low) from type-2 (high/normal); evaluates residual β-cell function.
  9. Islet autoantibodies — anti-GAD65, IAA, IA-2, ZnT8 — confirm type-1 diabetes in adults.
  10. Insulin level — high in insulin resistance (type-2, insulinoma); low in type-1.
  11. Lipid profile — high TG, low HDL, small dense LDL; cardiovascular risk.
  12. Renal function & urine microalbumin — ACR >30 mg/g = diabetic nephropathy.
  13. Fundus examination — retinopathy screening at diagnosis of type-2 DM and yearly thereafter.
  14. Foot examination — monofilament, vibration perception, ABI.

HbA1c is unreliable in pregnancy, haemolytic anaemia, recent transfusion, haemoglobinopathies and uraemia. For gestational diabetes mellitus screening, use 75 g OGTT at 24–28 weeks — one elevated value (fasting ≥92, 1-h ≥180, 2-h ≥153 mg/dL) diagnoses GDM (IADPSG).
q0_0_2_11:
Laboratory Diagnosis of HIV/AIDS

  1. Screening — 4th-generation combo ELISA/CIA — detects HIV-1 p24 antigen + HIV-1/2 antibodies; window period ~2–3 weeks. 5th-generation also distinguishes p24 from antibody.
  2. Confirmatory — HIV-1/2 differentiation immunoassay (e.g. Geenius) or Western blot. Distinguishes HIV-1 vs HIV-2.
  3. Nucleic acid tests (NAT)
    • HIV-1 RNA PCR (viral load) — diagnosis in window period, neonates (maternal antibody confounds), elite controllers, and treatment monitoring. <20 copies/mL is undetectable.
    • HIV-1 DNA PCR — for early infant diagnosis (<18 mo).
  4. Rapid tests — immunochromatographic finger-prick whole-blood / oral fluid; useful in voluntary counselling, OPD, labour ward. Three-test algorithm in India (NACO).
  5. Baseline staging
    • CD4+ T-lymphocyte count — normal >500; AIDS if <200; initiate ART if <350 or any AIDS-defining illness.
    • Plasma HIV-1 RNA viral load — baseline and at 2–8 wks, then every 3–6 months.
  6. Resistance testing — genotype (commonest) before starting ART and on virological failure; phenotype if complex.
  7. Co-infection & OI screening — HBsAg, anti-HCV, VDRL, TST/IGRA, CD4, toxoplasma serology, cryptococcal antigen (if CD4 <100), Pap smear, chest X-ray.
  8. Other baseline tests — CBC, LFT, KFT, fasting lipid profile & glucose, urinalysis, G6PD (before dapsone/sulfa), pregnancy test.

Clinical Pearl

In infants <18 months, maternal antibodies cross placenta — serology is unreliable. Use HIV-1 DNA PCR (or RNA) at 6 weeks (NACO), repeat at 6 months & 12 months. A positive result requires confirmation on a second sample before starting ART.
q0_0_2_12:
Stages of Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR)

The Westergren ESR measures the distance (in mm) that red cells fall in a vertical anticoagulated column over 1 hour. Three distinct phases occur:

  1. Stage of aggregation / rouleaux formation (0–10 min)
    • Red cells aggregate face-to-face forming rouleaux (coin-stack appearance).
    • Driven by plasma acute-phase proteins (fibrinogen, IgG, IgM, α2-macroglobulin, haptoglobin, CRP) which neutralise the negative zeta potential (sialic acid) on RBC surface.
    • Aggregates are heavier than individual cells and sediment faster.
  2. Stage of settling / sedimentation (10–40 min)
    • Rouleaux stacks fall under gravity at near-constant velocity; this is the linear phase that determines the 1-hour reading.
    • Sedimentation velocity follows Stokes' law: v ∝ r²; hence large aggregates settle fastest.
  3. Stage of packing (40–60 min)
    • Aggregates accumulate at the bottom and pack tightly; rate slows as cells reach the floor of the tube.
    • Final height of packed cell column at 1 h = ESR (mm/h).

Reference Ranges (Westergren)

  • Adult men: 0–15 mm/h
  • Adult women: 0–20 mm/h
  • Children: 0–10 mm/h
  • Elderly: up to ~30 (men) / ~35 (women)

Clinical Pearl

ESR reflects plasma viscosity and acute-phase reactants. CRP rises and falls faster (hours vs days) and is therefore preferred for monitoring acute inflammation. Markedly raised ESR (>100 mm/h) suggests multiple myeloma, polymyalgia rheumatica, temporal arteritis, malignancy or chronic infection (TB, endocarditis).
q0_0_2_13:
Causes of Increased ESR

  • Infections — pyogenic (pneumonia, abscess), TB, subacute infective endocarditis, osteomyelitis, pelvic inflammatory disease, HIV.
  • Inflammation / autoimmune — rheumatoid arthritis, SLE, polymyalgia rheumatica, giant-cell arteritis, vasculitis, inflammatory bowel disease.
  • Malignancy — multiple myeloma (often >100), lymphoma, leukaemia, carcinoma (especially with metastases), Waldenström macroglobulinaemia.
  • Tissue necrosis — MI, malignancy, surgery, trauma, infarction.
  • Pregnancy & menstruation — physiological rise; third trimester ESR may exceed 40 mm/h.
  • Drugs — OCPs, oestrogens, methyldopa, penicillamine, dextran, vitamin A.
  • Endocrine — hyperthyroidism, hypothyroidism.
  • Chronic renal failure / nephrotic syndrome — ↑ fibrinogen, ↑ globulins.
  • Anaemia — reduced haematocrit increases rouleaux.
  • Other — old age, female sex, obesity, smoking, recent vaccination.

Causes of Decreased ESR

  • Polycythaemia — Vera, secondary (hypoxia, tumour).
  • Severe leucocytosis (>50,000) — viscosity overshoots.
  • Abnormal RBC shape — sickle cell disease, spherocytosis, acanthocytosis, poikilocytosis (cannot form rouleaux).
  • Plasma protein abnormalities — hypofibrinogenaemia (DIC, severe liver disease), hypogammaglobulinaemia, agammaglobulinaemia.
  • Congestive heart failure — venous stasis & low flow.
  • Drugs — high-dose aspirin, corticosteroids, quinine, ACTH, TNF inhibitors.
  • Severe dehydration, shock.
  • Cryoglobulinaemia — at low temperature, plasma gels and RBCs cannot fall.
  • Technical — delayed testing >4 h, tilting tube >3° off vertical, bubbles, clot in sample, short Westergren tube.

Clinical Pearl

Very high ESR (>100 mm/h) should prompt a work-up for multiple myeloma (serum & urine electrophoresis, free light chains), giant-cell arteritis / polymyalgia rheumatica (especially in elderly with headache / shoulder stiffness), or occult malignancy / chronic infection (TB, IE).
q0_0_2_14:
Importance of Working in a Health-Care Team

Modern medicine is a team sport — no single professional has the breadth of expertise needed for safe, effective, patient-centred care. The team typically includes doctors, nurses, pharmacists, physiotherapists, dieticians, social workers, lab technicians, radiographers, hospital administrators and the patient's family — each contributing complementary skills.

  • Comprehensive care — combines medical, surgical, psychological, nutritional and social expertise, addressing the whole patient rather than one disease.
  • Reduced medical errors — cross-checks by pharmacists, nurses and second-physician reviewers catch prescribing errors, allergies, drug interactions and wrong-site surgery.
  • Improved outcomes — multidisciplinary stroke units, oncology tumour boards, and cardiac arrest teams have measurable mortality benefits over isolated care.
  • Better communication — structured handovers (SBAR) reduce information loss across shifts.
  • Patient safety — WHO Surgical Safety Checklist, time-outs and team briefing significantly reduce surgical morbidity & mortality.
  • Workload distribution — prevents burnout, ensures continuity of care, enables round-the-clock coverage.
  • Continuity & coordination — avoids duplicate investigations, contradictory plans, and gaps in follow-up.
  • Shared decision-making — patient & family are active partners, improving adherence & satisfaction.
  • Education & mentoring — junior staff learn from seniors; bedside rounds teach clinical reasoning, ethics and procedural skills.
  • Resource optimisation — administrators, microbiologists and infection-control nurses collaborate on antimicrobial stewardship and bed management.
  • Ethical & legal support — ethics committees, hospital lawyers and risk-management teams guide end-of-life decisions, consent, and adverse-event disclosure.

Clinical Pearl

Effective teams share three traits — clear roles, structured communication (closed-loop, SBAR), and psychological safety where any member can voice concerns without fear. The lowest-ranking nurse must be able to halt a surgery — that safety net has prevented countless wrong-site operations.

Indications for Semen Analysis

  • Male infertility workup — primary indication; couple unable to conceive after 12 months (or 6 months if partner >35) of unprotected intercourse.
  • Post-vasectomy confirmation — at 12 & 20 weeks / 20 ejaculations post-procedure to confirm azoospermia.
  • Pre-fertility treatment — IUI, IVF, ICSI; determines need & modality.
  • Assessment after illness / fever / varicocele repair / hormonal therapy.
  • Sperm donor screening — infectious disease, karyotype, sperm function tests.
  • Forensic / sexual assault cases — identification of semen (acid phosphatase, prostate-specific antigen, microscopy for spermatozoa, DNA profiling).
  • Cryopreservation — prior to chemotherapy, radiotherapy, vasectomy, orchiectomy, gender-reassignment.

Microscopic Examination (WHO 5th ed., 2021)

  • Sample collection — by masturbation after 2–7 days abstinence; delivered to lab within 1 h; kept at body temperature. Two samples 7–14 days apart for confirmation.
  • Liquefaction — within 15–30 min at 37°C (proteolytic enzymes from prostate).
  • Macroscopic — volume ≥1.4 mL (lower reference limit); pH ≥7.2; viscosity <2 cm thread; appearance grey-opalescent.
  • Sperm concentration — ≥16 million/mL (lower limit); haemocytometer or computer-assisted semen analysis (CASA).
  • Total sperm number — ≥39 million per ejaculate.
  • Total motility — ≥42% (PR + NP); progressive motility ≥30%.
  • Vitality — ≥54% live (eosin-nigrosin or hypo-osmotic swelling test).
  • Morphology — ≥4% normal forms (strict Kruger criteria); Papanicolaou, Shorr or Diff-Quik stain.
  • Leucocytes — <1 million/mL (peroxidase-positive); pyospermia suggests genital tract infection.
  • Agglutination — significant if >50% sperm agglutinated; suggests anti-sperm antibodies (MAR / IB test).
  • Other cells — immature germ cells, epithelial cells, debris.

Clinical Pearl

One abnormal semen analysis is not infertility — repeat after 12 weeks. Azoospermia with normal testicular volume & FSH suggests obstructive cause (post-infective, CFTR mutation, vasectomy) — surgical sperm retrieval (TESE / PESA) with ICSI can give biological paternity.
q0_0_2_16:
Molecular Mechanism of Apoptosis

Apoptosis is executed by a proteolytic cascade of caspases (cysteine-aspartate proteases). Initiator caspases (8, 9, 10) cleave and activate executioner caspases (3, 6, 7), which dismantle the cell.

1. Extrinsic (Death-Receptor) Pathway

  • FasL → Fas (CD95) trimerisation; TNF-α → TNFR1; TRAIL → DR4/5.
  • Receptor recruits adaptor FADD (or TRADD) via death domains.
  • FADD death-effector domain binds procaspase-8 → DISC (death-inducing signalling complex) → auto-activation of caspase-8.
  • Caspase-8 directly cleaves caspase-3, and cleaves Bid to truncated Bid (tBid) which feeds into the intrinsic pathway (cross-talk).

2. Intrinsic (Mitochondrial) Pathway

  • Stimuli: DNA damage, hypoxia, growth-factor withdrawal, ROS, radiation, ER stress, chemotherapy.
  • p53 & BH3-only proteins (Bid, Bim, Bad, Noxa, PUMA) neutralise Bcl-2 / Bcl-xL / Mcl-1 and activate Bax / Bak.
  • Bax/Bak oligomerise → mitochondrial outer-membrane permeabilisation (MOMP).
  • Cytochrome-c released into cytosol binds Apaf-1 + dATP → heptameric wheel-like apoptosome → recruits procaspase-9 → active caspase-9.
  • Caspase-9 cleaves caspase-3.
  • Smac/DIABLO & Omi/HtrA2 released simultaneously neutralise XIAP, cIAPs (inhibitors of apoptosis), removing the brake.

3. Execution Phase

  • Caspase-3 cleaves: PARP-1 (DNA repair), nuclear lamins (nuclear shrinkage), ICAD (liberates CAD DNase → internucleosomal 180-bp DNA ladder), cytoskeleton (membrane blebbing).
  • Phosphatidylserine translocated to outer leaflet (signals macrophages).
  • Membrane blebbing & fragmentation into apoptotic bodies.

4. Phagocytic Clearance

  • Macrophages / neighbouring cells recognise phosphatidylserine, thrombospondin, oxidised LDL via CD36, αvβ3 vitronectin receptor, MER-TK & LRP — engulf apoptotic bodies silently, without inflammation.
flowchart TD A[Death receptor] --> B[FADD → Caspase-8] B --> C[Caspase-3] B --> D[tBid] D --> E[Bax/Bak oligomerise] F[Stress → p53, BH3-only] --> E E --> G[MOMP → Cytochrome-c] G --> H[Apaf-1 Apoptosome → Caspase-9] H --> C C --> I[Chromatin condensation, DNA ladder, apoptotic bodies] I --> J[Phagocytosis without inflammation]

Clinical Pearl

Bcl-2 over-expression (e.g. follicular lymphoma t(14;18)) prevents apoptosis, allowing survival of malignant cells. p53 — "guardian of the genome" — induces apoptosis in damaged cells; its loss in ~50% of cancers allows genetically unstable cells to survive.
q0_0_2_17:
Phagocytosis

Phagocytosis ("cell eating") is the process by which specialised cells — neutrophils, macrophages, monocytes, dendritic cells (and eosinophils to a lesser degree) — internalise particles ≥0.5 µm (microbes, dead cells, debris) into a phagocytic vacuole (phagosome) for destruction and antigen presentation.

Steps

  1. Recognition & attachment
    • Direct — via mannose, scavenger, β-glucan, CD14 (LPS), CR3 (iC3b) receptors.
    • Opsonin-mediated — IgG (FcγR), C3b/iC3b (CR1, CR3), collectins, pentraxins (CRP) — greatly enhances uptake.
  2. Engulfment — pseudopodia zip around the particle (actin polymerisation, Rho-family GTPases Cdc42, Rac). Particle is internalised into a phagosome.
  3. Phagosome maturation — phagosome fuses with early endosome → late endosome → lysosome, progressively acidifying (pH drops to ~4.5–5.0) and acquiring degradative enzymes.
  4. Killing & digestion — Two mechanisms:
    • Oxygen-dependent (respiratory burst) — NADPH oxidase (phox) reduces O2 to superoxide (O2·−); superoxide dismutase converts to H2O2; myeloperoxidase (MPO) + Cl− → hypochlorous acid (HOCl). Other ROS: hydroxyl radical, singlet oxygen.
    • Oxygen-independent — lysosomal hydrolases, lysozyme (cleaves peptidoglycan), lactoferrin (iron chelation), defensins & cathelicidins (membrane pore-forming peptides), acidic pH.
    • Nitric oxide — iNOS generates NO·; combined with superoxide → peroxynitrite (ONOO−) — kills mycobacteria, intracellular pathogens.
  5. Exocytosis or antigen presentation — residual debris exocytosed; macrophages/dendritic cells process antigen and present peptide + MHC II to CD4 T-cells, linking innate to adaptive immunity.
flowchart TD A[Microbe + opsonin] --> B[Receptor recognition] B --> C[Actin-driven engulfment] C --> D[Phagosome] D --> E[Fusion with lysosome → Phagolysosome] E --> F[Oxygen-dependent: NADPH oxidase, MPO, HOCl] E --> G[Oxygen-independent: lysozyme, defensins, acid] E --> H[NO / peroxynitrite] F --> I[Microbial killing] G --> I H --> I I --> J[Digestion & exocytosis / antigen presentation]

Clinical Pearl

Defects in phagocytic pathways cause severe recurrent infections — chronic granulomatous disease (NADPH oxidase defect, catalase-positive organisms like S. aureus, Aspergillus), MPO deficiency (Candida), LAD-1 (β2 integrin CD18 defect, no pus formation), Chédiak-Higashi (lysosomal trafficking — giant granules, partial albinism).
q0_0_2_18:
Protein-Energy Malnutrition (PEM)

PEM is a group of clinical conditions caused by inadequate intake of protein and/or calories, broadly classified into Kwashiorkor, Marasmus and Marasmic kwashiorkor.

Etiopathogenesis

  • Inadequate intake — poverty, famine, ignorance, faulty weaning, anorexia, dysphagia.
  • Increased demand — pregnancy, lactation, infancy, adolescence, fever, sepsis, surgery, burns.
  • Malabsorption — chronic diarrhoea, celiac disease, tropical sprue, short bowel, cystic fibrosis, parasites.
  • Increased loss — nephrotic syndrome (proteinuria), protein-losing enteropathy, burns, fistulas, malignancy, chronic illness.
  • Social factors — poverty, illiteracy, poor maternal nutrition, large family, infections, lack of breastfeeding.

Classification & Comparison

Complications / Sequelae

  • Growth retardation, stunting, delayed milestones, intellectual disability.
  • Secondary immunodeficiency — cell-mediated immunity severely impaired → opportunistic infections (measles, TB, herpes, candidiasis).
  • Diarrhoeal disease — malabsorption, persistent diarrhoea cycle.
  • Hypothermia, hypoglycaemia, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, micronutrient deficiency (vit A, zinc, iron).
  • Dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, cardiac arrhythmia, sudden death.
  • Refeeding syndrome — hypophosphataemia, hypokalaemia, thiamine depletion on sudden refeeding.
  • Hepatic steatosis, fatty liver (kwashiorkor).
  • Apathy, developmental delay, permanent cognitive impairment.

Clinical Pearl

The WHO 10-step protocol for severe acute malnutrition stabilises first (Step 1–7: hypoglycaemia, hypothermia, dehydration, electrolytes, infection, micronutrients, careful feeding), then rehabilitates (Step 8–10: catch-up growth, sensory stimulation, follow-up). Never refeed aggressively in the first week — refeeding syndrome is fatal.

Most acute haemolytic reactions are preventable — they are usually clerical errors at the bedside. Always identify the patient and unit at the bedside with two identifiers before connecting the transfusion, and observe the patient closely during the first 15 minutes.

q0_0_2_21:
Complications in Healing of Skin Wounds

  • Infection — most common; staphylococcal/streptococcal; causes delayed healing, suppuration, cellulitis, abscess, wound dehiscence.
  • Dehiscence — splitting of opposed wound edges; usually day 5–8 before adequate collagen deposition; abdominal wound burst with evisceration is surgical emergency.
  • Incisional hernia — late complication of abdominal wound dehiscence; peritoneal sac protrudes through weakened scar.
  • Hypertrophic scar — raised, red scar confined to wound boundary; common in young, burns, tension areas; often regresses.
  • Keloid — scar extends beyond wound margins, does not regress; familial, dark-skinned individuals; over-production of collagen type III; common on sternum, earlobe, shoulder.
  • Contracture — shortening of scar across joints → deformity & limited motion; classic complication of burns.
  • Implantation (epidermal) cyst — epidermal cells trapped in dermis during closure.
  • Neuroma — traumatic neuroma at cut nerve end; painful.
  • Pigmentary changes — hyper- or hypopigmentation in scar.
  • Marjolin ulcer — SCC arising in chronic non-healing scar / chronic venous ulcer / burn scar; painless ulcer that suddenly enlarges.
  • Tattooing — foreign material embedded in wound leaves pigmented scar.
  • Cicatricial pemphigoid — scarring blistering disorder.
  • Delayed healing — malnutrition, diabetes, steroids, irradiation, anaemia, hypoxia, foreign body.

Clinical Pearl

Distinguish keloid from hypertrophic scar by the margins: keloid extends beyond the original wound, hypertrophic scar stays within it. Keloids tend to recur after excision — combine surgery with intralesional corticosteroid or silicone sheeting to reduce recurrence.
q0_0_2_22:
Morphological Lesions in Vitamin A Deficiency

  • Eye
    • Night blindness (nyctalopia) — earliest symptom; impaired rod function due to inadequate rhodopsin.
    • Xerophthalmia — conjunctival & corneal dryness; squamous metaplasia of conjunctiva; loss of goblet cells.
    • Bitot spots — silvery-grey foamy patches on bulbar conjunctiva (keratinised epithelium + Corynebacterium xerosis).
    • Corneal xerosis → keratomalacia → corneal ulceration, perforation, prolapse of iris, blindness.
    • Conjunctival impression cytology shows reduced goblet cells & squamous metaplasia (sub-clinical detection).
  • Skin — follicular hyperkeratosis (phrynoderma) — dry, rough, papular lesions over extensor surfaces of limbs, buttocks, back.
  • Respiratory tract — squamous metaplasia of respiratory epithelium → loss of ciliary clearance → recurrent respiratory infections.
  • GI tract — metaplasia of pancreatic ductal & salivary epithelium; diarrhoea & malabsorption.
  • Urinary tract — squamous metaplasia of urothelium → propensity to calculi & infection.
  • Reproductive tract — vaginal cornification; infertility, foetal malformations.
  • Growth retardation — impaired skeletal growth in children.
  • Impaired immunity — reduced T-cell function, fewer goblet cells → increased measles & diarrhoea severity.

Clinical Pearl

Vitamin A supplementation at high dose (200,000 IU) to children with measles reduces mortality by ~50% by preventing keratomalica and pneumonia. WHO classifies xerophthalmia into stages (XN, X1B Bitot spots, X2 corneal xerosis, X3A/B ulceration, XS scar, XF phthisis) for public-health action.
q0_0_2_23:
Tobacco-Related Diseases

Tobacco smoke contains >7,000 chemicals, >70 known carcinogens — including polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (benzo[a]pyrene), nitrosamines (NNK), aromatic amines, benzene, formaldehyde, cadmium, nickel, polonium-210. Smokeless tobacco (gutka, khaini, pan masala) contains nitrosamines and areca alkaloids.

  • Cardiovascular
    • Atherosclerosis, coronary artery disease, MI, sudden cardiac death
    • Hypertension, peripheral vascular disease, Buerger disease (thromboangiitis obliterans) — strongly tobacco-specific
    • Stroke, abdominal aortic aneurysm
  • Respiratory
    • COPD (chronic bronchitis & emphysema) — most important cause
    • Recurrent respiratory infections, pneumonia, TB
    • Aggravation of asthma
  • Malignancies — tobacco causes ~30% of all cancer deaths
    • Lung (90% of lung cancers in smokers — SCC, small cell, adenocarcinoma)
    • Upper aero-digestive tract — lip, oral cavity, tongue, oropharynx, larynx, oesophagus
    • Pancreas, urinary bladder, kidney (renal cell & transitional), uterine cervix, stomach, colon, AML
  • Reproductive

The lepromin test (Mitsuda reaction) is an intradermal delayed-type hypersensitivity (Type IV) test using heat-killed M. leprae (or armadillo-derived lepromin, Dharmendra antigen). It is not diagnostic of leprosy, but rather a prognostic and classification tool that reflects host cell-mediated immunity against M. leprae.

  • 0.1 mL lepromin injected intradermally on the volar surface of the forearm.
  • Fernandez reaction (early) — read at 48 h; erythema >10 mm indicates delayed hypersensitivity.
  • Mitsuda reaction (late) — read at 3–4 weeks; nodule >3–5 mm (or ulceration) indicates strong CMI.

  • Classification of leprosy along the Ridley-Jopling spectrum.

  • Not diagnostic — healthy individuals in endemic areas may be positive; some lepromatous patients may be negative even with active disease.

Diagnosis of leprosy is clinical — hypopigmented anaesthetic patch with thickened nerves, confirmed by slit-skin smear (Ziehl-Neelsen) showing acid-fast bacilli and histopathology (foamy macrophages with AFB in LL; epithelioid granulomas in TT). Wound Healing

Wound healing is the orchestrated, overlapping process by which damaged tissue is restored. Three phases:

1. Inflammation (0–3 days)

  • Haemostasis — vasoconstriction, platelet plug, fibrin clot. Platelets release PDGF, TGF-β, FGF, serotonin, histamine.
  • Acute inflammation — neutrophils (24 h) clear bacteria; monocytes convert to macrophages (48–72 h) — phagocytose debris, secrete cytokines (IL-1, TNF-α) and growth factors (PDGF, TGF-β, VEGF) that initiate repair.

2. Proliferation (3 days – 3 weeks)

  • Angiogenesis — VEGF, FGF drive capillary ingrowth; granulation tissue forms (pink, soft, granular).
  • Fibroblast proliferation & collagen deposition — type III initially, then remodelled to type I; provides tensile strength. Driven by TGF-β, PDGF.
  • Epithelialisation — keratinocytes migrate across wound surface (within 24 h for primary, longer for secondary), driven by EGF, KGF.
  • Wound contraction — myofibroblasts (specialised fibroblasts with α-smooth muscle actin) contract and pull edges together (esp. in secondary union).

3. Remodelling / Maturation (3 weeks – 12 months)

  • Type III collagen is replaced by type I; collagen reorganises along tension lines.
  • Vessels regress — scar becomes pale & avascular.
  • Wound tensile strength reaches ~70–80% of normal skin by 3 months; never reaches 100%.
flowchart LR A[Injury → Haemostasis] --> B[Inflammation: neutrophils → macrophages] B --> C[Proliferation: angiogenesis, fibroblasts, collagen III, epithelialisation, contraction] C --> D[Remodelling: collagen I, scar maturation]

Factors Affecting Healing

Local — infection, ischaemia, foreign body, haematoma, radiation, movement, oedema.
Systemic — diabetes, malnutrition (vit C, zinc, protein), steroids, chemotherapy, anaemia, age, smoking, obesity.

Clinical Pearl

Vitamin C deficiency (scurvy) impairs hydroxylation of proline & lysine → unstable collagen → poor wound healing & bleeding. Zinc is a co-factor for matrix metalloproteinases — zinc deficiency delays epithelialisation.

Glucose Tolerance Test (GTT) for Sugar

OGTT assesses the body's ability to handle a glucose load and is used when fasting / random glucose is borderline, in gestational diabetes mellitus screening, and to diagnose impaired glucose tolerance / diabetes.

Indications

  • Fasting glucose 100–125 mg/dL (impaired fasting glucose).
  • Symptomatic patient with normal fasting/random glucose.
  • Gestational diabetes screening at 24–28 weeks.
  • Patient with unexplained neuropathy, retinopathy, recurrent infections.
  • Past history of GDM, macrosomia, stillbirth, PCOS.

Preparation

  • Unrestricted carbohydrate diet (≥150 g/day) for 3 days prior.
  • Normal physical activity; avoid alcohol, smoking, caffeine, drugs (steroids, OCPs, thiazides, salicylates) for 24 h.
  • Fast 8–12 h overnight; only water allowed.
  • Rest 30 min before test; remain seated & non-smoking during test.

Procedure

  1. Collect fasting blood & urine sample.
  2. Give 75 g anhydrous glucose in 250–300 mL water over 5 min (1.75 g/kg, max 75 g in children; 100 g for some GDM protocols).
  3. Collect venous blood (& urine) at 30, 60, 90, 120 minutes.
  4. Plasma glucose measured by glucose oxidase method.

CategoryFasting2-h
Normal<110 mg/dL (<100 ADA)<140 mg/dL
Impaired Fasting Glucose110–125 (100–125 ADA)<140
Impaired Glucose Tolerance<126140–199

A "flat OGTT curve" (little rise over fasting) suggests malabsorption, insulinoma or hypopituitarism. A delayed peak with prolonged hyperglycaemia indicates impaired glucose tolerance / early type-2 diabetes.

Sputum Examination

Sputum is expectorated material from the lower respiratory tract (deep cough). Saliva is not sputum. Useful in pulmonary infections, malignancy, asthma, eosinophilic pneumonia, occupational lung disease.

Sample Collection

  • Early morning sample (overnight pooled secretions). Rinsing mouth with water reduces contamination.
  • Induced sputum — hypertonic saline nebulisation (3–5%) for patients who cannot expectorate.
  • For tuberculosis — 3 consecutive early-morning samples, or one pooled 24-h sample.
  • For cytology — fresh sample delivered to lab within 2 h.
  • Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) — when sputum is non-diagnostic.

Macroscopic Examination

  • Colour — clear/white (bronchitis); yellow-green (pyogenic); rusty (pneumococcal pneumonia); red (haemoptysis); black (anthracosis, aspergilloma); pink frothy (pulmonary oedema).
  • Consistency — mucoid, mucopurulent, purulent, tenacious (asthma — Curschmann spirals), viscid (cystic fibrosis).
  • Odour — foul (anaerobic abscess, bronchiectasis).
  • Dittrich plugs — in bronchiectasis, foul-smelling yellow-white plugs.

Microscopic Examination

  • Gram stain — assess squamous epithelial cells (<10/low power field = good sample) and neutrophils (>25/low power field); identify organisms (gram + cocci in pairs = pneumococcus; gram-negative diplococci = neisseria; gram-negative coccobacilli = Hib).
  • Ziehl-Neelsen / Auramine-rhodamine stain — acid-fast bacilli (M. tuberculosis, MOTT). Report graded 1+ to 3+ or negative (15-minute scan).
  • Wet mount — KOH — fungal hyphae (Aspergillus, Candida), Pneumocystis jirovecii (cysts with toluidine blue, Grocott silver stain).
  • Cytology — Papanicolaou, H&E, Wright-Giemsa; malignant cells, eosinophils (asthma, eosinophilic pneumonia), Charcot-Leyden crystals (asthma), Curschmann spirals (asthma), asbestos bodies, siderophages.
  • Culture — aerobic, anaerobic, mycobacterial (LJ, BACTEC MGIT), fungal (Sabouraud).
  • Sensitivity & molecular — CBNAAT (GeneXpert) for TB & rifampicin resistance; pneumococcal & legionella urinary antigen; viral PCR (respiratory panel).

Clinical Pearl

Bartlett's grading (0–3 score: neutrophils +10, mucus +2, squamous cells −5) helps decide whether a sputum sample is acceptable for culture. A score >1 generally warrants processing; a sample dominated by squamous epithelial cells represents saliva and should be rejected.

Pathological Calcification

Abnormal deposition of calcium salts in tissues other than osteoid or teeth. Two types:

Dystrophic Calcification

  • Definition — deposition of calcium in dead, degenerated or necrotic tissue with normal serum calcium & phosphate.
  • Pathogenesis — membrane damage releases phosphate; calcium binds to membrane phospholipids & denatured proteins. Hydroxyapatite crystals form, often with ammonium, magnesium, iron.
  • Examples
    • Caseous necrosis in TB ( Ghon complex), histoplasmosis.
    • Atheromatous plaques, damaged heart valves (calcific AS).
    • Old scars, healed infarcts, hyalinised leiomyomas.
    • Psammoma bodies — papillary thyroid carcinoma, serous ovarian cystadenocarcinoma, meningioma, papillary RCC.
    • Cysts — epidermoid, pilar, hydatid.
    • Dead parasites — schistosoma, guinea worm, cysticercus, echinococcus.
    • Fat necrosis (acute pancreatitis) — soap formation.
  • Microscopy — basophilic, amorphous, granular; H&E blue; von Kossa stain (silver) black.

Metastatic Calcification

  • Definition — deposition of calcium in normal tissue due to hypercalcaemia.
  • Causes of hypercalcaemia
    • Hyperparathyroidism (primary, secondary, tertiary).
    • Malignancy — PTHrP (squamous cell carcinoma, breast, renal), lytic bone metastases (breast, myeloma), multiple myeloma.
    • Vitamin D intoxication, sarcoidosis, milk-alkali syndrome.
    • Bone destruction — Paget disease, immobilisation, prolonged bed rest.
    • Renal failure (secondary hyperparathyroidism).
    • Thyrotoxicosis, thiazides, adrenal insufficiency.
  • Sites — kidney (nephrocalcinosis → renal failure), lungs (diffuse interstitial), stomach (fundic), blood vessels, cornea (band keratopathy), myocardium, alveolar walls.
  • Pathogenesis — Ca × P product >70; alkaline environment favours deposition (gastric fundus, lungs).

Clinical Pearl

Dystrophic calcification can be a helpful diagnostic clue — psammoma bodies in papillary thyroid carcinoma; caseating granulomas calcified in old TB; "egg-shell" calcification in silicotic lymph nodes. Metastatic calcification points to underlying hypercalcaemia — always check serum Ca, P, PTH, vitamin D, albumin, renal function.

Type IV (Cell-Mediated) Hypersensitivity

Delayed-type hypersensitivity (DTH) — T-cell mediated immune response that develops 24–72 h after antigen exposure. No antibody involvement; not transferred by serum but by T lymphocytes.

Mechanisms

  1. CD4+ T helper 1 (Th1) pathway — antigen presented by macrophage/dendritic cell on MHC-II → sensitised Th1 cell releases IFN-γ, IL-2, TNF-β → macrophage activation → epithelioid & giant-cell granuloma formation & tissue injury.
  2. CD8+ cytotoxic T-cell pathway — antigen on MHC-I → CTL directly kills target cell via perforin/granzyme & Fas-FasL.
  3. CD4+ Th17 pathway — IL-17, IL-22 recruits neutrophils; drives chronic inflammation & autoimmunity (psoriasis, IBD).

Role of Cytokines & Prostaglandins in Acute Inflammation

Cytokines

Small proteins secreted by activated macrophages, lymphocytes, endothelium, mast cells. Major ones in acute inflammation:

  • IL-1β, TNF-α — from macrophages; induce endothelial adhesion molecules (ICAM, VCAM, E-selectin); activate neutrophils; cause fever, anorexia, hypotension, acute-phase response (CRP, SAA); cachexia in chronic cases.
  • IL-6 — major stimulator of acute-phase proteins (CRP, fibrinogen, hepcidin) from liver; drives B-cell maturation.
  • Chemokines (IL-8 / CXCL8) — potent neutrophil chemoattractant & activator. Others: MCP-1 (CCL2), MIP-1α (CCL3), RANTES (CCL5), eotaxin (CCL11).
  • IL-12 — drives Th1 differentiation & NK activation.
  • IL-17 (from Th17) — recruits neutrophils via IL-8 induction.
  • IL-10, TGF-β — anti-inflammatory; resolve inflammation, promote repair & scarring.

Prostaglandins & Lipid Mediators

Derived from arachidonic acid released from membrane phospholipids by phospholipase A2.

  • Cyclo-oxygenase (COX) pathway
    • PGE2 — vasodilator, potentiate permeability, fever, pain sensitisation (hyperalgesia).
    • PGI2 (prostacyclin) — vasodilator, inhibits platelet aggregation.
    • TXA2 (thromboxane) — vasoconstrictor, platelet aggregation (platelets).
    • PGD2 — mast cells; vasodilator, chemoattractant.
  • Lipoxygenase (LOX) pathway
    • 5-HPETE → LTA4 → LTB4 (neutrophil chemoattractant & activator).
    • LTC4, LTD4, LTE4 — slow-reacting substance of anaphylaxis (SRS-A); bronchoconstriction, vasoconstriction, increased permeability.
  • Lipoxins (LXA4, LXB4) — generated during resolution; inhibit neutrophil recruitment, promote macrophage clearance of apoptotic cells.
  • Resolvins, protectins, maresins — derived from omega-3 fatty acids; actively terminate inflammation.

Clinical Pearl

NSAIDs (aspirin, ibuprofen) inhibit COX-1 & COX-2, reducing PGE2/PGI2 — relieving fever, pain & inflammation but also impairing gastric mucosal protection & renal perfusion. Steroids inhibit phospholipase A2 (lipocortin) and COX-2 induction, blocking both prostaglandins & leukotrienes — hence more potent anti-inflammatory effect.

Hemoparasites

  • Plasmodium spp. — P. falciparum, P. vivax, P. ovale, P. malariae, P. knowlesi — malaria
  • Babesia microti — babesiosis (USA, Europe)
  • Trypanosoma spp. — T. cruzi (Chagas), T. brucei gambiense / rhodesiense (sleeping sickness)
  • Leishmania spp. — L. donovani (kala-azar), L. tropica (cutaneous), L. braziliensis (mucocutaneous)

  1. Microscopy — Gold standard
    • Thick smear — concentration of parasites; sensitivity ~5–10 parasites/μL; species ID difficult.
    • Thin smear — species identification, parasite density (per 200 WBC or 1000 RBC), stage of parasite.
    • Stain — Giemsa, Leishman, JSB, Field's.
    • Reporting — parasitaemia % = (parasitised RBC / total RBC) × 100; >2% or >100,000/μL in falciparum = severe disease.
  2. Rapid Diagnostic Tests (RDT)
    • Immunochromatographic card tests detecting parasite LDH (pLDH), histidine-rich protein 2 (HRP-2 — P. falciparum only), aldolase (pan-malarial).
    • Useful in field; limit — does not quantify parasite load; HRP-2 deletions in some P. falciparum strains.
  3. Molecular — PCR
    • Species-specific 18S rRNA PCR; nested PCR for mixed infections.
    • Detects low parasitaemia; useful for species confirmation & research.
  4. Serology — IFA, ELISA for anti-malarial antibodies; useful for blood donor screening & retrospective diagnosis, not for acute.
  5. Other tests — buffy coat smear, quantitative buffy coat (QBC) fluorescent stain, loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP).
  6. Supportive tests — CBC (anaemia, thrombocytopenia), blood glucose (hypoglycaemia in falciparum), LFT, KFT, ABG (acidosis), urine for haemoglobinuria (blackwater fever), G6PD before primaquine.

In P. falciparum, only ring forms & gametocytes are seen in peripheral smear (trophozoites sequester in deep capillaries). Gametocytes are banana-shaped (crescent). Etiology

  • Genetic — HLA-DR2, HLA-DR3; C1q, C2, C4 deficiency; twin concordance ~25% monozygotic vs 2% dizygotic.
  • Hormonal — female : male 9:1; oestrogen enhances B-cell autoimmunity; flares in pregnancy & with OCPs.
  • Environmental triggers — UV light (keratinocyte apoptosis → nuclear antigen exposure); drugs (procainamide, hydralazine, isoniazid, anti-TNF → drug-induced lupus, anti-histone positive); infections (EBV).
  • Immune dysregulation — defective clearance of apoptotic bodies; polyclonal B-cell activation; T-helper bias.

Virchow's Triad & Thrombosis

Rudolf Virchow (1856) proposed that thrombosis results from a disturbance in three factors — endothelial injury, abnormal blood flow, and hypercoagulability.

  1. Endothelial injury — exposes subendothelial collagen & tissue factor, denudes antithrombotic surface, releases vWF. Platelets adhere via GP Ib-IX-V and are activated. Tissue factor activates the extrinsic coagulation cascade. Dominant in cardiac & arterial thrombi — atherosclerotic plaque rupture (MI), traumatic / catheter injury, vasculitis, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, cigarette smoking.
  2. Abnormal blood flow
    • Stasis — pool of blood allows activated clotting factors to accumulate; removes dilution effect; common in deep vein thrombosis (immobilisation, surgery, heart failure, AF, post-stroke). Sluggish venous flow also reduces endothelial clearance of activated factors.
    • Turbulence — damages endothelium at arterial bifurcations, aneurysms, around atherosclerotic plaques, prosthetic valves; causes platelet-endothelium interaction and counter-currents that favour coagulation.
  3. Hypercoagulability
    • Primary (genetic) — Factor V Leiden (most common), prothrombin G20210A, antithrombin III deficiency, protein C & S deficiency, dysfibrinogenaemia.
    • Secondary (acquired) — malignancy (Trousseau), pregnancy, OCPs, prolonged bed rest, surgery, trauma, burns, nephrotic syndrome, antiphospholipid syndrome, myeloproliferative neoplasms, homocysteinaemia, older age, obesity, smoking.

Most clinical thrombi arise from a combination of all three — e.g. a post-operative elderly patient with cancer and immobilisation has stasis + hypercoagulability + endothelial trauma from intravenous cannula.

Clinical Pearl

Stasis favours venous thrombi (red, fibrin-rich, do not propagate toward heart); endothelial injury favours arterial thrombi (white, platelet-rich). Recognition of which element predominates guides antithrombotic choice — antiplatelets for arterial, anticoagulants for venous.
q0_0_3_1:
Reversible Cell Injury

Reversible injury is the early stage of cell damage — cellular & functional alterations that can recover if the offending stimulus is removed. Two key targets are ATP depletion and membrane integrity.

Mechanisms

  1. Hypoxia / ischaemia → decreased oxidative phosphorylation → ↓ ATP.
  2. Failure of Na+/K+-ATPase → intracellular Na+ accumulation, K+ loss → cellular swelling (hydropic change), endoplasmic reticulum dilation.
  3. Switch to anaerobic glycolysis → ↑ lactate, ↓ intracellular pH → clumping of nuclear chromatin.
  4. Detachment of ribosomes from rough ER → ↓ protein synthesis → lipid deposition in injured cells (fatty change — especially in liver, heart).
  5. Ca2+ influx — ATP-depleted pumps fail to extrude Ca2+; mild rise activates phospholipases, proteases, endonucleases.
  6. ROS generation — at low levels can be detoxified; oxidative stress damages lipids, proteins, DNA.

Morphological Changes

  • Gross — pallor, swelling, increased weight, soft consistency.
  • Light microscopy
    • Cellular swelling (hydropic change) — earliest change.
    • Fatty change — triglyceride accumulation (steatosis).
    • Pigments — lipofuscin, haemosiderin, melanin.
  • EM (ultrastructure)
    • Plasma membrane blebbing.
    • Loss of microvilli.
    • Mitochondrial swelling & amorphous densities.
    • Dilation of ER with detachment of ribosomes.
    • Nuclear chromatin clumping.

Clinical Pearl

The key event that converts reversible to irreversible injury is severe mitochondrial dysfunction with MPTP opening, ATP depletion below the threshold for Na+/K+ pump, and profound membrane damage — leading to cell death by necrosis and/or apoptosis.
q0_0_3_2:
Role of Free Radicals in Cell Injury

Free radicals are chemical species with an unpaired electron in the outer orbit — highly reactive, initiate autocatalytic chain reactions. Major ROS in biology: superoxide anion (O2·−), hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), hydroxyl radical (·OH), peroxynitrite (ONOO−).

Sources

  • Endogenous — mitochondrial electron transport chain ( leakage); phagocyte oxidase during respiratory burst; peroxisomes; enzymes (xanthine oxidase in ischaemia-reperfusion; NADPH oxidase; cytochrome P450; NO synthase).
  • Exogenous — radiation (UV, ionising), oxygen toxicity (hyperbaric), chemicals (CCl4 → CCl3·), drugs (acetaminophen, doxorubicin, bleomycin), cigarette smoke, environmental pollutants, reperfusion after ischaemia.

Mechanisms of Injury

  1. Lipid peroxidation — radical attacks polyunsaturated fatty acids in membranes → destruction of membrane integrity, formation of malondialdehyde (MDA) & 4-HNE.
  2. Protein damage — oxidation of sulfhydryl groups, cross-linking, fragmentation → loss of enzyme activity & structural protein function.
  3. DNA damage — strand breaks, base modification (8-oxo-guanine) → mutagenesis, activation of p53 → apoptosis.
  4. Mitochondrial damage — opening of mitochondrial permeability transition pore (MPTP), cytochrome-c release → apoptosis; ATP depletion → necrosis.
  5. Activation of stress signalling — NF-κB, MAP kinases, inflammasome → cytokine release, inflammation.

Antioxidant Defence

  • Enzymatic — superoxide dismutase (SOD; O2·− → H2O2), catalase (H2O2 → H2O + O2), glutathione peroxidase (uses GSH).
  • Non-enzymatic — vitamin E (lipid membranes), vitamin C (aqueous), β-carotene, uric acid, bilirubin, glutathione, transferrin, ceruloplasmin.

Clinical Pearl

Ischaemia–reperfusion injury is the classic example — restoration of blood flow after ischaemia brings oxygen that fuels xanthine oxidase & mitochondrial electron leak, generating ROS that worsen tissue injury. This explains the benefit of early reperfusion in MI / stroke but also the paradox of reperfusion arrhythmias and stunning.
q0_0_3_3:
Mechanisms of Tumour Metastasis

Metastasis is the spread of tumour cells from the primary site to distant organs, forming secondary tumours. It is the hallmark of malignancy and accounts for >90% of cancer deaths.

Pathway

  1. Local invasion — tumour cells detach (loss of E-cadherin), degrade basement membrane & extracellular matrix via matrix metalloproteinases (MMP-2, MMP-9), and migrate (autocrine motility factors, integrins, chemokine receptors such as CXCR4).
  2. Intravasation — tumour cells enter capillaries / venules / lymphatics.
  3. Transport — circulated as single cells or emboli coated with platelets & fibrin (protects from shear stress & NK cells).
  4. Arrest & adhesion — bind to endothelium at distant site via selectins, integrins, CD44; site specificity dictated by chemokine gradients ("seed & soil" hypothesis — Paget).
  5. Extravasation — exit the vessel into the parenchyma.
  6. Survival & angiogenesis — survive in foreign microenvironment ("metastatic niche" primed by exosomes); induce angiogenesis (VEGF, FGF) to support growth into clinically detectable metastasis.
flowchart TD A[Primary tumour] --> B[Local invasion - MMP, loss of E-cadherin] B --> C[Intravasation into vessel] C --> D[Circulation as emboli] D --> E[Arrest in distant capillary] E --> F[Extravasation] F --> G[Survival in new microenvironment] G --> H[Angiogenesis & growth] H --> I[Clinical metastasis]

Routes of Spread

  • Lymphatic — carcinomas (regional nodes first).
  • Haematogenous — sarcomas, RCC (renal vein), HCC, lung, melanoma, choriocarcinoma; liver, lung, bone, brain.
  • Transcoelomic — ovarian (Krukenberg from stomach), gastric (Blumer shelf, Sister Mary Joseph nodule).
  • CSF / leptomeningeal — medulloblastoma, leukaemia, breast, lung.
  • Seeding of body cavities — thoracic, peritoneal, pericardial.
  • Iatrogenic — along biopsy tract, surgical wound.

Clinical Pearl

Seed and soil hypothesis (Paget, 1889) explains why different tumours metastasise to specific organs — breast to bone, lung, liver, brain; colorectal to liver; prostate to bone (osteoblastic); RCC to bone, lung (cannonball), thyroid to bone. Pre-metastatic niche is "prepared" by tumour exosomes & bone-marrow-derived cells.
q0_0_3_4:
Anaphylaxis — Why within Minutes

Anaphylaxis is a Type I (immediate / IgE-mediated) hypersensitivity reaction that develops within minutes (typically 5–30 min) of exposure to an allergen. The rapid time-course is dictated by the fact that the immune response is pre-formed — IgE is already bound to mast cells & basophils from prior sensitisation.

Mechanism

  1. Prior sensitisation — initial exposure to allergen (bee venom, peanut, drug, latex) → B-cell class-switching → production of allergen-specific IgE → binds FcεRI receptor on mast cells & basophils. No clinical reaction at first exposure.
  2. Re-exposure — allergen cross-links adjacent IgE molecules on the mast cell surface within seconds.
  3. Signal transduction — FcεRI aggregation activates Lyn & Syk tyrosine kinases → PLCγ → IP3 & DAG → Ca2+ release & PKC activation.
  4. Immediate (within seconds-minutes) — mast-cell degranulation releases preformed mediators stored in granules: histamine, tryptase, chymase, heparin, serotonin. These cause:
    • Vasodilation & increased vascular permeability → hypotension, urticaria, angioedema, laryngeal oedema.
    • Bronchoconstriction → wheeze, respiratory distress.
    • ↑ mucus secretion, ↑ gut motility → cramps, vomiting, diarrhoea.
  5. Late-phase (4–8 h) — newly synthesised lipid mediators (leukotrienes LTC4/D4/E4, prostaglandin D2, platelet-activating factor) and cytokines (TNF-α, IL-4, IL-5, IL-13) recruit eosinophils & basophils — late recrudescence of symptoms.
flowchart TD A[Prior sensitisation → IgE bound to mast cell FcεRI] --> B[Re-exposure to allergen] B --> C[Cross-linking of IgE] C --> D[FcεRI signalling → Ca2+] D --> E[Immediate: histamine, tryptase, heparin release] E --> F[Vasodilation, bronchospasm, oedema within minutes] D --> G[Late phase: leukotrienes, PGD2, PAF, cytokines] G --> H[Eosinophil & basophil recruitment 4-8 h later]

Clinical Pearl

IM injection of adrenaline (0.5 mg, 1:1000) at the anterolateral thigh is the first-line treatment and is most rapidly absorbed because of the high vascularity and large muscle mass. Repeat every 5 min if no response. Patient should be observed for ≥6 h because of biphasic reactions in 5–20% of cases.
q0_0_3_5:
Septic Shock & Multi-Organ Failure

Septic shock is a subtype of distributive shock characterised by systemic vasodilation, hypotension, and tissue hypoperfusion despite adequate fluid resuscitation, caused by an uncontrolled host response to infection. Multi-organ dysfunction syndrome (MODS) results when this cascade becomes self-sustaining.

Pathogenesis

  1. Trigger — microbial products (LPS / endotoxin of gram-negative bacteria; lipoteichoic acid of gram-positive; superantigens of S. aureus / S. pyogenes) bind pattern-recognition receptors (TLR4, TLR2, CD14).
  2. Cytokine storm — macrophages, monocytes & endothelium release TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8, IL-12, IFN-γ, HMGB1. These produce fever, hypotension, acute-phase response.
  3. Endothelial activation & dysfunction — ↑ adhesion molecules (ICAM, VCAM, E-selectin); ↑ NO (iNOS) → vasodilation & hypotension; ↑ permeability → capillary leak → tissue oedema & hypovolaemia; loss of glycocalyx → microvascular thrombosis.
  4. Coagulopathy — tissue factor expression → DIC; consumption of platelets & clotting factors; microvascular thrombi → tissue ischaemia.
  5. Mitochondrial dysfunction — "cytopathic hypoxia": cells cannot utilise oxygen even when delivered — oxygen extraction ratio falls; lactate rises. NO & H2S inhibit cytochrome c oxidase.
  6. Myocardial depression — circulating myocardial depressant factors (TNF, IL-1, NO) → reduced contractility → worsens hypotension.
  7. Organ failure — kidneys (AKI), lungs (ARDS), liver (jaundice, synthetic failure), brain (encephalopathy), heart (cardiomyopathy), gut (ileus, translocation), adrenals (relative adrenal insufficiency), coagulopathy, immune paralysis (compensatory anti-inflammatory response syndrome, CARS).
flowchart TD A[Infection: LPS / TLR4] --> B[Cytokine storm TNF, IL-1, IL-6] B --> C[iNOS → NO → Vasodilation, hypotension] B --> D[Endothelial leak → oedema, hypovolaemia] B --> E[Tissue factor → DIC → microthrombi] B --> F[Mitochondrial dysfunction → cytopathic hypoxia] B --> G[Myocardial depression] C --> H[Tissue hypoperfusion] D --> H E --> H F --> H G --> H H --> I[Multi-organ dysfunction syndrome]

Clinical Pearl

The qSOFA score (altered mentation, systolic BP ≤100, respiratory rate ≥22) identifies high-risk patients outside ICU. Early goal-directed therapy ( Surviving Sepsis Campaign "hour-1 bundle") — antibiotics within 1 h, 30 mL/kg crystalloid bolus, lactate, vasopressors to MAP ≥65 mm Hg — has reduced sepsis mortality substantially.

Key Determinants

  • Genetic programme — if cell has intact apoptotic machinery, ATP depletion triggers apoptosis; if ATP is profoundly depleted, necrosis predominates.
