Definition

Mutation is a stable, heritable change in the nucleotide sequence of the genome of an organism. It can occur spontaneously (due to errors in DNA replication, tautomeric shifts, deamination, depurination) or be induced by mutagens (physical — UV, X-ray, gamma-ray; chemical — nitrous acid, alkylating agents, base analogues; biological — transposons, viral integration).

Rate: ~10⁻⁶ to 10⁻¹⁰ per gene per generation in bacteria (E. coli ~10⁻⁷ per gene per generation).

Classification

A. By Mechanism / Molecular Nature (3 marks)

1. Point Mutation

Change in a single nucleotide. Sub-types:

  • Substitution
    • Transition — purine → purine (A ↔ G) or pyrimidine → pyrimidine (C ↔ T). Most common (≈70%).
    • Transversion — purine → pyrimidine or vice versa (A ↔ C, A ↔ T, G ↔ C, G ↔ T). Less common.
  • By functional consequence:
    • Silent (synonymous) — codon changes but encodes same amino acid (due to codon degeneracy); no phenotypic change.
    • Missense — codon changes to encode a different amino acid. Conservative (similar aa — mild effect) or non-conservative (dissimilar aa — severe, e.g., HbS — Glu→Val at position 6 of β-globin).
    • Nonsense — codon changes to a stop codon (UAA, UAG, UGA) → premature termination → truncated, usually non-functional protein (e.g., Duchenne muscular dystrophy).
    • Stop-loss — stop codon → sense codon → elongated protein.
2. Frameshift Mutation

Insertion or deletion of nucleotides in a number not divisible by 3 → shifts the reading frame → entirely different amino acid sequence downstream → usually premature stop codon → non-functional protein. E.g., Tay-Sachs (HEXA), Hb Wayne.

3. Insertions / Deletions (InDels)
  • Small (1–1000 bp) — frameshift if not multiple of 3.
  • Large — deletion of entire gene or exon; e.g., α-thalassaemia (--SEA deletion), Duchenne (deletion of dystrophin exons).
4. Dynamic / Expansion Mutation (Trinucleotide Repeat Expansion)

Expansion of unstable trinucleotide repeat sequences beyond a threshold during meiosis — causes anticipation (worse phenotype in successive generations). Examples:

  • Huntington disease — CAG in HTT (≥36 repeats).
  • Fragile X — CGG in FMR1 (>200 repeats; full mutation).
  • Myotonic dystrophy — CTG in DMPK (>50 repeats).
  • Friedreich ataxia — GAA in FXN (>66 repeats).
  • Spinocerebellar ataxias — CAG in various genes.
5. Copy Number Variation (CNV)

Duplication or deletion of large segments (>1 kb) — e.g., Hb Lepore (δβ fusion), dup 22q11.2 (cat eye); CMT1A (PMP22 duplication).

6. Chromosomal Mutations
  • Numerical
    • Aneuploidy — trisomy 21 (Down), 18 (Edward), 13 (Patau), X (Klinefelter XXY), monosomy X (Turner).
    • Polyploidy — triploidy, tetraploidy (lethal in humans; common in plants).
  • Structural
    • Deletion (5p- Cri-du-chat, 11p- aniridia/WAGR, 22q11.2 DiGeorge).
    • Duplication (Pallister-Killian 12p isochromosome).
    • Inversion (Factor VIII gene intron 22 inversion in Haemophilia A).
    • Translocation
      • Reciprocal — Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22)(q34;q11) — CML (BCR-ABL fusion).
      • Robertsonian — centromeric fusion of acrocentric chromosomes; t(14;21) — Down syndrome (translocation type).
    • Ring chromosome, isochromosome.
7. Conditional / Reversible
  • Suppressor mutation — second mutation that restores original phenotype (intragenic or intergenic).
  • Back mutation — reversion to wild-type.

B. By Effect on Phenotype (1 mark)

  • Loss-of-function — reduced or abolished protein activity; usually recessive (e.g., PKU, albinism).
  • Gain-of-function — new/ enhanced activity; usually dominant (e.g., Huntington disease, achondroplasia FGFR3, RET in MEN2).
  • Dominant-negative — mutant protein interferes with wild-type (e.g., p53, Marfan — mutant fibrillin disrupts normal fibrillin assembly).
  • Conditional / temperature-sensitive — phenotype only under certain conditions (e.g., Siamese cat coat colour — tyrosinase active only below body temperature).
  • Lethal — causes death (often embryonic).
  • Neutral / Silent — no phenotypic effect.

C. By Origin / Cell Type (1 mark)

  • Germ-line — in gametes; heritable; affects every cell of offspring (e.g., BRCA1 mutation in breast cancer family).
  • Somatic — in body cells; not heritable; causes cancer & mosaicism (e.g., TP53 mutation in lung cancer).

In Bacteria — Special Types

  • Auxotrophic mutant — loses ability to synthesise an essential nutrient; requires supplementation (e.g., his⁻ mutant of Salmonella in Ames test).
  • Antibiotic-resistant mutant — e.g., rifampicin-resistant rpoB mutant; MRSA (mecA).
  • Conditionally lethal / temperature-sensitive (ts) — grows at permissive temperature (30 °C), dies at restrictive (42 °C); useful for vaccine strains.
  • Phase variation — reversible on/off switching of gene expression (e.g., flagellin in Salmonella).
  • Antigenic variation — changes surface antigen (e.g., Neisseria pili, Borrelia VlsE, trypanosomes).

Causes / Mutagens

  • Base analogues — 5-bromouracil (mimics thymine); 2-aminopurine (mimics adenine).
  • Alkylating agents — EMS, MNNG, nitrogen mustard; add alkyl groups to bases → mispairing.
  • Deaminating agents — nitrous acid (HNO₂); converts adenine → hypoxanthine (pairs with C), cytosine → uracil.
  • Intercalating agents — acridine orange, proflavin, ethidium bromide; insert between base pairs → frameshift.
  • Hydroxylamine — modifies cytosine → pairs with adenine.
  • UV radiation — thymine dimers (cyclobutane pyrimidine dimer).
  • Ionising radiation — X-ray, gamma-ray; single- & double-strand breaks.
  • Replication errors — slippage (microsatellite instability); tautomeric shifts.
  • Transposons / Insertion sequences — move within genome; disrupt genes.
  • Viral integration — HPV E6/E7 inactivate p53/Rb.

DNA Repair Mechanisms (counteracting mutations)

  • Direct repair — photolyase (in bacteria; not humans); O⁶-methylguanine methyltransferase (MGMT).
  • Base excision repair (BER) — DNA glycosylase; for deaminated/oxidised bases.
  • Nucleotide excision repair (NER) — for bulky lesions (thymine dimers); defective in xeroderma pigmentosum.
  • Mismatch repair (MMR) — recognises mispaired bases; defective in hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer (Lynch syndrome).
  • Double-strand break repair — homologous recombination (BRCA1/2 — hereditary breast/ovarian cancer) & non-homologous end joining (NHEJ).

Clinical Pearl

The Ames test uses his⁻ Salmonella typhimurium to detect mutagens — if a chemical induces reverse mutation to his⁺, the bacteria grow on histidine-free medium → mutagen identified. Adding rat liver S9 fraction mimics mammalian metabolism — detects procarcinogens (e.g., aflatoxin B1, benzopyrene) that are activated in vivo. ~85% of known human carcinogens are mutagens in the Ames test — making it a powerful screening tool. In clinical practice, the most useful application is targeted cancer therapy based on mutation profile: EGFR mutation in lung adenocarcinoma → erlotinib/gefitinib; BCR-ABL in CML → imatinib; BRAF V600E in melanoma → vemurafenib; BRCA1/2 in breast/ovarian cancer → PARP inhibitor (olaparib); KRAS G12C → sotorasib. Next-generation sequencing (NGS) of tumours is now standard of care — exemplified by FoundationOne CDx covering 324 genes. Hotspot mutations (e.g., KRAS codon 12, TP53 codon 248, BRAF V600) recur across cancer types because they occur in critical functional domains.

Definition

Healthcare-associated infection (HAI) — also called nosocomial infection or hospital-acquired infection — is an infection occurring in a patient that was not present or incubating at the time of admission. The CDC/NHSN defines HAI by the following criteria:

  1. Infection develops ≥48 hours after admission to a healthcare facility.
  2. Infection develops within 30 days after discharge from a hospital (or 90 days if an implant was placed).
  3. Infection develops within 30 days (or 90 days with implant) of a surgical procedure.
  4. Infection develops in a patient receiving outpatient or home-care services (wound care, dialysis, IV therapy, catheterisation).
  5. Infection in a healthcare worker acquired through occupational exposure.

Epidemiology

  • WHO estimates 7–10% of hospitalised patients in developed countries and 10–25% in developing countries acquire an HAI.
  • ICU patients have 5–10× higher risk.
  • In India, HAI rates range from 10–30% depending on facility & surveillance methodology.
  • Commonest HAIs: urinary tract infection (UTI — 30–40%), surgical site infection (SSI — 20–25%), pneumonia (VAP — 10–15%), bloodstream infection (CLABSI — 5–10%).

Major Types of HAI

Type Criteria Common Pathogens
CAUTI — Catheter-Associated UTIUTI with urinary catheter in situ >2 calendar daysE. coli, Klebsiella, Proteus, Pseudomonas, Enterococcus, Candida
CLABSI — Central Line-Associated Bloodstream InfectionBacteraemia with central venous catheter in place >2 calendar daysCoNS, S. aureus (MRSA), Enterobacterales, Candida
VAP — Ventilator-Associated PneumoniaPneumonia >48 h after endotracheal intubationLate: Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter, Klebsiella, MRSA; Early (<5 d): S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae
SSI — Surgical Site InfectionWithin 30 days of surgery (or 90 d with implant)S. aureus, CoNS, Enterobacterales, anaerobes
CDI — C. difficile InfectionDiarrhoea >48 h after admission; positive toxinC. difficile (NAP1/027 hypervirulent strain)

Risk Factors

  • Patient — extremes of age, immunosuppression, malnutrition, diabetes, chronic illness, prolonged hospitalisation, severity of underlying disease.
  • Device-related — urinary catheter, central venous catheter, endotracheal tube, haemodialysis catheter, surgical drain.
  • Procedure-related — surgery, prolonged operative time, emergency procedure, contaminated wound class, improper antibiotic prophylaxis.
  • Environment — overcrowding, inadequate ventilation, contaminated water/air, poor sterilisation, contaminated disinfectants.
  • Antibiotic pressure — broad-spectrum antibiotic use selects multidrug-resistant organisms (MRSA, VRE, ESBL, CRE, CRPA, CRAB).

Sources of HAI

  • Endogenous — patient's own flora (skin, gut, respiratory); ~50% of HAIs.
  • Exogenous — healthcare workers' hands (most common cross-transmission), contaminated equipment, environment (fomites, water, air), other patients.
  • Parenteral — contaminated IV fluids, blood products, injections.

Mode of Transmission

  • Contact (most common) — direct (patient-to-patient, HCW-to-patient); indirect (via hands, equipment, environment).
  • Droplet — respiratory droplets >5 µm, <1 m distance (influenza, pertussis, RSV, mumps).
  • Airborne — droplet nuclei <5 µm, >1 m distance (TB, measles, varicella, aspergillosis).
  • Vehicle — contaminated food, water, medications, devices.
  • Vector — mosquitoes (malaria in hospital), flies.

Prevention — WHO Core Components

  1. Infection prevention & control (IPC) programme with dedicated team.
  2. National guidelines & facility SOPs.
  3. Surveillance — facility-based, with feedback.
  4. Antibiotic stewardship — restrict broad-spectrum use, de-escalate, monitor resistance.
  5. Hand hygiene — WHO 5 Moments; alcohol-based handrub.
  6. Personal protective equipment (PPE).
  7. Sterilisation & disinfection — Spaulding-based.
  8. Care bundles — VAP bundle (head-of-bed elevation, daily sedation interruption, oral chlorhexidine, subglottic secretion drainage, DVT prophylaxis); CLABSI bundle (full barrier precautions, chlorhexidine skin prep, avoidance of femoral site, daily review of line necessity); CAUTI bundle (sterile insertion, closed drainage, daily review, no routine bladder irrigation).
  9. Isolation precautions — standard; contact; droplet; airborne.
  10. Environmental cleaning & waste management.
  11. HCW vaccination & occupational health.

Surveillance — CDC NHSN

Site-specific definitions, device-associated infection rates reported as per 1000 device-days. Hospital infection control committee (HICC) reviews monthly data, performs root-cause analysis of clusters, feeds back to clinicians.

Clinical Pearl

WHO's 5 Moments for Hand Hygiene — before patient contact; before aseptic task; after body fluid exposure risk; after patient contact; after contact with patient surroundings — is the single most cost-effective intervention. Alcohol-based handrub (60–80% ethanol or isopropyl) reduces HAI rates by 30–50% and is faster than soap-and-water (20 sec vs 60 sec). However, alcohol does NOT kill C. difficile spores — use soap & water for suspected/confirmed CDI. The rise of carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (CRE — NDM, KPC, OXA-48) in Indian ICUs is alarming — a single CRE-positive patient can contaminate the entire environment (bed rails, IV poles, sinks) within 24 h, requiring aggressive contact precautions, dedicated equipment, and terminal room cleaning with bleach + UV-C. The MRSA nasal screen & decolonisation (mupirocin + chlorhexidine) in preoperative cardiac/orthopaedic patients reduces SSI by ~30%. The future is whole-genome sequencing for outbreak investigation — distinguishes true transmission events from coincidental unrelated strains within hours.

Introduction

Immunoglobulin M (IgM) is the largest antibody (≈900 kDa; 5 subunits) and the first immunoglobulin produced in the primary immune response. It is the third most abundant serum Ig (~5–10% of total Ig; 0.5–2 mg/mL). IgM is also the first immunoglobulin synthesised by the fetus (≈20 weeks gestation) and the first to appear in phylogeny (even in jawless fish — primitive IgM-like molecules).

Structure (1 mark)

  • Pentamer in serum — 5 IgM monomers (each 180 kDa) joined by a J-chain (joining chain, 15 kDa) via disulfide bonds. Total molecular weight ~900 kDa.
  • Monomer on B cell surface — expressed as membrane-bound monomer (mIgM) — functions as B-cell receptor (BCR) on naïve B cells.
  • Heavy chain (μ) — 5 domains (Vμ + 4 Cμ); lacks hinge region.
  • Light chain — κ or λ.
  • 10 antigen-binding sites (pentamer) — high avidity (functional affinity) despite lower intrinsic affinity per Fab than IgG.
  • Half-life — ~5 days (short; in serum ~5 days; on B cell surface longer).
  • Does NOT cross placenta — too large. Fetal IgM is self-produced; elevated fetal/neonatal IgM indicates congenital infection (TORCH).

Functions (4 marks)

  1. Primary immune response antibody
    • First Ig produced after antigen exposure (within 5–7 days; peaks 1–2 weeks).
    • Naïve B cells express surface IgM (BCR); on antigen binding, proliferate and secrete IgM before class-switching to IgG/IgA.
    • IgM is later replaced by IgG (class-switched) — but memory B cells retain IgM expression.
  2. Most potent complement activator (classical pathway)
    • Single pentameric IgM bound to antigen can activate complement — binds C1q via Fc.
    • IgM is ~400–1000× more efficient than IgG in activating complement (IgG requires ≥2 molecules spaced 30–40 nm apart).
    • C1q binds to Fc portion of μ chain → C1r–C1s → C4, C2 → C3 convertase → C3b → opsonisation & MAC lysis.
    • Important for bacteriolysis (Gram-negative), virus neutralisation.
  3. Agglutination
    • 10 antigen-binding sites (pentamer) → efficient cross-linking of particulate antigens (bacteria, RBCs).
    • IgM is ~100× more effective than IgG at agglutination.
    • Basis for blood typing (ABO) — anti-A and anti-B are IgM; cause immediate RBC agglutination → transfusion reactions.
    • Widal test (Salmonella O antigen), Weil-Felix (Rickettsia), VDRL (Treponema) — IgM-based agglutination tests.
  4. First line of defence — intravascular neutralisation
    • Largely confined to intravascular space (80%); limited extravascular penetration due to large size.
    • Important in bacteraemia & viraemia — rapidly activates complement & clears microbes.
  5. Opsonisation
    • Direct — via complement C3b (more important than IgG Fc for IgM).
    • Indirect — complement receptor on phagocytes (CR1, CR3) recognises C3b on IgM-coated microbe.
  6. Cytolysis (MAC — Membrane Attack Complex)
    • Complement activation → C5b-C9 → MAC → osmotic lysis of Gram-negative bacteria, enveloped viruses.
  7. Antigen receptor on naïve B cells (mIgM-BCR)
    • Naïve B cells co-express IgM & IgD on surface; BCR complex (Igα/Igβ) transduces signal → B-cell activation, proliferation, class-switching, memory.
    • Loss of surface IgM → B cell cannot respond to antigen.
  8. Natural antibodies
    • Polyreactive low-affinity IgM produced by B-1 cells (CD5+); without prior antigen exposure.
    • Recognise common microbial patterns (phosphorylcholine, LPS) & self antigens (e.g., ABO isohemagglutinins — anti-A, anti-B in individuals lacking that antigen).
    • First-line innate-like defence against blood-borne pathogens.
  9. Diagnostic marker of recent / acute infection
    • IgM appears first, peaks 1–2 weeks, declines by 6–8 weeks; replaced by IgG.
    • Detection of specific IgM indicates current or recent infection — TORCH (toxoplasma, rubella, CMV, HSV, HIV, hepatitis A/E, dengue, leptospirosis, syphilis VDRL, EBV VCA, mycoplasma).
    • In neonate — elevated IgM indicates congenital infection (maternal IgG crosses placenta, IgM does not).
  10. Rheumatoid factor (RF)
    • IgM antibody against Fc portion of IgG — diagnostic marker of rheumatoid arthritis (~70–80% sensitive).
    • Forms immune complexes → complement activation → joint damage.
  11. Cryoglobulins & cold agglutinins
    • IgM with anti-I specificity — cold agglutinin disease (mycoplasma pneumonia, EBV infection); haemolysis at low temperature.
    • Type II cryoglobulinaemia — monoclonal IgM with anti-IgG activity (HCV-associated).
  12. Waldenström macroglobulinaemia
    • IgM-secreting lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma; hyperviscosity syndrome (headache, visual disturbance, mucosal bleeding); treated with rituximab + chemotherapy.

Clinical Significance

  • Selective IgM deficiency — rare; recurrent sinopulmonary & GI infections, sepsis, autoimmune disease.
  • Hyper-IgM syndrome — CD40L deficiency (X-linked); failure of class switching → high IgM, low IgG/IgA/IgE; recurrent pyogenic & opportunistic infections (Pneumocystis, Cryptosporidium).
  • Neonatal screening — elevated IgM in cord blood or neonatal serum suggests congenital infection (TORCH).

Clinical Pearl

The single most useful diagnostic role of IgM is in acute infection diagnosis: detection of specific IgM antibodies in serum is a strong indicator of current or recent infection because IgM is the first antibody produced, peaks at 1–2 weeks, and disappears by 6–8 weeks (while IgG persists for years). For example, HEV IgM in a pregnant woman with acute hepatitis → recent hepatitis E (high mortality in pregnancy); rubella IgM in early pregnancy → risk of congenital rubella syndrome (consider termination); dengue IgM (NS1 + IgM) in febrile patient → dengue. However, IgM can persist for months in some infections (CMV, EBV, parvovirus B19) or even reappear on reactivation — so a positive IgM alone does not always mean acute infection. Cross-reactivity is also a problem — dengue IgM cross-reacts with other flaviviruses (Zika, JE, yellow fever vaccine). The pentameric structure of IgM (10 binding sites) explains why it is the most efficient complement activator — a single IgM molecule can trigger the classical pathway, whereas ≥2 IgG molecules are required. This is why IgM is the first responder in the immune response — it achieves what IgG achieves in quantity through quality.
q1_0_1_12:
Definition

A superantigen (SAg) is a class of microbial protein exotoxin that, unlike conventional antigens, bypasses normal antigen processing & presentation and potently activates a large fraction (5–30%) of the host's T cell population. This leads to massive pro-inflammatory cytokine release (cytokine storm), T-cell proliferation, and potentially toxic shock.

Mechanism of Action (3 marks)

  1. Conventional antigen
    • Antigen is taken up by antigen-presenting cell (APC); processed into short peptides (8–22 aa); peptide loaded onto MHC-II groove; presented to TCR.
    • Only T cells with the specific TCR Vβ complementary to that peptide-MHC are activated (frequency ~1 in 10⁵–10⁶ T cells).
  2. Superantigen mechanism
    • Binds outside the peptide-binding groove of MHC class II on APC (to the α-chain or β-chain, depending on SAg).
    • Binds the lateral face of the variable β-region (Vβ) of the TCR — outside the conventional peptide-binding site.
    • SAg does NOT require antigen processing or specific peptide — acts as a "bridge" between MHC-II and TCR Vβ.
    • Activates all T cells bearing that particular Vβ family — each Vβ family is used by 2–20% of total T cells; one SAg can activate 5–30% of all T cells → massive activation.
    • T cell activation triggers CD28 co-stimulation, IL-2 production, T cell proliferation (mitogenesis).
  3. Massive cytokine release (cytokine storm)
    • T cells — IL-2, IFN-γ, TNF-β, IL-4.
    • Macrophages (also activated by SAg) — IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α, IL-12, IL-8.
    • Endothelial activation, capillary leak, hypotension, multi-organ dysfunction.
  4. Consequences
    • Acute — toxic shock syndrome, food poisoning (enteric form), scarlet fever, cytokine storm.
    • Chronic — T-cell anergy, deletion (activation-induced cell death — AICD), immunosuppression; contributes to autoimmune disease (Kawasaki, multiple sclerosis, type 1 diabetes — molecular mimicry & Vβ expansion).
    • SAgs are also implicated in staphylococcal & streptococcal toxic shock, and atopic eczema (SAg-producing S. aureus on skin).

Important Superantigens (2 marks)

Source organism Superantigen(s) Clinical syndrome TCR Vβ target
Staphylococcus aureus
  • TSST-1 (Toxic Shock Syndrome Toxin-1)
  • Enterotoxins A, B, C1, C2, C3, D, E, G–U (24+)
  • Enterotoxin-like SEB, SEC
  • Toxic shock syndrome (menstrual — tampon; non-menstrual — surgical wound, burns, post-partum)
  • Staphylococcal food poisoning (enterotoxins)
  • Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS)
TSST-1: Vβ2; SEB: Vβ3, Vβ12, Vβ14; SEC: Vβ12
Streptococcus pyogenes (GAS)
  • SpeA, SpeC, SpeF, SpeG, SpeH, SpeI, SpeJ, SpeK, SpeL, SpeM (Streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxins)
  • Streptococcal mitogenic exotoxin Z (SMEZ)
  • Scarlet fever
  • Streptococcal toxic shock syndrome (STSS)
  • Necrotising fasciitis

Two Examples — Detailed

1. Toxic Shock Syndrome Toxin-1 (TSST-1)

  • 22 kDa protein produced by ~20% of S. aureus strains (especially phage group I).
  • Resistant to heat (100 °C × 30 min) & proteolysis.
  • Clinical: Toxic Shock Syndrome (TSS)
    • Original description (1980) — menstrual TSS associated with super-absorbent tampons (Rely brand).
    • Fever >38.9 °C, hypotension (SBP <90), diffuse maculopapular rash (sunburn-like) with desquamation (especially palms & soles after 1–2 weeks), multi-organ involvement (≥3 systems): vomiting/diarrhoea, myalgia, mucous membrane hyperaemia, renal, hepatic, haematological (thrombocytopenia), CNS (altered sensorium).
    • Pathogenesis — TSST-1 crosses mucosal barrier (no digestive destruction; absorbed intact); activates T cells bearing Vβ2 (5–30%); cytokine storm (TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6, IFN-γ) → capillary leak, hypotension, shock, ARDS.
    • Treatment — remove source (tampon, drain abscess, debride wound); aggressive fluid resuscitation; vasopressors; clindamycin (suppresses toxin synthesis) + vancomycin/oxacillin; IVIG; admission to ICU.
    • Mortality — 3–5% with prompt treatment; 50% untreated.

2. Staphylococcal Enterotoxin B (SEB)

  • 28 kDa heat-stable protein produced by S. aureus; one of the most common causes of staphylococcal food poisoning.
  • Clinical — Food poisoning:
    • Acute onset (2–6 h after ingestion) of severe nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps; diarrhoea less prominent.
    • Self-limited (24 h); no fever; resolves without specific treatment.
    • Source — contaminated food (cream pastries, salads, dairy products, meats) left at room temperature; S. aureus grows & produces toxin.
    • Pathogenesis — SEB acts on intestinal epithelium & submucosal mast cells (via Vβ3, Vβ12, Vβ14 T cells) → local cytokine release → vomiting reflex via vagal afferents & 5-HT3 receptors on enterochromaffin cells.
    • SEB is also a bioterrorism agent (Category B) — inhalation causes severe systemic illness resembling TSS.

Clinical Pearl

The defining hallmark of a superantigen is its ability to bypass antigen processing & bind directly to MHC-II outside the peptide groove + TCR Vβ outside the antigen-binding site — activating up to 30% of all T cells (vs <0.001% for conventional antigen). This explains the dramatic clinical presentations — toxic shock within hours, with high fever, hypotension, diffuse rash, multi-organ failure — and the rapid progression to death without treatment. The most common iatrogenic SAg-like syndrome is cytokine release syndrome (CRS) from CAR-T cell therapy or bispecific T-cell engagers — similar mechanism (massive T-cell activation → cytokine storm), different trigger (artificial CD3-tumour antigen linker). Both respond dramatically to tocilizumab (anti-IL-6R) — the basis for its FDA approval for CRS. Bacterial superantigens are not inactivated by routine cooking — SEB survives boiling for 30 min, so reheating contaminated food does not prevent food poisoning. The implicated foods (cream pastries, mayonnaise-based salads) must be refrigerated. For suspected toxic shock, remove the source (tampon, wound packing) immediately — every minute counts.

Definitions

Definitive Host

The definitive host (final host) is the host in which the parasite reaches sexual maturity and undergoes sexual reproduction (gamete formation, fertilisation). The parasite may also multiply in the definitive host, but the defining feature is sexual maturity.

Intermediate Host

The intermediate host is the host in which the parasite undergoes asexual reproduction (larval development, metamorphosis) but does NOT reach sexual maturity. The parasite passes through one or more larval stages in the intermediate host.

Other Host-Related Terms

  • Paratenic host (transport host) — a host in which the parasite does NOT undergo any development but remains viable & accumulates, serving as a vehicle for transmission to definitive host. E.g., rodents / pigs for Trichinella (no development, accumulates in muscle).
  • Reservoir host — a host (often animal) in which the parasite lives & multiplies, serving as a continuous source of infection for humans or other hosts. E.g., dog — Echinococcus granulosus; pig — Taenia solium; cattle — Taenia saginata.
  • Vector — an arthropod that transmits the parasite from one host to another. Biological vector (parasite develops/multiplies — Anopheles for malaria) vs mechanical vector (parasite carried passively — housefly for Entamoeba).
  • Accidental / incidental host — a host not normally part of the parasite's life cycle (e.g., humans for Echinococcus — dead-end host; for Angiostrongylus).

Examples — Parasites and Their Hosts (4 marks)

Clinical Pearl

Knowing which host the human plays is critical for understanding transmission & control. For Taenia solium, humans can be both definitive host (adult tapeworm in gut — taeniasis) AND accidental intermediate host (cysticercosis — cysticerci in brain, eye, muscle, subcutaneous tissue) when eggs are ingested from contaminated food/water or by autoinfection (fecal-oral). Neurocysticercosis is the most common cause of adult-onset epilepsy in endemic regions (Latin America, India, sub-Saharan Africa) — albendazole + corticosteroid is treatment. For Echinococcus granulosus, humans are accidental intermediate hosts — dogs are definitive hosts (adult worm in gut, eggs in faeces), sheep are normal intermediate hosts (hydatid cyst in liver/lung). Humans ingest eggs from dog faeces → hydatid cyst develops in liver (60%), lung (20%), other organs. Treatment — surgery (PAIR: puncture, aspiration, injection, reaspiration) + albendazole. For Schistosoma, humans are definitive hosts; snails are intermediate hosts that release cercariae which penetrate human skin — control requires snail elimination, safe water, sanitation & mass drug administration with praziquantel. For Toxoplasma, cats are definitive hosts (oocysts in faeces); humans are intermediate hosts — pregnant women should avoid cat litter & undercooked meat to prevent congenital toxoplasmosis (hydrocephalus, chorioretinitis, intracranial calcification).

Introduction

Louis Pasteur (1822–1895) — French chemist & microbiologist — is one of the founders of medical microbiology. His work laid the foundation for understanding microbial causation of disease, fermentation, vaccination, and aseptic practice. He pioneered the Germ Theory of Disease, displacing the prevailing theory of spontaneous generation.

Major Contributions

1. Germ Theory of Disease & Disproof of Spontaneous Generation (2 marks)

  • Pasteur demonstrated that microorganisms cause fermentation and disease — disproving the prevailing theory of spontaneous generation (held by Needham & Pouchet, that life arises de novo from non-living matter).
  • Swan-neck flask experiment (1859–64)
    • Boiled nutrient broth in flasks with long, curved (swan-neck) necks open to air.
    • Bent necks allowed air to enter but prevented dust & airborne microbes from reaching the broth.
    • Broth remained sterile indefinitely.
    • If the neck was broken or flask tipped so broth contacted dust in the neck, microbial growth appeared within days.
    • Conclusion: microbes come from other microbes (biogenesis), not spontaneous generation.
  • Pasteur's work extended the earlier work of Francesco Redi (1668 — meat & maggots) & Lazzaro Spallanzani (1765 — boiled broth in sealed flasks).
  • This work laid the foundation for Joseph Lister's antiseptic surgery (1867 — carbolic acid spray), hand hygiene (Semmelweis), and modern infection control.

2. Pasteurisation (1 mark)

  • Pasteur was asked by French wine industry (1856) to investigate why wine & beer were spoiling.
  • He discovered that spoilage was caused by contaminating microorganisms (acetic acid bacteria, lactic acid bacteria) — not chemical changes.
  • Pasteurisation — controlled heating of liquids (wine, beer, milk) to 60–65 °C for 30 min (holder method) — kills pathogenic/spoilage microbes without significantly altering taste.
  • Modern pasteurisation of milk
    • Holder — 63 °C × 30 min.
    • HTST (High Temperature Short Time) — 72 °C × 15 sec.
    • UHT (Ultra-High Temperature) — 132 °C × 1 sec; sterile; long shelf life without refrigeration.
  • Pasteurisation kills Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Coxiella burnetii (Q fever), Salmonella, Brucella, Streptococcus agalactiae, Listeria monocytogenes, Escherichia coli O157:H7 — preventing milk-borne disease.
  • Also applied to fruit juices, beer, wine, honey, eggs.

3. Vaccines — Attenuation & Rabies Vaccine (2 marks)

  • Pasteur extended Jenner's work on cowpox vaccination by developing artificially attenuated vaccines (microbes weakened so they no longer cause disease but retain antigenicity).
  • Chicken cholera vaccine (1879)
    • Accidental discovery — old culture of Pasteurella multocida (chicken cholera bacillus) lost virulence but protected chickens on subsequent challenge.
    • Coined the term "attenuation".
  • Anthrax vaccine (1881)
    • Attenuated Bacillus anthracis by growth at 42–43 °C (heat-attenuation).
    • Public demonstration at Pouilly-le-Fort — vaccinated 25 sheep, left 25 unvaccinated; all vaccinated survived anthrax challenge, all unvaccinated died.
    • Established principle of attenuated live vaccines.
  • Rabies vaccine (1885) — Pasteur's most famous achievement
    • Developed attenuated rabies virus by serial passage in rabbits (dried spinal cord of rabid rabbit — virus lost virulence after drying for 14 days).
    • Vaccine tested on Joseph Meister (9-year-old boy bitten by rabid dog, July 1885) — 14 days of subcutaneous inoculations with progressively less-dried (more virulent) spinal cord extract.
    • Meister survived — first successful rabies PEP.
    • Led to establishment of Pasteur Institute in Paris (1888).
  • Pasteur's attenuation principle later used to develop BCG (Calmette & Guérin, 1921 — 230 passages on bile-potato medium), Sabin oral polio vaccine, yellow fever vaccine (17D strain).

4. Fermentation & Industrial Microbiology (½ mark)

  • Demonstrated that fermentation is caused by living microorganisms, not chemical catalysis (Liebig's view).
  • Identified specific microbes for different fermentations — yeast for alcoholic fermentation (wine, beer); bacteria for lactic acid (souring of milk), acetic acid (vinegar), butyric acid.
  • Discovered anaerobic life — butyric acid fermentation by Clostridium butyricum in oxygen-free environment; coined the term "anaerobic".
  • Introduced pure culture concept — selected specific yeast strains for wine & beer production; founded the field of industrial microbiology.
  • Saved French silk industry by identifying pebrine disease of silkworms (caused by Nosema bombycis) and proposing microscopic screening of moths to eliminate infected stock.

5. Other Contributions

  • Molecular asymmetry (chirality) — discovered stereoisomerism of tartaric acid (1848); distinguished d- & l-tartaric acid using polarised light. Concept of chirality became fundamental to chemistry & pharmacology.
  • Founder of modern microbiology laboratory — developed techniques for sterile culture, pure culture isolation (enrichment, anaerobic cultivation), microbial identification.
  • Pasteur Institute (1888) — Paris; one of the world's leading biomedical research institutions; has produced 10 Nobel laureates. Discovered HIV (Barré-Sinoussi, Montagnier, 1983) at Pasteur Institute.
  • Established principles of aseptic technique in surgery (influenced Lister).
  • Coined terms "vaccine", "attenuation", "anaerobic", "microorganism".

Clinical Pearl

Pasteur's rabies vaccination of Joseph Meister (1885) is the prototype of post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP). Today's rabies PEP follows the same principle — passive (RIG) + active (vaccine) immunisation — refined into WHO-recommended regimens (Essen 5-dose intramuscular on days 0, 3, 7, 14, 28; or 2-site intradermal on days 0, 3, 7). Modern cell-culture vaccines (HDCV — human diploid cell vaccine; PCECV — purified chick embryo cell vaccine) replaced Pasteur's nervous-tissue vaccine (which had serious neurological adverse effects). India still uses the nervous tissue vaccine (BPL-inactivated sheep brain — Semple vaccine) in some government centres despite WHO recommendation against it — due to cost considerations. Pasteur's broader legacy: every aseptic practice in modern medicine — hand hygiene, sterile surgical instruments, sterile dressings, sterilisation of fluids, food safety — derives from his disproof of spontaneous generation. His aphorism: "Chance favours only the prepared mind" — refers to his accidental discovery of chicken cholera attenuation, which led to the entire field of vaccinology. The Pasteur Institute, founded with global donations after his rabies vaccine triumph, remains a major research institution — and was where HIV-1 was first isolated in 1983 (Luc Montagnier & Françoise Barré-Sinoussi, Nobel Prize 2008).

Introduction

The WHO Five Moments for Hand Hygiene — launched in 2009 as part of the "Clean Care is Safer Care" campaign — defines the five critical moments during patient care when hand hygiene must be performed. The strategy simplifies earlier (CDC) guidelines and provides a unified, evidence-based framework for healthcare workers in all settings. It is the single most effective measure to prevent healthcare-associated infections (HAI).

The Five Moments

Moment 1: Before touching a patient

  • When — before any physical contact with the patient (shaking hands, helping patient move, taking pulse/BP, abdominal examination, turning patient).
  • Why — protects the patient from microbes carried on the healthcare worker's hands (transient flora acquired from surfaces, other patients, environment).
  • Zone — patient zone (the patient and their immediate surroundings).
  • Method — alcohol-based handrub (preferred) or soap-and-water.

Moment 2: Before clean / aseptic procedure

  • When — before any procedure that requires aseptic technique — dressing a wound, inserting a peripheral or central venous catheter, urinary catheterisation, preparing an injection, oral care, eye care, drawing blood.
  • Why — protects the patient from microbes (including their own resident flora) entering sterile sites (bloodstream, bladder, subcutaneous tissue, wound). Most critical moment — directly prevents healthcare-associated bloodstream infection (CLABSI), CAUTI, SSI.
  • Method — alcohol-based handrub; if hands visibly soiled, wash with soap & water first. For surgical procedures, surgical hand scrub with chlorhexidine/povidone-iodine (3–5 min).

Moment 3: After body fluid exposure risk

  • When — immediately after any procedure involving contact with body fluids, mucous membranes, non-intact skin, or wound dressings — e.g., after drawing blood, changing a wound dressing, handling a used bedpan, oral suctioning, removing an IV line.
  • Why — protects the healthcare worker and the healthcare environment from microbial colonisation by patient-derived microbes (transient hand contamination).
  • Method — wash with soap & water if hands visibly soiled; otherwise alcohol-based handrub. Always remove gloves & perform hand hygiene before leaving the patient zone.

Moment 4: After touching a patient

  • When — after any physical contact with the patient (shaking hands, helping move, examination).
  • Why — protects the healthcare worker & other patients from microbes acquired from the patient.
  • Method — alcohol-based handrub or soap & water.

Moment 5: After touching patient surroundings

  • When — after contact with any inanimate object in the patient's immediate vicinity — bed rails, IV pole, bedside table, monitor, door handle, blood pressure cuff, thermometer, chart, laptop, phone.
  • Why — protects the healthcare worker & other patients from microbes left on surfaces by previous patient contact.
  • Method — alcohol-based handrub or soap & water.

Hand Hygiene Methods

Method Indication Time
Alcohol-based handrub (ABHR)Routine hand hygiene — all 5 moments (when hands not visibly soiled)20–30 sec; 3–5 mL
Soap & waterVisibly dirty hands; before eating; after toilet; suspected/confirmed C. difficile, norovirus, anthrax, spore-formers (alcohol does NOT kill spores)40–60 sec
Surgical hand scrubBefore surgical procedure2–5 min; chlorhexidine or povidone-iodine

WHO Technique — Alcohol-Based Handrub

  1. Apply enough product (3–5 mL) to cover both hands.
  2. Rub palms together.
  3. Right palm over left dorsum; left palm over right dorsum.
  4. Palm to palm with fingers interlaced.
  5. Backs of fingers to opposing palms with fingers interlocked.
  6. Rotational rubbing of left thumb clasped in right palm & vice versa.
  7. Rotational rubbing, backwards & forwards, with clasped fingers of right hand in left palm & vice versa.
  8. Once dry, hands are safe.

Indications for Soap & Water Instead of Alcohol Handrub

  • Hands visibly soiled with blood, body fluids, dirt.
  • Before eating, after using the toilet.
  • Suspected or confirmed C. difficile infection (alcohol does not kill spores).
  • Norovirus outbreak (alcohol has limited efficacy).
  • Bacillus anthracis (spores).
  • After caring for a patient with clostridial infection.

Glove Use — Key Principles

  • Gloves are NOT a substitute for hand hygiene — they have microscopic defects and can be contaminated during removal.
  • Wear gloves when contact with blood/body fluids, mucous membranes, non-intact skin is anticipated.
  • Change gloves between patients and between dirty & clean tasks on the same patient.
  • Remove gloves immediately after task — perform hand hygiene.
  • Do NOT wear the same pair of gloves for multiple patients.

Indications for Hand Hygiene — Beyond Five Moments

  • Before & after eating.
  • After using the toilet.
  • After coughing/sneezing into hands.
  • Before & after smoking.
  • Before putting on & after removing PPE.
  • After handling contaminated waste or laundry.

Why Hand Hygiene Saves Lives

  • Healthcare workers' hands are the most common vehicle of cross-transmission in hospitals.
  • Compliance with hand hygiene can reduce HAIs by 30–50%.
  • WHO estimates that improving hand hygiene could save 5–8 million lives annually worldwide.
  • Cost-effective — alcohol-based handrub is cheaper than soap-and-water (time, water, towels).
  • Reduces spread of multidrug-resistant organisms (MRSA, VRE, ESBL, CRE, CRAB, CRPA).

Clinical Pearl

The single most important lesson from the WHO campaign is: alcohol-based handrub is the gold standard for routine hand hygiene (20 sec, more effective, faster, better tolerated by skin, no need for water/sink/towels) — except when hands are visibly dirty or when spore-forming organisms (C. difficile, anthrax, norovirus) are suspected (then soap-and-water is mandatory because alcohol does not kill spores). The 5 Moments framework is intentionally simple — easy to remember, easy to audit, easy to teach. Compliance is monitored by direct observation (gold standard), product consumption (litres per 1000 patient-days), and increasingly by automated monitoring systems. The WHO "My 5 Moments" framework has been adopted in over 180 countries — it is the most successful patient-safety intervention in history. The rise of carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales (NDM, KPC, OXA-48) in Indian ICUs makes hand hygiene non-negotiable — these organisms are spread almost exclusively by contaminated hands. Wearing the same pair of gloves for multiple patients is the most dangerous hand-hygiene violation — gloves do not protect the next patient.

Definition

Enriched media are culture media that have been supplemented with additional nutrients (such as blood, serum, egg, yeast extract, haemin, vitamin K, chocolate agar) to support the growth of fastidious microorganisms — bacteria or fungi that require complex or specific growth factors and cannot grow on simple media like nutrient agar.

Fastidious organisms need growth factors such as:

  • Vitamins — NAD (V factor), hemin (X factor), vitamin K, vitamin B12, folate.
  • Amino acids, nucleotides.
  • Blood — for haemin, iron, growth factors.
  • Carbon dioxide — for capnophiles (Streptococcus, Neisseria gonorrhoeae).
  • Serum proteins, lipids, cholesterol.

Enriched media may be basal media supplemented with enrichments (e.g., blood agar = nutrient agar + 5–10% sheep blood), or complex defined media from the start (e.g., chocolate agar, Lowenstein-Jensen medium).

Difference from Related Media Types

Type Function Example
Simple / basal mediumSupports non-fastidious organismsNutrient agar, peptone water
Enriched mediumSupplemented to grow fastidious organismsBlood agar, chocolate agar
Enrichment brothSelective for pathogen (inhibits competitors, favours pathogen)Selenite F broth (Salmonella), Alkaline peptone water (Vibrio)
Selective mediumContains antibiotics/chemicals that inhibit some organisms & favour othersMacConkey agar, TCBS, Lowenstein-Jensen
Differential mediumDistinguishes organisms by colour / colony morphologyMacConkey (lactose fermenter), Blood agar (haemolysis)
Transport mediumMaintains viability without multiplication during transportStuart, Cary-Blair, Amies

Two Examples — Detailed

1. Blood Agar

  • Composition — nutrient agar base (peptone, beef extract, sodium chloride, agar, water, pH 7.2–7.6) supplemented with 5–10% defibrinated sheep/horse/human blood.
  • Why enriched — provides X factor (hemin), V factor (NAD — partially), iron, amino acids, vitamins; supports growth of fastidious organisms (Streptococcus, Staphylococcus, Neisseria, Corynebacterium, Haemophilus — partial, Listeria, enterococci, pneumococci).
  • Types
    • Sheep blood agar — preferred for streptococcal differentiation; α, β, γ haemolysis.
    • Human blood agar — less ideal (may contain antibodies, antibiotics).
    • Horse blood agar — used in UK; similar haemolysis patterns.
  • Preparation — autoclave base medium; cool to 45–50 °C; add sterile defibrinated blood (5–10%); mix gently (avoid bubbles); pour into plates; incubate at 37 °C for 24 h to check sterility.
  • Haemolysis patterns
    • α-haemolysis — partial haemolysis; greenish discolouration around colony due to oxidation of haemoglobin to methaemoglobin (e.g., Streptococcus pneumoniae, Streptococcus viridans group — S. mitis, S. salivarius, S. sanguinis, S. mutans). Aerial view: green.
    • β-haemolysis — complete lysis of RBCs; clear transparent zone around colony (e.g., Streptococcus pyogenes, Streptococcus agalactiae, Listeria monocytogenes — narrow; Staphylococcus aureus; Clostridium perfringens). Due to streptolysin O & S (Group A Strep), CAMP factor (Group B Strep).
    • γ-haemolysis (no haemolysis) — no change in blood agar around colony (e.g., Enterococcus faecalis, Staphylococcus epidermidis).
  • Special tests on blood agar
    • Optochin test — differentiates S. pneumoniae (sensitive, ≥14 mm zone) from viridans streptococci (resistant).
    • Bacitracin test — differentiates S. pyogenes (sensitive) from other β-haemolytic strep.
    • CAMP test — identifies S. agalactiae (arrowhead-shaped haemolysis enhancement with Staphylococcus aureus β-lysin).
    • Satellitism test — identifies Haemophilus influenzae (grows around Staphylococcus aureus streak — provides V factor; or on nutrient agar with NAD disc).

2. Chocolate Agar

  • Composition — blood agar that has been heated to 70–80 °C after adding blood (until colour changes from red to brown — "chocolate"). Heating lyses RBCs, releasing intracellular X factor (hemin) and V factor (NAD) — these are normally unavailable in unheated blood agar (V factor is intracellular in RBCs).
  • Why enriched — supports growth of more fastidious organisms than blood agar, particularly those needing both X & V factors.
  • Organisms that grow on chocolate agar but NOT blood agar
    • Haemophilus influenzae (requires X + V factor).
    • Neisseria gonorrhoeae & Neisseria meningitidis (require V factor; improved growth on chocolate agar; also need 5% CO₂ — capnophilic).
    • Moraxella catarrhalis.
  • Uses
    • Respiratory specimens — sputum for H. influenzae.
    • Genital specimens — urethral/cervical swab for N. gonorrhoeae (Thayer-Martin is selective chocolate).
    • CSF — meningitis workup (N. meningitidis, H. influenzae).
    • Eye swab — for H. influenzae biogroup aegyptius (Koch-Weeks bacillus; Brazilian purpuric fever).
  • Variants
    • Thayer-Martin medium — chocolate agar + vancomycin + colistin + nystatin (VCN inhibitor) — selective for pathogenic Neisseria; inhibits normal flora in genital/oropharyngeal specimens.
    • Modified Thayer-Martin (MTM) — adds trimethoprim (VCNT).
    • New York City (NYC) medium — alternative selective medium for N. gonorrhoeae.
    • Martin-Lewis — chocolate agar + vancomycin + colistin + anisomycin.
    • GC-Lect — selective for N. gonorrhoeae.

Other Important Enriched Media (brief)

  • Loeffler's serum slope — serum + egg + glucose — for Corynebacterium diphtheriae (emphasises granules & metachromatic granules).
  • Dorset egg medium — egg yolk + saline — for Mycobacterium tuberculosis (slower than LJ).
  • Lowenstein-Jensen (LJ) — egg + malachite green + glycerol + asparagine — for M. tuberculosis (selective & enriched).
  • Todd-Hewitt broth — enriched broth for Streptococcus.
  • Trypticase soy agar (TSA) / Tryptic soy broth (TSB) — general-purpose enriched medium.
  • Brain heart infusion (BHI) — enriched for fastidious organisms, yeast, mould.
  • Cooked meat broth (Robertson's) — enriched + anaerobic; for Clostridium.
  • Serum agar / serum broth — for fastidious organisms requiring serum proteins.
  • Fildes medium — peptic digest of blood; for H. influenzae.

Clinical Pearl

The single most important practical lesson: chocolate agar is needed for suspected Haemophilus influenzae and Neisseria infections — these organisms will not grow on blood agar (or grow poorly) because they require the V factor (NAD) which is intracellular in RBCs and only released when blood is heated. For a febrile child with meningitis, always plate CSF on both blood agar & chocolate agar (in 5% CO₂ candle jar) — and incubate overnight. Adding a chocolate agar plate to routine meningitis workup increases yield for H. influenzae and N. meningitidis dramatically. Thayer-Martin selective chocolate agar is mandatory for genital swabs in suspected gonorrhoea — non-selective chocolate agar will be overgrown by normal flora. For group A streptococcus pharyngitis, a single blood agar plate (incubated anaerobically or with 5% CO₂) is sufficient — S. pyogenes shows β-haemolysis within 24 h. Always keep enrichment broth (e.g., BHI or tryptic soy broth) for blood culture — fastidious organisms like H. influenzae, S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis, viridans streptococci are common blood culture pathogens; BACTEC automated systems use enriched resins to neutralise antibiotics in patient serum.

Definition

Infective endocarditis (IE) is an infection of the endocardial surface of the heart — most commonly the heart valves (native or prosthetic), but also the mural endocardium or septum, or implanted devices (pacemaker leads, ICD). It is characterised by vegetation — a mass of platelets, fibrin, microorganisms, and inflammatory cells — on the valve.

Classification

  • By onset — Acute (fulminant over days — virulent organisms like S. aureus); Subacute (weeks–months — less virulent like viridans streptococci).
  • By valve type — Native valve endocarditis (NVE); Prosthetic valve endocarditis (PVE — early <2 months post-surgery; late >2 months); Pacemaker/ICD lead endocarditis.
  • By acquisition — Community-acquired; Healthcare-associated (nosocomial & non-nosocomial).
  • By culture result — Culture-positive; Culture-negative (5–10% — prior antibiotics, fastidious organisms, intracellular — Coxiella, Bartonella, Tropheryma).

Causative Organisms (modified Duke criteria)

Setting Common organisms
Native valve (community)Viridans streptococci (S. sanguinis, S. mutans — 30–40%); S. aureus (30%); Enterococcus (10%); HACEK group (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) — 5%; Group A, B, G streptococci; S. pneumoniae
Native valve (healthcare-associated)S. aureus (incl. MRSA — 40–50%); CoNS; Enterococcus; Gram-negative bacilli (E. coli, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas); Candida
Prosthetic valve — early (<2 mo)CoNS (S. lugdunensis, S. epidermidis — 30%); S. aureus; Gram-negative bacilli; Candida; Enterococcus; diphtheroids
Prosthetic valve — late (>2 mo)Viridans streptococci; Enterococcus; S. aureus; CoNS; HACEK
IV drug usersS. aureus (incl. MRSA — 60%); often right-sided (tricuspid); Pseudomonas, Candida, Bacillus, Corynebacterium
Culture-negativeCoxiella burnetii; Bartonella; Tropheryma whipplei; Legionella; Mycoplasma; Chlamydia psittaci; Brucella; HACEK (fastidious, slow-growing); fungi (Aspergillus, Histoplasma ); prior antibiotics

Risk Factors

  • Pre-existing valve disease — rheumatic, bicuspid aortic valve, mitral valve prolapse with regurgitation, calcific aortic stenosis, congenital heart disease (VSD, PDA, TOF).
  • Prosthetic valve / pacemaker / ICD.
  • IV drug use.
  • Indwelling central venous catheter, haemodialysis.
  • Immunosuppression, diabetes, malignancy.
  • Poor dental hygiene, dental procedures (viridans strep); GU procedures (enterococci).

Clinical Features

  • Constitutional — fever (90%), rigors, night sweats, fatigue, weight loss, anorexia.
  • Cardiac — new or changing murmur (85%; particularly regurgitant), heart failure, conduction block (AV block — aortic root abscess).
  • Vascular phenomena — splinter haemorrhages (nail beds); Janeway lesions (painless erythematous macules on palms/soles — septic microemboli); conjunctival petechiae; Osler nodes (painful nodules on pulp of fingers/toes — immune complex); Roth spots (retinal haemorrhages with pale centre).
  • Embolic — systemic emboli (brain — stroke; mesenteric — abdominal pain; splenic, renal, coronary; limb — gangrene); septic pulmonary emboli (right-sided IE).
  • Immunological — glomerulonephritis (immune complex); arthritis; positive rheumatoid factor.
  • Splenomegaly; clubbing (chronic cases).

Modified Duke Criteria — Diagnosis

Definite IE Possible IE Rejected
2 major OR 1 major + 3 minor OR 5 minor criteria1 major + 1 minor OR 3 minorFirm alternative diagnosis; resolution with <4 days antibiotics; no pathologic evidence at surgery/autopsy

Major criteria:

  1. Typical microorganism in 2 separate blood cultures (viridans strep, S. aureus, HACEK, enterococci) OR persistent bacteraemia (≥2 positive cultures >12 h apart; or ≥3 of ≥4 positive cultures >1 h apart); OR single positive Coxiella burnetii blood culture / anti-phase I IgG >1:800.
  2. Evidence of endocardial involvement — echocardiogram positive (oscillating intracardiac mass on valve / supporting structures / implanted material; abscess; new partial dehiscence of prosthetic valve); OR new valvular regurgitation.

Minor criteria:

  • Predisposition — predisposing heart condition or IV drug use.
  • Fever >38 °C.
  • Vascular phenomena — arterial emboli, septic pulmonary infarcts, mycotic aneurysm, intracranial haemorrhage, conjunctival haemorrhages, Janeway lesions.
  • Immunological phenomena — glomerulonephritis, Osler nodes, Roth spots, rheumatoid factor.
  • Microbiological evidence — positive blood culture not meeting major criterion, or serological evidence of active infection with organism consistent with IE.

Laboratory Diagnosis (3 marks)

1. Blood Cultures — Cornerstone

  • Three sets from separate venepuncture sites, >1 h apart, before antibiotic administration (if possible).
  • Volume critical — adult: 20–30 mL per set (10 mL per bottle × 2 bottles per set); paediatric: 1–4 mL per bottle depending on weight.
  • Aerobic & anaerobic BACTEC bottles; incubated 5 days (extended to 14 days for HACEK, nutritionally variant strep, Brucella, Candida).
  • Positive bottles — Gram stain, subculture on blood agar, chocolate agar, MacConkey; biochemical identification; antimicrobial susceptibility testing (MIC, synergy testing for enterococci).
  • If prior antibiotics — use antimicrobial removal device (ARD) resin bottles; or prolonged incubation.
  • Culture-negative workup — serology (Coxiella, Bartonella, Brucella, Mycoplasma); PCR (16S rRNA, 18S rRNA for fungi); autohalophilic organisms; ask lab to hold cultures for 14 days.

2. Complete Blood Count

  • Anaemia — normocytic normochromic (anaemia of chronic disease).
  • Leucocytosis with neutrophilia (acute); normal or low in subacute.
  • Thrombocytopenia.
  • ESR raised (often >50 mm/h); CRP raised.

3. Urine

  • Proteinuria, microscopic haematuria — immune complex glomerulonephritis.
  • RBC casts — proliferative glomerulonephritis.

4. Immunological

  • Rheumatoid factor — positive in ~50% (subacute).
  • Hypocomplementaemia (low C3, C4) — immune complex.
  • Cryoglobulins; circulating immune complexes.

5. ECG

  • May show new AV block (aortic root abscess), bundle branch block, non-specific ST-T changes.
  • Atrial fibrillation.

6. Echocardiography

  • Transthoracic echo (TTE) — first-line; sensitivity 60% (NVE), 70% (PVE); good for anterior structures.
  • Transoesophageal echo (TOE/TEE) — sensitivity >90% (NVE), 90% (PVE); preferred for prosthetic valves, suspected abscess, periannular complications, small vegetations (<5 mm).
  • Findings — oscillating mass (vegetation) on valve; abscess; new regurgitation; dehiscence of prosthetic valve; perforation of leaflet.

7. Molecular & Serological Tests

  • 16S rRNA PCR on blood or excised valve tissue — culture-negative endocarditis.
  • Serology — Coxiella (phase I IgG >1:800), Bartonella henselae/quintana, Brucella, Mycoplasma, Chlamydia psittaci.
  • 18S rRNA / mannan / anti-mannan antibody for Candida endocarditis.

8. Histopathology of Excised Valve

  • Gram stain, PAS, Grocott methenamine silver (GMS), Ziehl-Neelsen; PCR on tissue.
  • Acute inflammation, vegetation with fibrin-platelet microorganisms; granulomatous reaction (Bartonella, Coxiella, T. whipplei).

Treatment Principles

  • Empirical antibiotics (before culture results) — vancomycin + gentamicin ± cefepime (native valve); vancomycin + gentamicin + ciprofloxacin + rifampin (prosthetic valve early).
  • Targeted therapy based on organism & MIC — typically 4–6 weeks IV; for viridans strep: ceftriaxone 2 g IV OD × 4 wk or penicillin G + gentamicin × 2 wk; for S. aureus: nafcillin/oxacillin × 6 wk (vancomycin if MRSA); for enterococci: ampicillin + gentamicin × 4–6 wk.
  • Surgery — heart failure, uncontrolled infection (perivalvular abscess, persistent bacteraemia, fungal IE, prosthetic valve IE), large vegetations (>10 mm) with emboli, S. aureus PVE.
  • Anticoagulation — not routinely indicated; may continue for pre-existing indication.

Prevention — Antibiotic Prophylaxis

  • Indicated for high-risk cardiac conditions — prosthetic valve, previous IE, congenital heart disease (unrepaired cyanotic; repaired with prosthetic material within 6 months; repaired with residual defect), cardiac transplant with valvulopathy, rheumatic heart disease (in endemic areas).
  • Procedures — dental (extractions, scaling); respiratory tract procedures involving incision; infected skin/musculoskeletal procedures.
  • Amoxicillin 2 g PO 30–60 min before procedure (ampicillin 2 g IV / cefazolin / clindamycin if penicillin-allergic). Not for routine GI/GU procedures.

Clinical Pearl

The single most important rule for IE diagnosis is: draw 3 sets of blood cultures from separate sites BEFORE starting antibiotics — the diagnosis of IE rests primarily on bacteraemia documentation, not on a single positive culture. Culture-negative endocarditis (5–10% of cases) is most often due to prior antibiotic exposure — but always consider Coxiella burnetii (Q fever — check phase I IgG >1:800), Bartonella, and HACEK organisms. For HACEK, ask the lab to hold blood cultures for 14 days (slow grower). For suspected IE, always start with transthoracic echo (TTE), but proceed to transoesophageal echo (TOE) if TTE negative — TOE has >90% sensitivity and is essential for prosthetic valves, suspected abscess, or small vegetations. The modified Duke criteria are essential for case classification — a single major criterion (typical organism in blood culture + echo evidence of vegetation) makes the diagnosis definite. A common viva trap: S. aureus bacteraemia from any source (line infection, skin infection, IV drug use) — should always prompt echocardiography to look for IE because S. aureus has high affinity for valves and a high mortality (25–40%). Always involve cardiology, infectious disease, microbiology, and cardiac surgery early — multidisciplinary "endocarditis team" approach reduces mortality.

Definition

Fever of unknown origin (FUO) / Pyrexia of unknown origin (PUO) — classically defined by Petersdorf & Beeson (1961) as:

  1. Fever >38.3 °C (101 °F) on several occasions.
  2. Duration >3 weeks.
  3. Failure to reach a diagnosis despite 1 week of inpatient investigation (or 3 outpatient visits with 2 days of intelligent invasive tests).

Modern (Durack & Street, 1991) classification — 4 subtypes:

  • Classic FUO — as above, in community or hospital setting.
  • Nosocomial FUO — fever developing in hospitalised patient, ≥3 days, not present/incubating at admission; cultures negative after 48 h.
  • Neutropenic FUO — fever in neutropenic patient (neutrophils <500/µL or expected to fall below 500); cultures negative after 48 h.
  • HIV-associated FUO — fever in HIV-positive patient, ≥4 weeks outpatient or ≥3 days inpatient; cultures negative after 48 h.

Etiology — Major Categories (4 marks)

Traditionally divided into 4 categories — infections (~30%), neoplasms (~20%), non-infectious inflammatory diseases (~30%), and miscellaneous/undiagnosed (~20%). The pattern varies by geography & age.

A. Infections (25–40% in developed; 40–50% in developing countries)

Type Examples
TuberculosisPulmonary, miliary, disseminated, extrapulmonary (lymphadenitis, meningitis, osteomyelitis, abdominal TB, adrenal TB — Addison's) — most common cause of infection-related FUO in India
EndocarditisSubacute bacterial endocarditis — viridans strep, enterococci; culture-negative (Coxiella, Bartonella, HACEK)
AbscessIntra-abdominal (subphrenic, hepatic, pelvic), renal, perinephric, dental, brain; often require CT to localise
BacteraemiaOccult bacteraemia — Salmonella (enteric fever — typhoid, paratyphoid), Brucellosis, Leptospirosis
Viral infectionsEBV (infectious mononucleosis), CMV, HIV (seroconversion illness, opportunistic infection), viral hepatitis (HCV), dengue, chikungunya
FungalDisseminated histoplasmosis, cryptococcosis, candidiasis, aspergillosis (immunocompromised)
ParasiticMalaria (esp. P. falciparum, P. knowlesi), visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar), amebic liver abscess, toxoplasmosis, trypanosomiasis, schistosomiasis
Rickettsial & intracellularScrub typhus, murine typhus, Indian tick typhus, Q fever (Coxiella), ehrlichiosis
OthersWhipple's disease (Tropheryma whipplei), Cat scratch disease (Bartonella henselae), Rat bite fever (Streptobacillus), Leptospirosis

B. Neoplasms (15–25%)

  • Lymphoma — both Hodgkin (Pel-Ebstein fever — cyclic) and non-Hodgkin; most common neoplastic cause of FUO; check LDH, CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, lymph node biopsy.
  • Leukaemia — acute myeloid leukaemia, hairy cell leukaemia.
  • Renal cell carcinoma — classic triad (haematuria, flank pain, mass) often absent; paraneoplastic fever.
  • Hepatocellular carcinoma, hepatic metastases.
  • Atrial myxoma — mimic of IE; systemic symptoms, emboli, elevated ESR; echo diagnostic.
  • Other — ovarian, pancreatic, gastric, colon cancer (especially with hepatic metastases); bone tumours.

C. Non-Infectious Inflammatory Diseases (20–30%)

  • Adult-onset Still's disease (AOSD) — quotidian (spiking) fever, evanescent salmon-pink rash, arthritis, ferritin >1000 ng/mL.
  • Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) — particularly early stage; ANA, anti-dsDNA, low complement.
  • Rheumatoid arthritis — extra-articular.
  • Vasculitis
    • Giant cell arteritis / temporal arteritis — age >50, headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, raised ESR.
    • Polymyalgia rheumatica — shoulder/hip girdle pain & stiffness; high ESR.
    • ANCA-associated — granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener's), microscopic polyangiitis, eosinophilic GPA (Churg-Strauss).
    • Polyarteritis nodosa.
    • Takayasu arteritis — young women, absent pulses.
  • Sarcoidosis — bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, uveitis, erythema nodosum.
  • Inflammatory bowel disease — Crohn's disease.
  • Reactive arthritis,ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic arthritis.
  • Behçet's disease — oral & genital aphthae, uveitis, skin lesions.
  • Cryoglobulinaemia — HCV-associated.
  • Autoinflammatory syndromes — Familial Mediterranean Fever (FMF), TNF receptor-associated periodic syndrome (TRAPS), Hyper-IgD syndrome (HIDS), periodic fever, aphthous stomatitis, pharyngitis, adenitis (PFAPA).

D. Miscellaneous Causes (10–15%)

  • Drug fever — β-lactams, sulfa, anticonvulsants (phenytoin), allopurinol, quinidine, methyldopa, isoniazid, minocycline; resolves within 72 h of stopping.
  • Factitious fever / self-induced — Munchausen syndrome; thermometers manipulated, injected contaminants; suspected when fever doesn't follow diurnal pattern or disappears in observer's presence.
  • Habitual hyperthermia — usually young women; low-grade fever (37.5–38.2 °C), normal ESR/CRP; stress-related.
  • Endocrine — hyperthyroidism, Addison's disease, pheochromocytoma.
  • Haematological — haemolytic anaemia, multiple pulmonary emboli, deep vein thrombosis.
  • Granulomatous hepatitis.
  • Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease (histiocytic necrotising lymphadenitis).
  • Subacute thyroiditis, Hashitoxicosis.
  • Cirrhosis with hepatic failure.
  • Cyclic neutropenia.

E. Undiagnosed (5–20%)

  • Despite extensive workup, no cause found; many resolve spontaneously; some recur.
  • Prognosis generally good if no underlying cause identified in 6 months.

Approach to FUO — Diagnostic Strategy (1 mark)

Phase 1 — Initial Workup (history, exam, basic tests)

  • Detailed history — onset, pattern, travel, occupation, animal exposure, sexual, drug, family history, transfusion, surgery, immunisation.
  • Examination — rash, lymph nodes, heart murmur, abdominal tenderness, hepatosplenomegaly, joint, eye (uveitis), temporal artery (tenderness).
  • Tests — CBC, ESR, CRP, peripheral smear; LFT, RFT, electrolytes, glucose, TFT; urinalysis & urine culture; blood cultures × 3 sets; chest X-ray; HIV, HBsAg, anti-HCV; Mantoux / IGRA; ECG.

Phase 2 — Targeted Second-Line

  • Serology — Salmonella (Widal), Brucella, Leptospira, Rickettsia (Weil-Felix, IgM ELISA), Dengue NS1 + IgM, EBV VCA IgM, CMV IgM, scrub typhus IgM.
  • ANA, anti-dsDNA, ANCA, RF, anti-CCP, complement, serum electrophoresis.
  • Ferritin, iron studies (haemophagocytic syndrome).
  • CT chest/abdomen/pelvis with contrast — look for abscess, lymphadenopathy, malignancy.
  • Echocardiography — TTE & TOE (endocarditis).
  • Ultrasound abdomen — hepatic/renal abscess, biliary obstruction.
  • PPD / IGRA (QuantiFERON-TB Gold).
  • Stool — culture, ova/cyst/parasite, occult blood.

Phase 3 — Invasive / Specialised

  • Bone marrow aspiration & biopsy — TB, leukaemia, lymphoma, leishmaniasis.
  • Liver biopsy — granulomatous hepatitis, miliary TB, sarcoidosis, lymphoma.
  • Lymph node biopsy — TB, lymphoma, Kikuchi; excisional preferred over FNAC.
  • Temporal artery biopsy — if GCA suspected (age >50, high ESR, headache).
  • FDG-PET/CT — increasingly used in FUO; identifies occult malignancy, large-vessel vasculitis, focal infection.
  • Endoscopy — colonoscopy for IBD/malignancy; upper GI for Crohn's.
  • Surgical exploration (rare) — exploratory laparotomy (rarely done now with CT).

Approach Principles

  • Stop unnecessary drugs — empirical withdrawal of medications (consider drug fever).
  • Document fever pattern — quotidian (single daily spike), intermittent, remittent, sustained, Pel-Ebstein (cyclical in Hodgkin).
  • Avoid empirical antibiotics, steroids, antipyretics (unless clinically unstable) — they obscure diagnosis.
  • Treat specifically once cause identified.
  • Watchful waiting if stable & diagnosis elusive — many resolve spontaneously.

Clinical Pearl

The most important rule in FUO: repeat the history & examination — repeatedly. New findings emerge over days–weeks (e.g., new murmur of endocarditis, lymphadenopathy of lymphoma, temporal artery tenderness of GCA). In Indian FUO, the three most common final diagnoses are: tuberculosis (especially extrapulmonary / miliary), enteric fever, and lymphoma — workup should focus on these. Always get an FDG-PET/CT early — it is the most useful second-line test in modern FUO workup, with sensitivity 80–90% for occult malignancy, vasculitis, and focal infection. Empirical therapy with antitubercular therapy (ATT) or steroids should be reserved for last resort — only after all diagnostic avenues exhausted or patient deteriorating. In older patients (>65 yr), giant cell arteritis / polymyalgia rheumatica should always be considered — they are easily missed and respond dramatically to low-dose steroids (with temporal artery biopsy confirmation if possible). Never give empirical steroids without excluding infection — particularly TB and fungal infections which flare catastrophically. Finally, up to 25% of FUO remains undiagnosed despite extensive workup; in such patients, prognosis is generally good (~50% resolve spontaneously without sequelae).

Introduction

Escherichia coli is a Gram-negative, facultatively anaerobic, lactose-fermenting bacillus of the family Enterobacteriaceae — a normal commensal of the human gut. However, certain strains acquire virulence genes (plasmid-encoded, bacteriophage-encoded, or pathogenicity islands) that enable them to cause intestinal disease. Based on their virulence factors, clinical presentation, and pathogenic mechanism, diarrheagenic E. coli are classified into six major pathotypes.

The Six Pathotypes

Pathotype Mechanism Clinical features Key virulence factors
ETEC — Enterotoxigenic E. coli Non-invasive; adheres to small bowel via CFAs; produces enterotoxins → secretory diarrhoea Traveller's diarrhoea (50–80%); watery, afebrile, no blood; self-limiting in 3–5 days; severe in infants in developing countries (dehydration) Heat-labile toxin (LT) — cholera-like AB toxin → ADP-ribosylates Gsα → ↑cAMP → Cl⁻ & water secretion
Heat-stable toxin (STa) — activates guanylate cyclase → ↑cGMP → Cl⁻ secretion
Colonisation factor antigens (CFAs — CFA/I–IV)
EPEC — Enteropathogenic E. coli Adherent to small bowel enterocytes; produces "attaching & effacing" (A/E) lesion; microvillus destruction Infantile diarrhoea in developing countries — acute watery diarrhoea, vomiting, low-grade fever; severe & prolonged; major cause of infant mortality Bundle-forming pilus (Bfp) — initial attachment
Tir (translocated intimin receptor) — injected by T3SS
Intimin (eae gene) — tight adherence; A/E lesion
Locus of enterocyte effacement (LEE pathogenicity island)
EHEC / STEC — Enterohaemorrhagic / Shiga toxin-producing E. coli Adherent to colon (A/E lesion like EPEC); produces Shiga toxin (Stx1, Stx2) — inhibits 60S ribosomal subunit → cell death Haemorrhagic colitis — bloody diarrhoea with abdominal cramps, no fever (afebrile); <10% develop haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS) — triad of microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, AKI (especially children <5 yr); serotype O157:H7 most common Shiga toxins (Stx1, Stx2) — encoded by lysogenic bacteriophage
Intimin (eae)
Plasmid-encoded enterohaemolysin (EhxA)
EIEC — Enteroinvasive E. coli Invasive — invades & multiplies within colonic epithelial cells → cell death → mucosal ulceration; resembles Shigella biochemically & antigenically Bacillary dysentery-like illness — bloody mucoid diarrhoea with fever, tenesmus, abdominal cramps; less severe than shigellosis 140 MDa virulence plasmid (pINV) — encodes T3SS
ipaBCD (invasion plasmid antigens) — invasion & cell-to-cell spread
icsA (VirG) — actin-based intracellular motility
Non-motile (no H antigen); late/ non-lactose fermenter
EAEC — Enteroaggregative E. coli Adheres to small & large bowel mucosa in "stacked-brick" aggregative pattern; produces toxins; biofilm formation Persistent paediatric diarrhoea in developing countries (≥14 days); also traveller's diarrhoea; associated with HIV; cause of Shiga-toxin-producing EAEC outbreak in Germany 2011 (O104:H4 — HUS) Aggregative adherence fimbriae (AAF/I–V)
PET (plasmid-encoded toxin) — enterotoxin
EAST1 (enteroaggregative heat-stable toxin 1)
AggR — master transcription regulator
SepA, Pic proteins
DAEC — Diffusely adherent E. coli Diffuse adherence to HEp-2 cells; Afa/Dr family of adhesins; induces finger-like projections (elongation) Watery diarrhoea in children >1 yr; UTI (uro-pathogenic strain); recently associated with Crohn's disease Afa/Dr adhesins — bind decay-accelerating factor (DAF, CD55)
Diffuse adherence phenotype

Detailed Pathophysiology of Each Pathotype

1. ETEC — Enterotoxigenic E. coli

  • Adhesion — CFAs bind small intestinal enterocyte receptors.
  • LT (Heat-labile toxin) — AB₅ toxin similar to cholera toxin; B subunit binds GM1 ganglioside → A subunit ADP-ribosylates Gsα → ↑adenylate cyclase → ↑cAMP → PKA phosphorylates CFTR → Cl⁻ secretion + inhibits NaCl absorption → secretory watery diarrhoea.
  • STa (Heat-stable toxin) — binds guanylate cyclase C receptor → ↑cGMP → PKG phosphorylates CFTR → Cl⁻ & water secretion. (STb — pig pathogen).
  • Diagnosis — PCR (LT, ST genes), bioassay (rabbit ileal loop, Y-1 adrenal cell, CHO cell, infant mouse assay); culture on MacConkey (lactose fermenter); sorbitol-MacConkey.
  • Treatment — ORS, antibiotics (rarely needed in adults; doxycycline, ciprofloxacin, azithromycin); prevention — hygiene, ETEC vaccine (ETEC + cholera B subunit).

2. EPEC — Enteropathogenic E. coli

  • A/E lesion — bundle-forming pilus (BfpA) mediates initial attachment → T3SS injects Tir into enterocyte → Tir inserts into membrane → binds intimin (encoded by eae in LEE island) → tight attachment → actin polymerisation (pedestal) → microvillus effacement → malabsorption & tight junction disruption.
  • Classical — infantile diarrhoea ( outbreaks in nurseries); atypical EPEC lacks EAF plasmid but retains eae.

3. EHEC / STEC — Enterohaemorrhagic E. coli

  • Serotype O157:H7 — most common in US/Europe; non-sorbitol-fermenting (distinguishable on SMAC — sorbitol-MacConkey agar).
  • Source — undercooked beef (esp. ground beef), unpasteurised milk, contaminated water, leafy greens (spinach, lettuce), petting zoos.
  • Shiga toxin (Stx1, Stx2) — encoded by lambda-like bacteriophage; AB₅ toxin — B subunit binds globotriaosylceramide (Gb3) on endothelial cells (especially renal glomerulus, colon) → A subunit cleaves 28S rRNA → inhibits protein synthesis → cell death. Stx2 is more associated with HUS.
  • HUS — Stx damages renal glomerular endothelium → microthrombi → MAHA + thrombocytopenia + AKI. Triad: microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (schistocytes), thrombocytopenia, AKI.
  • Diagnosis — SMAC agar (non-sorbitol fermenter), latex agglutination for O157, PCR for stx1/stx2 + eae, serotyping for non-O157 STEC (Top 6: O26, O45, O103, O111, O121, O145).
  • Treatment — supportive; avoid antibiotics (especially fluoroquinolones, TMP-SMX — increase Stx release via phage induction → ↑HUS risk); avoid antimotility agents; eculizumab (anti-C5) for complement-mediated aHUS; dialysis for AKI; blood transfusion.

4. EIEC — Enteroinvasive E. coli

  • Biochemically similar to Shigella — non-motile, late/ non-lactose fermenter.
  • Invades colonic epithelial cells via M cells → escapes phagosome → multiplies in cytoplasm → spreads cell-to-cell via actin polymerisation (icsA/VirG) → mucosal ulceration → dysentery.
  • Sereny test — keratoconjunctivitis in guinea pig (invasiveness).
  • Treatment — fluoroquinolones, azithromycin; self-limiting in most.

5. EAEC — Enteroaggregative E. coli

  • Stacked-brick aggregative adherence to HEp-2 cells.
  • Biofilm formation; release of enterotoxins (EAST1, PET) → mucosal damage → persistent watery diarrhoea with mucus.
  • Germany 2011 outbreak — Shiga-toxin-producing EAEC O104:H4 — caused >4000 cases of HUS/death; sprouts as source.

6. DAEC — Diffusely adherent E. coli

  • Afa/Dr adhesins bind DAF (CD55) on enterocytes → elongation of microvilli.
  • Cause watery diarrhoea in children >12 months; sometimes UTI.

Laboratory Diagnosis

  • Culture — MacConkey (lactose fermenter); SMAC for O157 STEC; chromogenic agar (CHROMagar STEC).
  • Biochemical identification — TSI (A/A, gas +), IMViC (++--); Urease negative; motile (except EIEC).
  • Serotyping — O (somatic), H (flagellar), K (capsular) antigens.
  • Molecular — multiplex PCR for pathotype-specific genes (lt, st for ETEC; eae, bfpA for EPEC; stx1, stx2, eae for EHEC; ipaH, ial for EIEC; aggR, aaiC for EAEC; daaE, afa for DAEC); whole genome sequencing.
  • HEp-2 adherence assay — gold standard for EPEC (localized), EAEC (aggregative), DAEC (diffuse).
  • Bioassays — rabbit ileal loop (LT — fluid accumulation); Y-1 adrenal cell (LT — rounding); infant mouse (ST — fluid / weight ratio); Sereny test (EIEC — keratoconjunctivitis); Vero cell cytotoxicity (Stx).

Clinical Pearl

The most important clinical rule for diarrheagenic E. coli is DO NOT give antibiotics or antimotility agents in suspected EHEC/STEC (especially O157:H7) — both increase Shiga toxin release (antibiotics induce phage lysis → Stx release) and HUS risk. Antimotility agents (loperamide) prolong gut transit → more toxin absorption. Suspect EHEC in any patient with bloody diarrhoea without fever (afebrile is key — distinguishes from invasive causes like Shigella, Campylobacter, Salmonella which cause fever). The 2011 German outbreak of O104:H4 EAEC that acquired Stx2 gene — was initially mistaken for EHEC but was actually an enteroaggregative strain that had lysogenised the Stx2 phage — causing >4000 cases and 50 deaths; fenugreek sprouts were the source. For laboratory diagnosis, request PCR for pathotype-specific genes when clinical suspicion is high — culture alone cannot differentiate pathotypes from commensal E. coli. For traveller's diarrhoea (ETEC), self-treatment with azithromycin or rifaximin for 3 days is effective; ORS remains mainstay. For infantile EPEC in developing countries, exclusive breastfeeding (IgA protection) is the single best preventive measure.

Introduction

Both amoebic dysentery (caused by Entamoeba histolytica) and bacillary dysentery (caused by Shigella spp.) present with bloody mucoid diarrhoea, abdominal cramps, and tenesmus — but they differ significantly in pathogenesis, clinical features, stool examination, complications, and treatment. Differentiating them is critical for appropriate therapy.

Comparison Table

VaccineNoneNone widely available; candidate vaccines in trials

Clinical Pearl

The most reliable bedside discriminator between amoebic and bacillary dysentery is the stool microscopy: in amoebic dysentery, you see trophozoites of E. histolytica with ingested RBCs (pathognomonic) and clumped RBCs with few pus cells; in bacillary dysentery, you see sheets of pus cells with discrete RBCs and no parasite. The "anchovy sauce" appearance of stool is classic for amoebic — but the single best test for an amoebic liver abscess is abdominal ultrasound (single, hypoechoic lesion in right lobe of liver) combined with serology (E. histolytica-specific antigen or antibody — TechLab ELISA) — stool examination is often negative in liver abscess because trophozoites have invaded beyond the gut. Remember the geographic patterns: in India, both amoebic and bacillary dysentery are common — but amoebic liver abscess is the most common extra-intestinal complication in adult men (alcoholism is a risk factor). For bacillary dysentery, S. flexneri is the dominant serogroup in India, but S. dysenteriae type 1 causes epidemic bacillary dysentery with high mortality (especially from Shiga toxin-induced HUS). Always avoid antimotility agents (loperamide) in either condition — they prolong pathogen contact with mucosa and worsen outcome (especially HUS risk in S. dysenteriae type 1).
