Introduction

IgG is the most abundant serum immunoglobulin (75–80% of total Ig; 8–16 mg/mL), the principal antibody of the secondary immune response, and the only Ig that crosses the placenta.

Structure

  • Y-shaped monomer, 150 kDa — 2 heavy (γ) chains + 2 light (κ or λ) chains linked by disulfide bonds.
  • Heavy chain (γ) — 4 domains: VH + Cγ1, Cγ2, Cγ3; lacks hinge between Cγ2 & Cγ3.
  • Hinge region — flexible proline-rich segment between Cγ1 & Cγ2; allows Fab arms to open & bind epitopes at variable distances; susceptible to papain & pepsin.
  • Enzymatic cleavage
    • Papain → 2 Fab (antigen-binding, monovalent) + 1 Fc (effector functions).
    • Pepsin → 1 F(ab')₂ (bivalent) + small pFc' fragments.
  • Fab — VH + VL; contains paratope (CDR1–3) that binds epitope.
  • Fc — Cγ2 + Cγ3; mediates complement activation (C1q binds Cγ2) & Fcγ receptor binding (Cγ3).
  • Subclasses (4) — IgG1 (66%), IgG2 (23%, polysaccharide antigens — encapsulated bacteria), IgG3 (7%, strongest complement), IgG4 (4%, chronic antigen exposure, IgG4-related disease).
  • Half-life — 21 days (longest of all Igs; due to FcRn-mediated recycling).

Functions

  1. Neutralisation — blocks viral/bacterial attachment & toxin action.
  2. Opsonisation — Fc binds FcγRI (CD64) on phagocytes → enhanced phagocytosis.
  3. Complement activation (classical pathway) — C1q binds Fc of adjacent IgG molecules → C3b → MAC lysis.
  4. ADCC — FcγRIII (CD16) on NK cells binds Fc of IgG-coated target → perforin/granzyme-mediated killing.
  5. Transplacental transfer — FcRn (neonatal Fc receptor) in placental syncytiotrophoblast actively transports IgG to fetal circulation; provides passive immunity to neonate for first 6 months.
  6. Half-life extension — FcRn in endothelial cells recycles IgG, protecting from lysosomal degradation.
  7. Immune complex clearance — IgG-antigen complexes bind RBC CR1; transported to liver/spleen.
  8. Feedback inhibition — IgG-antigen complex binds FcγRIIb on B cells → inhibits further B-cell activation.

Clinical Significance

  • Maternal IgG protects neonate for 6 months.
  • Used as therapeutic IVIG for immunodeficiency, ITP, Guillain-Barré, Kawasaki.
  • IgG2 subclass deficiency — recurrent sinopulmonary infection with encapsulated bacteria.
  • IgG4-related disease — autoimmune pancreatitis, Mikulicz syndrome, Riedel thyroiditis.
  • Most therapeutic monoclonal antibodies are IgG1 or IgG4 (trastuzumab, rituximab, infliximab).

Clinical Pearl

IgG is the only immunoglobulin that crosses the placenta — mediated by FcRn (Brambell receptor). This explains why maternal IgG anti-D (Rh) causes haemolytic disease of the newborn — maternal anti-Rh IgG crosses to fetal circulation and destroys Rh+ fetal RBCs. The same mechanism is exploited therapeutically: anti-D immunoglobulin (RhoGAM) given to Rh-negative mothers at 28 weeks & within 72 h of delivery clears fetal Rh+ cells before maternal B cells are sensitised. Because IgG has the longest half-life (21 d), it is the basis for monoclonal antibody therapy and IVIG replacement therapy (400–600 mg/kg every 3–4 weeks).
q1_0_2_15:
Definition

Enriched media are culture media supplemented with additional nutrients (blood, serum, egg, yeast extract, haemin, vitamin K, growth factors) to support the growth of fastidious microorganisms — bacteria or fungi that require complex growth factors and cannot grow on simple media like nutrient agar.

Fastidious organisms need:

  • Vitamins — NAD (V factor), hemin (X factor), vitamin K, vitamin B12, folate.
  • Amino acids, nucleotides.
  • Blood — for haemin, iron, growth factors.
  • CO₂ (capnophiles — Streptococcus, Neisseria gonorrhoeae).
  • Serum proteins, lipids.

Examples (2 detailed)

1. Blood Agar

  • Composition — nutrient agar base (peptone, beef extract, NaCl, agar, water, pH 7.4) + 5–10% defibrinated sheep/horse blood.
  • Why enriched — provides X factor (hemin), V factor (NAD — partially), iron, amino acids, vitamins; supports growth of fastidious organisms — Streptococcus, Staphylococcus, Neisseria, Corynebacterium, Listeria, enterococci, pneumococci.
  • Preparation — autoclave base; cool to 45–50 °C; add sterile defibrinated blood; pour plates.
  • Haemolysis patterns
    • α-haemolysis — partial; greenish discolouration (methaemoglobin) — S. pneumoniae, viridans strep.
    • β-haemolysis — complete; clear zone — S. pyogenes, S. agalactiae, S. aureus.
    • γ-haemolysis — no change — Enterococcus, CoNS.
  • Special tests — Optochin (S. pneumoniae), Bacitracin (S. pyogenes), CAMP (S. agalactiae), Satellitism (Haemophilus).

2. Chocolate Agar

  • Composition — blood agar heated to 70–80 °C until colour changes to brown ("chocolate"). Heating lyses RBCs, releasing intracellular X (hemin) & V factor (NAD — normally intracellular in RBCs).
  • Why enriched — supports growth of more fastidious organisms than blood agar; especially those needing both X & V factors.
  • Organisms that grow on chocolate agar but NOT blood agar
    • Haemophilus influenzae (requires X + V).
    • Neisseria gonorrhoeae & N. meningitidis (require V factor; capnophilic — 5% CO₂).
    • Moraxella catarrhalis.
  • Uses — sputum (H. influenzae); urethral/cervical swab (N. gonorrhoeae — Thayer-Martin selective); CSF (meningitis); eye swab (H. aegyptius).
  • Variants — Thayer-Martin (chocolate + vancomycin + colistin + nystatin — selective for pathogenic Neisseria); NYC medium; Martin-Lewis; GC-Lect.

Other Enriched Media (brief)

  • Loeffler's serum slope — serum + egg + glucose — for Corynebacterium diphtheriae.
  • Lowenstein-Jensen — egg + malachite green + glycerol — for M. tuberculosis.
  • Todd-Hewitt broth — for Streptococcus.
  • Trypticase soy agar (TSA) / Brain heart infusion (BHI) — general-purpose enriched.
  • Cooked meat broth (Robertson's) — enriched + anaerobic — for Clostridium.
  • Fildes medium — peptic digest of blood — for H. influenzae.

Difference from Related Media

Type Function Example
Simple / basalSupports non-fastidious organismsNutrient agar, peptone water
EnrichedSupplemented to grow fastidiousBlood agar, chocolate agar
Enrichment brothSelective for pathogen (inhibits competitors)Selenite F (Salmonella), Alkaline peptone water (Vibrio)
SelectiveAntibiotics inhibit some, favour othersMacConkey, TCBS, LJ
DifferentialDistinguishes by colour/morphologyMacConkey (LF/NLF), Blood agar (haemolysis)

Clinical Pearl

The single most important practical lesson: chocolate agar is needed for suspected Haemophilus influenzae and Neisseria infections — these organisms will not grow on blood agar because they require V factor (NAD) which is intracellular in RBCs and only released when blood is heated. For a febrile child with meningitis, always plate CSF on both blood agar & chocolate agar (in 5% CO₂). For suspected gonorrhoea, use Thayer-Martin selective chocolate agar — non-selective chocolate agar will be overgrown by normal flora.
q1_0_2_16:
Definition

Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) — invented by Kary Mullis (1983; Nobel Prize 1993) — is an in vitro enzymatic method for exponential amplification of a specific DNA sequence by repeated cycles of denaturation, primer annealing, and extension, using a thermostable DNA polymerase (Taq polymerase from Thermus aquaticus).

Principle — Three-Step Cycle

  1. Denaturation — heat to 94–95 °C for 30 sec → separates double-stranded DNA into single strands.
  2. Annealing — cool to 50–65 °C for 30 sec → sequence-specific primers (forward & reverse) bind (hybridise) to complementary sequences flanking the target.
  3. Extension — heat to 72 °C for 1 min → Taq polymerase extends primers, synthesising new DNA strand complementary to template, using free dNTPs.

Each cycle doubles the target DNA; 30 cycles produce ~10⁹ copies (2³⁰) from a single template.

Components

  • Template DNA (sample — blood, tissue, CSF, sputum).
  • Sequence-specific primers (forward + reverse, 20–30 bp).
  • Thermostable DNA polymerase (Taq, Pfu, Tth — has 5'→3' polymerase activity; lacks 3'→5' exonuclease proofreading in Taq).
  • dNTPs (dATP, dTTP, dGTP, dCTP).
  • Mg²⁺ (cofactor).
  • Buffer (Tris-HCl, KCl, pH 8.3).

Types of PCR

1. Conventional / End-point PCR

  • Detects product at end of cycling by gel electrophoresis (agarose + ethidium bromide).
  • Qualitative (presence/absence).
  • Limit — cannot quantify; contamination risk; post-PCR processing.

2. Real-time / Quantitative PCR (qPCR)

  • Monitors amplification in real-time using fluorescent dyes or probes.
  • SybR Green — binds dsDNA; non-specific.
  • TaqMan probe — sequence-specific; hydrolysis probe with fluorescent reporter & quencher; fluorescence emitted when probe cleaved.
  • FRET probes (HybProbe) — two probes; fluorescence resonance energy transfer.
  • Molecular beacons — hairpin probes.
  • Quantitative — Ct (cycle threshold) value; lower Ct = higher initial template.
  • Faster; closed-tube (low contamination); quantitative; sensitive.

3. Reverse Transcription PCR (RT-PCR)

  • For RNA targets — first convert RNA to cDNA using reverse transcriptase (MMLV, AMV); then PCR amplify.
  • Used for RNA viruses — HIV, HCV, influenza, SARS-CoV-2, dengue; mRNA expression studies.

4. Multiplex PCR

  • Multiple primer pairs in one reaction → amplifies multiple targets simultaneously.
  • Examples — respiratory virus panel (BioFire FilmArray — 20+ pathogens); STI panel (CT/NG/MG/TV); meningitis/encephalitis panel; gastrointestinal panel.

5. Nested PCR

  • Two rounds of PCR — outer primers, then inner (nested) primers; increased sensitivity & specificity.
  • Used for low-copy targets — HIV proviral DNA, Toxoplasma in CSF.
  • Limit — high contamination risk.

6. Reverse Line Blot / PCR-RFLP

  • PCR + restriction enzyme digestion + electrophoresis — detects mutations; HLA typing; HPV genotyping.

7. Loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP)

  • Isothermal (60–65 °C, no thermal cycler); uses Bst polymerase with strand displacement activity; 4–6 primers.
  • Field-deployable; result in 30–60 min; readout by turbidity, fluorescence, or colour change.
  • Used for TB (TB-LAMP), malaria, COVID-19, dengue.

8. Digital PCR (dPCR / ddPCR)

  • Sample partitioned into thousands of droplets; PCR in each; counts positive partitions.
  • Absolute quantification without standard curve; high precision.
  • Used for rare allele detection, copy number variation, liquid biopsy (circulating tumour DNA).

9. Other Types

  • Hot-start PCR — polymerase activated only at high temperature; reduces non-specific amplification.
  • Touchdown PCR — annealing temperature decreases over cycles; increases specificity.
  • Asymmetric PCR — generates single-stranded DNA (sequencing probes).
  • Colony PCR — directly from bacterial colony.
  • Quantitative RT-PCR (RT-qPCR) — RT-PCR + qPCR; quantifies RNA expression; gold standard for SARS-CoV-2 viral load.
  • Whole Genome Amplification (MDA, WGA) — for single-cell genomics.

Diagnostic Applications

Field Examples
Infectious diseaseTB (CBNAAT/Xpert MTB-RIF — detects rifampicin resistance); HIV (viral load, infant diagnosis); HCV (viral load, genotyping); HBV (viral load); SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR; dengue; influenza; HSV encephalitis (CSF); CMV; EBV; malaria; leishmaniasis; Toxoplasma; syphilis (PCR of lesion); gonorrhoea/chlamydia; pertussis; Mycoplasma
GeneticsHLA typing; triplet repeat disorders (Huntington, fragile X); sickle cell (HbS); thalassaemia mutations; cystic fibrosis; Duchenne; breast cancer (BRCA1/2); pharmacogenomics (CYP2D6, CYP2C19, HLA-B*5701)
OncologyBCR-ABL (CML); PML-RARA (APL); JAK2 V617F (MPN); BRAF V600E (melanoma); KRAS (colon cancer); EGFR (lung cancer); HER2; liquid biopsy (ctDNA)
ForensicDNA fingerprinting (STR profiling); paternity testing; identification of remains; crime scene analysis
Antibiotic resistancemecA (MRSA); vanA/B (VRE); blaCTX-M (ESBL); blaKPC, blaNDM, blaOXA-48 (CRE); rpoB (rifampin resistance in TB); katG/inhA (isoniazid); gyrA (fluoroquinolone)
Food & waterDetection of Salmonella, E. coli O157, Listeria, GMO screening

Advantages

  • High sensitivity (detects <10 copies); high specificity.
  • Rapid (2–4 h); can be automated.
  • Can detect non-cultivable or fastidious organisms.
  • Can detect antimicrobial resistance genes.
  • Quantitative (qPCR).

Limitations

  • Cannot distinguish live vs dead organisms (detects DNA from both).
  • Contamination risk (carryover from previous amplifications).
  • Inhibitors in sample (haemoglobin, heparin).
  • Requires expensive equipment & trained personnel.
  • False positives due to contamination; false negatives due to inhibitors or mutations in primer binding sites.

Clinical Pearl

The most widely used PCR in Indian clinical microbiology is CBNAAT (Cartridge-Based Nucleic Acid Amplification Test) — Xpert MTB/RIF (Cepheid) — detects M. tuberculosis DNA & rifampicin resistance (rpoB gene mutations) in 2 hours from sputum. This revolutionised TB diagnosis — replaced sputum smear microscopy (sensitivity 50–60%) with sensitivity 90%+ and simultaneous drug resistance detection. The COVID-19 pandemic made RT-PCR a household term — it remains the gold standard for SARS-CoV-2 diagnosis (E, N, RdRp genes; Orf1a/b). For HCV, HCV RNA PCR is the test of cure — target undetectable at 12 weeks post-treatment (SVR12). HIV-1 DNA PCR on dried blood spot is the test of choice for infant diagnosis (maternal IgG confounds antibody tests until 18 months). The future is point-of-care multiplex PCR panels — BioFire FilmArray respiratory panel (20+ pathogens in 1 hour), gastrointestinal panel (22 pathogens), meningitis/encephalitis panel (14 pathogens) — these transform clinical decision-making at the bedside.
q1_0_2_17:
Introduction

Anaerobic bacteria require reduced oxygen tension (or absence of O₂) for growth — they cannot grow in 21% O₂ (atmospheric). Important human pathogens include Clostridium spp. (C. perfringens, C. tetani, C. botulinum, C. difficile), Bacteroides fragilis, Prevotella, Fusobacterium, Peptostreptococcus, Actinomyces, Propionibacterium acnes.

Methods of Anaerobic Culture

1. Anaerobic Jar (McIntosh & Filde's jar) — Most commonly used

  • Principle — H₂ + O₂ → H₂O (catalysed by palladium catalyst) removes O₂ from sealed jar.
  • Procedure
    1. Inoculated plates placed inside jar.
    2. Place gas-generating sachet (GasPak — sodium borohydride + citric acid + cobalt chloride; produces H₂ & CO₂ on adding water).
    3. Palladium catalyst (in lid) catalyses H₂ + O₂ → H₂O.
    4. Seal jar; incubate at 37 °C for 48 h.
    5. Methylene blue indicator strip (blue in O₂, colourless in anaerobic) confirms anaerobiosis.
  • Indicators
    • Methylene blue — blue (oxidised, O₂ present) → colourless (reduced, anaerobic).
    • Resazurin — pink (O₂) → colourless.
  • Limit — does not achieve strict anaerobiosis (some O₂ remains).

2. Anaerobic Chamber / Glove Box (Coy, Whitley)

  • Largest & most sophisticated method — sealed chamber filled with gas mixture (N₂ 85%, H₂ 5%, CO₂ 10%); operator handles cultures through gloves.
  • Strictest anaerobiosis; allows processing of specimens & subculture without O₂ exposure.
  • Expensive; needs continuous gas supply.

3. Anaerobic Bags / Pouches (GasPak EZ)

  • Single-plate system — plate + gas-generating sachet sealed in transparent pouch.
  • Convenient for small labs; no jar needed; individual plate incubation.
  • Result read directly without opening.

4. Robertson's Cooked Meat (RCM) Broth

  • Liquid medium containing minced cooked meat (beef heart) — provides nutrients, reducing agents (sulphydryl groups in cysteine, glutathione), anaerobic environment at the bottom.
  • Meat particles act as reducing agents (maintain low Eh).
  • For Clostridium — gas production, "stormy fermentation" in milk (C. perfringens); digestion of meat particles (proteolytic species).
  • Useful for recovery from blood cultures & wound swabs.

5. Thioglycollate Broth (Brewer's)

  • Sodium thioglycollate — reducing agent (lowers Eh); maintains anaerobic conditions at the bottom of tube.
  • Methylene blue indicator — pink at top (O₂), colourless at bottom.
  • Used for sterility testing of biological products; blood culture.

6. Brain Heart Infusion (BHI) with Vitamin K & Hemin

  • Enriched broth for fastidious anaerobes.
  • Used in automated blood culture systems (BACTEC, BacT/ALERT) with anaerobic bottles.

7. PRAS (Pre-Reduced Anaerobically Sterilised) Media

  • Media prepared, poured, sterilised, and stored under anaerobic conditions throughout — never exposed to O₂.
  • Roll tubes (Hungate tubes) — agar slants in tubes flushed with O₂-free gas.
  • For fastidious anaerobes (Bacteroides, Fusobacterium).

8. Special Media for Anaerobes

  • Brucella blood agar — enriched with vitamin K, hemin; for Bacteroides, Prevotella.
  • Bacteroides bile esculin agar (BBE) — selective for B. fragilis group (bile-tolerant, esculin hydrolysis).
  • Kanamycin-vancomycin laked blood agar (KVLB) — selective for Prevotella, Bacteroides.
  • Egg yolk agar (Nagler) — for Clostridium perfringens (lecithinase positive — opacity around colonies; inhibited by anti-α-toxin = positive Nagler reaction).
  • Cycloserine-cefoxitin-fructose agar (CCFA) — selective for C. difficile.
  • TPYG agar — Trypticase phytone yeast extract glucose.

9. Automated Anaerobic Blood Culture Systems

  • BACTEC (BD), BacT/ALERT (bioMérieux) — continuous monitoring; anaerobic bottles with reducing agents; alarm when CO₂ produced by growth detected.

Specimen Collection for Anaerobes

  • Avoid contamination with normal flora — collect from sites normally sterile.
  • Use aspirate (syringe) rather than swab where possible — aspirate in anaerobic transport tube.
  • Transport media — Stuart's, Cary-Blair, Amies; or PRAS tubes.
  • Rapid transport to lab (<2 h); refrigeration kills some anaerobes.
  • Sites acceptable — deep wound aspirate, blood, CSF, pleural fluid, peritoneal fluid, deep abscess, tissue biopsy, transtracheal aspirate.
  • Sites NOT acceptable (contaminated with normal flora) — throat, sputum (unless bronchial wash), stool (except C. difficile), vaginal swab (except culdocentesis), urethra, superficial wound.

Identification

  • Gram stain morphology — Gram-positive bacilli (Clostridium, Actinomyces, Propionibacterium); Gram-negative bacilli (Bacteroides, Prevotella, Fusobacterium); Gram-positive cocci (Peptostreptococcus); Gram-negative cocci (Veillonella).
  • Colonial morphology, pigment production (Prevotella melaninogenica — black colonies), haemolysis, fluorescence under UV (B. fragilis — red; Prevotella — brick-red).
  • Biochemical tests — catalase, indole, nitrate, bile tolerance, sugar fermentation.
  • MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry — rapid identification (minutes).
  • 16S rRNA gene sequencing — gold standard for difficult identifications.
  • Molecular tests — PCR for toxin genes (C. perfringens alpha toxin; C. difficile toxin A/B; C. botulinum neurotoxin A/B/E/F; C. tetani tetanospasmin).

Clinical Pearl

The single most important clinical clue to anaerobic infection is foul-smelling (fetid) pus — caused by volatile short-chain fatty acids produced by anaerobic metabolism. Other clues — gas in tissue (gas gangrene — C. perfringens), tissue necrosis, location near mucosal surfaces (oral, GI, GU tract infections), infection after bite wounds (Bacteroides, Fusobacterium, Prevotella + Pasteurella), aspiration pneumonia (Bacteroides, Peptostreptococcus, Fusobacterium), intra-abdominal abscess (B. fragilis), pelvic inflammatory disease (Bacteroides, Prevotella), brain abscess (Peptostreptococcus, Bacteroides, Fusobacterium), infected diabetic foot ulcer (polymicrobial with anaerobes). Always suspect anaerobes when: (1) foul smell, (2) gas in tissue, (3) necrosis, (4) failure to grow on aerobic culture with pus on Gram stain, (5) infection near mucosa, (6) bite wound, (7) post-abdominal/pelvic surgery. Empirical antibiotics covering anaerobes — metronidazole (drug of choice for Bacteroides, Clostridium); clindamycin (anaerobic cocci, Actinomyces); carbapenems (imipenem, meropenem); β-lactam + β-lactamase inhibitor (ampicillin-sulbactam, piperacillin-tazobactam); moxifloxacin; tigecycline. C. difficile requires oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin (not metronidazole first-line anymore per 2021 IDSA guidelines).

Definition

Mutation is a stable, heritable change in the nucleotide sequence of the genome. It can occur spontaneously (errors in DNA replication, tautomeric shifts, deamination, depurination) or be induced by mutagens (physical — UV, X-ray; chemical — nitrous acid, alkylating agents, base analogues; biological — transposons, viral integration). Rate: ~10⁻⁶ to 10⁻¹⁰ per gene per generation in bacteria.

Types of Mutation

1. Point Mutation — Single nucleotide change

  • Transition — purine → purine (A↔G) or pyrimidine → pyrimidine (C↔T). Most common (70%).
  • Transversion — purine → pyrimidine or vice versa (A↔C, A↔T, G↔C, G↔T). Less common.

By Functional Consequence

  • Silent (synonymous) — codon changes but encodes same amino acid (codon degeneracy); no phenotypic change.
  • Missense — codon changes to encode different amino acid. Conservative (similar aa — mild) or non-conservative (dissimilar — severe). Example — HbS (sickle cell): Glu→Val at position 6 of β-globin (GAG→GTG transversion).
  • Nonsense — codon changes to a stop codon (UAA, UAG, UGA) → premature termination → truncated, usually non-functional protein. Example — Duchenne muscular dystrophy (dystrophin truncation).
  • Stop-loss — stop codon → sense codon → elongated protein.

2. Frameshift Mutation

  • Insertion or deletion of nucleotides in a number not divisible by 3 → shifts reading frame → different amino acid sequence downstream → premature stop codon → non-functional protein.
  • Example — Tay-Sachs disease (HEXA 4-bp insertion); Hb Wayne.

3. Insertion / Deletion (InDel)

  • Small (1–1000 bp) — frameshift if not multiple of 3.
  • Large — deletion of entire gene/exon. Example — α-thalassaemia (--SEA deletion); Duchenne (dystrophin exon deletion).

4. Dynamic / Expansion Mutation (Trinucleotide Repeat)

Expansion of unstable trinucleotide repeat beyond threshold during meiosis — causes anticipation. Examples:

  • Huntington disease — CAG in HTT (≥36 repeats).
  • Fragile X — CGG in FMR1 (>200 repeats).
  • Myotonic dystrophy — CTG in DMPK (>50 repeats).
  • Friedreich ataxia — GAA in FXN (>66 repeats).
  • Spinocerebellar ataxias — CAG in various genes.

5. Copy Number Variation (CNV)

  • Duplication or deletion of large segments (>1 kb). Examples — Hb Lepore (δβ fusion); CMT1A (PMP22 duplication).

6. Chromosomal Mutations

  • Numerical — aneuploidy (trisomy 21 Down, 18 Edward, 13 Patau, XXY Klinefelter, X Turner); polyploidy (lethal in humans).
  • Structural
    • Deletion (5p- Cri-du-chat, 22q11.2 DiGeorge).
    • Duplication.
    • Inversion (Factor VIII intron 22 inversion in Haemophilia A).
    • Translocation — Philadelphia t(9;22) in CML (BCR-ABL); t(14;18) follicular lymphoma (BCL2); t(8;14) Burkitt lymphoma (MYC).
    • Ring chromosome, isochromosome.

7. Conditional / Reversible

  • Suppressor mutation — second mutation restores phenotype.
  • Back mutation — reversion to wild-type.

By Effect on Phenotype

  • Loss-of-function — reduced/abolished activity; recessive (PKU, albinism).
  • Gain-of-function — new/enhanced activity; dominant (Huntington, achondroplasia FGFR3).
  • Dominant-negative — mutant interferes with wild-type (Marfan, p53).

By Origin

  • Germ-line — heritable (BRCA1 in familial breast cancer).
  • Somatic — not heritable; causes cancer (TP53 in lung cancer).

Clinical Significance

  1. Genetic diseases — sickle cell anaemia, thalassaemia, cystic fibrosis (ΔF508), Huntington, Duchenne, haemophilia A, phenylketonuria, Tay-Sachs, fragile X, hereditary cancer syndromes (BRCA1/2, Lynch, Li-Fraumeni).
  2. Cancer — somatic mutations drive oncogenesis (TP53, KRAS, EGFR, BRAF, BCR-ABL, MYC); guide targeted therapy (EGFR mutation → erlotinib; BCR-ABL → imatinib; BRAF V600E → vemurafenib; BRCA1/2 → PARP inhibitor olaparib).
  3. Pharmacogenomics — CYP2D6 polymorphisms affect codeine metabolism; HLA-B*5701 predisposes to abacavir hypersensitivity; TPMT variants affect thiopurine metabolism; G6PD deficiency — haemolysis with primaquine, sulfonamides, fava beans.
  4. Antibiotic resistance — mutations in rpoB (rifampicin resistance in TB), gyrA (fluoroquinolone resistance), katG & inhA (isoniazid), rpsL & rrs (streptomycin); HBV polymerase mutations (lamivudine, entecavir resistance); HIV reverse transcriptase & protease mutations.
  5. Forensic & paternity — DNA fingerprinting (STR profiling).
  6. Prenatal & carrier diagnosis — chorionic villus sampling, amniocentesis; preimplantation genetic diagnosis (PGD).
  7. Evolution & biodiversity — mutations are the raw material for natural selection.
  8. Immune diversity — V(D)J recombination in T & B cell receptors generates >10¹⁰ unique specificities.

Mutagens (Inducers)

  • Base analogues — 5-bromouracil, 2-aminopurine.
  • Alkylating agents — EMS, MNNG, nitrogen mustard.
  • Deaminating agents — nitrous acid (HNO₂) — converts adenine → hypoxanthine (pairs with C), cytosine → uracil.
  • Intercalating agents — acridine orange, proflavin, ethidium bromide — frameshift.
  • UV radiation — thymine dimers (cyclobutane pyrimidine dimer).
  • Ionising radiation — X-ray, gamma-ray — single & double-strand breaks.

DNA Repair Mechanisms

  • Direct repair — photolyase (bacteria); O⁶-methylguanine methyltransferase (MGMT).
  • Base excision repair (BER) — for deaminated/oxidised bases.
  • Nucleotide excision repair (NER) — for bulky lesions; defective in xeroderma pigmentosum.
  • Mismatch repair (MMR) — defective in Lynch syndrome (hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer).
  • Double-strand break repair — homologous recombination (BRCA1/2); non-homologous end joining (NHEJ).

Clinical Pearl

The Ames test uses his⁻ Salmonella typhimurium to detect mutagens — if a chemical induces reverse mutation to his⁺, the bacteria grow on histidine-free medium → mutagen identified. ~85% of known human carcinogens are mutagens in the Ames test. In clinical practice, the most useful application is targeted cancer therapy based on mutation profile: EGFR mutation in lung adenocarcinoma → erlotinib/gefitinib; BCR-ABL in CML → imatinib; BRAF V600E in melanoma → vemurafenib; BRCA1/2 in breast/ovarian cancer → PARP inhibitor (olaparib); KRAS G12C → sotorasib. Next-generation sequencing (NGS) of tumours is now standard of care. Hotspot mutations (KRAS codon 12, TP53 codon 248, BRAF V600) recur across cancer types because they occur in critical functional domains.

Definition

Antimicrobial stewardship is a coordinated set of interventions and strategies designed to optimise the use of antimicrobial agents — selecting the right drug, right dose, right route, right duration, and right indication — to maximise clinical cure while minimising adverse effects, toxicity, emergence of resistance, and healthcare costs. It is a core component of every healthcare facility's infection prevention & control (IPC) programme.

Goals / Aims

  • Optimise clinical outcomes — improved cure rates, reduced treatment failure, shorter length of stay.
  • Minimise unintended consequences — reduce antimicrobial resistance, Clostridioides difficile infection, adverse drug reactions, disruption of normal microbiome.
  • Reduce healthcare costs — minimise unnecessary or duplicate prescriptions; use cheaper equivalents when appropriate.
  • Preserve antimicrobial effectiveness for future use.

Core Elements of an Antimicrobial Stewardship Program (AMSP)

  1. Accountability — physician lead + pharmacist co-lead + microbiologist + infection control nurse.
  2. Drug expertise — clinical pharmacist.
  3. Key interventions
    • Pre-authorisation (restrictive) — certain antibiotics require approval before dispensing (e.g., meropenem, linezolid, colistin, tigecycline, echinocandins).
    • Prospective audit & feedback — review of ongoing therapy with recommendation to prescriber.
    • Formulary restriction — limited antibiotic availability.
    • Cycling & mixing — scheduled rotation to limit resistance.
    • Guidelines & care bundles — for empiric therapy of common infections (UTI, pneumonia, sepsis, SSI prophylaxis).
    • Dose optimisation — PK/PD-based dosing (extended infusion of β-lactams).
    • IV-to-oral conversion — switch when patient tolerates oral & clinically stable.
    • De-escalation — narrow spectrum once culture & sensitivity available.
    • Stop orders / automatic stop dates — review at 48–72 h and 5–7 days.
    • Duplicate therapy alerts — e.g., two drugs with overlapping spectra.
  4. Tracking & monitoring — antibiotic consumption (DDD/1000 patient-days); resistance patterns (antibiogram); C. difficile rates; clinical outcomes.
  5. Reporting — to prescribers, hospital administration, infection control committee.
  6. Education — regular training of medical, nursing, pharmacy staff.

Why AMSP Matters

  • Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) — >1.27 million deaths globally attributable to bacterial AMR in 2019 (Lancet); India has among the highest rates of multidrug-resistant organisms (MRSA, VRE, ESBL, CRE, CRAB, CRPA).
  • Misuse of antibiotics — ~50% of antibiotic prescriptions in hospitals are inappropriate (unnecessary, wrong drug, wrong dose, wrong duration).
  • Without effective antibiotics — chemotherapy, surgery, neonatal care, and transplantation become life-threatening.
  • WHO calls AMR one of the top 10 global public health threats.

Indian Context — ICMR AMSP

  • ICMR initiated AMSP network in 2017–2018; >150 hospitals enrolled.
  • Annual AMR surveillance reports — publish antibiograms.
  • "Red Line Campaign" — distinguishes prescription-only antibiotics (red line on packaging) from OTC.
  • National Action Plan on AMR (NAP-AMR, 2017–2021) — multi-sectoral "One Health" approach.

Clinical Pearl

The single most effective stewardship intervention is prospective audit & feedback — a pharmacist or ID physician reviews all antibiotic prescriptions after 48–72 h and recommends continuation, narrowing, switching to oral, or stopping. This reduces broad-spectrum antibiotic use by 20–30% without compromising outcomes. The second is pre-authorisation of last-resort antibiotics (carbapenems, colistin, linezolid, tigecycline) — approval by ID physician before dispensing. Always send cultures before starting antibiotics — this enables de-escalation from broad empiric to narrow targeted therapy within 48–72 h. The "Start Smart, Then Focus" approach (UK Department of Health) is the simplest bedside mnemonic — start with appropriate empiric therapy within 1 h of severe sepsis, then review at 48–72 h based on cultures and clinical response. Avoid antibiotics for viral upper respiratory infections — the single most common misuse of antibiotics in outpatient practice.

Definition

Cell-mediated immunity (CMI) is the arm of adaptive immunity mediated by T lymphocytes and other immune cells (rather than by antibodies). It defends against intracellular pathogens (viruses, intracellular bacteria — TB, Listeria, Salmonella; protozoa — Leishmania, Toxoplasma, Plasmodium; fungi — Candida, Histoplasma), malignant cells, and transplanted tissue. CMI is also responsible for Type IV (delayed-type) hypersensitivity.

Cells Involved in CMI

1. T Lymphocytes — Central

  • CD4+ Helper T cells — recognise antigen presented on MHC class II by professional APCs (dendritic cells, macrophages, B cells). Subsets:
    • Th1 — secrets IFN-γ, IL-2 — activates macrophages; defends against intracellular pathogens (TB, viruses); DTH. Transcription factor T-bet.
    • Th2 — secrets IL-4, IL-5, IL-13 — allergy, asthma, parasites; B cell help for IgE. GATA3.
    • Th17 — secrets IL-17, IL-22 — extracellular bacteria & fungi at mucosa; autoimmune inflammation. RORγt.
    • Tfh (follicular helper) — secrets IL-21 — germinal centre formation & B cell help. Bcl-6.
    • Treg (regulatory) — FoxP3+, IL-10, TGF-β — immune tolerance, suppresses effector T cells.
  • CD8+ Cytotoxic T Lymphocytes (CTLs) — recognise antigen presented on MHC class I (all nucleated cells); kill virus-infected, tumour, transplant cells via:
    • Perforin/granzyme — perforin creates pores; granzyme enters & activates caspases → apoptosis.
    • FasL-Fas — Fas ligand on CTL binds Fas (CD95) on target → caspase-8 → apoptosis.
    • Cytokines — IFN-γ, TNF-α, TNF-β — inhibit viral replication, recruit other immune cells.
  • γδ T cells — TCR γδ; MHC-independent; mucosal & skin intraepithelial; rapid cytokine response.
  • NKT cells — express NK markers + TCR; recognise lipid antigen on CD1d; rapid IFN-γ, IL-4.

2. Antigen-Presenting Cells (APCs)

  • Dendritic cells — most potent APC; bridge innate & adaptive; primary naïve T cell activator.
  • Macrophages — phagocytose; present antigen on MHC-II to effector/memory CD4+ T cells; activated by Th1 IFN-γ to kill intracellular pathogens.
  • B cells — antigen-specific uptake via BCR; present to CD4+ Tfh cells.

3. Effector Cells of CMI

  • Activated macrophages — enhanced phagocytosis, ROS/RNS production (respiratory burst, iNOS); granuloma formation.
  • NK cells — kill virus-infected & tumour cells (missing-self); ADCC via FcγRIII (CD16) binds IgG-coated target.
  • Eosinophils — parasite defence (MBP, ECP); allergy.

4. Cytokines

  • IL-2 (T cell proliferation); IFN-γ (macrophage activation, Th1); IL-4, IL-5, IL-13 (Th2); IL-17, IL-22 (Th17); IL-12 (Th1 polarisation); TNF-α (inflammation, granuloma); TGF-β (Treg, fibrosis, IgA switching); IL-10 (immunosuppression).

Mechanism of CMI

Phase 1 — Antigen Recognition & T Cell Priming

  1. Pathogen engulfed by dendritic cell → processed intracellularly → peptide loaded onto MHC class I (endogenous — viral/cytosolic proteins) or MHC class II (exogenous — phagolysosomal).
  2. Dendritic cell migrates to draining lymph node; matures (upregulates MHC, B7 co-stimulator, CCR7).
  3. Naïve T cell in lymph node paracortex recognises peptide-MHC via TCR (signal 1).
  4. Co-stimulation — CD28 on T cell binds B7 (CD80/86) on DC (signal 2) — essential for activation; without it, anergy.
  5. Cytokines from DC (IL-12 → Th1; IL-4 → Th2; IL-6 + TGF-β + IL-23 → Th17; IL-10 + TGF-β → Treg) polarise naïve T cell (signal 3).
  6. T cell proliferates 10⁴–10⁶-fold (clonal expansion, blast transformation); differentiates into effector & memory cells.

Phase 2 — Effector Function

  • CD4+ Th1 cells — migrate to site of infection; recognise antigen on macrophage MHC-II; release IFN-γ → activates macrophage → enhanced phagocytosis, ROS, RNS, granuloma formation; kills intracellular pathogens (TB, Listeria, Salmonella).
  • CD4+ Th17 cells — recruit neutrophils via IL-17 → extracellular bacteria & fungi.
  • CD8+ CTLs — migrate to infected tissue; recognise peptide-MHC I on infected cell; release perforin/granzyme → apoptosis; FasL-Fas; cytokines IFN-γ, TNF-α inhibit viral replication.
  • γδ T cells & NKT cells — rapid innate-like response; cytokine release.
  • NK cells — kill cells with downregulated MHC-I (virus, tumour); ADCC.

Phase 3 — Resolution & Memory

  • Effector cells undergo apoptosis (activation-induced cell death — AICD) as antigen cleared.
  • Memory T cells persist — central memory (TCM) in lymph nodes; effector memory (TEM) in tissues; resident memory (TRM) in epithelial barriers.
  • Memory response — faster, larger, higher affinity on re-exposure.

Functions of CMI

  • Defence against intracellular pathogens — viruses, TB, Listeria, Salmonella, Brucella, Leishmania, Toxoplasma, Plasmodium, fungi.
  • Tumour surveillance — CD8+ CTLs kill tumour cells; basis of cancer immunotherapy (checkpoint inhibitors — nivolumab anti-PD-1, ipilimumab anti-CTLA-4; CAR-T cell therapy).
  • Transplant rejection — host T cells recognise foreign MHC (alloreactivity); acute cellular rejection of solid organ transplant.
  • Graft-versus-host disease (GvHD) — donor T cells attack host tissues post-HSCT.
  • Type IV hypersensitivity — tuberculin skin test, contact dermatitis (poison ivy, nickel), granulomatous disease.
  • Autoimmunity — T cell-mediated tissue damage — type 1 diabetes (β-cell destruction), multiple sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, Hashimoto thyroiditis.

Assessment of CMI

  • Tuberculin skin test (Mantoux) — DTH reaction; measures prior sensitisation to TB.
  • IGRA (QuantiFERON-TB Gold) — IFN-γ release assay; measures T cell response to TB antigens (ESAT-6, CFP-10).
  • Flow cytometry — CD3, CD4, CD8 counts; CD4/CD8 ratio.
  • Lymphocyte proliferation assay — tritiated thymidine incorporation.
  • DCM (delayed cutaneous hypersensitivity) — Candida, mumps, tetanus antigens; anergy panel.

Examples of CMI Deficiency

  • DiGeorge syndrome — thymic aplasia; T cell deficiency.
  • SCID (severe combined immunodeficiency) — T + B cell defect.
  • HIV/AIDS — CD4+ T cell depletion; opportunistic infections (PJP, Toxoplasma, CMV, MAC, Cryptococcus); Kaposi sarcoma.
  • Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis — IL-17 pathway defects (STAT1, AIRE — APECED).
  • IFN-γ pathway defects — disseminated BCG, environmental mycobacteria, Salmonella.

Clinical Pearl

The thymus is essential for T cell development — DiGeorge syndrome (22q11.2 deletion, CATCH-22) causes thymic aplasia → absent T cells → severe viral, fungal, and intracellular bacterial infections; if untreated, fatal in infancy. Thymic transplantation can rescue. The CD4 count is the most important laboratory marker in HIV — guides when to start ART (<500 cells/µL per WHO; <350 cells/µL symptomatic; <200 cells/µL requires PCP prophylaxis with TMP-SMX; <100 cells/µL requires MAC prophylaxis with azithromycin; <50 cells/µL requires CMV surveillance). Granuloma formation (TB, sarcoidosis, fungal, foreign body) is the hallmark of intense Th1-mediated CMI — epithelioid macrophages & multinucleated giant cells surround the pathogen, containing it. Checkpoint inhibitor cancer therapy (nivolumab anti-PD-1, ipilimumab anti-CTLA-4) unleashes pre-existing anti-tumour CD8+ T cells — has revolutionised melanoma, lung, and renal cancer treatment, but causes immune-related adverse events (colitis, pneumonitis, hepatitis, endocrinopathy) — because the brake is removed from self-reactive T cells too.

Definition

Herd immunity (community immunity, population immunity) is the indirect protection from infectious disease that occurs when a large proportion of a population becomes immune to that disease — either through vaccination or prior infection — such that even unvaccinated or non-immune individuals are protected because the disease has little opportunity to spread within the community.

The principle is that when the proportion of immune individuals exceeds a threshold, the effective reproduction number (Re or Rt) falls below 1, and the infection cannot sustain transmission — eventually dying out.

Concept — Reproduction Number & Threshold

  • R₀ (basic reproduction number) — average number of secondary infections from one case in a fully susceptible population.
  • Re = R₀ × (1 – p), where p = proportion immune.
  • Herd immunity threshold (HIT) = 1 – (1/R₀).
Disease R₀ HIT (≥%)
Measles12–1892–95%
Pertussis12–1792–94%
Diphtheria6–783–85%
Polio5–780–86%
Rubella5–780–85%
Mumps4–775–86%
COVID-19 (ancestral)2–360–70% (Delta ~80%, Omicron ~90%+)
Influenza1.5–233–50%

Clinical Significance in Public Health

1. Protection of Vulnerable Individuals Who Cannot Be Vaccinated

  • Infants <6 months (too young for most vaccines).
  • Immunocompromised (HIV, chemotherapy, transplant recipients, primary immunodeficiency).
  • Pregnant women (live vaccines contraindicated).
  • Individuals with severe vaccine allergy (e.g., egg allergy for yellow fever, MMR).
  • Elderly with poor vaccine response.
  • When herd immunity is high, these individuals are protected indirectly.

2. Disease Elimination & Eradication

  • Elimination — zero cases in a defined geographic area (e.g., polio eliminated from India in 2011; measles eliminated from many countries).
  • Eradication — global zero cases — only achieved for smallpox (1980) and rinderpest (2011); polio & Guinea worm on track.
  • Herd immunity is essential — even a single imported case will not spread if Re < 1.
  • Pulse polio immunisation in India achieved >95% coverage → herd immunity → interrupted wild poliovirus transmission.

3. Outbreak Prevention & Control

  • When coverage falls below threshold, outbreaks occur.
  • Measles outbreaks in communities with low MMR coverage (vaccine hesitancy, antivaxx movement).
  • Diphtheria outbreaks — former Soviet Union (1990s); Yemen (recent conflict-related).
  • Coverage gaps create clusters of susceptible individuals.

4. Vaccine Strategy Design

  • Coverage target must exceed HIT for each vaccine-preventable disease.
  • Uniform coverage is more important than average coverage — pockets of low coverage sustain transmission.
  • Pulse campaigns — NIDs for polio; supplementary immunisation activities (SIAs) for measles.
  • Catch-up campaigns — reach missed children.

5. COVID-19 Pandemic & Herd Immunity

  • Initial HIT estimate for COVID-19 was ~60–70%; revised upward with more transmissible variants (Delta ~80%, Omicron >90%).
  • Hybrid immunity (vaccination + prior infection) gives stronger protection.
  • Waning immunity & immune escape variants (Omicron) mean sterilising herd immunity may be unattainable — but herd protection against severe disease remains achievable.
  • Vaccine inequity (high-income vs low-income countries) prolonged the pandemic.

Factors Affecting Herd Immunity

  • R₀ of pathogen — higher R₀ needs higher coverage.
  • Vaccine efficacy — imperfect vaccines need higher coverage; some provide only protection against disease (not infection).
  • Waning immunity — booster doses needed.
  • Uniformity of coverage — clusters of unvaccinated sustain transmission.
  • Pathogen evolution — antigenic drift (influenza), variants (COVID-19) reduce herd immunity.
  • Population mixing patterns — schools, mass gatherings.

Clinical Pearl

Measles is the most contagious human disease — R₀ of 12–18 — meaning one case infects 12–18 susceptibles; herd immunity threshold of 92–95% is required to prevent outbreaks. This explains why measles is the first disease to re-emerge when vaccine coverage falls — even a small dip below 95% leads to outbreaks (e.g., 2019 US outbreaks linked to international travel + pockets of vaccine refusal). The MMR-autism myth (Wakefield 1998, retracted 2010) caused lasting vaccine hesitancy and measles resurgence in the UK, Europe, and US. India's Universal Immunisation Programme (UIP) targets >90% coverage for all vaccines — Mission Indradhanush (since 2014) intensifies efforts in low-coverage districts. The COVID-19 pandemic underscored both the power and limitations of herd immunity — vaccines dramatically reduced severe disease, but Omicron's immune escape means we may never reach true sterilising herd immunity for SARS-CoV-2. The future is herd protection against severe disease through continued vaccination + boosters for high-risk groups, rather than preventing all infection.
q1_0_3_1:
Introduction

Fungi are eukaryotic organisms with chitin-containing cell walls and ergosterol-containing cell membranes. Morphologically classified into 4 groups: yeasts, yeast-like fungi, moulds, and dimorphic fungi.

1. Yeasts

  • Unicellular, round/oval (3–8 µm); reproduce asexually by budding (blastogenesis).
  • Colony on SDA — creamy, pasty.
  • Examples: Candida albicans (oral thrush, vulvovaginitis); Cryptococcus neoformans (meningitis in HIV; India ink positive); Malassezia furfur (pityriasis versicolor); Saccharomyces cerevisiae.

2. Yeast-like Fungi

  • Intermediate; grow as yeast at 37 °C, but form pseudohyphae at lower temperatures.
  • Examples: Candida albicans (germ tube positive); C. tropicalis, C. parapsilosis, C. krusei, C. glabrata (non-albicans Candida).

3. Moulds (Filamentous Fungi)

  • Multicellular; grow as branching hyphae (tubular cells); mass of hyphae = mycelium.
  • Two types of hyphae:
    • Septate — cross-walls (septa); e.g., Aspergillus, dermatophytes.
    • Aseptate (coenocytic) — no cross-walls; broad, ribbon-like; e.g., Mucor, Rhizopus (Mucorales).
  • Colony — cottony, woolly, powdery with various pigments.

Subtypes of Moulds

Type Examples Disease
Zygomycetes (Mucorales)Rhizopus, Mucor, AbsidiaRhinocerebral mucormycosis (DKA); angioinvasive
Hyaline septateAspergillus fumigatus, Fusarium, Penicillium marneffeiInvasive aspergillosis, aspergilloma, ABPA, keratitis
Dermatophytes (keratinophilic)Trichophyton, Microsporum, Epidermophyton floccosumTinea (capitis, corporis, cruris, pedis, unguium)
Dematiaceous (pigmented)Alternaria, Cladosporium, Bipolaris, CurvulariaPhaeohyphomycosis, chromoblastomycosis, eumycetoma

4. Dimorphic Fungi

  • Exist as mould at 25 °C (environmental) & yeast (or spherule) at 37 °C (host).
  • Temperature-dependent dimorphism = virulence factor.
Fungus Mould (25 °C) Tissue form (37 °C)
Histoplasma capsulatumTuberculate macroconidiaSmall intracellular yeast (2–4 µm)
Blastomyces dermatitidisPear-shaped conidiaBroad-based budding yeast
Coccidioides immitisArthroconidiaSpherule with endospores
Paracoccidioides brasiliensisChlamydospore-like"Captain's wheel" multiple budding yeast
Sporothrix schenckiiFlower-like conidiaCigar-shaped yeast
Talaromyces (Penicillium) marneffeiBrush conidiophoreFission yeast (transverse septum)

Special Mention — Pneumocystis jirovecii

Originally classified as protozoan (Pneumocystis carinii); now recognised as a fungus based on rRNA & ergosterol synthesis. Cysts seen on silver stain (GMS) in bronchoalveolar lavage — "crushed ping-pong balls". Causes PCP pneumonia in HIV (CD4 <200). Does not grow on SDA.

Clinical Pearl

The single most important bedside clue to fungal morphology is the KOH mount with calcofluor white: yeasts = oval budding cells; pseudohyphae = constrictions at septa (like sausages); true hyphae = parallel walls & true septa; aseptate (Mucorales) hyphae = broad (6–15 µm), ribbon-like, branching at 90°. This distinction is critical — Mucorales require urgent liposomal amphotericin B + surgical debridement (poor response to voriconazole, first-line for Aspergillus). The COVID-19 pandemic saw a surge of COVID-associated mucormycosis (CAM) in India — uncontrolled diabetes, steroid therapy, iron overload. Remember: hyaline septate acute-angle branching = Aspergillus; broad aseptate right-angle branching = Mucorales.
q1_0_3_2:
Introduction

Concentration techniques in stool examination are used to increase the yield of detecting parasites (ova, cysts, larvae, trophozoites) by separating them from faecal debris. They are essential when parasite load is low. Two commonly used concentration methods are formalin-ether (ethyl acetate) sedimentation and zinc sulphate flotation.

Method 1 — Formalin-Ether Sedimentation (Ritchie's method)

  • Principle — formalin fixes & preserves parasites; ether/ethyl acetate dissolves lipids & debris, which float; parasites (heavier) sediment.
  • Procedure
    1. Emulsify ~1 g stool in 10 mL 10% formalin (sieves through gauze to remove debris).
    2. Add 3 mL ether (or ethyl acetate — safer); shake vigorously for 30 sec.
    3. Centrifuge at 500 g for 5 min.
    4. Four layers form: top (ether), debris plug, formalin layer, sediment (parasites).
    5. Decant supernatant; resuspend sediment; mount on slide with iodine or saline; examine under microscope.
  • Recovers — most ova, cysts, larvae, coccidia (Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora, Isospora), tapeworm eggs.
  • Does NOT recover — trophozoites (formalin distorts them); live parasites (formalin kills).

    1. Emulsify stool in tap water; filter through gauze.
    2. Add ZnSO₄ solution (33% w/v, SG 1.18).
    3. Centrifuge at 500 g for 2 min, or let stand 10 min (gravity).
    4. Carefully collect surface film with wire loop or coverslip.
    5. Mount on slide with iodine; examine.
  • Recovers — most nematode eggs (Ascaris, hookworm, Trichuris), cestode eggs (Taenia, Hymenolepis), protozoan cysts (Giardia, Entamoeba).

  • Modified acid-fast stain — for Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora, Isospora.

Definition

High-level disinfectants (HLDs) are chemical agents that destroy all vegetative bacteria (including mycobacteria), viruses, fungi, and some bacterial spores (with prolonged contact — become sterilants). They are used for semi-critical items (contact mucous membranes or non-intact skin — endoscopes, respiratory therapy equipment, vaginal specula, laryngoscope blades) per Spaulding classification.

Two High-Level Disinfectants

1. Glutaraldehyde 2% (Cidex)

  • Properties — colourless liquid; activated by alkalising to pH 7.5–8.5; reuse for 14–28 days (check MRC ≥1.5% with test strip).
  • Action — alkylates proteins, nucleic acids → cell death.
  • Exposure — 20–45 min for HLD; 10 h for sterilisation.
  • Uses
    • Flexible endoscopes (gastroscope, colonoscope, bronchoscope).
    • Respiratory therapy equipment, anaesthesia equipment.
    • Laryngoscope blades, vaginal specula.
    • Dialysers, blood tubing.
    • Rubber & plastic items that cannot be autoclaved.
  • Limitations — irritant vapour (use closed container, PPE); fixes protein (must pre-clean items); inactivated by organic matter; M. chelonei outbreak risk if reused too long; not sporicidal at short exposure.

2. Ortho-Phthalaldehyde (OPA) 0.55%

  • Properties — clear pale-blue liquid; no activation needed; less irritating vapour; faster action; reuse for 14 days.
  • Exposure — 12 min for HLD at 20 °C; 6 h for sterilisation.
  • Uses
    • Replacement for glutaraldehyde — endoscopes, respiratory therapy equipment.
    • Manual & automated endoscope reprocessors.
  • Limitations — stains skin/proteins grey (repeated exposure); sensitises urology staff (occupational asthma); higher cost.

Other HLDs

  • Hydrogen peroxide 7.5% — no toxic residue; for endoscopes & instruments.
  • Peracetic acid 0.2–0.35% — Steris System 1; single-use; for rigid endoscopes & surgical instruments.
  • Hypochlorite 1% (5000 ppm) — for blood spills; surfaces.

Spaulding Classification

  • Critical items (enter sterile tissue) — require sterilisation.
  • Semi-critical items (contact mucous membranes) — require HLD.
  • Non-critical items (contact intact skin) — require intermediate/low-level disinfection.

Clinical Pearl

The most important practical lesson: HLD reduces microbial load but does not sterilise. For instruments entering sterile tissue (critical items — surgical instruments, implants), only true sterilisation is acceptable. The biggest source of endoscope-related outbreaks is atypical mycobacteria (M. abscessus, M. chelonei) — they survive standard glutaraldehyde by forming biofilm in instrument channels. Prevention: (1) meticulous manual cleaning with enzymatic detergent before disinfection; (2) discard glutaraldehyde after 14 days; (3) use automated endoscope reprocessors with filtered water & 70% alcohol flush; (4) store endoscopes vertically in drying cabinet. For duodenoscopes (ERCP), FDA (2015) recommends EtO sterilisation or peracetic acid after HLD due to repeated MDR-organism outbreaks.

WHO Five Moments for Hand Hygiene

The WHO Five Moments (2009) define the 5 critical moments during patient care when hand hygiene must be performed. It is the single most effective measure to prevent healthcare-associated infections.

  1. Before touching a patient
    • Before any physical contact — shaking hands, helping patient move, taking pulse/BP, examination.
    • Why — protects patient from microbes on healthcare worker's hands.
  2. Before clean/aseptic procedure
    • Before dressing a wound, inserting IV/urinary catheter, preparing injection, oral care, drawing blood.
    • Why — protects patient from microbes (including own flora) entering sterile sites. Most critical moment — directly prevents CLABSI, CAUTI, SSI.
  3. After body fluid exposure risk
    • After any procedure with body fluids, mucous membranes, non-intact skin, wound dressings — drawing blood, changing dressing, handling bedpan, suctioning.
    • Why — protects healthcare worker & environment from patient-derived microbes.
  4. After touching a patient
    • After any physical contact — handshake, examination, helping move.
    • Why — protects healthcare worker & other patients.
  5. After touching patient surroundings
    • After contact with bed rails, IV pole, bedside table, monitor, door handle, BP cuff, chart.
    • Why — protects healthcare worker & other patients from microbes left on surfaces.

Hand Hygiene Methods

  • Alcohol-based handrub (ABHR) — preferred; 20–30 sec; 60–80% ethanol/isopropanol; for all 5 moments when hands not visibly soiled.
  • Soap & water — 40–60 sec; when hands visibly dirty; before eating; after toilet; suspected/confirmed C. difficile (alcohol does NOT kill spores); norovirus outbreak.
  • Surgical hand scrub — 2–5 min with chlorhexidine or povidone-iodine.

WHO Technique for Alcohol Handrub

  1. Apply 3–5 mL product.
  2. Palm to palm.
  3. Right palm over left dorsum & vice versa.
  4. Palm to palm with fingers interlaced.
  5. Backs of fingers to opposing palms with fingers interlocked.
  6. Rotational rubbing of left thumb clasped in right palm & vice versa.
  7. Rotational rubbing with clasped fingers of right hand in left palm & vice versa.
  8. Once dry — hands are safe.

Why Hand Hygiene Saves Lives

  • Healthcare workers' hands are the most common vehicle of cross-transmission in hospitals.
  • Compliance can reduce HAIs by 30–50%.
  • WHO estimates improving hand hygiene could save 5–8 million lives annually.
  • Cost-effective — alcohol handrub is cheaper than soap-and-water.
  • Reduces spread of multidrug-resistant organisms (MRSA, VRE, ESBL, CRE, CRAB, CRPA).

Clinical Pearl

The single most important lesson: alcohol-based handrub is the gold standard for routine hand hygiene (20 sec, faster, more effective, better tolerated) — except when hands are visibly dirty or spore-forming organisms (C. difficile, anthrax, norovirus) are suspected (then soap-and-water mandatory). Wearing the same pair of gloves for multiple patients is the most dangerous hand-hygiene violation — gloves do not protect the next patient. The 5 Moments framework has been adopted in >180 countries — most successful patient-safety intervention in history.

(A) Clinical Diagnosis & Causative Organism (2 marks)

The clinical picture — chronic cough (≥2–4 weeks), low-grade evening fever, weight loss, loss of appetite, night sweats, haemoptysis (streaky or frank), and chest radiograph showing cavitary lesion typically in the right upper lobe (apical/posterior segments), with sputum showing acid-fast bacilli (AFB) — long, slender, beaded bacilli — is the classic presentation of pulmonary tuberculosis (PTB).

Causative organism: Mycobacterium tuberculosis — an acid-fast, obligate aerobe, non-motile, non-spore-forming, slow-growing (generation time 18–24 h) bacillus of family Mycobacteriaceae. The characteristic acid-fastness (red bacilli on Ziehl-Neelsen stain; auramine-rhodamine fluorescent on auramine O) is due to high mycolic acid content in the cell wall. Other components — arabinogalactan, peptidoglycan, lipoarabinomannan (LAM), wax D, phenolic glycolipid — make the wall impervious to Gram stain.

Other mycobacteria causing TB-like disease: M. bovis (unpasteurised milk), M. africanum (West Africa), M. microti (rodents). M. canettii. These are grouped as M. tuberculosis complex. Non-tuberculous mycobacteria (NTM) — M. avium-intracellulare, M. kansasii, M. abscessus — cause opportunistic infection in immunocompromised.

(B) Pathogenesis (6 marks)

1. Source & Transmission

  • Source — open (sputum-positive) pulmonary TB case. Untreated smear-positive patient infects ~10–15 contacts/year.
  • Transmission — airborne droplet nuclei (1–5 µm) generated by coughing, sneezing, singing; remain suspended for hours; inhaled into terminal alveoli. NOT spread by fomites, food, or casual contact.
  • Infective dose — as few as 1–10 bacilli.
  • Incubation — 2–10 weeks for primary infection; years for reactivation.
  • Risk factors for infection & disease — HIV (highest risk — 5–15% annual risk of TB vs 5–15% lifetime in HIV-negative), malnutrition, diabetes, silicosis, smoking, immunosuppression (anti-TNF, steroids, transplant), chronic renal failure, malignancy, poverty, overcrowding.

2. Entry & Primary Infection (Ghon Complex)

  1. Inhalation — droplet nuclei reach terminal bronchioles & alveoli (upper lobe preferred — high oxygen tension).
  2. Phagocytosis by alveolar macrophages — bacilli ingested but resist killing due to:
    • Cell wall mycolic acid prevents fusion of phagosome with lysosome.
    • Trehalose dimycolate ("cord factor") causes serpentine cording & inhibits macrophage function.
    • Lipoarabinomannan (LAM) blocks macrophage activation, scavenges ROS, induces TNF-α.
    • Phagosome maturation arrest (blocks Rab5 → Rab7 conversion; retains TACO protein).
  3. Intracellular multiplication — bacilli multiply within macrophages; macrophage eventually ruptures, releasing bacilli to infect new macrophages.
  4. Dendritic cell migration — bacilli & antigen carried to draining hilar lymph nodes; presented to naïve T cells → CMI develops in 2–6 weeks.
  5. Granuloma formation
    • Activated macrophages (epithelioid cells), Langhans giant cells (multinucleated), CD4+ T cells (Th1), CD8+ T cells, B cells, fibroblasts.
    • Central caseous necrosis (cheese-like; due to TNF-α, IFN-γ, ischaemia).
    • Fibrosis & calcification contain the bacilli; bacilli dormant but viable for years.
  6. Ghon complex — subpleural parenchymal lesion (Ghon focus) + draining hilar lymph node involvement. Heals by fibrosis & calcification (Ranke complex). Visible on chest X-ray as calcified nodule.

3. Latent TB Infection (LTBI)

  • After primary infection, CMI contains the bacilli in granulomas; patient is asymptomatic, not infectious, but infected.
  • Tuberculin skin test (Mantoux) positive; IGRA (QuantiFERON-TB Gold) positive.
  • Lifetime risk of reactivation ~5–10% in immunocompetent; 5–15% per year in HIV.
  • Reactivation typically in upper lobes (high oxygen tension).

4. Post-Primary (Adult/Reactivation) TB

  • Occurs years–decades after primary infection; due to waning immunity or new infection.
  • Location — apical & posterior segments of upper lobes (85%); superior segment of lower lobe (10%).
  • Pathology
    • Caseous necrosis with cavitation — erosion into bronchus allows bacilli to be coughed up (sputum positive; highly infectious).
    • Fibrocaseous lesions; endobronchial TB; haematogenous spread (miliary TB).
  • Immunology — Th1 cytokines (IFN-γ, TNF-α, IL-2); CD8+ CTL killing; DTH reaction. TNF-α is critical for granuloma maintenance — anti-TNF therapy (infliximab, adalimumab, etanercept) reactivates TB.

5. Spread

  • Local — endobronchial spread to other lobes (leading to "aspiration pneumonia" pattern).
  • Lymphatic — hilar, mediastinal, cervical lymph nodes (scrofuloderma).
  • Haematogenous — miliary TB (lung, liver, spleen, bone marrow, meninges); solitary extrapulmonary sites (Pott's spine, TB meningitis, GI, renal, pericardial, adrenal — Addison's).
  • Direct extension — pleural effusion, empyema, pericarditis, Pott's spine.

6. Pathological Stages

  1. Exudative — acute inflammation, exudate in alveoli; neutrophil & macrophage infiltrate.
  2. Caseative — caseous necrosis; epithelioid & giant cells; central cheesy material.
  3. Fibrocaseous — fibrosis surrounds caseum; cavity formation.
  4. Fibrous / calcified — healed lesion.

(C) Laboratory Diagnosis (7 marks)

1. Specimen Collection

  • Sputum — early morning, deep cough specimen (≥3 mL); 3 samples (spot-morning-spot or 3 consecutive mornings).
  • Induced sputum — hypertonic saline nebulisation for patients who cannot expectorate.
  • Bronchoscopy — bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL), transbronchial biopsy for smear-negative.
  • Gastric lavage — early morning; for children <5 yr who swallow sputum (cannot expectorate); aspirate overnight-swallowed sputum from stomach.
  • Other specimens — CSF (TB meningitis), urine (renal TB), pleural fluid, pericardial fluid, ascitic fluid, synovial fluid, pus, tissue biopsy (lymph node, bone marrow, liver).
  • Transport — sterile wide-mouth container; refrigerate if delay >1 h; cetylpyridinium chloride (CPC) for transport if long delay.

2. Smear Microscopy

  • Ziehl-Neelsen (ZN) stain — hot carbol fuchsin, acid-alcohol decolourisation, methylene blue counterstain. AFB appear red/pink against blue background.
  • Grading (WHO/RNTCP)
    • 3+ — >10 AFB per field (examine 20 fields).
    • 2+ — 1–10 AFB per field (50 fields).
    • 1+ — 10–99 AFB per 100 fields.
    • Scanty — 1–9 AFB per 100 fields (report exact number).
    • Negative — no AFB in 100 fields.
  • Sensitivity — 5,000–10,000 bacilli/mL sputum required for smear positivity; ~50–60% sensitivity vs culture. Negative smear does NOT exclude TB.
  • Auramine O (fluorescent stain) — yellow-orange bacilli on black background under UV; examine 40× objective (faster); preferred in high-burden settings.

3. Culture — Gold Standard

  • Solid media
    • Löwenstein-Jensen (LJ) — egg-based, malachite green (inhibits contaminants); colonies in 2–8 weeks (M. tuberculosis grows slowly — 18–24 h generation time).
    • Middlebrook 7H10/7H11 agar — faster (1–3 weeks).
  • Liquid culture (faster — 1–3 weeks)
    • MB/BacT, BACTEC MGIT 960 (Mycobacterial Growth Indicator Tube — fluorescent sensor detects O₂ consumption); BACTEC 460 (radiometric — 14C-palmitic acid; now obsolete).
    • VersaTREK.
  • Colony morphology — M. tuberculosis: buff-coloured, rough, dry, cauliflower-like colonies (cord factor causes serpentine growth); non-pigmented (photochromogen — M. kansasii; scotochromogen — M. scrofulaceum; non-chromogen — M. tuberculosis, M. avium).
  • Sensitivity — detects 10–100 bacilli/mL; gold standard for diagnosis; required for drug susceptibility testing.

4. Identification

  • Niacin test — M. tuberculosis produces niacin (positive); M. bovis negative.
  • Nitrate reduction — M. tuberculosis positive; M. bovis negative.
  • Catalase — variable; M. tuberculosis loses catalase at 68 °C (thermolabile).
  • Arylsulphatase — M. tuberculosis negative; M. fortuitum positive.
  • Tween 80 hydrolysis — M. tuberculosis positive (5 days); M. avium negative.
  • Pyrazinamidase — M. tuberculosis positive; M. bovis negative.
  • MTP40 antigen, MPT64 antigen — immunochromatographic rapid test (Capilia TB-Neo); confirms M. tuberculosis complex.
  • HPLC — mycolic acid pattern.
  • MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry — rapid identification.
  • Molecular — PCR (IS6110, 16S rRNA); line probe assay (GenoType MTBDRplus, MTBDRsl).

5. Molecular Tests — CBNAAT (Xpert MTB/RIF)

  • Cepheid Xpert MTB/RIF — automated real-time PCR; detects M. tuberculosis DNA + rifampicin resistance (rpoB gene mutations) in 2 hours.
  • Sensitivity — 90%+ in smear-positive; 70–80% in smear-negative; >95% specificity.
  • WHO-endorsed as first-line test for TB diagnosis (replaces smear microscopy in many settings).
  • Xpert Ultra — improved sensitivity (LOD 16 bacilli/mL vs 131 in MTB/RIF); useful in HIV, children, extrapulmonary TB.
  • Truenat MTB — Indian-made portable PCR; also detects rifampicin resistance.
  • Line Probe Assays (LPAs)
    • GenoType MTBDRplus — detects M. tuberculosis + rifampicin + isoniazid resistance (rpoB, katG, inhA).
    • GenoType MTBDRsl — second-line: fluoroquinolones (gyrA), aminoglycosides (rrs), ethambutol (embB) resistance.
    • Useful in MDR-TB diagnosis & management.
  • Whole Genome Sequencing (WGS) — comprehensive resistance profiling; research/specialised labs.

6. Tuberculin Skin Test (TST / Mantoux)

  • 5 TU PPD (purified protein derivative) intradermally on volar forearm; read induration at 48–72 h.
  • Positive — ≥5 mm (HIV, immunosuppressed, recent TB contact); ≥10 mm (healthcare workers, high-risk); ≥15 mm (low-risk general population).
  • Does NOT distinguish latent vs active TB; NOT diagnostic for active disease.
  • False positive — BCG vaccination, NTM infection.
  • False negative — anergy (HIV, malnutrition, measles, immunosuppression, military TB, severe active TB).

7. Interferon-Gamma Release Assays (IGRA)

  • QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus (QFT-Plus) — ELISA measuring IFN-γ released by T cells in response to ESAT-6 & CFP-10 antigens (absent from BCG & most NTM).
  • T-SPOT.TB — ELISPOT counting IFN-γ-producing T cells.
  • Advantages over TST — single visit; no booster effect; not affected by BCG; more specific.
  • Does NOT distinguish latent vs active TB.
  • Useful for LTBI screening in healthcare workers, BCG-vaccinated individuals, before anti-TNF therapy.

8. Drug Susceptibility Testing (DST)

  • Phenotypic DST — solid (LJ proportion method) or liquid (MGIT 960 — gold standard); 1–4 weeks.
  • Genotypic DST — molecular (CBNAAT, line probe assays) — hours; detect specific resistance mutations.
  • First-line drugs tested — rifampicin (rpoB), isoniazid (katG, inhA), pyrazinamide (pncA), ethambutol (embB), streptomycin (rpsL, rrs, gidB).
  • Second-line — fluoroquinolones (gyrA/B), aminoglycosides (rrs), ethionamide (inhA promoter), PAS (thyA), cycloserine (alr, ddl).

9. Other Investigations

  • Chest X-ray — apical/posterior upper lobe infiltrates, cavitation, fibrosis, calcification; miliary ("millet seed" shadows); pleural effusion; hilar lymphadenopathy (primary).
  • CBG — anaemia of chronic disease; raised ESR.
  • HIV test — mandatory in every TB patient.
  • CRP, LFT, RFT, blood glucose (baseline before starting ATT).
  • Urinalysis — sterile pyuria (renal TB).
  • ADA (adenosine deaminase) in body fluids — >40 U/L in pleural/ascitic/CSF fluid supports TB.
  • CBNAAT on extrapulmonary specimens — CSF, pleural, pericardial, ascitic, synovial, tissue.
  • Histopathology — caseating granuloma with epithelioid cells & Langhans giant cells; AFB stain (ZN) on tissue section.

Treatment — DOTS / RNTCP / NTEP

  • NTEP (National TB Elimination Program, formerly RNTCP) — India's national programme; provides free diagnosis & treatment.
  • Drug-sensitive TB — 6-month course:
    • Intensive phase (2 months) — HRZE (Isoniazid + Rifampicin + Pyrazinamide + Ethambutol).
    • Continuation phase (4 months) — HRE (Isoniazid + Rifampicin + Ethambutol).
  • MDR-TB (rifampicin-resistant) — shorter MDR regimen (9–12 months: Bedaquiline + Pretomanid + Linezolid — BPaL; or longer 18–20-month regimen).
  • XDR-TB (extensively drug-resistant) — individualised regimen.
  • Treatment adherence — DOTS (Directly Observed Treatment, Short-course); digital adherence technologies (99DOTS, video-supported therapy).

Prevention

  • BCG vaccine — live attenuated M. bovis; given at birth; protects against disseminated TB & TB meningitis in children (70–80% efficacy); less effective against adult pulmonary TB (variable 0–80%).
  • Infection control — airborne precautions (negative-pressure isolation, N95 respirators, UV light); cough etiquette.
  • Active case finding — contact tracing; intensified case finding in HIV.
  • LTBI treatment — Isoniazid 300 mg daily × 6–9 months; or Rifampicin × 4 months; or 3HP (Isoniazid + Rifapentine weekly × 3 months).
  • Address social determinants — poverty, nutrition, housing.

Clinical Pearl

CBNAAT (Xpert MTB/RIF) has replaced sputum smear microscopy as the first-line diagnostic test for TB in India under NTEP — it detects M. tuberculosis DNA and rifampicin resistance in 2 hours, with sensitivity >90% (smear-positive) and 70–80% (smear-negative). For extrapulmonary TB (TB meningitis, pleural, pericardial, lymph node), CBNAAT on the relevant body fluid is the test of choice, though sensitivity may be lower than for pulmonary specimens. Always send 3 sputum samples (spot-morning-spot) for smear if CBNAAT unavailable. For suspected MDR-TB, send for line probe assay (LPA) — detects resistance to first-line (MTBDRplus: rifampicin + isoniazid) and second-line drugs (MTBDRsl: fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides, ethambutol). The most important recent advance is the BPaL regimen (Bedaquiline + Pretomanid + Linezolid, 6 months) for MDR-TB — much shorter and more effective than the 18–24-month traditional regimen. Always test for HIV in every TB patient. TB is the leading cause of death in people living with HIV — screen every HIV-positive patient for TB at every visit (4-symptom screen: cough, fever, night sweats, weight loss); if positive, send CBNAAT. The WHO goal of ending TB by 2030 (Sustainable Development Goal 3.3) requires intensified case finding, universal DST, MDR-TB scale-up, and TB preventive treatment.

(A) Clinical Diagnosis & Causative Organism (2 marks)

The clinical picture — crush injury 4–5 days ago, wound contaminated with soil, necrotic muscle, oedema, severe pain, crepitus on palpation (gas in tissue), and black discoloration at the wound site — is the textbook presentation of gas gangrene (clostridial myonecrosis).

Causative organism: Clostridium perfringens (formerly C. welchii) — a Gram-positive, anaerobic, spore-forming, non-motile, encapsulated bacillus. Responsible for ~80% of gas gangrene cases. Other clostridia causing gas gangrene: C. septicum, C. novyi, C. histolyticum, C. sordellii, C. bifermentans. Rare cases from polymicrobial infection (anaerobic streptococci, Bacteroides, peptostreptococci — synergistic non-clostridial anaerobic myonecrosis).

Taxonomy: family Clostridiaceae, genus Clostridium; obligate anaerobe (cannot grow in O₂); spores survive in soil for years.

(B) Pathogenesis (6 marks)

1. Source & Transmission

  • Source — C. perfringens spores in soil, dust, faeces, sewage; also normal flora of human colon & vagina.
  • Transmission
    • Traumatic gas gangrene — wounds contaminated with soil/dust (war injuries, road traffic accidents, agricultural injuries, crush injuries, compound fractures, surgical wounds).
    • Spontaneous / non-traumatic gas gangrene — C. septicum bacteraemia from GI tract (colorectal cancer, neutropenia, diabetes); no obvious wound.
    • Uterine gas gangrene — septic abortion, prolonged rupture of membranes, retained products of conception.
  • Incubation — 6 hours to 3 days (usually <24 h).

2. Predisposing Factors

  • Wound conditions that favour anaerobic growth:
    • Necrotic/devitalised tissue (provides nutrients & reduces O₂).
    • Foreign body (bullet, shrapnel, dirt).
    • Impaired blood supply (vascular injury, tourniquet, compartment syndrome).
    • Crush injury (tissue damage, haematoma).

(A) Clinical Diagnosis (1 mark)

The clinical picture — 7-year-old unimmunised child with high-grade fever, toxicity, severe sore throat, inability to swallow, and white patch on the fauces that bleeds when touched — is the classic presentation of pharyngeal diphtheria.

(B) Etiological Agent (1 mark)

Corynebacterium diphtheriae — a Gram-positive, non-spore-forming, non-motile, non-capsulated pleomorphic bacillus. Characteristic morphology — Chinese letter / cuneiform (club-shaped) arrangement; metachromatic granules (volutin granules) on Loeffler's methylene blue or Albert stain. The club shape is due to presence of polyphosphate granules at poles.

Biotypes (based on colony morphology & haemolysis on tellurite blood agar):

  • gravis — large, grey, daisy-head colonies; most severe; associated with epidemics.
  • intermedius — small, flat, black colonies; intermediate severity.
  • mitis — small, glossy, black colonies; mildest; common in endemic areas.
  • belfanti — non-lipophilic variant.

Toxigenic strains carry the tox gene (encoded by corynephage β — a lysogenic bacteriophage); non-toxigenic strains cause mild pharyngitis but not classic diphtheria. Only toxigenic strains produce diphtheria toxin.

(C) Pathogenesis (5 marks)

1. Source & Transmission

  • Source — cases (symptomatic) & asymptomatic carriers (nasopharyngeal colonisation).
  • Transmission — droplet (coughing, sneezing); direct contact with wound exudate (cutaneous diphtheria); fomites (rare).
  • Incubation — 2–5 days (range 1–10 days).
  • Risk factors — unimmunised or incompletely immunised child; overcrowding; poor nutrition; immunocompromise; travel to endemic area.

2. Colonisation & Pseudomembrane Formation

  1. Adherence — via pili & surface proteins (DIP0733, DIP1281); C. diphtheriae colonises mucosa of tonsils, pharynx, larynx, nose; occasionally conjunctiva, genital mucosa, or skin (cutaneous diphtheria in tropics).
  2. Local invasion — bacteria remain superficial; do NOT invade deeper tissues or bloodstream.
  3. Pseudomembrane formation — bacteria + necrotic epithelial cells + fibrin + neutrophils + RBCs form a tough, adherent, grey-white membrane. Bleeds on attempted removal — characteristic. Extends from tonsils → uvula → soft palate → pharynx → larynx → trachea (causing airway obstruction).
  4. "Bull neck" — marked cervical lymphadenopathy with subcutaneous oedema; severe case sign.

3. Diphtheria Toxin — Mode of Action

  • Structure — AB toxin; 62 kDa single polypeptide.
    • A subunit (Fragment A, 21 kDa) — active catalytic moiety; released by proteolytic cleavage of disulfide bond.
    • B subunit (Fragment B, 41 kDa) — binding & translocation; binds heparin-binding epidermal growth factor-like (HB-EGF) receptor on host cells.
  • Cell entry
    1. B subunit binds HB-EGF receptor (all nucleated cells express; heart, nerves, kidneys particularly sensitive).
    2. Receptor-mediated endocytosis → endosome.
    3. Acidification of endosome triggers conformational change → B subunit forms pore in endosomal membrane.
    4. A subunit translocates through pore into cytoplasm.
    5. Disulfide bond reduced → A subunit released.
  • Enzymatic action
    • A subunit catalyses ADP-ribosylation of Elongation Factor 2 (EF-2) at diphthamide residue (unique modified histidine).
    • Uses NAD⁺ as cofactor → transfers ADP-ribose to diphthamide.
    • Modified EF-2 cannot bind ribosome → protein synthesis inhibited → cell death.
  • Toxin gene regulation
    • tox gene encoded by corynephage β (lysogenic phage); only toxigenic strains produce toxin.
    • DtxR (diphtheria toxin repressor) — iron-dependent regulatory protein.
      • High iron (Fe²⁺) → DtxR-Fe²⁺ binds tox operator → represses toxin gene.
      • Low iron → DtxR releases → toxin gene transcribed → toxin produced.
    • Explains why diphtheria is worse in iron-deficient hosts (low iron → high toxin).

  • Local — necrotic pharyngitis; pseudomembrane; airway obstruction (laryngeal diphtheria — "membranous croup"); cervical adenitis with oedema ("bull neck").

  • Neuropathy
    • Palatal paralysis (early — 2–3 weeks) — nasal regurgitation, nasal voice.
    • Oculomotor, facial, pharyngeal paralysis (3–5 weeks).
    • Polyneuropathy (paralytic syndrome) — symmetric, descending; resembles Guillain-Barré; occurs 1–3 months after onset.
  • Renal — acute tubular necrosis.
  • Adrenal — haemorrhage & insufficiency.

  • Efficacy — >95% after complete primary series; wanes over 10 years → boosters needed.

2. Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (PEP) for Contacts

  • Identify close contacts — household, school, daycare; clinical & microbiological surveillance for 7 days.
  • Immunisation status
    • <3 doses or unknown — start primary series + booster.
    • ≥3 doses, last >5 years ago — booster dose.
    • Fully immunised, recent booster — no vaccine.
  • Antibiotic prophylaxis
    • Benzathine penicillin G 600,000–1,200,000 U IM single dose (children <30 kg → 600,000; ≥30 kg → 1,200,000).
    • Or azithromycin 500 mg OD × 5 days (children 10 mg/kg) — alternative if penicillin allergy.
    • Or erythromycin 500 mg QID × 7 days.
    • Or clindamycin.
  • Cultures — baseline & post-prophylaxis to confirm clearance.

3. Treatment of Cases

  • Diphtheria antitoxin (DAT) — equine-derived; given IV/IM ASAP (do NOT wait for culture confirmation if clinical suspicion high).
    • Dose — 20,000–40,000 U for pharyngeal/laryngeal disease <48 h; 80,000–120,000 U for extensive disease >48 h or neck swelling.
    • Always test for hypersensitivity (skin test or slow IV test dose) — risk of anaphylaxis or serum sickness.
    • Neutralises circulating toxin only — does NOT reverse tissue-bound toxin; therefore must be given early.
  • Antibiotics
    • IV Penicillin G (or procaine penicillin) × 14 days; or erythromycin × 14 days (penicillin allergy).
    • Eliminates organism, stops toxin production, prevents transmission.
    • Does NOT neutralise existing toxin — must be combined with antitoxin.
  • Supportive
    • Airway management — tracheostomy if laryngeal obstruction.
    • Bed rest (2–3 weeks) — minimises cardiac stress.
    • Cardiac monitoring — ECG, echocardiography; treat arrhythmias, heart failure.
    • Aspiration precautions for palatal paralysis; NG tube feeding.
    • ICU support if severe.
  • Isolation — droplet precautions until 2 negative cultures (24 h apart) after antibiotics completed.

Diphtheria is a re-emerging infection in India — outbreaks reported in Kerala, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Assam, Delhi in last decade; largely due to waning immunity in adults (booster doses missed) & pockets of unimmunised children. The pseudomembrane that bleeds on touching is pathognomonic — but do NOT attempt to remove it (causes bleeding, aspiration, sudden airway obstruction). Always give diphtheria antitoxin (DAT) immediately on clinical suspicion — do NOT wait for culture confirmation — because antitoxin neutralises only free (unbound) toxin; once toxin binds to tissues, it cannot be reversed. Mortality is 5–10% even with treatment; respiratory obstruction or myocarditis are the main causes of death. The Schick test (intradermal toxin injection) is historical — replaced by serology; an antitoxin level >0.1 IU/mL is considered protective. The most important prevention is complete childhood immunisation + adult Td boosters every 10 years. All healthcare workers should have current Tdap vaccination. The recent shift from DTP to DTaP in many countries (less reactogenic) has reduced adverse events but may reduce durability — acellular pertussis immunity wanes faster.
