Introduction

Syphilis is a chronic systemic sexually transmitted infection caused by Treponema pallidum subspecies pallidum — a thin (0.1 × 5–20 µm), coiled (6–14 spirals), delicate, motile spirochete that cannot be cultured on artificial media. Untreated, syphilis progresses through characteristic stages — primary, secondary, latent, and tertiary — each with distinct clinical features.

Stages of Syphilis

1. Primary Syphilis

  • Incubation — 9–90 days (average 3 weeks) after sexual exposure.
  • Chancre — at site of inoculation (genital — glans penis, prepuce, vulva, cervix, labia; extragenital — lip, tongue, tonsil, anus, rectum, finger).
    • Single, painless, clean, indurated ulcer with raised edge ("cartilaginous" induration); 1–2 cm diameter; base clean, red, exudes clear serum.
    • Painless (distinguishes from herpes — painful; chancroid — painful; LGV — painful).
    • Regional lymphadenopathy — non-tender, rubbery, discrete, non-suppurating inguinal nodes ("satellite bubo"); bilateral.
    • Heals spontaneously in 3–6 weeks without scarring (even without treatment).
    • Does NOT bleed on touch (distinguishes from diphtheria pseudomembrane).
    • Extragenital chances are more atypical.
  • Highly infectious — teeming with spirochaetes; dark-field microscopy positive.
  • Serology may be negative in early primary (window period); becomes positive after 1–4 weeks.

2. Secondary Syphilis

  • Onset — 2 weeks to 6 months after primary chancre (average 6 weeks); may overlap with healing chancre.
  • Represents haematogenous dissemination of spirochaetes.
  • Constitutional — low-grade fever, malaise, fatigue, headache, anorexia, weight loss, generalised lymphadenopathy (epitrochlear node pathognomonic), arthralgia, myalgia.
  • Skin rash:
    • Macular / maculopapular rash on trunk, palms, soles, extremities; copper-red; non-pruritic (or mildly pruritic); symmetric; 5–10 mm.
    • Rash on palms & soles is highly suggestive of secondary syphilis (distinguishes from most other rashes).
    • Annular papular rash — face (especially black patients).
    • Condylomata lata — broad, moist, wart-like, highly infectious plaques in moist intertriginous areas (perianal, vulva, scrotum, inner thigh, axilla, submammary).
    • Patchy hair loss (moth-eaten alopecia) — eyebrows, beard, scalp; non-scarring.
    • Mucous patches — painless silver-grey erosions on tongue, buccal mucosa, lips, pharynx, genitalia; highly infectious.
  • Systemic manifestations:
    • Hepatitis (mild transaminitis); perihepatitis (Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome).
    • Glomerulonephritis, nephrotic syndrome (immune complex).
    • Uveitis, optic neuritis, retinitis.
    • Meningitis, cranial nerve palsies (VII, VIII — sensorineural hearing loss), stroke.
    • Osteitis, periostitis, arthritis.
    • Malaise, fever, generalised lymphadenopathy (epitrochlear, inguinal, cervical).
  • Resolves spontaneously in 3–12 weeks → latent syphilis.
  • Highest spirochaete load → highly infectious.

3. Latent Syphilis

  • Asymptomatic phase after resolution of secondary syphilis; diagnosis by positive serology with no clinical signs.
  • Early latent — <1 year after infection (or unknown, but within last year); infectious (relapse possible).
  • Late latent — >1 year after infection (or unknown duration); not infectious (except transplacentally); can still transmit to fetus.
  • Can last for years to decades before progressing to tertiary.
  • ~30% progress to tertiary syphilis if untreated.

4. Tertiary (Late) Syphilis

Occurs in ~30% of untreated patients, 3–30 years after primary infection. Three main forms:

4a. Gummatous Syphilis (Late Benign Syphilis)

  • Gumma — granulomatous lesion with central caseous necrosis surrounded by plasma cells, lymphocytes, epithelioid cells, giant cells; paucibacillary (few or no treponemes); destructive but localised.
  • Skin — nodular ulcerative lesions with punched-out edges, scarring ("tissue paper" scars); annular pattern.
  • Mucous membranes — palate perforation (cleft palate); nasal septum perforation (saddle nose).
  • Bones — periostitis, osteitis (tibia, skull, clavicle); Charcot joints (neuropathic).
  • Viscera — gumma of liver (hepar lobatum), testis, stomach, lung, brain.
  • Responds dramatically to penicillin.

4b. Cardiovascular Syphilis

  • Occurs 10–30 years after primary infection.
  • Aortitis — infection of vasa vasorum of aorta → ischaemic necrosis of aortic media → aneurysm of ascending aorta & arch.
  • Clinical:
    • Aortic regurgitation — dilatation of aortic root & valve ring; diastolic murmur; water-hammer pulse; collapsing pulse; de Musset's sign (head bobbing); Corrigan's sign (visible carotid pulsation); Quincke's pulse (nail bed pulsation).
    • Aortic aneurysm — expanding mass in mediastinum; pressure on trachea (stridor), oesophagus (dysphagia), recurrent laryngeal nerve (hoarseness); risk of rupture.
    • Coronary ostial stenosis — angina.
    • Syphilitic aortitis — "tree-bark" appearance of intima (atherosclerosis-like).
  • Often asymptomatic until complications; leading cause of death in tertiary syphilis.

4c. Neurosyphilis

Can occur at any stage but typically tertiary. Four main forms:

  • Asymptomatic neurosyphilis — CSF abnormalities (pleocytosis, raised protein, positive CSF VDRL) without symptoms.
  • Meningovascular syphilis — 5–10 years after primary; chronic basal meningitis, vasculitis of cerebral vessels → stroke (especially middle cerebral artery); cranial nerve palsies (VII, VIII); seizures; headache.
  • General paresis (General Paralysis of the Insane — GPI) — 15–20 years after primary; direct parenchymal invasion of brain.
    • Psychiatric — personality change, dementia, delusions of grandeur, mania, depression, psychosis ("general paresis of the insane").
    • Neurological — Argyll Robertson pupils (small, irregular, accommodate but do not react to light — "prostitute's pupil"); tremor of tongue & hands (flapping); dysarthria; hyperreflexia; seizures; Babinski sign.
    • Progressive dementia & death within 3–5 years if untreated.
  • Tabes dorsalis (Locomotor ataxia) — 15–30 years after primary; degeneration of posterior columns & dorsal roots of spinal cord.
    • Sensory ataxia — wide-based gait, positive Romberg, foot slap; loss of position & vibration sense; loss of deep tendon reflexes (especially knee & ankle).
    • Lightning pains — sudden, severe, lancinating pains in legs, abdomen, throat.
    • Visceral crises — abdominal pain, vomiting (gastric crisis); rectal pain (rectal crisis); laryngeal stridor.
    • Charcot joints — neuropathic arthropathy (knee, hip, ankle); painless joint destruction.
    • Argyll Robertson pupil — accommodation present, light reflex absent.
    • Bladder & bowel dysfunction — urinary retention, constipation; trophic ulcers (perforating ulcers of foot).
    • Optic atrophy — blindness.

5. Congenital Syphilis

Transplacental transmission from mother to fetus — can occur at any stage of pregnancy but highest risk in primary & secondary maternal syphilis.

  • Early congenital syphilis (0–2 years):
    • "Snuffles" — profuse blood-tinged nasal discharge (highly infectious).
    • Maculopapular rash — palms, soles, perioral, perianal; desquamation.
    • Hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, anaemia, thrombocytopenia.
    • Osteochondritis & periostitis (Parrot's pseudoparalysis — infant does not move limb due to pain).
    • Lymphadenopathy.
    • Low birth weight, failure to thrive.
  • Late congenital syphilis (>2 years):
    • Hutchinson's triad: (1) Hutchinson's teeth — notched, peg-shaped permanent central incisors; (2) interstitial keratitis — bilateral corneal inflammation → opacity, blindness; (3) eighth nerve deafness (sensorineural, late onset).
    • Mulberry molars — multiple small cusps on first molars.
    • Saddle nose deformity, frontal bossing (Parrot's nodes), short maxilla, high arched palate, protuberant mandible ("bulldog" facies).
    • Saber shins (anterior bowing of tibia), scaphoid scapula, Clutton joints (painless knee effusion).
    • Rhagades — linear scars radiating from angles of mouth, nose, anus.
    • Mental retardation, seizures.

Laboratory Diagnosis

  • Direct detection
    • Dark-field microscopy — exudate from chancre, condyloma latum, mucous patch, snuffles → characteristic corkscrew motility.
    • DFA-TP (direct fluorescent antibody) — more sensitive & specific.
    • PCR — research; detects T. pallidum DNA.
  • Non-treponemal serology (reagin tests) — detect anti-lipoidal antibodies (reagin) produced in response to lipoidal antigens released from damaged tissues & T. pallidum cell wall.
    • VDRL (Venereal Disease Research Laboratory) — flocculation test; quantitative (titre); screening.
    • RPR (Rapid Plasma Reagin) — similar to VDRL; macroscopic flocculation; faster.
    • USR (Unheated Serum Reagin), TRUST.
    • Titres correlate with disease activity — used to monitor treatment response (4-fold fall in titre at 6 months indicates adequate therapy).
    • False positive — pregnancy, autoimmune disease (SLE), malaria, leprosy, HIV, vaccination, IV drug use, old age.
    • False negative — prozone phenomenon (high antibody titre in secondary syphilis → false negative; dilute serum & retest).
  • Treponemal serology (specific tests) — detect antibodies against T. pallidum antigens.
    • FTA-ABS (Fluorescent Treponemal Antibody Absorption) — indirect immunofluorescence; sensitive & specific.
    • TPHA (T. pallidum Haemagglutination Assay) — passive haemagglutination.
    • TPPA (T. pallidum Particle Agglutination) — gelatin particle agglutination.
    • Western blot — confirms.
    • Rapid point-of-care treponemal tests — immunochromatographic; useful in field & screening.
    • EIA (enzyme immunoassay) — detects IgG, IgM; used for screening in many labs now.
  • Diagnostic algorithm:
    • Screen with VDRL/RPR → if positive, confirm with TPHA/FTA-ABS (treponemal test).
    • "Reverse algorithm": screen with EIA (treponemal) → if positive, do RPR (non-treponemal) for disease activity.
  • CSF examination — for suspected neurosyphilis: CSF VDRL (specific but insensitive), CSF protein, cells (lymphocytic pleocytosis), CSF FTA-ABS (sensitive but less specific).

Treatment

  • Drug of choice — Penicillin G (only antibiotic with proven efficacy for syphilis, especially neurosyphilis & pregnancy).
    • Primary, secondary, early latent — Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM single dose.
    • Late latent, gumma, cardiovascular — Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM weekly × 3 doses.
    • Neurosyphilis — IV Aqueous crystalline penicillin G 18–24 million units/day (3–4 MU every 4 h) × 10–14 days.
    • Congenital syphilis — IV or IM aqueous crystalline penicillin G 50,000 U/kg every 12 h × 10 days.
  • Penicillin allergy (non-pregnant):
    • Doxycycline 100 mg BD × 14 days (early syphilis).
    • Tetracycline 500 mg QID × 14 days.
    • Ceftriaxone 1–2 g IV/IM daily × 8–10 days (early syphilis; cross-reactivity with penicillin, test dose).
    • Azithromycin 2 g single dose — resistance reported (macrolide resistance — 23S rRNA mutation A2058G).
    • For late syphilis — doxycycline × 28 days.
  • Pregnancy — penicillin is the only option; desensitise if allergic.
  • Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction
    • Acute worsening of symptoms within 2–12 h of treatment (fever, chills, myalgia, headache, hypotension); due to massive release of lipopolysaccharide-like endotoxin from killed spirochaetes.
    • Most common in secondary syphilis.
    • Self-limiting (24 h); treat with antipyretics, fluids.
    • Risk in pregnancy — fetal distress, preterm labour; monitor.

Prevention

  • Safe sexual practices — condoms, mutual monogamy.
  • Screening — pregnant women (first antenatal visit, repeat in 3rd trimester if high risk); MSM; HIV-positive; sexual contacts of infected individuals.
  • Notification & treatment of partners — primary (3 months), secondary (6 months), latent (1 year).
  • Education — importance of completing treatment; follow-up serology.

Clinical Pearl

The single most important clinical clue to secondary syphilis is a painless rash on the palms & soles — few other conditions cause palmar-plantar rashes ( Rocky Mountain spotted fever, meningococcaemia, hand-foot-mouth disease, Kawasaki). Hutchinson's triad (Hutchinson's teeth, interstitial keratitis, 8th nerve deafness) is pathognomonic of late congenital syphilis. Argyll Robertson pupil (accommodates but does not react to light — "prostitute's pupil: accommodates but does not react") is classic for neurosyphilis (tabes dorsalis & general paresis) — also seen in diabetes. VDRL/RPR titre falls 4-fold (2 dilutions) within 6–12 months after adequate treatment — failure to fall suggests treatment failure, reinfection, or co-infection with HIV. Prozone phenomenon — false-negative VDRL in secondary syphilis due to very high antibody levels; if suspicion high, dilute serum 1:16 or 1:32 & retest. Penicillin is the only drug proven effective for syphilis in pregnancy & neurosyphilis — desensitise penicillin-allergic pregnant women. Always test for HIV in syphilis patients (co-infection common; HIV accelerates syphilis progression & may cause treatment failure). Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction — warn patient; self-limiting; antipyretics. Syphilis is resurging globally — especially in MSM, HIV-positive, and bisexual men; screen high-risk groups annually.
q1_1_1_7:
Introduction

Neurocysticercosis (NCC) — infection of the central nervous system by the larval stage of Taenia solium (pork tapeworm) — is the most common parasitic disease of the CNS worldwide and the leading cause of acquired epilepsy in adults in endemic regions (Latin America, India, sub-Saharan Africa, China, SE Asia).

Etiology

  • Taenia solium — pork tapeworm.
    • Definitive host — human (adult tapeworm in small intestine; taeniasis).
    • Intermediate host — pig (cysticercus cellulosae in muscle); humans (accidental — cysticercosis).
  • Humans develop NCC by ingesting T. solium eggs (faecal-oral route) — NOT by eating undercooked pork (that causes intestinal taeniasis).
  • Sources of eggs — food/water contaminated with human faeces from a tapeworm carrier; autoinfection (reverse peristalsis brings gravid proglottids/eggs from intestine to stomach; or faecal-oral self-infection).
  • Eggs hatch in stomach & upper small intestine → oncospheres (hexacanth embryos) penetrate intestinal wall → enter bloodstream → disseminate to brain, eye, muscle, subcutaneous tissue → develop into cysticerci (fluid-filled cysts with invaginated scolex).

Types of Cysts in Brain

  • Parenchymal — most common; cerebral cortex (especially near grey-white junction); single or multiple; size 5–20 mm.
  • Subarachnoid/intraventricular — basal cisterns; may cause hydrocephalus; racemose (grape-like, no scolex) form in basal cisterns.
  • Intraventricular — 4th ventricle most common; obstructive hydrocephalus; can be fatal.
  • Spinal cord — rare; subarachnoid or intramedullary.
  • Ocular — subretinal, vitreous; visual loss.
  • Stages of cyst evolution:
    1. Vesicular — viable cyst; clear fluid; viable scolex; minimal inflammation (immune evasion).
    2. Colloidal vesicular — degenerating cyst; turbid fluid; surrounding inflammation (oedema); clinical symptoms begin.
    3. Granular nodular — cyst retracts; oedema decreases; scolex calcifies.
    4. Calcified — dead cyst; calcified nodule; no oedema; may still cause seizures (focus of gliosis).

Clinical Manifestations

Depends on number, location, size, and stage of cysts; immune response of host.

1. Seizures — Most Common Presentation

  • Acute symptomatic seizures — when cyst degenerates (colloidal stage); inflammatory oedema irritates cortex → focal seizures with or without secondary generalisation; most common presentation (~70–80% of patients).
  • Late-onset seizures — after cyst calcifies; gliosis around calcified lesion acts as epileptic focus; may persist for years.
  • NCC is the most common cause of adult-onset partial epilepsy in endemic areas.

2. Headache

  • Due to raised intracranial pressure (multiple cysts, hydrocephalus, arachnoiditis) or cyst degeneration.
  • Migraine-like or tension-type; chronic.

3. Raised Intracranial Pressure

  • Multiple parenchymal cysts with oedema; intraventricular cyst with obstructive hydrocephalus; racemose cyst in basal cisterns causing communicating hydrocephalus.
  • Papilloedema, nausea, vomiting, altered sensorium; sixth nerve palsy (false localising sign).
  • Cysticercal encephalitis — diffuse brain oedema in patients with massive cyst load; life-threatening.

4. Meningitis

  • Chronic cysticercal arachnoiditis — chronic basal meningitis; lymphocytic pleocytosis in CSF; may mimic TB meningitis.
  • Cranial nerve palsies (especially II, III, VI, VII, VIII); communicating hydrocephalus.

5. Focal Neurological Deficits

  • Stroke — cysticercal vasculitis (inflammation of arteries in subarachnoid space); small vessel ischaemic stroke.
  • Cranial nerve palsy.
  • Spinal cord compression (rare).

6. Cognitive & Psychiatric

  • Dementia, behavioural changes (especially in chronic NCC with multiple calcifications).
  • Developmental delay in children.

7. Ocular Cysticercosis

  • Subretinal cyst — visual loss, retinal detachment.
  • Vitreous cyst — floaters, visual disturbance.
  • Conjunctival, extraocular muscle cyst — pain, diplopia.

8. Subcutaneous/Muscular Cysticercosis

  • Palpable subcutaneous nodules (rice-grain size); painless; may calcify (visible on X-ray as elliptical "cigar-shaped" calcifications in muscle).

Diagnosis

1. Neuroimaging — CT / MRI

  • CT findings:
    • Vesicular stage — cyst with scolex ("hole-with-dot" sign); CSF-density cyst in brain parenchyma; no oedema.
    • Colloidal stage — ring-enhancing lesion with surrounding oedema; scolex may be visible.
    • Granular stage — shrinking cyst; less oedema; nodular enhancement.
    • Calcified stage — small hyperdense calcified nodules (1–5 mm); no oedema; no enhancement.
    • Multiple cysts — "starry sky" appearance.
    • Hydrocephalus, basal arachnoiditis — in subarachnoid/intraventricular NCC.
  • MRI findings:
    • Better than CT for:
      • Intraventricular cysts (CSF flow void; may need CISS/FIESTA sequence).
      • Subarachnoid cysts (basal cisterns).
      • Spinal cysts.
      • Scolex ("hole-with-dot") — hyperintense on T1, hypointense on T2.
      • Oedema assessment.
    • Vesicular cyst — CSF signal on T1 & T2; scolex visible as eccentric nodule.
    • Colloidal cyst — T1 hyperintense (proteinaceous fluid); T2 hyperintense with surrounding oedema; ring enhancement post-gadolinium.
    • Calcified — hypointense on T2* (susceptibility sequence); may be missed on routine MRI — CT better for calcifications.

2. Immunological Tests

  • ELISA for anti-cysticercal antibodies — serum; sensitivity 65–85%; specificity 90% (lower in endemic areas due to background seroprevalence).
  • EITB (Enzyme-linked immunoelectrotransfer blot) — CDC-50 kd lentil lectin-agglutinated glycoprotein blot:
    • Gold standard serology; sensitivity 98% (multiple cysts), 60–70% (single cyst).
    • Specificity 100%.
    • Detects antibodies to 7 specific T. solium glycoproteins (50, 42–48, 39, 24, 21, 14, 13 kDa); positive if any one band present.
  • CSF ELISA / EITB — more sensitive than serum for subarachnoid/intraventricular NCC; CSF eosinophilia supportive.
  • Antigen detection — detects circulating cysticercal antigen (HP10 antigen); useful for viable cysts; monitors treatment response. Monoclonal antibody-based.

3. Stool Examination

  • Detect T. solium eggs or proglottids in stool — identifies tapeworm carrier (source of eggs); treat carrier to prevent autoinfection & spread.
  • Eggs — spherical, 30–40 µm, thick brown striated embryophore with hexacanth embryo (oncosphere) with 3 pairs of hooklets; indistinguishable from T. saginata eggs.
  • Proglottids — T. solium has 7–13 lateral uterine branches per side; T. saginata has 15–20.
  • Sensitive — perianal swab (NIH swab) or Scotch tape test.

4. Other Tests

  • CSF analysis — pleocytosis (lymphocytic/eosinophilic), raised protein, low glucose (in arachnoiditis); positive CSF EITB.
  • X-ray soft tissue (thigh, calf) — "cigar-shaped" or "rice-grain" calcifications in muscle (pathognomonic).
  • Biopsy of subcutaneous nodule — cysticercus cellulosae (cyst with invaginated scolex, hooklets).
  • Fundus examination — to exclude ocular cysticercosis (before starting antiparasitic treatment; ocular cysts can be worsened by albendazole → irreversible blindness).

5. Diagnostic Criteria — Del Brutto et al. (Revised 2017)

Absolute (1): cysticercal cyst on biopsy or imaging (scolex within cyst).

Neuroimaging (major): lesion with scolex; multilobulated cyst in basal cisterns; enhancing lesion; calcification(s).

Clinical (major): seizures; typical CT/MRI features.

Immunological (major): EITB positive.

Epidemiological (minor): household contact with T. solium; travel to endemic area.

Definitive diagnosis — 1 absolute OR 2 major + 1 minor + imaging.

Treatment

1. Antiparasitic Therapy

  • Albendazole 15 mg/kg/day (max 1200 mg/day) in 2 divided doses × 7–14 days — drug of choice; kills cysts by inhibiting microtubule polymerisation.
  • Praziquantel 50–100 mg/kg/day in 3 divided doses × 15 days — alternative.
  • Combination (albendazole + praziquantel) — more effective for multiple cysts.
  • Contraindicated: ocular cysticercosis (irreversible blindness from inflammation); spinal cord cyst (risk of oedema → paralysis) — surgical removal preferred.
  • Indications: viable cysts (vesicular & colloidal stages); multiple cysts; symptomatic subarachnoid cysts.
  • Not indicated for calcified cysts (dead cysts — no antiparasitic effect; just seizure management).

2. Corticosteroids

  • Dexamethasone or prednisolone — given before & during antiparasitic therapy to prevent inflammatory response to dying cysts (oedema → raised ICP → seizures, encephalitis).
  • Dexamethasone 8–12 mg/day starting 1–2 days before albendazole; continue for 4–7 days, then taper.
  • For cysticercal encephalitis — high-dose IV steroids; delay antiparasitic until oedema controlled.

3. Anticonvulsants

  • Levetiracetam, phenytoin, carbamazepine, valproate — for seizure control.
  • Continue for 1–2 years after seizure-free; may be lifelong if calcified lesion remains epileptogenic.
  • Withdrawal of AED after calcification — controversial; recurrence risk ~40%.

4. Surgical / Interventional

  • VP shunt — for hydrocephalus (intraventricular cyst, basal arachnoiditis); may need revision (shunt malfunction from high CSF protein).
  • Neuroendoscopic removal — for intraventricular cysts; preferred over open surgery.
  • Resective surgery — for drug-resistant epilepsy with calcified epileptic focus.
  • Ocular cysticercosis — surgical removal (vitrectomy); no antiparasitic.
  • Spinal cyst — surgical decompression & removal.

5. Symptomatic & Supportive

  • Osmotic agents (mannitol) for raised ICP.
  • Analgesics for headache.
  • Treat tapeworm carrier (source) — niclosamide or praziquantel single dose.

Prevention

  • Proper sanitation & safe water.
  • Avoid eating undercooked pork (kills cysticerci).
  • Wash hands before eating; wash vegetables thoroughly.
  • Treat tapeworm carriers — screen household contacts of NCC patients.
  • Pig vaccination (TSOL18 vaccine) & deworming (oxfendazole) — control in endemic areas.
  • Meat inspection; proper cooking (≥60 °C internal temperature); freezing (-10 °C × 4 days) kills cysticerci.
  • Health education.

Clinical Pearl

NCC is the most common cause of adult-onset partial epilepsy in India — always suspect in any adult presenting with new-onset seizures, especially from an endemic area (UP, Bihar, Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan, Andhra Pradesh). The "hole-with-dot" sign (cyst with eccentric scolex) on CT/MRI is pathognomonic. Always examine fundus before starting albendazole — ocular cysticercosis can be worsened by antiparasitic-induced inflammation → irreversible blindness; requires surgical removal. Always give corticosteroids (dexamethasone) before & during antiparasitic therapy — dying cysts release antigens causing intense inflammation → oedema, raised ICP, seizures, encephalitis. Calcified cysts do not require antiparasitic treatment — they are dead; treat seizures with anticonvulsants only. Intraventricular cysts require neuroendoscopic removal (not antiparasitic) — risk of sudden hydrocephalus & death if cyst obstructs foramen of Monro or 4th ventricle. CSF EITB is more sensitive than serum for subarachnoid/intraventricular NCC. Always check stool of patient & household contacts for T. solium eggs — the tapeworm carrier is the source of eggs; treating the carrier prevents further transmission & autoinfection. Pig vaccination & deworming in endemic areas is the most effective public health intervention — India's National Taeniasis/Cysticercosis Control Programme is being piloted in high-burden districts.

Introduction

Rabies — a fatal acute viral encephalomyelitis caused by Lyssavirus (family Rhabdoviridae) — is transmitted through saliva of rabid animals (dogs in 99% of human cases; also cats, monkeys, bats, foxes, jackals, mongooses, cows). Once symptoms appear, rabies is virtually 100% fatal. Therefore, post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) immediately after exposure is the only way to prevent death. India accounts for ~36% of global rabies deaths (~20,000 annually).

Categories of Exposure (WHO)

Category Type of exposure Recommended PEP
ITouching, feeding animal; licks on intact skinNone — wash with soap & water; no vaccine
IINibbling uncovered skin; minor scratches without bleedingWound care + vaccine (no RIG)
IIISingle/multiple bites/scratches that break skin; contamination of mucous membrane with saliva; licks on broken skin; exposure to bats; head/neck bitesWound care + RIG + vaccine

Steps in PEP

Step 1 — Immediate Wound Care (most important & often neglected)

  1. Wash wound immediately & thoroughly with soap & running water for at least 15 minutes — mechanical removal of virus.
  2. Then wash with povidone-iodine or 70% alcohol — virucidal action.
  3. Do NOT suture the wound — if unavoidable, delay suturing; infiltrate wound with RIG first.
  4. Do NOT apply irritants — chillies, oil, turmeric, lime (traditional remedies; harmful; increase viral spread).
  5. Apply sterile dressing.
  6. Tetanus prophylaxis — tetanus toxoid + TIG if indicated.
  7. Antibiotics — broad-spectrum (amoxicillin-clavulanate; or doxycycline + metronidazole) if wound infected or deep puncture; cover Pasteurella, anaerobes, S. aureus, Capnocytophaga.

Step 2 — Rabies Immunoglobulin (RIG) — for Category III exposure

  • Equine Rabies Immunoglobulin (ERIG) — 40 IU/kg body weight; cheaper; risk of serum sickness & anaphylaxis (skin test required previously; WHO now says no skin test needed if properly purified).
  • Human Rabies Immunoglobulin (HRIG) — 20 IU/kg body weight; safer; more expensive; no skin test required.
  • Administration:
    • Infiltrate as much as possible into & around the wound — neutralises virus at site of inoculation.
    • Remaining dose — IM at distant site (deltoid or anterolateral thigh; NOT gluteal — fat reduces absorption).
    • If multiple wounds — dilute RIG with sterile normal saline to infiltrate all wounds.
    • If wound is on a digit — infiltrate carefully (avoid compartment syndrome); use a 25-gauge needle.
    • Must be given within 7 days of first vaccine dose — after that, antibody from vaccine is forming; RIG not needed.
  • Contraindication — RIG is given once in lifetime; never repeat (immune complex disease).

Step 3 — Rabies Vaccine — Active Immunisation

Types of Vaccine
  • Modern cell-culture vaccines (CCV):
    • HDCV (Human Diploid Cell Vaccine) — Mérieux; gold standard; expensive.
    • PCECV (Purified Chick Embryo Cell Vaccine) — Rabipur; widely used.
    • PDEV (Purified Duck Embryo Vaccine) — Vaxirab.
    • Vero cell vaccine — Abhayrab, Indirab; cost-effective; widely used in India.
    • Recombinant vaccine — experimental.
  • Nerve tissue vaccine (NTV) — Semple vaccine (sheep brain — BPL-inactivated); obsolete & not recommended by WHO; still used in some Indian government centres due to cost; high risk of neuroparalytic complications (1 in 200–2000).
Dose & Route
  • Single dose — 1 vial (1.0 mL) regardless of age or weight (intramuscular) OR 0.1 mL (intradermal).
  • Reconstitute immediately before use; discard if not used within 6 hours.
Routes of Administration
  • Intramuscular (IM):
    • Adult & child >2 years — deltoid muscle (arm).
    • Child <2 years — anterolateral thigh.
    • NEVER gluteal — fat reduces absorption; lower immunogenicity.
  • Intradermal (ID):
    • 0.1 mL at one site (raises a visible & palpable bleb).
    • WHO pre-qualifies ID route — cost-saving (60–80% less vaccine); immunogenic equivalent to IM.
    • Used in India, Thailand, Sri Lanka, Philippines.
    • Site — deltoid (adults); anterolateral thigh (children <2 years).
    • Contraindicated — chloroquine therapy (reduces ID response; use IM), immunosuppression.
Schedules
Schedule Route Days Indication
Essen (5-dose IM)IM, deltoidDays 0, 3, 7, 14, 28 (5 doses)Standard PEP — previously unvaccinated
Essen (4-dose IM)IM, deltoidDays 0 (2 sites), 7, 21Alternative
Updated Thai Red Cross (2-2-2-0-2 ID)ID, 2 sitesDays 0, 3, 7, 28 (2 injections per visit at 2 different sites) — total 8 injectionsStandard ID PEP — WHO recommended
IPC (1-week ID)ID, 2 sitesDays 0, 3, 7 — 2 injections per visitShorter schedule; WHO approved 2018
4-site IDID, 4 sites on day 0 + 1 site days 7 & 28Day 0 (4 sites), Day 7 (1 site), Day 28 (1 site)Alternative
Previously vaccinated (any PEP schedule)IM (1 dose) or ID (2 sites)Days 0 & 3 — 2 doses onlyFor re-exposure — no RIG needed

Step 4 — Observe the Animal

  • If dog/cat available for observation — confine & observe for 10 days.
    • If animal remains healthy for 10 days — rabies ruled out; can discontinue vaccination after day 3 (no need for full course).
    • If animal dies or shows rabies signs — continue full course + RIG.
  • For other animals (wild, stray, livestock) — assume rabid; give full PEP.
  • If animal escapes — assume rabid; full PEP.
  • Laboratory confirmation of animal — fluorescent antibody test (FAT) on brain tissue (hippocampus, cerebellum, brainstem); mouse inoculation test (historical); PCR (research).

Step 5 — Special Situations

  • Previously vaccinated patients — 2 doses on days 0 & 3 (IM or ID); NO RIG.
  • Immunocompromised patients — full course + RIG (Category II & III); check seroconversion (neutralising antibody titre ≥0.5 IU/mL) 2–4 weeks after last dose; if inadequate, repeat dose.
  • Pregnancy — not a contraindication; rabies vaccine & RIG are safe.
  • Infants & children — same dose as adults (ID 0.1 mL; IM 1.0 mL); site varies.
  • HIV-positive — full course; check seroconversion; consider extra dose if CD4 <200.
  • Chloroquine therapy — avoid ID route; use IM.
  • Delayed presentation — even months/years after exposure, start PEP (incubation may be prolonged).

Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP) — for High-Risk Individuals

  • Veterinarians, animal handlers, laboratory staff, travellers to endemic areas, children in endemic areas.
  • Schedule — days 0, 7, 21 (or 0, 7, 28); IM (1 mL) or ID (0.1 mL).
  • Booster — every 2–5 years; or check antibody titre (<0.5 IU/mL → booster).
  • If exposed later — only 2 doses on days 0 & 3 (no RIG needed).

Failure of PEP — Causes

  • Delay in initiating treatment.
  • Incomplete/inadequate wound care.
  • Failure to give RIG (Category III).
  • Incorrect RIG administration (not infiltrated into wound).
  • Incorrect vaccine schedule or route (gluteal injection).
  • Immunosuppression (HIV, steroids, malignancy).
  • Use of chloroquine with ID route.
  • Use of NT vaccine (Semple).
  • Severe facial/neck wounds (short incubation; virus reaches CNS before antibody).

Prevention

  • Vaccinate dogs — mass dog vaccination (>70% coverage) interrupts transmission; most effective public health intervention.
  • Stray dog control — animal birth control (ABC) programme.
  • Public education — wash wounds immediately; seek medical care; avoid traditional remedies; vaccinate pets.
  • PrEP for high-risk groups.
  • Surveillance — report animal bites; track rabies cases.

Clinical Pearl

Rabies is 100% fatal once symptoms appear — PEP must be started immediately after exposure. The single most important intervention is thorough wound washing with soap & water for 15 minutes — mechanical removal of virus reduces infection risk by up to 90%, yet is often neglected. For Category III exposure (bite breaking skin, mucosal contamination, head/neck, bat exposure) — give BOTH RIG and vaccine. RIG provides passive immunity (neutralising antibody at wound site) during the 7–10 days before vaccine-induced antibody appears. Infiltrate RIG into & around the wound — if dose insufficient for all wounds, dilute with saline; if wound on digit, use 25-gauge needle to avoid compartment syndrome. Never inject RIG & vaccine at the same site — RIG will neutralise vaccine. Never give RIG after day 7 of vaccination — antibody already forming; RIG can cause immune complex disease. Never inject vaccine in the gluteal region — fat reduces absorption; use deltoid (adults & children ≥2 yr) or anterolateral thigh (infants). Intradermal route saves 60–80% of vaccine cost — India's National Rabies Control Programme uses ID route widely. Observe dog for 10 days — if healthy, discontinue vaccination after day 3. The Milwaukee Protocol (induced coma + antiviral cocktails) has saved ~5 patients worldwide with clinical rabies — experimental, not standard; PEP remains the only reliable prevention. India's National Action Plan for Dog Mediated Rabies Elimination (NAPRE) by 2030 aims to eliminate rabies through mass dog vaccination & PEP access.
q1_1_1_9:
Introduction

Tetanus is an acute fatal disease caused by Clostridium tetani — a Gram-positive, anaerobic, spore-forming, drumstick-shaped bacillus — through its exotoxin tetanospasmin (a neurotoxin that blocks inhibitory neurotransmitter release at spinal synapses, causing severe muscle spasms). Diagnosis is clinical; lab tests are supportive.

Laboratory Diagnosis

1. Specimen

  • Wound swab/pus from entry wound (umbilical stump in neonatal tetanus, post-natal septic abortion, surgical wound, chronic ulcer, injection site).
  • Tissue biopsy from wound edge.
  • CSF — usually normal (helps exclude other causes of meningismus); no organisms.

2. Direct Microscopy

  • Gram stain — Gram-positive bacilli with terminal drumstick-shaped spores (round terminal spore gives characteristic drumstick appearance); may be Gram-variable in old cultures.
  • Spores are heat-resistant (boil 100 °C × 1 h survives); survive in soil for years.
  • Limit — microscopy alone is non-diagnostic (C. tetani may be present in normal flora; morphology alone cannot confirm toxin production).

3. Culture

  • Robertson's cooked meat (RCM) broth — anaerobic; C. tetani grows with gas, digests meat slowly; produces "drumstick" bacilli.
  • Blood agar — anaerobic incubation; swarming growth (translucent film) due to motility; important to identify.
  • Nitrate-mannitol agar — selective.
  • Trypticase sulfite neomycin agar.
  • Incubation — 37 °C, 24–48 h, anaerobic (GasPak jar, anaerobic chamber).

4. Identification

  • Gram stain — terminal drumstick spores; Gram-positive bacilli.
  • Motility — motile (swarming on blood agar).
  • Biochemical tests — indole positive, nitrate negative, gelatin liquefaction positive, no sugar fermentation.
  • Toxigenicity testing — most important.
    • Animal inoculation (mouse bioassay) — gold standard; inject culture filtrate into mice: one group unprotected, one protected with tetanus antitoxin. Unprotected mice develop tetanic spasms & die; protected mice survive.
    • PCR — detects tetX gene (toxin gene); faster but not widely available.
    • ELISA — detects toxin in culture filtrate.

5. Serology

  • Anti-tetanus antibody titre — to assess immune status; ≥0.1 IU/mL is protective.
  • Useful for diagnosing inadequate immunity in patients with tetanus (most have <0.01 IU/mL).
  • Not diagnostic of acute disease — tetanus toxin is so potent that disease can occur without measurable antibody response.

6. Other Tests

  • Clinical diagnosis — based on trismus (lockjaw), risus sardonicus, opisthotonus, muscle spasms, intact sensorium, normal CSF.
  • CBC — leucocytosis.
  • Electromyography (EMG) — continuous motor unit discharges; loss of silent period after masseter reflex.
  • Wound culture — supports diagnosis but not necessary if clinical signs present.

Prevention

1. Active Immunisation — Tetanus Toxoid (TT)

  • Toxoid — formaldehyde-treated tetanospasmin; loses toxicity but retains antigenicity; adsorbed on aluminium hydroxide adjuvant.
  • Types
    • DTP — diphtheria + tetanus + whole-cell pertussis.
    • DTaP — diphtheria + tetanus + acellular pertussis.
    • Td / Tdap — reduced-dose diphtheria + tetanus ± acellular pertussis (booster for adolescents/adults).
    • TT (tetanus toxoid alone) — for adults.
    • Pentavalent vaccine — DTP + Hepatitis B + Hib (used in India's UIP).
  • Schedule (India — NIS):
    • Primary — 3 doses at 6, 10, 14 weeks.
    • Boosters — at 16–18 months & 5 years.
    • Then Td at 10 & 16 years.
    • Adults — booster every 10 years (Td).
  • Efficacy — >95% after complete primary series; wanes over 10 years.
  • Pregnancy — Td given during each pregnancy (2 doses in 1st pregnancy; 1 dose in subsequent); protects neonate via transplacental antibody.

2. Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (PEP) for Wounds

Wound type Immune status (vaccinated) PEP
Clean, minor wound (<6 h old, no contamination)≥3 doses TT, last <10 yrNo TT needed
<3 doses or unknown / last >10 yrTT booster
Tetanus-prone wound (contaminated, >6 h, deep puncture, crush, foreign body, animal bite, burn, frostbite, septic abortion, unsterile delivery)≥3 doses TT, last <5 yrNo TT or TIG needed
<3 doses or unknown / last >5 yrTT booster + TIG 250 IU IM

3. Passive Immunisation — Tetanus Immune Globulin (TIG)

  • Human tetanus immune globulin (HTIG) — 250 IU IM (for tetanus-prone wounds in unimmunised); 3000–6000 IU IM/IV (for treatment of clinical tetanus).
  • Equine tetanus antitoxin (ATS) — 1500 IU SC/IM after skin test (cheaper; risk of serum sickness; mostly replaced by HTIG in modern practice).
  • Given at separate site from TT (different syringe, different limb).

4. Treatment of Clinical Tetanus

  • Supportive — ICU admission; quiet dark environment; avoid stimuli; muscle relaxants (diazepam IV — drug of choice for spasms; midazolam, propofol, magnesium sulphate infusion); mechanical ventilation if respiratory compromise; tracheostomy.
  • Neutralise unbound toxin — HTIG 3000–6000 IU IM (or IV preparation) — neutralises circulating toxin only (does NOT reverse bound toxin); give ASAP.
  • Eliminate organism — IV Metronidazole 500 mg QID × 7–10 days (drug of choice); Penicillin G (alternative; theoretical concern — GABA antagonist may worsen spasms); debride wound.
  • Active immunisation — TT must be given at recovery (clinical tetanus does NOT confer immunity — toxin amount too small to trigger antibody response); full primary series.
  • Autonomic dysfunction — labetalol, morphine, clonidine for sympathetic overactivity; atropine for bradycardia.

5. Other Preventive Measures

  • Proper wound care — clean with soap & water; debride necrotic tissue; remove foreign bodies.
  • Sterile technique in surgery & deliveries.
  • Safe abortion & clean cord care in newborns.
  • Health education.

Clinical Pearl

Tetanus is a clinical diagnosis — do NOT wait for lab confirmation. The classic tetrad is trismus (lockjaw), risus sardonicus (sardonic smile), opisthotonus, and intact sensorium. The incubation period inversely correlates with severity — <7 days portends severe disease & poor prognosis. Neonatal tetanus — from cutting umbilical cord with unsterile instrument or applying cow dung/ash — remains a leading cause of neonatal mortality in unimmunised populations; preventable by maternal TT immunisation & clean delivery practices. Cephalic tetanus — cranial nerve palsies (especially VII) after head/face wound or otitis media; may progress to generalised tetanus. Always immunise recovered tetanus patients — the disease does not confer immunity (toxin dose too small); full primary TT series is mandatory. Magnesium sulphate infusion is now standard adjunct for severe tetanus — controls spasms & autonomic dysfunction; reduces need for mechanical ventilation. Metronidazole is preferred over penicillin — penicillin is a GABA antagonist that may worsen spasms. India's Maternal & Neonatal Tetanus Elimination (MNTE) — achieved WHO elimination status in 2015 (<1 case per 1000 live births in every district) through universal TT immunisation of pregnant women & clean delivery practices.

Introduction

Vaginal candidiasis (vulvovaginal candidiasis — VVC) is a fungal infection of the vulva & vagina caused by Candida species — most commonly Candida albicans (~85–90%). Affects ~75% of women at least once in lifetime; 5–8% develop recurrent VVC (≥4 episodes/year).

Etiology

  • Candida albicans — most common (~85–90%); forms germ tubes & chlamydospores.
  • Non-albicans Candida — C. glabrata (5–10%; increasingly resistant to azoles), C. tropicalis, C. parapsilosis, C. krusei (intrinsic fluconazole resistance), C. lusitaniae (amphotericin B resistance).
  • Candida — dimorphic fungus; yeast form in vagina; forms pseudohyphae & true hyphae in tissue; budding yeast (blastoconidia) 3–6 µm.
  • Normal commensal of vagina in ~20% of women; overgrowth causes infection.

Risk Factors

  • Antibiotic use — destroys normal vaginal lactobacilli → loss of acidic pH → Candida overgrowth (most common risk factor).
  • Pregnancy — high oestrogen → increased glycogen in vaginal epithelium → Candida growth; 2–10× more common.
  • Diabetes mellitus — uncontrolled; high vaginal glucose.
  • Immunosuppression — HIV/AIDS, steroids, chemotherapy, malignancy.
  • Oestrogen-containing oral contraceptives or hormone replacement therapy.
  • Intrauterine device (IUD).
  • Poor hygiene, tight synthetic underwear (warm, moist environment).
  • Douching — disrupts normal flora.
  • Iron deficiency anaemia, hypothyroidism, Cushing's syndrome.

Clinical Features

  • Pruritus vulvae — intense itching; most prominent symptom.
  • Vaginal discharge — thick, white, curdy ("cottage cheese"-like), odourless; adherent to vaginal walls.
  • Burning — vulva, especially on urination (dysuria) or intercourse (dyspareunia).
  • Erythema & oedema of vulva & vagina; fissures, excoriations from scratching.
  • Satellite lesions — pustules surrounding erythematous area on vulva/perineum.
  • Vaginal pH — normal (4.0–4.5); distinguishes from bacterial vaginosis (pH >4.5) and trichomoniasis (pH >5.0).
  • Whiff test (KOH) — negative (distinguishes from BV — positive "fishy" odour).

Laboratory Diagnosis

1. Clinical Specimen

  • Vaginal discharge — collected with speculum using sterile swab; from posterior fornix & lateral vaginal wall.

2. Direct Microscopy

  • Wet mount (saline) — budding yeast cells (3–6 µm), pseudohyphae; few WBCs.
  • 10% KOH mount — dissolves epithelial cells & debris; easier to see yeast & pseudohyphae (sensitivity 50–70%).
  • Gram stain — Gram-positive budding yeast cells & pseudohyphae; sensitivity higher than wet mount (~80%).

3. Culture

  • Sabouraud dextrose agar (SDA) — creamy white pasty colonies in 24–48 h at 37 °C.
  • Chromogenic Candida agar (CHROMagar) — differentiates species by colony colour:
    • C. albicans — green.
    • C. tropicalis — blue/purple.
    • C. krusei — pink, fuzzy.
    • C. glabrata — pink/white.
    • C. parapsilosis — cream/pink.
  • Culture is more sensitive than microscopy — detects low-grade infection; but positive culture alone does not prove infection (20% colonisation); must correlate with symptoms.

4. Identification

  • Germ tube test — subculture in human/animal serum at 37 °C × 2–3 h; C. albicans forms germ tubes (short hyphal projections); >95% specific.
  • Chlamydospore formation — on corn meal agar; C. albicans forms chlamydospores at tips of pseudohyphae.
  • Sugar fermentation & assimilation tests — identify species.
  • API 20C AUX — commercial identification system.
  • MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry — rapid identification.
  • PCR — species identification; PNA FISH.

5. Other Tests

  • Vaginal pH measurement — normal (4.0–4.5) in candidiasis; elevated in BV & trichomoniasis.
  • Whiff (amine) test — KOH added to discharge; negative in candidiasis (positive "fishy" in BV).
  • STD screen — for recurrent or atypical cases; rule out co-infections (HIV, diabetes check).
  • Blood glucose — if recurrent; rule out diabetes.
  • HIV test — if recurrent, severe, or non-albicans species.

Differential Diagnosis

Condition Discharge pH Whiff test Microscopy
Vaginal candidiasisThick, white, curdy, odourlessNormal (4.0–4.5)NegativeYeast, pseudohyphae
Bacterial vaginosisThin, grey, homogenous, "fishy" odour>4.5Positive (fishy)Clue cells
TrichomoniasisYellow-green, frothy, malodorous>5.0VariableMotile trichomonads, many WBCs

Treatment

Uncomplicated VVC (immunocompetent, mild-moderate, <4 episodes/year, C. albicans)

  • Topical azoles (intravaginal) — clotrimazole 1% cream 5 g PV × 7–14 days; miconazole 2% cream 5 g PV × 7 days; tioconazole 6.5% ointment PV single dose; terconazole 0.4% cream × 7 days or 0.8% × 3 days; butoconazole 2% sustained release × 1 dose.
  • Oral — fluconazole 150 mg single oral dose — preferred for convenience; alternative itraconazole 200 mg BD × 1 day.
  • Cure rate 80–95%.

Complicated VVC (severe, recurrent, pregnancy, diabetes, non-albicans)

  • Severe (extensive erythema, oedema, fissures) — fluconazole 150 mg PO × 2 doses (72 h apart); or topical azole × 7–14 days.
  • Recurrent VVC (≥4 episodes/year) — induction with fluconazole 150 mg every 3 days × 3 doses; then maintenance fluconazole 150 mg weekly × 6 months.
  • Pregnancy — topical azoles only (7-day course preferred); fluconazole contraindicated in 1st trimester (teratogenic).
  • Non-albicans Candida — often azole-resistant; treat with terconazole or boric acid 600 mg PV capsule daily × 14 days (effective against C. glabrata); amphotericin B suppository rare.
  • HIV — same regimen; recurrent disease common; suppressive fluconazole weekly.

Prevention

  • Avoid unnecessary antibiotics.
  • Wear loose cotton underwear; avoid tight synthetic clothing.
  • Avoid douching; maintain natural flora.
  • Control diabetes; check blood glucose.
  • Avoid prolonged wet swimsuits; dry genital area thoroughly.
  • Probiotics (Lactobacillus) — controversial; may help prevent recurrent VVC.
  • Treat sexual partner only if symptomatic (balanitis).

Clinical Pearl

The single most useful bedside diagnostic test is the 10% KOH mount — dissolves epithelial cells, allowing clear visualisation of budding yeast & pseudohyphae. Vaginal pH is the key differentiator — normal (4.0–4.5) in candidiasis; elevated (>4.5) in bacterial vaginosis & trichomoniasis. Fluconazole 150 mg single oral dose is the standard first-line for uncomplicated VVC — convenient, effective, well-tolerated; 80–95% cure rate. Recurrent VVC (≥4 episodes/year) — check HIV, diabetes, thyroid; consider maintenance fluconazole weekly × 6 months. Non-albicans Candida (especially C. glabrata & C. krusei) are often fluconazole-resistant — use boric acid vaginal capsules (600 mg PV daily × 14 days) or terconazole. Pregnancy — topical azoles only (7-day course); avoid oral fluconazole (teratogenic in 1st trimester — case-control studies show increased risk of miscarriage & congenital anomalies). Always exclude diabetes in recurrent VVC — uncontrolled diabetes is the most common underlying cause; control blood glucose to prevent recurrences. Asymptomatic Candida colonisation does not require treatment — 20% of women have Candida in vagina without symptoms; treat only symptomatic cases.

Introduction

Oncogenic viruses (oncoviruses) are viruses that can cause cancer in humans. Approximately 15–20% of all human cancers are virus-associated. The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) has classified several viruses as Group 1 carcinogens. They cause cancer through mechanisms including insertional mutagenesis, oncogene activation, tumour suppressor inactivation, chronic inflammation, and immunosuppression.

Mechanism of Viral Oncogenesis

1. Direct Mechanism

  • Insertional mutagenesis — viral DNA integrates into host genome near proto-oncogene → activates it (e.g., HBV integration near c-myc, cyclin A).
  • Oncogene expression — virus carries viral oncogene (v-onc) homologous to cellular proto-oncogene (c-onc) → uncontrolled proliferation (e.g., HTLV-1 tax; EBV LMP1 mimics CD40 signalling; HHV-8 vGPCR).
  • Tumour suppressor inactivation — viral proteins bind & degrade/inactivate p53 & Rb:
    • HPV E6 → E6AP ubiquitin ligase → p53 degradation.
    • HPV E7 → Rb sequestration → E2F release → S-phase entry.
    • SV40/MCV large T antigen → Rb & p53 binding.
    • HBV HBx → p53 sequestration; transcriptional transactivator.
    • EBV LMP1 → BCL-2 upregulation (anti-apoptotic); NF-κB activation.
  • Anti-apoptotic mechanisms — EBV BHRF1 (BCL-2 homologue); HPV E5, E6.
  • Genomic instability — viral proteins cause DNA damage, centrosome amplification (HPV E6, E7).

2. Indirect Mechanism

  • Chronic inflammation — HBV/HCV → chronic hepatitis → cirrhosis → HCC (80% of virus-associated HCC arises in cirrhotic liver); inflammatory mediators (ROS, cytokines) cause DNA damage.
  • Immunosuppression — HIV (indirectly; causes immunodeficiency → allows EBV, KSHV, HPV, HBV to cause cancer — Kaposi sarcoma, non-Hodgkin lymphoma, cervical cancer). HIV itself is not oncogenic.

  • ~15–20% of human cancers are virus-associated.
  • Most common virus-associated cancers worldwide — HCC (HBV, HCV), cervical cancer (HPV), Burkitt lymphoma & nasopharyngeal carcinoma (EBV), Kaposi sarcoma (HHV-8).
  • In developing countries (including India), virus-associated cancers are more common due to high prevalence of HBV, HCV, HPV, EBV.
  • Preventable through vaccination (HBV, HPV) and antiviral therapy (HCV).

Clinical Pearl

The single most important preventive intervention against virus-associated cancer is vaccination — HBV vaccine (first anti-cancer vaccine; prevents HCC; given at birth) and HPV vaccine (Gardasil 9 — prevents cervical cancer & other HPV-associated cancers). The HPV vaccine — recommended at ages 9–14 (before sexual debut); 2-dose schedule if <15 years, 3-dose if ≥15 years or immunocompromised; gender-neutral vaccination now recommended (prevents anal, oropharyngeal, penile cancers in males). Hepatitis B vaccine — given at birth, 6, 10, 14 weeks in India's UIP; first vaccine to prevent cancer (HBV-related HCC). HCV cure with direct-acting antivirals (DAAs — sofosbuvir/velpatasvir × 12 weeks; ≥95% cure rate) prevents HCC. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma — EBV + genetic susceptibility (HLA) + nitrosamines (salted fish) — Southern China, SE Asia. Kaposi sarcoma — HHV-8 + HIV (epidemic KS); also classic (Mediterranean elderly men), endemic (Africa), iatrogenic (transplant). Merkel cell carcinoma — MCV in 80% of cases; aggressive neuroendocrine skin cancer; elderly, immunosuppressed. Always consider viral aetiology in cancer workup — tumour viral PCR may guide prognosis & therapy (e.g., EBV-positive Hodgkin lymphoma has different prognosis; HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancer responds better to treatment).

Clinical Identification

The 28-year-old woman with high-grade fever, vomiting, flank pain, and likely urinary symptoms (dysuria, frequency, urgency) — consistent with acute pyelonephritis (upper urinary tract infection). If lower urinary symptoms alone — acute cystitis. Women are at higher risk due to short urethra & proximity to anus.

Definition

Urinary tract infection (UTI) is an infection of any part of the urinary tract — bladder (cystitis), urethra (urethritis), prostate (prostatitis), kidneys (pyelonephritis). Most common bacterial infection in women; ~50% of women experience UTI in their lifetime.

Classification

  • By site — lower (cystitis, urethritis); upper (pyelonephritis).
  • By complexity — uncomplicated (healthy non-pregnant adult woman); complicated (pregnancy, male, child, catheter, urinary abnormality, diabetes, immunosuppression, recent instrumentation, recurrent, severe).
  • By acquisition — community-acquired; catheter-associated (CAUTI).

Etiology

Organism Frequency Comment
E. coli75–85%Most common; uropathogenic strains with P fimbriae (pyelonephritis), K1 capsule, haemolysin, siderophores
Klebsiella pneumoniae5–10%Diabetics, catheterised
Proteus mirabilis5%Urease producer → struvite stones; alkaline urine
Enterococcus faecalis3–5%Catheter, instrumentation
Staphylococcus saprophyticus5–10% (young women)Sexually active young women; coagulase-negative, novobiocin-resistant
Pseudomonas aeruginosa2–3%Catheterised, instrumentation, complicated
Enterobacter, Citrobacter, Serratia, Acinetobacter<5%Hospital-acquired, MDR
Staphylococcus aureus<2%Haematogenous spread — consider renal abscess, endocarditis
Candida spp.—Catheterised, diabetes, immunosuppressed, broad-spectrum antibiotics
Mycobacterium tuberculosis—Sterile pyuria; chronic; UTB

Pathogenesis

  1. Route — ascending (most common; periurethral flora → urethra → bladder → kidneys); haematogenous (S. aureus, TB); lymphatic (rare).
  2. Adherence — uropathogenic E. coli (UPEC) with type 1 fimbriae (binds uroplakin on bladder epithelium — cystitis) & P fimbriae (binds globoside on renal epithelium — pyelonephritis).
  3. Host defences — urinary flow (flushing); acidic pH; osmolality; Tamm-Horsfall protein (uromodulin); secretory IgA; bladder mucopolysaccharide; neutrophils.
  4. Risk factors:
    • Female sex (short urethra, proximity to anus).
    • Sexual activity ("honeymoon cystitis"); diaphragm + spermicide use.
    • Pregnancy (progesterone → ureteral dilatation & reflux; mechanical obstruction).
    • Postmenopause (loss of oestrogen → loss of lactobacilli → vaginal pH rises).
    • Urinary obstruction — stones, BPH, strictures, tumours, reflux (VUR).
    • Catheterisation (most common hospital risk).
    • Diabetes (immunocompromise, glycosuria, neurogenic bladder).
    • Immunosuppression.
    • Instrumentation.

Clinical Features

Lower UTI (Cystitis)

  • Dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic pain, haematuria.
  • Low-grade fever; no flank pain.

Upper UTI (Pyelonephritis)

  • High fever with chills & rigors.
  • Flank pain & costovertebral angle (CVA) tenderness.
  • Nausea, vomiting.
  • Symptoms of cystitis may or may not be present.
  • Severe — sepsis, septic shock, ARDS.

Laboratory Diagnosis

1. Urine Specimen Collection

  • Clean-catch midstream urine (MSU) — most common; clean perineum; spread labia; discard first portion; collect midstream in sterile container.
  • Catheter specimen — from port (not from bag); preferred if catheterised.
  • Suprapubic aspiration — neonates & infants; sterile bladder puncture.
  • In-out catheterisation — if MSU not possible.
  • Transport — within 2 h; refrigerate (4 °C) if delayed; boric acid preservative.

2. Urinalysis (Dipstick)

  • Leukocyte esterase — detects pus cells (WBC esterase); sensitivity 75–95%; specificity 85–95%.
  • Nitrite — bacterial reduction of nitrate to nitrite (by Enterobacterales — E. coli, Klebsiella, Proteus, Enterobacter); sensitivity 35–85%; specificity 95%; not produced by S. saprophyticus, Enterococcus, Pseudomonas.
  • Blood — haematuria (cystitis, stones, malignancy).
  • Protein — mild in UTI; nephrotic if heavy.
  • pH & specific gravity.

3. Urine Microscopy

  • Pyuria — >5–10 WBCs/HPF; indicates infection.
  • Bacteriuria — bacteria seen on Gram stain of uncentrifuged urine (≥1 organism/OIF correlates with ≥10⁵ CFU/mL).
  • Hematuria — RBCs.
  • Cast — WBC cast (pyelonephritis — distinguishes from cystitis).
  • Crystals — struvite (infection stones); calcium oxalate.

4. Urine Culture — Gold Standard

  • Semiquantitative culture — calibrated loop (0.001 mL or 0.01 mL) streaked on blood agar & MacConkey agar; incubated 37 °C × 24–48 h.
  • Significant bacteriuria:
    • ≥10⁵ CFU/mL — symptomatic women, asymptomatic (2 specimens), men.
    • ≥10⁴ CFU/mL — symptomatic women, catheterised.
    • ≥10² CFU/mL — symptomatic young women (acute cystitis); suprapubic aspirate (any number).
  • Identification — biochemical tests, MALDI-TOF, automated (Vitek 2).
  • Antibiotic susceptibility — disk diffusion or MIC; guide therapy.
  • Sterile pyuria — pyuria with negative culture — TB, Chlamydia, Ureaplasma, fungal, fastidious organisms, stones, tumour, NSAIDs.

5. Other Tests

  • Blood culture — in pyelonephritis, sepsis (positive in 10–20%).
  • CBG — leucocytosis.
  • Renal function — urea, creatinine (baseline; AKI in severe).
  • Blood glucose — rule out diabetes.
  • Imaging:
    • Ultrasound — for recurrent UTI, pyelonephritis, obstruction, stones, renal abscess.
    • CT abdomen — for complications (emphysematous pyelonephritis — diabetics; abscess; stones; obstruction).
    • MCUG (micturating cystourethrogram) — for children with recurrent UTI (VUR).

Treatment

Uncomplicated Cystitis (Female)

  • Nitrofurantoin 100 mg BD × 5 days (first-line; safe in pregnancy).
  • Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (co-trimoxazole) 960 mg BD × 3 days (first-line if local E. coli resistance <20%; avoid in pregnancy 1st trimester).
  • Fosfomycin 3 g single dose.
  • Pivmecillinam 400 mg BD × 3–7 days.
  • Fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin) — reserve; resistance rising.

Pyelonephritis (Mild — Outpatient)

  • Ciprofloxacin 500 mg BD × 7 days OR levofloxacin 750 mg OD × 5 days.
  • Co-trimoxazole 960 mg BD × 14 days (if susceptible).
  • Cefixime 400 mg OD × 7 days (alternative).

Pyelonephritis (Severe — Hospitalised)

  • IV Ceftriaxone 1–2 g OD.
  • IV Ciprofloxacin 400 mg BD.
  • IV Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g 6-hourly (if MDR suspected).
  • IV Amoxicillin-clavulanate.
  • IV Carbapenem (meropenem) — if ESBL/CRE suspected.
  • Switch to oral when afebrile 24–48 h & clinically stable; total course 7–14 days.

Special Situations

  • Pregnancy — nitrofurantoin (avoid term — haemolysis in G6PD), cephalosporins (cephalexin); avoid fluoroquinolones, co-trimoxazole (1st & 3rd trimester), tetracyclines.
  • CAUTI — remove/change catheter; treat with antibiotics targeting Enterococcus, Pseudomonas, MDR organisms.
  • Recurrent UTI — investigate (postmenopausal, diabetes, stones); consider prophylactic nitrofurantoin or co-trimoxazole (low dose, post-coital or daily); vaginal oestrogen in postmenopause.
  • Catheter-associated asymptomatic bacteriuria — do NOT treat (except pregnancy, urological procedure, neutropenia); antibiotic stewardship.

Prevention

  • Hydration — 2–3 L/day; frequent urination.
  • Post-coital voiding — flushes bacteria.
  • Wipe front to back.
  • Avoid spermicide/diaphragm in recurrent UTI.
  • Cranberry products (proanthocyanidins prevent E. coli adherence) — modest benefit.
  • Vaginal oestrogen (postmenopausal).
  • Probiotics (Lactobacillus).
  • Antibiotic prophylaxis — for recurrent UTI.
  • Vaccine (Uro-Vaxom — E. coli extract; Stirbaum; ExPEC4V conjugate in trials).
  • Catheter care — aseptic insertion, closed drainage, minimal dwell.

Clinical Pearl

The single most important diagnostic test for UTI is urine culture with susceptibility testing — guides therapy, especially with rising antibiotic resistance. Significant bacteriuria is ≥10⁵ CFU/mL in asymptomatic women (2 specimens), ≥10⁴ CFU/mL in symptomatic women/catheterised, ≥10² CFU/mL in acute cystitis in young women. Sterile pyuria (pyuria + negative routine culture) — always consider M. tuberculosis (3 early morning urines for AFB), Chlamydia trachomatis, Ureaplasma, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, fungi, fastidious organisms; also non-infectious (NSAIDs, stones, tumour, interstitial nephritis). Emphysematous pyelonephritis — gas-forming infection (E. coli, Klebsiella) in diabetics; life-threatening; requires IV antibiotics + percutaneous drainage or nephrectomy. Pregnancy UTI — always treat (even asymptomatic bacteriuria); risk of pyelonephritis, preterm labour, low birth weight; use nitrofurantoin (avoid term), cephalosporins. Acute uncomplicated cystitis in young women — empiric treatment without culture is acceptable; 3–5 days of nitrofurantoin or co-trimoxazole (if local E. coli resistance <20%). Always send culture before antibiotics for pyelonephritis, complicated UTI, recurrent UTI, pregnancy, catheterised, males — to guide targeted therapy. India has high rates of ESBL-producing E. coli in community UTI — empiric fluoroquinolones often fail; nitrofurantoin, fosfomycin, oral cephalosporins preferred first-line; carbapenems reserved for severe / MDR.

Introduction

Acute bacterial meningitis is a medical emergency — inflammation of meninges (pia, arachnoid) caused by bacterial infection. Mortality 10–30% even with treatment; permanent neurological sequelae in 20–30% of survivors. Early recognition & treatment are critical.

Etiological Agents (by age)

Age group Common organisms
Neonates (0–1 month)
  • Group B Streptococcus (S. agalactiae) — most common; maternal vaginal colonisation.
  • E. coli (K1 capsule).
  • Listeria monocytogenes — acquired transplacentally or during birth.
  • Klebsiella, other Gram-negative bacilli.
Infants & children (1 month – 5 years)
  • Streptococcus pneumoniae — most common post-Hib & pneumococcal vaccine.
  • Neisseria meningitidis — adolescents; epidemics in sub-Saharan Africa meningitis belt.
  • Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) — where vaccine not used.
Children 5–18 yr & young adults
  • N. meningitidis — most common; dormitory, military, Hajj outbreaks.
  • S. pneumoniae.
Adults 18–50 yr
  • S. pneumoniae — most common.
  • N. meningitidis.
Adults >50 yr; alcoholics; immunocompromised
  • S. pneumoniae.
  • Listeria monocytogenes — increasing; cell-mediated immunity defect.
  • Gram-negative bacilli (including Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter in neurosurgery/post-trauma).
Post-neurosurgery; CSF shunt; head trauma
  • Coagulase-negative staphylococci (CoNS — S. epidermidis).
  • S. aureus.
  • Gram-negative bacilli (Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter).
  • Propionibacterium acnes (shunt).

Other Risk Factors

  • Sickle cell disease, asplenia, complement deficiency (C5–C9) — N. meningitidis, S. pneumoniae.
  • HIV, immunosuppression — Listeria, S. pneumoniae, Cryptococcus (fungal).
  • CSF leak (otorrhoea, rhinorrhoea) — S. pneumoniae.
  • Pneumococcal pneumonia, endocarditis.
  • Pregnancy — Listeria.
  • Alcoholism — S. pneumoniae, Listeria.

Clinical Features

  • Classic triad — fever, neck stiffness, altered mental status (present in >95% of cases when at least 2 of 3 present).
  • Headache — severe, generalized; photophobia.
  • Nausea, vomiting.
  • Altered sensorium — confusion, lethargy, seizures, coma.
  • Signs of meningeal irritation — neck stiffness, Kernig's sign (inability to extend knee when hip flexed at 90°), Brudzinski's sign (neck flexion → hip/knee flexion).
  • Petechial/purpuric rash — N. meningitidis (meningococcaemia); Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome (adrenal haemorrhage, DIC, shock).
  • Focal neurological deficit — cranial nerve palsy, hemiparesis.
  • Seizures (30% in adults; 50%+ in children).
  • Infants — bulging fontanelle, irritability, poor feeding, high-pitched cry, seizures; meningeal signs may be absent.

Laboratory Diagnosis

1. Blood Culture

  • 2 sets before antibiotics — positive in 50–80% of bacterial meningitis; guides therapy.
  • Always draw before starting empiric antibiotics (but do not delay antibiotics if lumbar puncture delayed).

2. CSF Analysis — Gold Standard

Lumbar Puncture
  • Site — L3–L4 or L4–L5 intervertebral space.
  • Contraindications:
    • Raised ICP with focal signs or papilloedema — risk of herniation; do CT head first.
    • Coagulopathy (INR >1.4; platelets <50,000).
    • Overlying skin infection.
    • Haemodynamically unstable.
  • Collect 3 tubes (1–2 mL each):
    • Tube 1 — cell count & differential.
    • Tube 2 — glucose & protein.
    • Tube 3 — Gram stain, culture, antigen tests, molecular.
  • Open pressure — measured with manometer; elevated (>20 cm H₂O in adults; >15 cm in children) in bacterial meningitis.
CSF Findings in Bacterial Meningitis
Parameter Bacterial Viral (aseptic) TB Fungal
Opening pressure↑ (>20 cm H₂O)Normal/slightly ↑↑↑↑
WBC count↑↑↑ (100–10,000/µL)↑ (10–500/µL)↑ (50–500/µL)↑ (20–500/µL)

Glucose↓↓ (<40 mg/dL or <1/3 of serum)Normal↓↓ (<40)↓
Protein↑↑ (100–500 mg/dL)Normal/slightly ↑↑↑↑ (100–5000)↑↑

CulturePositive (70–85%)Negative (viral culture rare)Positive (low yield; long incubation)Positive (Cryptococcus; Candida)
Latex agglutinationPositive (specific antigen — S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis, Hib, E. coli K1, Group B Strep)Negative—Cryptococcal antigen positive
Specific CSF Tests
  • Gram stain — rapid, identifies organism type:
    • Gram-positive diplococci (lancet-shaped) — S. pneumoniae.
    • Gram-negative diplococci (kidney bean-shaped, intracellular) — N. meningitidis.
    • Gram-negative pleomorphic coccobacilli — H. influenzae.
    • Gram-positive bacilli — Listeria.
    • Gram-negative bacilli — E. coli, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas.
  • Bacterial antigen detection (latex agglutination) — S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis (A, B, C, Y, W135), Hib, E. coli K1, Group B Streptococcus; rapid; useful if prior antibiotics.
  • CSF culture — blood agar, chocolate agar (for N. meningitidis, H. influenzae — capnophilic); MacConkey for Gram-negative bacilli; incubated 37 °C 5% CO₂ × 48–72 h.
  • PCR (16S rRNA) — broad-range bacterial PCR; identifies organism in culture-negative; specific PCR for N. meningitidis (ctrA), S. pneumoniae (lytA, pneumolysin), Hib (bexA); multiplex FilmArray meningitis/encephalitis panel.
  • Limulus lysate test — detects endotoxin (Gram-negative).
  • Lactate — elevated (>4 mmol/L) in bacterial; helps distinguish from viral.
  • CSF adenosine deaminase (ADA) — elevated in TB meningitis (>10 U/L).

3. Other Tests

  • CBG — leucocytosis, neutrophilia.
  • CRP, procalcitonin — elevated in bacterial; helps distinguish from viral.
  • Coagulation profile — before LP; rule out DIC (N. meningitidis).
  • Serum glucose — to compare with CSF (CSF glucose <1/3 serum = bacterial).
  • Serum electrolytes — SIADH common; hyponatraemia.
  • Renal & liver function.
  • HIV test — in all adults; immunocompromised host.

4. Imaging

  • CT head before LP — if focal signs, papilloedema, seizures, immunocompromised, history of CNS disease, altered consciousness, bleeding disorder; rule out mass lesion/hydrocephalus before LP.
  • MRI — for complications (subdural empyema, cerebral abscess, ventriculitis, cortical vein thrombosis, infarction).
  • Chest X-ray — for pneumonia, TB.
  • Sinus/skull X-ray — for CSF leak.

Empirical Antibiotic Therapy (start within 1 hour of presentation)

Age/risk Empirical antibiotics
Neonate (<1 month)Ampicillin + Cefotaxime (or Ampicillin + Gentamicin); add Aminoglycoside if Listeria
Infants 1–3 monthsAmpicillin + Cefotaxime/Ceftriaxone + Vancomycin (if S. pneumoniae resistant)
Children >3 months & adults <50 yrCeftriaxone 2 g IV BD + Vancomycin 15–20 mg/kg IV 8-hourly ± Dexamethasone
Adults >50 yr; alcoholics; immunocompromisedCeftriaxone + Vancomycin + Ampicillin (for Listeria)
Post-neurosurgery; CSF shuntVancomycin + Ceftazidime (or Meropenem); add Aminoglycoside intraventricular if shunt
Penicillin allergyVancomycin + Chloramphenicol (or Meropenem)
  • Dexamethasone 10 mg IV QID × 4 days — given before or with first antibiotic dose; reduces hearing loss & neurological sequelae in S. pneumoniae meningitis (proof in European trials; controversial in low-income settings).
  • Duration — S. pneumoniae 10–14 days; N. meningitidis 7 days; Hib 7 days; Listeria 21 days (ampicillin/gentamicin); Gram-negative bacilli 21 days.
  • De-escalate — based on culture & sensitivity results.

Prophylaxis

  • N. meningitidis exposure — close contacts (household, daycare, kiss contacts): Rifampicin 600 mg BD × 2 days; or Ciprofloxacin 500 mg single dose; or Ceftriaxone 250 mg IM single dose (pregnancy).
  • Hib exposure — household contacts (if unvaccinated child <4 yr): Rifampicin 20 mg/kg (max 600 mg) OD × 4 days.

Prevention — Vaccines

  • Hib conjugate vaccine — included in India's pentavalent vaccine.
  • Pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV13) — protects against 13 serotypes; given in India's UIP.
  • Meningococcal vaccine:
    • Quadrivalent conjugate (A, C, Y, W135) — Menactra, Menveo; for Hajj pilgrims, military, asplenia, complement deficiency.
    • Men B vaccine (Bexsero, Trumenba) — for serogroup B.
  • BCG — protects against TB meningitis.

Clinical Pearl

Acute bacterial meningitis is a medical emergency — empiric antibiotics must be given within 1 hour of presentation; do NOT wait for LP or imaging if unstable or LP delayed. The classic triad of fever, neck stiffness, altered mental status is present in >95% (if at least 2 of 3). Petechial/purpuric rash with shock suggests meningococcal septicaemia (Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome — adrenal haemorrhage) — give ceftriaxone IM/IV immediately, isolate (droplet precautions until 24 h antibiotics), notify public health, give chemoprophylaxis to contacts. CSF Gram stain is the single most useful rapid test — Gram-positive diplococci (S. pneumoniae), Gram-negative diplococci (N. meningitidis), Gram-negative coccobacilli (Hib), Gram-positive bacilli (Listeria). Bacterial antigen tests (latex agglutination) useful if prior antibiotics; multiplex PCR (FilmArray ME panel) detects 14 pathogens in 1 hour — transforming diagnostics. Always add Ampicillin for Listeria in patients >50 yr, alcoholics, immunocompromised, pregnant — Listeria is resistant to cephalosporins. Give dexamethasone before or with first antibiotic dose — reduces hearing loss & neurological sequelae in S. pneumoniae meningitis (especially in high-income settings; less clear benefit in low-income). Repeat LP at 48–72 h if no clinical improvement (persistent fever, worsening mental status) — assess response; consider complications (subdural empyema, ventriculitis, abscess).

Introduction

Congenital Rubella Syndrome (CRS) is a constellation of birth defects caused by transplacental transmission of Rubella virus (family Togaviridae, genus Rubivirus) from a mother who acquires primary rubella infection during pregnancy. The classic Gregg triad (1941) — cataract, cardiac defects, deafness — defines the syndrome.

Etiology & Pathogenesis

  • Virus — Rubella virus (RNA, Togaviridae); humans only reservoir; transmitted by droplets & transplacentally.
  • Maternal infection — primary rubella during pregnancy (most damaging in 1st trimester).
  • Transplacental transmission — virus crosses placenta → infects fetus → causes:
    1. Cell division inhibition — slows fetal cell mitosis → growth retardation, organ hypoplasia.
    2. Chromosomal damage — breaks, apoptosis.
    3. Vasculitis — vascular injury in developing organs → stenosis, atresia, hypoplasia.
    4. Chronic persistent infection — virus remains in fetal tissues for months–years after birth; sheds in urine, saliva, CSF for up to 1–2 years.

Risk by Gestational Age

Gestational age at infection Risk of CRS Severity
1st 4 weeks90%Most severe; multiple defects; spontaneous abortion
5–8 weeks50–80%Severe; multiple defects
9–12 weeks25–35%Single defect (often deafness)
13–16 weeks10–20%Usually deafness only
17–20 weeks5–10%Rare; mild
>20 weeks<1%Rare; normal outcome

Clinical Features

1. Classic Triad (Gregg Triad)

  1. Sensorineural deafness
    • Most common manifestation (~60–75% of CRS).
    • May be unilateral or bilateral; progressive.
    • Cochlear damage (organ of Corti).
  2. Ocular abnormalities
    • Cataract — bilateral or unilateral; nuclear; "pearl-like".
    • Congenital glaucoma — cloudy cornea, buphthalmos.
    • Pigmentary retinopathy — "salt-and-pepper" appearance; most common ocular finding.
    • Microphthalmia, strabismus.
  3. Congenital heart disease
    • Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) — most common cardiac defect.
    • Pulmonary artery stenosis.
    • Ventricular septal defect (VSD); tetralogy of Fallot.

2. Other Features

  • Intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR) — small for gestational age.
  • Thrombocytopenic purpura — "blueberry muffin baby" (extramedullary haematopoiesis in skin); transient; resolves in weeks.
  • Hepatosplenomegaly, hepatitis, jaundice.
  • Anaemia (haemolytic).
  • Meningoencephalitis — lethargy, irritability, seizures; chronic.
  • Microcephaly, intellectual disability, developmental delay, autism.
  • Radiolucent bone disease — metaphyseal lucencies (long bones).
  • Pneumonitis, interstitial lung disease.
  • Endocrine disorders — diabetes mellitus (Type 1, late onset — due to pancreatic insufficiency); thyroiditis, hypothyroidism, growth hormone deficiency.
  • Progressive rubella panencephalitis (PRP) — rare; late-onset neurodegenerative disorder (2nd decade); fatal.

Diagnosis

1. Maternal Diagnosis

  • Serology:
    • Rubella-specific IgM — indicates recent infection (persists 1–3 months).
    • Rubella-specific IgG avidity — low avidity suggests recent infection (<3 months); high avidity = past infection.
    • Four-fold rise in IgG titre between paired sera (acute & convalescent).
  • RT-PCR — detect rubella RNA in maternal throat, urine, blood.
  • Clinical — maternal rash, lymphadenopathy, arthralgia; often subclinical.

2. Prenatal Diagnosis

  • RT-PCR on amniotic fluid or fetal blood (after 18–22 weeks).
  • Fetal blood — rubella-specific IgM (after 22 weeks when fetal immune system is mature).
  • Ultrasound — IUGR, cardiac defects, microcephaly, echogenic bowel.
  • Chorionic villus sampling — PCR.

3. Postnatal Diagnosis of Newborn

  • Rubella-specific IgM in neonatal blood — indicates congenital infection (IgM does not cross placenta; produced by fetus). Persists 6–12 months.
  • Rubella-specific IgG — persists at high titre beyond 6–12 months (maternal IgG wanes by 6 months); high IgG in infant at 6 months suggests congenital infection.
  • RT-PCR / viral culture — throat swab, urine, CSF, rectal swab, lens aspirate (cataract); virus shed for months.
  • Complete blood count — thrombocytopenia, anaemia.
  • Liver function tests — elevated transaminases.
  • Audiology evaluation — brainstem auditory evoked potentials (BAER); often missed at birth; assess serially.
  • Ophthalmologic examination — cataract, glaucoma, retinopathy.
  • Echocardiography — PDA, pulmonary stenosis, VSD.
  • Ultrasound brain — calcifications, ventriculomegaly.
  • X-ray long bones — metaphyseal lucencies.

Differential Diagnosis — Other TORCH Infections

  • T — Toxoplasma gondii — chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, intracranial calcifications (periventricular).
  • O — Other — Syphilis, VZV, Parvovirus B19, Listeria.
  • R — Rubella — cataract, PDA, deafness.
  • C — Cytomegalovirus (CMV) — petechiae, hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, sensorineural hearing loss, periventricular calcifications, microcephaly.
  • H — Herpes simplex virus (HSV) — vesicular skin lesions, encephalitis, hepatitis.

Treatment

  • No specific antiviral therapy.
  • Supportive:
    • Cataract — surgery (lensectomy, IOL implantation).
    • Glaucoma — surgical.
    • Cardiac defects — surgical correction (PDA ligation, pulmonary valvotomy).
    • Hearing aids, cochlear implant.
    • Developmental intervention — physiotherapy, speech therapy, special education.
    • Thrombocytopenia — IVIG if severe.
    • Diabetes — insulin.
  • Isolation — infant sheds virus for months; droplet precautions in hospital.

Prevention

  • Rubella vaccine:
    • Live attenuated — RA 27/3 strain.
    • Given as MMR (measles, mumps, rubella) — at 12–15 months + booster at 4–6 years.
    • Or MR (measles-rubella) — used in India's UIP.
    • India's MR campaign (2017–2019) — mass vaccination of children 9 months–15 years.
  • Pre-pregnancy screening:
    • Check rubella IgG before conception.
    • If negative — vaccinate; avoid pregnancy for 1 month after vaccination.
  • Pregnancy:
    • Antenatal screening — rubella IgG at first antenatal visit.
    • If IgG negative — avoid exposure; vaccinate postpartum.
    • Live vaccine is CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy — theoretical risk to fetus; inadvertent vaccination is not indication for termination (no confirmed CRS cases from vaccine strain).
  • Post-exposure prophylaxis:
    • Immune globulin (IG) within 72 h of exposure — for exposed pregnant women who are seronegative; does not prevent infection but may reduce severity; not routinely recommended.
  • Public health:
    • Universal childhood immunisation — herd immunity.
    • Outbreak investigation.
    • Surveillance of CRS cases.

Clinical Pearl

The Gregg triad — cataract, cardiac defects (PDA), and deafness — is the classic presentation of CRS. Sir Norman Gregg, an Australian ophthalmologist, first described the association in 1941 after observing a cluster of congenital cataract cases following a rubella epidemic. Risk of CRS is highest in 1st trimester (90% at <4 weeks; 50% at 5–8 weeks) and drops sharply after 20 weeks. Sensorineural deafness is the most common manifestation and may be the only defect in late 2nd trimester infection — always include hearing assessment (BAER) in newborn screening for CRS. Thrombocytopenic purpura ("blueberry muffin baby") — extramedullary haematopoiesis in skin — is a transient but striking neonatal presentation. Diabetes mellitus (Type 1) may develop in adolescence as a late complication — due to gradual pancreatic β-cell destruction. Rubella vaccine is the most effective preventive intervention — India's MR campaign (2017–2019) targeted 410 million children; CRS incidence has dropped dramatically. Live rubella vaccine is contraindicated in pregnancy but inadvertent vaccination is NOT an indication for termination (no confirmed CRS cases from RA 27/3 strain). Always check rubella IgG in pre-pregnancy counselling — vaccinate seronegative women before conception. CRS is now rare in countries with universal rubella vaccination but remains a problem in countries without routine vaccination.
