Introduction

Several parasites can form cysts in human skeletal muscle, typically as part of their life cycle or as aberrant migration. The two most important are Taenia solium (Cysticercus cellulosae — cysticercosis) and Trichinella spiralis (trichinellosis).

Two Important Parasites Forming Cysts in Skeletal Muscle

1. Taenia solium — Cysticercus cellulosae (Cysticercosis)

  • Parasite — pork tapeworm; T. solium.
  • Life cycle:
    • Definitive host — human (adult tapeworm in small intestine → eggs in faeces).
    • Intermediate host — pig (cysticercus cellulosae in muscle); human (accidental intermediate — cysticercosis).
  • Transmission to humans (cysticercosis):
    • Ingestion of T. solium eggs from contaminated food/water (faecal-oral).
    • Autoinfection — reverse peristalsis brings gravid proglottids/eggs from intestine to stomach; or faecal-oral self-infection.
    • NOT from eating undercooked pork (that causes intestinal taeniasis, not cysticercosis).
  • Pathogenesis:
    1. Eggs hatch in stomach & upper small intestine → oncospheres (hexacanth embryos).
    2. Oncospheres penetrate intestinal wall → bloodstream → disseminate to brain, eye, muscle, subcutaneous tissue.
    3. Develop into cysticerci (cysticercus cellulosae) — fluid-filled cyst (5–20 mm) with invaginated scolex (has suckers & hooklets).
    4. Live cysts cause minimal inflammation (immune evasion).
    5. When cyst dies (after 2–5 years) → intense inflammatory reaction → symptoms (seizures in brain; painful nodules in muscle; visual loss in eye).
    6. Eventually calcifies.
  • Skeletal muscle involvement:
    • Common site — skeletal muscle (along with brain, eye, subcutaneous tissue).
    • Usually asymptomatic; may cause myalgia, weakness.
    • Calcified cysticerci — visible on X-ray as elliptical ("cigar-shaped") calcifications in muscle, oriented along long axis of muscle fibres; pathognomonic.
    • Subcutaneous nodules — palpable; rice-grain size; biopsy shows cysticercus.
  • Clinical features:
    • Neurocysticercosis (NCC) — most common manifestation; seizures, headache, raised ICP, focal deficits; leading cause of adult-onset epilepsy in endemic areas.
    • Ocular cysticercosis — visual loss, retinal detachment.
    • Muscle/subcutaneous — usually asymptomatic; calcified nodules.
  • Diagnosis:
    • Clinical + imaging.
    • CT/MRI brain — cyst with scolex ("hole-with-dot" sign); calcified lesions.
    • X-ray soft tissue — "cigar-shaped" calcifications in muscle.
    • Serology — EITB (enzymatic immunotransfer blot) for T. solium antibodies; ELISA.
    • Biopsy of subcutaneous nodule — cysticercus cellulosae.
    • Stool examination — for T. solium eggs/proglottids (identifies tapeworm carrier — source).
  • Treatment:
    • Albendazole 15 mg/kg/day × 7–14 days OR Praziquantel 50 mg/kg/day × 15 days — kills viable cysts.
    • Corticosteroids (dexamethasone/prednisolone) — before & during antiparasitic therapy to prevent inflammatory response to dying cysts.
    • Anticonvulsants — for seizures.
    • Surgical — for ocular, spinal cysts; ventricular shunt for hydrocephalus.
    • Calcified cysts — no antiparasitic needed (dead); anticonvulsants only.

2. Trichinella spiralis — Trichinellosis (Trichinosis)

  • Parasite — nematode (roundworm); Trichinella spiralis; other species — T. nativa (arctic), T. britovi, T. pseudospiralis, T. nelsoni.
  • Life cycle:
    • All stages occur in a single host (no environmental stage).
    • Adult worms in small intestine (intracellular in epithelial cells); male 1.5 mm × 40 µm; female 3–4 mm × 60 µm.
    • Viviparous — female releases larvae (100 µm) into bloodstream; larvae disseminate.
    • Larvae encyst in skeletal muscle — preferentially diaphragm, extraocular muscles, masseter, tongue, intercostal muscles, pectoral, deltoid, biceps, gastrocnemius (muscles with high blood flow).
    • Larvae coil inside nurse cells (modified muscle cell); encyst within 4–6 weeks; calcify within 6–18 months; remain viable for years (10+ years).
    • When another animal eats the encysted larvae (e.g., pig eats rat; human eats undercooked pork), larvae mature into adults in the new host's intestine → cycle continues.
  • Transmission to humans:
    • Eating undercooked pork (most common).
    • Eating undercooked wild game — bear, boar, walrus, horse meat (T. nativa in arctic — resistant to freezing).
    • Horse meat — Europe outbreaks.
  • Incubation — 1–2 weeks (range 1–35 days).
  • Clinical phases:
    • Phase 1 — Intestinal (1–7 days): nausea, abdominal pain, diarrhoea, vomiting; due to adult worms in intestine.
    • Phase 2 — Migration (1–2 weeks): fever, myalgia (especially extraocular, masseter, diaphragm), periorbital oedema (pathognomonic), headache, weakness; eosinophilia; allergic reactions (urticaria); myocarditis, pneumonitis, encephalitis (severe).
    • Phase 3 — Encystment (2–3 weeks): symptoms subside; larvae encyst in muscle; persistent myalgia, weakness; calcification over months-years.
  • Diagnosis:
    • Clinical — triad of fever, periorbital oedema, myalgia; eosinophilia; history of undercooked pork/wild game.
    • Serology — ELISA, immunoblot for Trichinella antibodies; appears 2–3 weeks after infection.
    • Muscle biopsy — gold standard; press muscle tissue between 2 slides & examine under microscope for coiled larvae; or histopathology with H&E; larvae in nurse cells.
    • CBG — eosinophilia (10–70%); leucocytosis; raised CPK, LDH (muscle breakdown).
    • PCR — investigational.
    • Other — ECG (myocarditis), chest X-ray (pneumonitis).
  • Treatment:
    • Albendazole 400 mg BD × 8–14 days OR Mebendazole 200–400 mg TID × 3 days then 400 mg TID × 10 days — kills adult worms & larvae.
    • Corticosteroids (prednisolone 30–60 mg/day) — for severe symptoms, myocarditis, CNS involvement, allergic reactions; reduces inflammation from dying larvae.
    • Analgesics — NSAIDs for myalgia.
    • Supportive — fluids, antipyretics, cardiac monitoring.
  • Prevention:
    • Cook pork & wild game thoroughly (≥71 °C / 160 °F internal temperature).
    • Freeze pork <15 cm thick at –15 °C for 20 days (kills T. spiralis; NOT effective against T. nativa — arctic, freeze-resistant).
    • Avoid eating undercooked wild game (bear, walrus).
    • Proper pig husbandry — cook feed; rodent control.
    • Meat inspection in slaughterhouses.

Other Parasites That Can Form Cysts/Encyst in Muscle (Less Common)

  • Echinococcus granulosus — hydatid cyst; rare in muscle (liver 60%, lung 20%); when in muscle — slowly growing cyst; surgical excision.
  • Toxoplasma gondii — tissue cysts (bradyzoites) in muscle, brain, eye; usually asymptomatic; reactivation in immunocompromised.
  • Sarcocystis spp. — rare; encyst in skeletal & cardiac muscle; usually asymptomatic; may cause myositis.
  • Trypanosoma cruzi — amastigote forms pseudocysts in cardiac muscle (Chagas disease); not skeletal muscle typically.
  • Gnathostoma spinigerum — larval migration through muscle; visceral & cutaneous larva migrans; eosinophilia.
  • Sparganum (Spirometra) — sparganosis; larval cestode in subcutaneous tissue & muscle; from applying frog/fish flesh to skin or eating undercooked frog/snake/fish.
  • Dracunculus medinensis — Guinea worm; adult worm in subcutaneous tissue (not muscle); emerging through skin blister.

Clinical Pearl

The two most important parasites forming cysts in skeletal muscle are Taenia solium (cysticercosis) and Trichinella spiralis (trichinellosis). Cysticercosis — acquired by ingesting T. solium eggs (faecal-oral); not from eating pork (that causes taeniasis); skeletal muscle cysts are usually asymptomatic but visible on X-ray as elliptical "cigar-shaped" calcifications; neurocysticercosis is the most important manifestation (seizures, headache). Trichinellosis — acquired by eating undercooked pork or wild game (bear, walrus); classic triad of fever, periorbital oedema, & myalgia with eosinophilia; larvae encyst in muscle (diaphragm, extraocular, masseter, tongue); muscle biopsy diagnostic. Always ask about dietary history — undercooked pork/wild game for trichinellosis; exposure to T. solium carrier (food handler) for cysticercosis. Periorbital oedema with eosinophilia & myalgia after pork ingestion = trichinellosis until proven otherwise. "Cigar-shaped" calcifications in muscle on X-ray = cysticercosis. Albendazole is the drug of choice for both; add corticosteroids to prevent inflammatory reaction to dying parasites (especially in neurocysticercosis — dexamethasone before albendazole). India — cysticercosis is endemic (especially UP, Bihar, Punjab, Rajasthan); neurocysticercosis is the most common cause of adult-onset epilepsy. Trichinellosis is rare in India (pork consumption varies by region; religious restrictions in Hindus & Muslims).

Definition

Darling's disease — also called Histoplasmosis — is a systemic fungal infection caused by the dimorphic fungus Histoplasma capsulatum. Named after Samuel Darling who described it in 1905 in Panama. Endemic in Ohio & Mississippi River valleys (USA), parts of Central & South America, Africa, India (along Ganges & Brahmaputra riverbeds), SE Asia.

Causative Agent

Histoplasma capsulatum — dimorphic fungus of family Ajellomycetaceae.

  • Mould form (25 °C, environmental):
    • Septate hyphae with microconidia (2–5 µm) — infectious; inhaled.
    • Tuberculate macroconidia (8–15 µm) — characteristic spiny ("sea urchin") appearance; diagnostic on culture.
    • Found in soil enriched with bird/bat guano (chicken coops, starling roosts, bat caves, old buildings).
  • Yeast form (37 °C, host tissue):
    • Small (2–4 µm) oval yeast cells; narrow-based budding.
    • Intracellular — within macrophages ("Histoplasma packed in macrophages looks like cluster of grapes").
    • Found in tissue biopsy, peripheral blood (in disseminated disease), bone marrow.

Two Varieties

  • H. capsulatum var. capsulatum — worldwide (classic histoplasmosis); small yeast (2–4 µm).
  • H. capsulatum var. duboisii — Africa (African histoplasmosis); larger yeast (8–15 µm); cutaneous, subcutaneous, bone lesions predominant.

Transmission

  • Inhalation of microconidia from soil enriched with bird/bat guano — activities like cave exploration (spelunking), chicken farming, cleaning old barns, demolition, excavation.
  • NOT transmitted person-to-person.
  • Incubation — 5–18 days (average 10 days) for acute pulmonary; weeks-months for disseminated.

Clinical Syndromes

Syndrome Features
Acute pulmonary histoplasmosisMost cases asymptomatic. Symptomatic — fever, cough, headache, myalgia, chest pain; patchy pneumonia on CXR; hilar lymphadenopathy. May cause erythema nodosum & arthritis (acute rheumatological). Self-limited in 1–3 weeks.
Severe acute pulmonary (diffuse)Heavy exposure; diffuse reticulonodular infiltrates; hypoxaemia; ARDS; may need antifungals.
Chronic pulmonary histoplasmosisUnderlying lung disease (emphysema); cavitary upper lobe lesions mimicking TB; cough, sputum, weight loss, haemoptysis. Progressive if untreated.
Disseminated histoplasmosisImmunocompromised (HIV with CD4 <100, transplant, steroids); infants; elderly. Fever, weight loss, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, pancytopenia, mucocutaneous lesions (oral ulcers), adrenal insufficiency (Addison's), meningitis, endocarditis. Fatal if untreated.
Ocular histoplasmosis syndrome (OHS)Presumed ocular; choroiditis; macular scarring; visual loss.
HistoplasmomaSolitary pulmonary nodule (residual); central calcification ("target lesion"); often incidental finding.
Fibrosing mediastinitisRare; excessive fibrotic response to healed infection; compresses SVC, bronchi, pulmonary vessels.

Pathogenesis

  1. Inhaled microconidia reach alveoli; phagocytosed by macrophages.
  2. Convert to yeast form at 37 °C (dimorphism — virulence factor).
  3. Multiply within macrophages (resist killing by inhibiting phagosome-lysosome fusion; alkalinise phagosome).
  4. Drain to regional lymph nodes → disseminate haematogenously (especially to reticuloendothelial system — liver, spleen, bone marrow) within macrophages.
  5. Cell-mediated immunity (Th1, TNF-α) develops in 2–3 weeks → granuloma formation (caseating); controls infection.
  6. In immunocompromised — uncontrolled replication → disseminated disease.
  7. Calcified granulomas in lung, spleen, liver ("scatterred buckshot" calcifications); heal over years.

Laboratory Diagnosis

1. Specimen

  • Sputum, BAL, induced sputum.
  • Blood (EDTA, isolate buffy coat for intracellular yeasts in disseminated disease).
  • Bone marrow aspirate/biopsy.
  • Tissue biopsy — lung, lymph node, liver, skin, oral mucosa.
  • CSF — for meningitis.
  • Urine, serum — for antigen detection.

2. Direct Microscopy

  • Giemsa or Wright stain of peripheral blood smear, bone marrow aspirate, or buffy coat — small (2–4 µm) oval yeast cells inside macrophages ("cluster of grapes"); narrow-based budding.
  • KOH mount — yeast in tissue.
  • Histopathology — H&E shows granuloma (caseating) with yeasts in macrophages; GMS (Grocott methenamine silver) & PAS stain reveal yeasts (2–4 µm, narrow-based budding, surrounded by clear halo — pseudocapsule).

3. Culture

  • Sabouraud dextrose agar (SDA) with antibiotics (without cycloheximide — inhibits H. capsulatum) — incubate at 25–30 °C for 4–6 weeks (slow grower).
  • BACTEC MGIT, BHI agar.
  • Colony morphology (mould phase at 25 °C) — cottony white to tan/buff colonies; reverse white.
  • Microscopy (lactophenol cotton blue) — septate hyphae with tuberculate macroconidia (8–15 µm, spiny surface — like sea urchin) — pathognomonic; also microconidia (2–5 µm).
  • Conversion to yeast phase — subculture on brain heart infusion (BHI) blood agar at 37 °C; confirms dimorphism.
  • Nucleic acid probe (AccuProbe) — rapid confirmation; species-specific DNA probe hybridisation.
  • Biohazard — mould form highly infectious; BSL-3 lab required for culture.

4. Antigen Detection

  • Histoplasma galactomannan antigen:
    • Detected in urine (most sensitive), serum, BAL, CSF.
    • Sensitivity — 90%+ for disseminated disease; 80% for acute pulmonary; lower for chronic pulmonary.
    • Useful for diagnosis & monitoring treatment response (antigen level falls with effective therapy).
    • Cross-reactivity — Blastomyces (~50%), Talaromyces (Penicillium) marneffei, Paracoccidioides.

5. Antibody Detection (Serology)

  • Complement fixation (CF):
    • Antibody titres ≥1:32 (yeast antigen) or ≥1:8 (mycelial antigen) suggest active infection.
    • 4-fold rise in paired sera more specific.
    • Sensitivity 80–95%.
  • Immunodiffusion (ID):
    • H & M bands — H band indicates active infection; M band indicates recent or past infection.
    • Specific but less sensitive (70–80%).
  • ELISA — for antibodies; useful for screening.
  • Limitations — antibody response impaired in immunocompromised (HIV); false negative in disseminated disease; positive for years after infection.

6. Molecular Tests

  • PCR — detects H. capsulatum DNA in tissue, blood, BAL; investigational; not widely available.
  • Real-time PCR.

7. Other Tests

  • CBC — pancytopenia in disseminated (bone marrow involvement); anaemia; leucopenia; thrombocytopenia.
  • LFT — elevated (hepatic involvement).
  • Adrenal function — cortisol, ACTH stimulation test (adrenal involvement → Addison's disease).
  • Chest X-ray — patchy pneumonia; hilar lymphadenopathy; cavitary lesions (chronic); miliary pattern (disseminated); calcified nodules (healed).
  • CT chest — more detailed.
  • Skin test (histoplasmin) — for epidemiological surveys (delayed hypersensitivity); not for diagnosis (positive for years after exposure).

Treatment

Syndrome Treatment
Acute pulmonary (mild-moderate)Usually self-limited; rest, NSAIDs. If symptoms >4 weeks: Itraconazole 200 mg TID × 3 days then 200 mg BD × 6–12 weeks.
Severe acute pulmonaryLiposomal Amphotericin B 3 mg/kg/day × 2 weeks → Itraconazole × 12 weeks.
Chronic pulmonaryItraconazole 200 mg BD × 12–24 months.
Disseminated (moderate-severe)Liposomal Amphotericin B 3 mg/kg/day × 2 weeks → Itraconazole 200 mg BD × ≥12 months.
Disseminated (mild)Itraconazole 200 mg BD × 12 months.
MeningitisLiposomal Amphotericin B 5 mg/kg/day × 4–6 weeks → Itraconazole × 12 months (or longer).
HIV (maintenance)Itraconazole lifelong OR secondary prophylaxis until immune reconstitution on ART (CD4 >150 for 6 months).

Prevention

  • Avoid areas with high bird/bat guano — caves, chicken coops, old buildings.
  • Wear N95 mask, protective clothing when cleaning chicken coops, exploring caves, demolishing old buildings.
  • Wet soil before excavation to reduce dust.
  • Prophylaxis — Itraconazole for immunocompromised (HIV with CD4 <150) in endemic areas (controversial).
  • No vaccine available.

Clinical Pearl

Think histoplasmosis in any patient with prolonged fever, weight loss, hepatosplenomegaly, pancytopenia, & mucocutaneous lesions — especially if immunocompromised (HIV with CD4 <100) or from endemic area (Ohio-Mississippi valley, India's Ganges belt). The buffy coat of peripheral blood or bone marrow aspirate stained with Giemsa showing small (2–4 µm) intracellular yeasts in macrophages is the most rapid diagnostic test for disseminated disease. Histoplasma antigen in urine is the most sensitive non-culture test (90%+); falls with treatment response — useful for monitoring. Adrenal involvement is common — bilateral adrenal enlargement; may cause Addison's disease (check cortisol, ACTH stimulation). Distinguish from TB — both cause granulomatous disease with similar features; culture or antigen detection is essential. India — endemic along Ganges (UP, Bihar, Bengal) & Brahmaputra (Assam) riverbeds; bat caves in Andamans; underdiagnosed. The tuberculate macroconidia on culture (25 °C) are pathognomonic — spiny "sea urchin" appearance. Mould form is highly infectious to laboratory workers — BSL-3 required for culture; opening a Petri dish of mould-form H. capsulatum can cause laboratory-acquired infection. Itraconazole is the oral drug of choice; liposomal amphotericin B for severe disease. Monitor itraconazole levels — ensure therapeutic; check drug interactions (CYP3A4 — many). HIV patients need lifelong secondary prophylaxis until CD4 >150 for 6 months on ART.

Introduction

Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A Streptococcus, GAS) — Gram-positive cocci in chains, β-haemolytic, bacitracin-sensitive — is a pyogenic (pus-forming) pathogen causing a wide spectrum of suppurative (purulent) infections of skin, soft tissue, respiratory tract, & systemic sites.

Four Suppurative Infections Caused by S. pyogenes

1. Pharyngitis ("Strep Throat") — Most Common

  • Acute inflammation of pharynx & tonsils.
  • Clinical — sudden onset sore throat, fever, tonsillar exudate, tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, absence of cough/coryza (Centor criteria).
  • Complications — peritonsillar abscess (quinsy), retropharyngeal abscess, otitis media, sinusitis, meningitis.
  • Non-suppurative sequelae — acute rheumatic fever (ARF), post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN).
  • Diagnosis — throat swab culture (blood agar — β-haemolytic, bacitracin-sensitive); rapid antigen detection test (RADT); ASO titre.
  • Treatment — oral penicillin V or amoxicillin × 10 days; azithromycin if allergic.

2. Impetigo (Pyoderma)

  • Superficial skin infection; two forms:
    • Non-bullous impetigo — most common; honey-coloured crusts on erythematous base; face, extremities; common in children.
    • Bullous impetigo — flaccid bullae that rupture, leaving thin flat varnish-like crust; caused by S. aureus exfoliative toxin A/B (less commonly GAS).
    • Ecthyma — deeper ulcerative form; punched-out ulcers with necrotic scab; legs.
  • Complications — cellulitis, lymphangitis; PSGN (especially M type 49).
  • Treatment — topical mupirocin; oral antibiotics (cephalexin, dicloxacillin) for extensive.

3. Cellulitis & Erysipelas

  • Cellulitis — deep dermal & subcutaneous infection; spreading erythema, warmth, swelling, tenderness, indistinct margins; lower limbs common; portal of entry (fissure, ulcer, trauma, tinea pedis).
  • Erysipelas — more superficial; raised, sharply demarcated borders; "orange-peel" appearance; face (classic), legs.
  • Complications — abscess, necrotising fasciitis, bacteraemia, sepsis.
  • Treatment — oral dicloxacillin/cephalexin; IV for severe, diabetic, immunocompromised.

4. Necrotising Fasciitis ("Flesh-Eating Disease")

  • Rapidly progressive necrosis of subcutaneous tissue & fascia; spreads along fascial planes.
  • Two types:
    • Type II (monomicrobial) — S. pyogenes (GAS) — classic "flesh-eating" form; often with STSS; trauma, surgery, IV drug use; rapid progression (hours).
    • Type I (polymicrobial) — mixed aerobes & anaerobes; perineum (Fournier gangrene), diabetic foot, post-surgical.
  • Clinical — severe pain out of proportion to findings; erythema, swelling, crepitus (gas), skin discolouration (purple/grey), bullae, necrosis; systemic toxicity; septic shock.
  • Complications — Streptococcal Toxic Shock Syndrome (STSS); multi-organ failure; limb loss; death (mortality 20–40%).
  • Treatment — emergency surgical debridement (life-saving); IV penicillin + clindamycin (suppresses toxin); IVIG; supportive ICU.

Other Suppurative Infections (brief)

  • Puerperal sepsis (post-partum endometritis — historical "childbed fever").
  • Surgical wound infection.
  • Septic arthritis, osteomyelitis (less common than S. aureus).
  • Pneumonia (post-viral, e.g., after influenza/measles).
  • Meningitis, brain abscess (rare).
  • Peritonsillar abscess, retropharyngeal abscess, Ludwig's angina.
  • Otitis media, sinusitis.
  • Bacteraemia, sepsis, STSS.

Clinical Pearl

S. pyogenes (GAS) is one of the few bacteria capable of causing the full spectrum from trivial (impetigo, pharyngitis) to life-threatening (necrotising fasciitis, STSS). The key virulence factor is the M protein — anti-phagocytic; antibodies against M protein are protective but specific to serotype (so recurrent infections with different serotypes possible). Always consider GAS in any rapidly progressive soft tissue infection — pain out of proportion to findings, systemic toxicity, rapid spread → necrotising fasciitis until proven otherwise; emergency surgical debridement + IV penicillin + clindamycin. Penicillin remains the drug of choice — no resistance reported in GAS; macrolide resistance ~5–20%. Always check for non-suppurative sequelae — acute rheumatic fever (ARF) 2–3 weeks after pharyngitis (mitral regurgitation, migratory polyarthritis, carditis, chorea, erythema marginatum, subcutaneous nodules — Jones criteria); post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN) 1–3 weeks after pharyngitis or impetigo (haematuria, oedema, hypertension, oliguria). India — rheumatic heart disease (RHD) remains common — secondary prophylaxis with benzathine penicillin G every 3–4 weeks for 5–10 years after ARF; primary prevention — treat strep throat with penicillin × 10 days.

Introduction

Lepromatous leprosy (LL) — the multibacillary, anergic pole of the leprosy spectrum — occurs in hosts with weak cell-mediated (Th1) immunity & strong humoral (Th2) response. Bacilli multiply unchecked; high bacterial load; systemic involvement.

Four Characteristic Features of Lepromatous Leprosy

1. Skin Lesions — Multiple, Symmetric, Diffuse

  • Multiple, symmetrical, bilateral distribution — face, trunk, extremities.
  • Macules, papules, plaques, nodules — erythematous or copper-coloured; poorly defined (unlike tuberculoid — sharply defined).
  • Diffuse infiltration of skin — thickened, waxy, doughy texture.
  • Leonine facies — coarse, furrowed facial skin with nodular infiltration (forehead, eyebrows, cheeks, nose, ears) — "lion-like" appearance; classic.
  • Madarosis — loss of eyebrows (lateral third first) & eyelashes.
  • Saddle-nose deformity — destruction of nasal cartilage.
  • Pendulous ear lobes.
  • Hypopigmentation (mild — lesions not sharply demarcated).
  • Sensation relatively preserved early (unlike TT — anaesthesia is late in LL).

2. Nerve Involvement — Symmetric, Widespread, Glove-Stocking Pattern

  • Symmetric peripheral neuropathy — glove & stocking anaesthesia; distal > proximal.
  • Multiple nerves thickened — great auricular, ulnar, radial cutaneous, common peroneal, posterior tibial; palpable, tender.
  • Claw hand (ulnar), foot drop (peroneal), claw toes (posterior tibial), lagophthalmos & corneal anaesthesia (facial nerve) — late.
  • Trophic ulcers — painless plantar ulcers; autoamputation of digits.
  • Nerve damage is slower than in TT but more widespread.

3. Mucosal Involvement — Nasal, Oral, Laryngeal

  • Nasal mucosa — earliest & most common; nasal stuffiness, epistaxis, discharge (highly bacillated — "lepromatous nodules"); perforation of nasal septum → saddle nose; collapse of nasal bridge.
  • Oral mucosa — nodular infiltration of palate, uvula, tongue; ulceration; tooth loss.
  • Larynx — hoarseness, stridor; nodular infiltration of epiglottis, vocal cords.

4. Systemic Involvement & High Bacillary Load

  • Very high bacterial load — skin smears strongly positive (BI 4–6+); globi (clusters of bacilli in foamy macrophages / Virchow cells) on microscopy — pathognomonic.
  • Lymphadenopathy — generalised; bacilli in nodes.
  • Hepatosplenomegaly — reticuloendothelial involvement.
  • Testicular involvement — orchitis, infertility, gynaecomastia (↓testosterone, ↑oestrogen from testicular damage).
  • Eye — uveitis, keratitis, blindness.
  • Bone — periostitis, osteitis, absorption of digits.
  • Kidney — amyloidosis (secondary AA); glomerulonephritis.
  • Reactions — Type 2 (ENL — erythema nodosum leprosum) common in LL.

Other Features

  • Lepromin (Mitsuda) test — negative (absent CMI against M. leprae).
  • Serology (PGL-1 IgM) — strongly positive.
  • Histology — diffuse infiltrate of foamy macrophages (Virchow cells) loaded with bacilli (globi); Grenz zone (subepidermal clear zone separating infiltrate from atrophic epidermis); few lymphocytes; no granuloma (unlike TT).
  • Eye involvement — uveitis, episcleritis, keratitis, lagophthalmos leading to exposure keratitis & blindness.
  • Immunology — anergy to M. leprae (specific); normal immunity to other antigens; high antibody levels (IgM anti-PGL-1) but no protection (humoral response ineffective against intracellular pathogen).

Treatment

  • MB-MDT (Multibacillary regimen) — Rifampicin 600 mg + Clofazimine 300 mg monthly (supervised) + Dapsone 100 mg + Clofazimine 50 mg daily (self-administered) × 12 months.
  • Monitor for reactions — Type 1 (reversal) & Type 2 (ENL); treat with prednisolone (Type 1) or thalidomide (Type 2 — strictly contraindicated in pregnancy).
  • Long-term follow-up — relapse, deformity, reactions.

Clinical Pearl

The leonine facies (coarse furrowed face with nodular infiltration) is the classic physical sign of lepromatous leprosy — combined with madarosis (eyebrow loss) & saddle nose deformity, the diagnosis is clinical. Symmetrical multiple skin lesions with relatively preserved sensation early (anaesthesia develops late in LL) distinguishes LL from tuberculoid leprosy (TT — single/few sharply defined anaesthetic lesions). Skin smear strongly positive (BI 4–6+) with globi (clusters of bacilli in Virchow cells) — pathognomonic. Lepromin test is negative (absent CMI); serology (PGL-1 IgM) strongly positive. Histology shows foamy macrophages (Virchow cells) with Grenz zone — no granuloma. Nasal mucosa is the primary site & source of transmission — bacilli shed in nasal discharge; highly infectious. Type 2 reaction (ENL) — crops of painful erythematous nodules on face & extensor surfaces; fever, malaise, neuritis, iritis, orchitis, dactylitis; treat with thalidomide (strictly avoid in pregnancy — severe phocomelia) or prednisolone. Always check for systemic involvement — eye (uveitis, blindness), testis (infertility, gynaecomastia), kidney (amyloidosis). MB-MDT for 12 months — rifampicin kills 99.9% of bacilli with single dose; clofazimine anti-inflammatory; dapsone antibacterial. India's NLEP (National Leprosy Eradication Programme) provides free MDT; achieved elimination (<1/10,000) in 2005 but new cases (~120,000/year) continue — early detection & complete treatment essential to prevent deformity & transmission.

Introduction

Streptococcus pneumoniae (pneumococcus) — Gram-positive, lancet-shaped diplococci, α-haemolytic, optochin-sensitive, bile-soluble — causes pneumonia, meningitis, otitis media, sinusitis, bacteraemia. Virulence factors enable colonisation, evasion of host defences, & tissue invasion.

Two Important Virulence Factors

1. Polysaccharide Capsule — Most Important

  • Structure — thick polysaccharide capsule surrounding cell wall; capsular serotype determines antigenicity (>90 serotypes identified; ~13 covered by PCV13 vaccine, 23 by PPSV23).
  • Mechanism:
    • Anti-phagocytic — prevents opsonisation by complement & antibodies; resists phagocytosis by neutrophils & macrophages.
    • Hinders complement activation — capsule impairs C3b deposition on bacterial surface; alternative pathway less effective.
    • Resists mucosal clearance — facilitates colonisation of nasopharynx & invasion.
    • Strains without capsule (rough colonies) are non-pathogenic — avirulent.
  • Protection — type-specific IgG antibodies against capsule → opsonisation → phagocytosis. Basis of pneumococcal vaccines (PCV13 — conjugate; PPSV23 — polysaccharide).
  • Serotype distribution — 6A, 6B, 9V, 14, 19A, 19F, 23F most common in children; 3, 4, 6B, 9V, 14, 19F, 23F in adults.
  • Serotype replacement — after PCV7 introduction, non-vaccine serotypes (especially 19A, 6A) emerged; PCV13 expanded coverage.

2. Pneumolysin — Cytolytic Toxin

  • Structure — 53 kDa cholesterol-dependent cytolysin (CDC); produced by virtually all pneumococcal strains; intracellular (released on autolysis).
  • Mechanism:
    • Pore formation — binds cholesterol in host cell membranes → oligomerises → forms transmembrane pores (β-barrel) → osmotic lysis & cell death.
    • Haemolysis — lyses RBCs (α-haemolysis on blood agar — partial; pneumolysin contributes; also O₂-labile pneumolysin — enhanced under anaerobic conditions).
    • Cytotoxic to ciliated epithelium — damages respiratory epithelium; impairs mucociliary clearance.
    • Complement activation — classical pathway (binds Fc portion of IgG); depletes complement; reduces opsonisation.
    • Pro-inflammatory — activates NLRP3 inflammasome → IL-1β release; neutrophil recruitment.
    • Neurotoxic — damages brain microvascular endothelial cells; contributes to meningitis pathogenesis & hearing loss.
    • Cardiotoxic — damages myocardium; contributes to cardiac complications of pneumococcal pneumonia.
  • Role in disease — worsens pneumonia severity; meningitis; otitis media; invasive pneumococcal disease (IPD).

Other Virulence Factors

  • Surface proteins:
    • Pneumococcal surface protein A (PspA) — anti-complement; anti-phagocytic; vaccine candidate.
    • Pneumococcal surface protein C (PspC / CbpA) — binds polymeric Ig receptor & factor H; colonisation & immune evasion.
    • Pneumococcal surface antigen A (PsaA) — manganese transporter; adhesion; vaccine candidate.
    • Choline-binding proteins — adhere to epithelial cells (CbpA).
  • Cell wall components:
    • Teichoic acid — activates complement; pro-inflammatory (TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6).
    • Peptidoglycan — activates alternative complement; cytokine release.
    • C-polysaccharide — activates CRP (C-reactive protein) in host.
  • Enzymes:
    • IgA1 protease — cleaves host secretory IgA1; evades mucosal immunity; facilitates colonisation.
    • Neuraminidase (NanA, NanB, NanC) — cleaves sialic acid from host glycoproteins; exposes receptors for adhesion; contributes to otitis media & meningitis.
    • Hyaluronidase — tissue invasion.
    • Autolysin (LytA) — causes bacterial lysis at stationary phase → releases pneumolysin & cell wall components; contributes to inflammation & virulence.
  • Pili (type IV) — adhesion to epithelial cells; colonisation; some strains only.

Clinical Pearl

The polysaccharide capsule is the single most important virulence factor of S. pneumoniae — strains without capsule are non-pathogenic; antibodies against capsule (opsonising IgG) are protective; basis of pneumococcal vaccines. >90 capsular serotypes identified — vaccine covers subset (PCV13: 13 serotypes causing >80% of invasive disease in children; PPSV23: 23 serotypes for adults). Serotype replacement — non-vaccine serotypes emerge after vaccination (especially 19A after PCV7; replaced by PCV13); ongoing surveillance essential. Pneumolysin — pore-forming toxin; cytotoxic to respiratory epithelium, RBC, neurons, myocardium; worsens severity; vaccine candidate. IgA1 protease — cleaves secretory IgA1; evades mucosal immunity — explains high colonisation rate in children. Always suspect S. pneumoniae in: acute community-acquired pneumonia (rusty sputum), acute bacterial meningitis (Gram-positive diplococci in CSF), otitis media in children, sinusitis, bacteraemia in asplenic patients. Quellung reaction (Neufeld) — historical capsular typing test; capsule swells visibly when specific antiserum added. Bile solubility test — pneumococcus lysed by bile/SDS (activates autolysin LytA); distinguishes from viridans streptococci. Optochin sensitivity — pneumococcus sensitive (≥14 mm zone); viridans streptococci resistant. India — PCV13 introduced in UIP (2017); reduces pneumococcal pneumonia, meningitis, otitis media, & antimicrobial resistance.

Introduction

Staphylococcus aureus — Gram-positive cocci in clusters, catalase-positive, coagulase-positive — produces a remarkable array of virulence factors. Here are two of the most important.

Two Virulence Factors of Staphylococcus

1. Coagulase — Free & Bound

  • Free coagulase (secreted enzyme):
    • Activates prothrombin → thrombin → converts fibrinogen → fibrin → clot formation.
    • Walls off infection → abscess formation; protects bacteria from phagocytes & antibiotics.
    • Tube coagulase test detects this; definitive for S. aureus identification.
  • Bound coagulase (clumping factor):
    • Surface protein (ClfA, ClfB) that binds fibrinogen directly → fibrin coat on bacterial surface.
    • Resists phagocytosis.
    • Slide coagulase test detects this.
  • Role in disease — abscess formation (boils, carbuncles, abscesses); endocarditis (vegetation); foreign body infection (biofilm on catheter); distinguishes S. aureus from CoNS.

2. Protein A — Surface Protein

  • Structure — 42 kDa cell wall surface protein anchored to peptidoglycan; expressed by all S. aureus strains.
  • Mechanism:
    • Binds Fc portion of IgG in wrong orientation — the Fab (antigen-binding) ends face outward, Fc faces inward.
    • Prevents opsonisation — phagocytes cannot recognise Fc.
    • Resists phagocytosis by neutrophils & macrophages.
    • Also a B-cell superantigen — binds VH3 region of B-cell receptor → polyclonal B-cell activation → immune evasion.
  • Role in disease — major immune evasion mechanism; enables colonisation & invasive infection; basis for clinical identification (staphylococcal slide agglutination tests — bound protein A & clumping factor detected simultaneously).
  • Clinical use — protein A columns used therapeutically to remove IgG-mediated antibodies (immunoadsorption) in autoimmune disease (ITP, myasthenia gravis, SLE).

Other Important Virulence Factors

  • Hemolysins — α-toxin (pore-forming; dermonecrotic), β-haemolysin (sphingomyelinase), γ-haemolysin, δ-toxin.
  • Leucocidins — Panton-Valentine leucocidin (PVL — destroys neutrophils; CA-MRSA; necrotising pneumonia); LukAB, LukED.
  • Superantigens — TSST-1 (toxic shock syndrome), enterotoxins A–U (food poisoning), exfoliative toxins A & B (scalded skin syndrome).
  • Capsule — anti-phagocytic (type 5 & 8).
  • Teichoic acid — adherence to mucosa & prosthetic devices.
  • Catalase — neutralises H₂O₂ (survives neutrophil oxidative burst).
  • Enzymes — hyaluronidase ("spreading factor"), fibrinolysin, DNase, lipase, protease.
  • Biofilm — polysaccharide intercellular adhesin (PIA); device infections.
  • Antibiotic resistance — β-lactamase (penicillin resistance); PBP2a/mecA (MRSA).

Clinical Pearl

The coagulase test is the single most important lab test to differentiate S. aureus (positive) from coagulase-negative staphylococci (CoNS — S. epidermidis, S. saprophyticus). Protein A is unique to S. aureus — binds Fc of IgG in wrong orientation, preventing opsonisation; enables the bacteria to evade phagocytosis & complement; basis for slide agglutination tests. Together, coagulase & protein A explain why S. aureus is so virulent — coagulase walls off infection (abscess, vegetation); protein A evades immune clearance. PVL (Panton-Valentine Leucocidin) — marker of CA-MRSA; causes necrotising pneumonia (mortality 30–50%), recurrent skin abscesses, necrotising fasciitis. TSST-1 — superantigen; toxic shock syndrome (menstrual — tampon; non-menstrual — surgical wound); fever, hypotension, diffuse desquamating rash, multi-organ failure. Exfoliative toxins — scalded skin syndrome (SSSS) in neonates; cleaves desmoglein 1 → intraepidermal split; Nikolsky sign positive; mucosa spared (distinguishes from TEN). Enterotoxins — heat-stable; staphylococcal food poisoning (rapid vomiting, 2–6 h after ingestion of contaminated cream pastries, mayonnaise, dairy). Biofilm on prosthetic devices — PIA; reason device removal often needed for cure; rifampin has biofilm activity.

Introduction

For suspected tuberculosis (pulmonary or extrapulmonary), proper specimen collection & transport are critical because M. tuberculosis is slow-growing & sensitive to environmental conditions. Delay or improper transport reduces culture yield significantly.

Clinical Specimen Preferred

1. Pulmonary TB (Most Common)

  • Sputum (3 samples) — preferred:
    • Spot-morning-spot (SMS) — Day 1 spot, Day 2 morning, Day 2 spot; WHO & India's NTEP recommended.
    • OR 3 consecutive early morning samples.
    • Volume — at least 3 mL (5 mL ideal); mucoid or mucopurulent (not saliva).
    • Collected in sterile wide-mouth, leak-proof, disposable container.
  • Induced sputum — if patient cannot expectorate (hypertonic 3% saline nebulisation).
  • Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) or bronchial washings — if sputum smear-negative but suspicion high; via bronchoscopy.
  • Gastric aspirate/lavage — children <5 years who swallow sputum (cannot expectorate); early morning, fasting; 3 consecutive days; neutralise immediately (sodium carbonate) as gastric acid kills mycobacteria.
  • Tracheal aspirate — intubated patients.

2. Extrapulmonary TB

Site Specimen
TB lymphadenitisLymph node aspirate (FNAC) or biopsy
TB meningitisCSF (≥5 mL; collect last fraction for culture)
Pleural TBPleural fluid (thoracocentesis); pleural biopsy (culture yield higher from tissue than fluid)
Peritoneal TBAscitic fluid (≥50 mL); peritoneal biopsy
Pericardial TBPericardial fluid; pericardial biopsy
Bone & joint TB (Pott's spine)Pus from sinus; bone biopsy; aspirate from paravertebral abscess (CT-guided)
Genitourinary TBEarly morning urine (3 samples — midstream); renal tissue; semen; endometrial biopsy
Miliary / disseminated TBBlood (BACTEC — lysis-centrifugation); bone marrow aspirate/biopsy; liver biopsy
Cutaneous TBSkin biopsy (punch — full thickness)
Intestinal TBColonoscopic biopsy; ascitic fluid; mesenteric lymph node biopsy

Transport Medium

  • Sputum & most specimens:
    • Transport to lab within 2 hours at room temperature (do NOT refrigerate immediately as some mycobacteria are sensitive to cold).
    • If delay expected (>2 h): refrigerate at 4 °C for up to 24–48 h.
    • For longer delays: add cetylpyridinium chloride (CPC) 0.5% — preservative; kills contaminating bacteria but allows mycobacteria to survive up to 7 days at room temperature; widely used in NTEP.
  • Sodium carbonate (Na₂CO₃) 1% — for gastric aspirate; neutralise gastric acid immediately (HCl kills mycobacteria within hours).
  • CSF:
    • Collect in sterile container; transport immediately at room temperature.
    • Do NOT refrigerate — M. tuberculosis sensitive to cold in CSF (low bacillary load).
    • Use last fraction (highest cell pellet).
  • Blood for disseminated TB:
    • Collect in ISOLATOR tube (lysis-centrifugation) or BACTEC Myco/F Lytic bottle; lyses RBCs & WBCs → releases intracellular mycobacteria.
    • Transport at room temperature; do NOT refrigerate.
  • Tissue biopsy:
    • Place in sterile saline (not formalin) — formalin kills mycobacteria (no culture possible from formalin-fixed tissue; only histopathology).
    • Transport on ice within 1 hour.
    • For histopathology — separate piece in 10% formalin.
  • Urine:
    • 3 early morning midstream urine specimens; ≥50 mL each.
    • Transport within 2 h or refrigerate at 4 °C; centrifuge & pool sediment for culture.
  • Pus / aspirate:
    • Collect in sterile container; transport immediately at room temperature.
    • If contaminated — add CPC or NaOH for decontamination (N-acetyl-L-cysteine-NaOH method in lab).

Specimen Processing in Laboratory

  • Decontamination — N-acetyl-L-cysteine-NaOH (NALC-NaOH) method; kills contaminating bacteria & fungi while preserving mycobacteria; liquifies mucus.
  • Concentration — centrifugation (3000 g × 15 min); sediment used for smear & culture.
  • Smear — Ziehl-Neelsen (hot carbol fuchsin) or auramine O (fluorescent); AFB.
  • Culture:
    • LJ (Löwenstein-Jensen) — solid; 2–8 weeks.
    • MGIT (BACTEC MGIT 960) — liquid; 1–3 weeks (faster; gold standard).
    • BACTEC 460 (historical; radiometric).
  • CBNAAT (Xpert MTB/RIF) — automated PCR; detects M. tuberculosis DNA + rifampicin resistance (rpoB gene mutations) in 2 hours; WHO-endorsed first-line test; India's NTEP uses widely.
  • Line probe assay (LPA) — GenoType MTBDRplus (rifampicin + isoniazid resistance); MTBDRsl (second-line — fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides, ethambutol).

Biosafety

  • Mycobacterium tuberculosis — BSL-3 required for culture & manipulation (aerosol transmission risk).
  • Smear preparation — BSL-2 acceptable.
  • CBNAAT — BSL-2 acceptable (closed cartridge system).
  • Biosafety cabinet (Class II) for processing.

Clinical Pearl

The single most important specimen for pulmonary TB is sputum — collect 3 samples (spot-morning-spot); early morning sputum has highest bacillary load. For children <5 yr who cannot expectorate — gastric aspirate (early morning, fasting; neutralise with sodium carbonate immediately). For smear-negative suspected pulmonary TB — bronchoscopy with BAL or induced sputum (3% saline nebulisation). For extrapulmonary TB — tissue biopsy is better than body fluid (higher bacillary load); always send part in saline (for culture) & part in formalin (for histopathology). NEVER refrigerate CSF — M. tuberculosis sensitive to cold in CSF; transport at room temperature, process immediately. CPC (cetylpyridinium chloride) — preferred preservative for sputum if delay >2 h; kills contaminants but preserves mycobacteria up to 7 days. CBNAAT (Xpert MTB/RIF) has replaced smear microscopy as the first-line diagnostic test in India's NTEP — detects TB + rifampicin resistance in 2 hours. Always send specimens before starting ATT — even 1 dose of ATT reduces culture yield by 50%; PCR (CBNAAT) less affected. BSL-3 required for culture — laboratory-acquired TB is a real risk for laboratory workers handling specimens without proper containment.

Introduction

Acute pyogenic (septic) arthritis in sexually active young adults has a distinctive microbiology — sexually transmitted pathogens predominate. The two most important causative agents are Neisseria gonorrhoeae (most common) & Chlamydia trachomatis.

Two Common Causative Agents

1. Neisseria gonorrhoeae (Gonococcus) — Most Common

  • Gram-negative diplococcus (kidney-bean shaped, intracellular); oxidase & catalase positive; ferment glucose only.
  • Most common cause of septic arthritis in sexually active adults <30 yr (50–70% of cases).
  • Transmission — sexual contact; asymptomatic genital carriage common in women.
  • Pathogenesis:
    • Mucosal infection (urethra, cervix, rectum, pharynx) → haematogenous spread to joints.
    • Pili (adherence), Por (invasion), Opa (adhesion), LOS (endotoxin), IgA protease (immune evasion).
    • Complement resistance — sialylation of LOS.
  • Clinical features:
    • Disseminated Gonococcal Infection (DGI) — two clinical forms:
      1. Arthritis-dermatitis syndrome (more common) — migratory polyarthralgia → settles in 1–2 joints (knee, wrist, ankle); tenosynovitis; painless skin lesions (pustules on extremities — fingers, toes, palms, soles); fever; low-grade.
      2. Localised septic arthritis (less common) — single joint (knee); more acute, purulent; positive culture.
    • Genital symptoms may be absent or mild.
  • Diagnosis:
    • Synovial fluid — Gram stain (intracellular Gram-negative diplococci; positive in 25–50%); culture (Thayer-Martin — positive in 25–50% of purulent arthritis, <10% in arthritis-dermatitis); PCR (NAAT — more sensitive).
    • Genital/rectal/pharyngeal swab — NAAT (PCR) for N. gonorrhoeae; positive in most DGI cases even if joint culture negative.
    • Blood culture — positive in arthritis-dermatitis syndrome; negative in localised arthritis.
    • Skin lesion culture/PCR — positive in 50%.
  • Treatment:
    • Ceftriaxone 1 g IV/IM daily × 7 days (+ azithromycin 1 g PO single dose for co-existing chlamydia & to slow resistance).
    • Alternative — cefotaxime, ceftizoxime.
    • Fluoroquinolones — no longer recommended (widespread resistance).
    • Joint drainage — needle aspiration or arthroscopy.
    • Treat sexual partner(s).

2. Chlamydia trachomatis — Reactive Arthritis

  • Obligate intracellular bacterium; Gram-negative (cell wall lacks muramic acid).
  • Serovars D–K cause genital infection (urethritis, cervicitis).
  • Most common bacterial STI globally; often asymptomatic.
  • Pathogenesis of arthritis:
    • Reactive arthritis (Reiter syndrome) — sterile inflammatory arthritis 1–4 weeks after chlamydial urethritis/cervicitis; immune-mediated (not infection of joint).
    • Triad — arthritis (asymmetric, lower limbs — knee, ankle), conjunctivitis, urethritis ("can't see, can't pee, can't climb a tree"); HLA-B27 association (50–80%).
    • Additional features — circinate balanitis, keratoderma blennorrhagicum (palms/soles), enthesitis (Achilles tendon), dactylitis ("sausage digit"), sacroiliitis, oral ulcers.
    • Joint fluid — sterile (negative culture); inflammatory (WBC 2,000–50,000/µL, neutrophils).
  • Diagnosis:
    • NAAT (PCR) — first-void urine, urethral/cervical swab for C. trachomatis.
    • Synovial fluid — sterile; PCR may detect C. trachomatis DNA in synovium (controversial — persistence vs contamination).
    • Serology — IgM, IgG; not diagnostic of active infection.
    • HLA-B27 — positive in 50–80% of reactive arthritis (supportive, not diagnostic).
    • Exclude gonococcal arthritis — NAAT for both organisms.
  • Treatment:
    • Azithromycin 1 g PO single dose OR doxycycline 100 mg BD × 7 days — treats genital chlamydia (does not change arthritis course but prevents transmission & reinfection).
    • NSAIDs — first-line for arthritis.
    • DMARDs (sulfasalazine, methotrexate) — for persistent >6 months.
    • Local corticosteroid injection — for refractory single joint.
    • Anti-TNF — for severe refractory.
    • Treat sexual partner(s).

Other Agents in Sexually Active Adults

  • Ureaplasma urealyticum & Mycoplasma genitalium — rare causes of reactive arthritis.
  • Treponema pallidum — syphilitic arthritis (secondary syphilis; neuropathic Charcot joint in tertiary).
  • HIV — indirect; immunosuppression → opportunistic septic arthritis (S. aureus, Salmonella, fungi); also HIV-associated arthropathy & Reiter syndrome.
  • Haemophilus ducreyi — chancroid; not arthritis.
  • HSV — rarely; reactive.

Comparison: Gonococcal vs Reactive Arthritis

Feature Gonococcal arthritis Reactive arthritis (Chlamydia)
MechanismSeptic (live organism in joint)Sterile (immune-mediated)
TimingDuring/after genital infection1–4 weeks after genital infection
PatternMigratory polyarthralgia → settles; or single jointAsymmetric oligoarthritis (lower limbs)
Skin lesionsPainless pustules (palms/soles)Keratoderma blennorrhagicum, circinate balanitis
ConjunctivitisRareYes (Reiter triad)
Synovial culturePositive (25–50%)Sterile (negative)
HLA-B27No associationPositive (50–80%)
TreatmentCeftriaxone IV/IMNSAIDs + treat chlamydia (azithromycin/doxycycline)

Clinical Pearl

N. gonorrhoeae is the most common cause of septic arthritis in sexually active young adults (<30 yr) — characterised by migratory polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis, & painless pustular skin lesions (Disseminated Gonococcal Infection — DGI). Always test for chlamydia co-infection (30–50%) — treat with ceftriaxone + azithromycin/doxycycline. Reactive arthritis (Reiter syndrome) — sterile arthritis 1–4 weeks after chlamydial urethritis; classic triad of arthritis + conjunctivitis + urethritis; HLA-B27 positive (50–80%); joint culture sterile (distinguishes from gonococcal); treat with NSAIDs + treat chlamydia. Synovial fluid Gram stain & culture — gonococcal arthritis: intracellular Gram-negative diplococci; positive culture 25–50%; reactive arthritis: sterile, inflammatory WBC 2,000–50,000/µL. NAAT (PCR) on urine or genital swab — best test for detecting both N. gonorrhoeae & C. trachomatis; positive in most DGI & reactive arthritis cases even if joint culture negative. Always treat sexual partner(s) — prevent reinfection & further transmission. Emerging ceftriaxone-resistant N. gonorrhoeae (FC428 clone) — global concern; monitor & report.

Introduction

Clostridium tetani — Gram-positive, anaerobic, spore-forming, drumstick-shaped bacillus — produces two potent exotoxins. The most important is tetanospasmin (tetanus toxin) — responsible for clinical tetanus.

Two Toxins of C. tetani

1. Tetanospasmin (Tetanus Toxin, TeNT) — Most Important

  • Structure:
    • 150 kDa A-B toxin (similar to botulinum, diphtheria toxins).
    • Single polypeptide; cleaved by protease into:
      • Heavy chain (100 kDa, B subunit) — binding & translocation; binds neurons; mediates entry.
      • Light chain (50 kDa, A subunit) — active moiety; Zn²⁺-dependent endopeptidase (metalloprotease).
    • Linked by disulfide bond.
  • Mechanism of action:
    1. Toxin released at site of infection; enters peripheral motor neurons (via SV2A/SV2B receptor + polysialogangliosides on neuron surface).
    2. Retrograde axonal transport to spinal cord (anterior horn) & brainstem.
    3. Heavy chain mediates translocation across synaptic membrane into synaptosome.
    4. Light chain cleaves SNARE protein synaptobrevin (VAMP-2) — vesicle-associated membrane protein.
    5. Cleaved synaptobrevin cannot mediate vesicle fusion → prevents release of inhibitory neurotransmitters (GABA & glycine) from interneurons (Renshaw cells) onto motor neurons.
    6. Loss of inhibition → uncontrolled motor neuron firing → severe sustained muscle spasms.
  • Clinical effects:
    • Trismus (lockjaw) — masseter spasm; earliest sign.
    • Risus sardonicus — sardonic smile from facial muscle spasm.
    • Opisthotonus — arching of back; severe hyperextension.
    • Generalised tetanus — sustained muscle spasms; respiratory compromise; autonomic dysfunction (sympathetic overactivity — labile BP, arrhythmias); intact sensorium.
    • Cephalic tetanus — cranial nerve palsies (especially VII) after head/face wound or otitis media.
    • Neonatal tetanus — from unsterile umbilical cord care.
    • Mortality 10–40% even with treatment; near 100% untreated.
  • Treatment:
    • HTIG (Human Tetanus Immune Globulin) 3000–6000 IU IM/IV — neutralises unbound toxin only (does NOT reverse bound toxin).
    • IV Metronidazole × 7–10 days — kills organism.
    • Surgical debridement of wound.
    • Supportive — diazepam (muscle relaxant), mechanical ventilation, magnesium sulphate (autonomic dysfunction).
    • Active immunisation with TT (tetanus toxoid) at recovery — clinical tetanus does NOT confer immunity (toxin amount too small).
  • Prevention:
    • Tetanus toxoid (TT) vaccine — formaldehyde-treated toxin; loses toxicity but retains antigenicity; adsorbed on aluminium hydroxide.
    • Given as DTP/DTaP/Tdap/Td in childhood & adulthood.
    • India — 3 primary doses at 6, 10, 14 weeks; boosters at 16–18 months & 5 years; Td at 10 & 16 years; adults every 10 years.
    • Pregnancy — Td in each pregnancy.

2. Tetanolysin — Less Important

  • Structure:
    • 49 kDa cholesterol-dependent cytolysin (CDC).
    • Oxygen-labile (inactivated by O₂); heat-labile.
    • Member of cholesterol-binding toxin family (similar to streptolysin O, pneumolysin, listeriolysin O, perfringolysin O).
  • Mechanism:
    1. Binds cholesterol in host cell membranes.
    2. Oligomerises into ring-shaped pre-pore (40–50 monomers).
    3. Undergoes conformational change → inserts into membrane → forms transmembrane β-barrel pore (large; 30 nm diameter).
    4. Osmotic lysis & cell death.
  • Effects:
    • Haemolysis — lyses RBCs; contributes to local tissue destruction.
    • Cytotoxic — damages leukocytes, macrophages, platelets, myocardium (in vitro).
    • Degranulation of mast cells & platelets.
    • Complement activation — classical pathway.
  • Role in disease — uncertain; less important than tetanospasmin; may contribute to local necrosis & create anaerobic environment favourable for C. tetani growth; may aid in iron acquisition (from lysed RBCs).
  • Antigenically related to streptolysin O, pneumolysin — anti-tetanolysin antibodies cross-react.

Comparison of C. tetani Toxins

Feature Tetanospasmin Tetanolysin
Size150 kDa (AB toxin)49 kDa (CDC)
Site of actionCNS (spinal cord, brainstem)Local (membrane of cells at infection site)
MechanismCleaves synaptobrevin (VAMP-2) → blocks GABA/glycine releasePore-forming in cholesterol-containing membranes
Clinical importanceMajor — causes tetanusMinor — local necrosis; may aid anaerobic environment
Toxoid vaccineYes (formaldehyde-inactivated)No
HTIG neutralisesYes (unbound toxin only)No

Clinical Pearl

Tetanospasmin (TeNT) is one of the most potent toxins known — minimum lethal dose in humans ~2.5 ng/kg; acts by cleaving synaptobrevin (VAMP-2) → blocks release of inhibitory neurotransmitters (GABA & glycine) → uncontrolled motor neuron firing → tetanus. The toxin acts in CNS but is produced at peripheral wound site — travels retrograde along motor neurons to spinal cord. HTIG neutralises only unbound (circulating) toxin — once toxin binds to neurons (irreversible), it cannot be reversed; recovery requires sprouting of new synapses (4–6 weeks). Clinical tetanus does NOT confer immunity — toxin amount too small to trigger antibody response; always vaccinate recovered patients with full TT series. Always give tetanus toxoid (TT) booster for tetanus-prone wounds in incompletely immunised patients (>5 years since last dose); for clean minor wounds, booster if >10 years. Pregnant women — Td in each pregnancy (2 doses in 1st pregnancy, 1 dose in subsequent); protects neonate via transplacental antibody; India achieved MNTE (Maternal & Neonatal Tetanus Elimination) in 2015. Magnesium sulphate infusion is now standard adjunct for severe tetanus — controls spasms & autonomic dysfunction; reduces need for mechanical ventilation. Metronidazole is preferred over penicillin for tetanus — penicillin is GABA antagonist and may theoretically worsen spasms. Tetanolysin — less clinically important; cholesterol-binding cytolysin; may contribute to local tissue destruction but not the neurotoxic effects of tetanus.

Introduction

Acute gastroenteritis is a leading cause of childhood mortality globally, especially in developing countries. Viruses are the most common cause in children <5 years. The two most important are Rotavirus (most common cause of severe dehydrating diarrhoea) & Norovirus (most common cause of outbreaks / sporadic gastroenteritis).

Two Common Viruses Causing Acute Gastroenteritis in Young Children

1. Rotavirus — Most Common Cause of Severe Dehydrating Diarrhoea

  • Family: Reoviridae; genus Rotavirus.
  • Structure:
    • Non-enveloped; icosahedral; double capsid (triple-layered).
    • Wheel-like appearance ("rota" = wheel) under electron microscopy.
    • Double-stranded RNA (dsRNA); 11 segments.
    • Outer capsid proteins — VP4 (P-type protease-sensitive) & VP7 (G-type glycoprotein) — define serotype; basis of vaccine strains.
    • Inner capsid — VP6 (most abundant; antigenic; defines group A–G; Group A most common in humans).
  • Transmission — faecal-oral; contaminated food/water; fomites; respiratory droplets (possible).
  • Incubation — 1–3 days.
  • Pathogenesis:
    1. Virus ingested → infects mature enterocytes of small intestinal villi (especially proximal small intestine).
    2. VP4 binds enterocyte receptors (integrins, gangliosides, HbA).
    3. VP4 cleaved by intestinal trypsin → enhances infectivity.
    4. Virus enters cell; replicates in cytoplasm.
    5. NSP4 (non-structural protein 4) — enterotoxin; triggers calcium influx → chloride secretion → watery diarrhoea; also induces apoptosis of enterocytes.
    6. Destruction of mature absorptive enterocytes → villous atrophy; malabsorption; decreased disaccharidases (especially lactase) → osmotic diarrhoea.
    7. Resolves in 5–7 days; lifelong immunity develops (but multiple serotypes possible reinfection).
  • Clinical features:
    • Sudden onset fever, vomiting (prominent; 1–2 days), profuse watery diarrhoea (5–10 days).
    • Dehydration — mild to severe; leading cause of hospitalisation in infants <2 yr.
    • Seizures (febrile) in some children.
    • Death from dehydration & electrolyte imbalance if untreated.
  • Diagnosis:
    • Stool antigen ELISA (VP6) — most common; rapid (15 min); high sensitivity/specificity.
    • Latex agglutination, immunochromatographic rapid tests.
    • PAGE (polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis) of stool RNA — characteristic 11-segment pattern ("electropherotype").
    • RT-PCR — gold standard; detects & genotypes.
    • Electron microscopy — wheel-like particles.
    • Stool microscopy — no RBCs or WBCs (non-invasive).
  • Treatment:
    • ORS (oral rehydration solution) — WHO formula; low-osmolarity (Na 75, glucose 75 mmol/L) — mainstay.
    • IV fluids (Ringer's lactate) for severe dehydration.
    • Zinc supplementation — 20 mg/day × 10–14 days; reduces duration & severity; WHO recommended.
    • Probiotics (Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG).
    • No antivirals; avoid antimotility agents.
  • Prevention:
    • Rotavirus vaccine:
      • Rotarix (RV1) — monovalent; G1P[8]; 2 doses at 6 & 10 weeks (or 6 & 14 weeks).
      • RotaTeq (RV5) — pentavalent; G1, G2, G3, G4, P[8]; 3 doses at 6, 10, 14 weeks.
      • ROTAVAC (116E) — Indian indigenous (Bharat Biotech); neonatal strain; 3 doses at 6, 10, 14 weeks.
      • ROTASIIL — Indian (Serum Institute); thermostable; lyophilised; 3 doses.
      • India — included in UIP (2016); reduced rotavirus diarrhoea mortality by ~50%.
      • Contraindication — severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID); history of intussusception.
      • Small increased risk of intussusception (~1 in 50,000–100,000) — benefit outweighs risk.
    • Hand hygiene, safe water, sanitation, exclusive breastfeeding (6 months).

2. Norovirus — Most Common Cause of Outbreaks

  • Family: Caliciviridae; genus Norovirus.
  • Structure:
    • Non-enveloped; icosahedral; small (27–40 nm).
    • Cup-shaped depressions on surface (calici = cup).
    • Positive-sense single-stranded RNA (+ssRNA).
    • Single major capsid protein (VP1) + minor VP2.
    • Genogroups GI, GII (most common in humans); GIV.
    • GII.4 (Sydney variant) — most common cause of outbreaks globally.
  • Transmission:
    • Faecal-oral — contaminated food (shellfish, salads, fruits, ready-to-eat food handled by infected food handler).
    • Person-to-person — direct contact; aerosolised vomitus.
    • Fomites — surfaces (door handles, keyboards); survives 7 days on surfaces.
    • Waterborne — recreational water, drinking water.
  • Incubation — 12–48 h.
  • Infective dose — very low (~18 viral particles); highly contagious.
  • Pathogenesis:
    1. Virus infects mature enterocytes of proximal small intestine (jejunum).
    2. Receptors — histo-blood group antigens (HBGA); secretor status determines susceptibility.
    3. Villus blunting; crypt hyperplasia; transient malabsorption.
    4. Inflammatory response — minimal (no RBCs/WBCs in stool).
    5. Decreased brush border enzymes (lactase, sucrase, maltase) → osmotic diarrhoea.
    6. Delayed gastric emptying → vomiting.
    7. Resolves in 1–3 days; viral shedding in stool for 2–3 weeks.
  • Clinical features:
    • Acute onset nausea, vomiting (prominent), abdominal cramps, watery diarrhoea.
    • Low-grade fever, malaise, headache, myalgia.
    • Dehydration — usually mild-moderate; severe in young, elderly, immunocompromised.
    • Self-limiting in 1–3 days.
  • Diagnosis:
    • RT-PCR (real-time) — gold standard; detects & genotypes.
    • ELISA for norovirus antigen — rapid.
    • Electron microscopy — small round structured viruses (SRSV).
    • Stool — no RBCs/WBCs (non-invasive).
  • Treatment — supportive; ORS; IV fluids if severe; antiemetics (ondansetron) for severe vomiting; no antivirals; no vaccine (in development).
  • Prevention:
    • Hand hygiene (soap & water better than alcohol handrub — norovirus relatively resistant).
    • Food safety — cook shellfish thoroughly; sick food handlers should not work for 48–72 h after recovery.
    • Environmental disinfection — bleach (sodium hypochlorite 1000–5000 ppm); quaternary ammonium less effective.
    • Isolation of affected patients (cohorting); contact precautions in hospitals.
    • Outbreak control in cruise ships, nursing homes, hospitals, schools.

Other Viruses Causing Acute Gastroenteritis in Children

Virus Features
Adenovirus (types 40, 41 — enteric)2nd most common viral cause in infants; prolonged diarrhoea (5–14 days); respiratory symptoms may coexist
AstrovirusMild; infants <2 yr; winter; 2–4 days
Sapovirus (Caliciviridae)Milder than norovirus; outbreaks & sporadic
Enterovirus (some)Mild diarrhoea; often with other symptoms
Cytomegalovirus (CMV)Immunocompromised (HIV); colitis

Clinical Pearl

Rotavirus is the most common cause of severe dehydrating diarrhoea in children <5 yr — responsible for ~40% of hospitalisations for childhood gastroenteritis globally; mortality ~200,000/year (mostly developing countries). Rotavirus vaccine (ROTAVAC / ROTASIIL — India-made) included in India's UIP (2016) — reduced rotavirus hospitalisation & mortality by ~50%. Norovirus is the most common cause of gastroenteritis outbreaks — cruise ships, nursing homes, schools, hospitals; very low infective dose (~18 particles); survives on surfaces 7 days; vomiting prominent. Alcohol-based handrubs are LESS effective against norovirus — soap & water preferred; bleach for environmental disinfection. Rotavirus & norovirus are non-invasive — stool shows no RBCs or WBCs (distinguishes from bacterial dysentery — Shigella, Salmonella, Campylobacter, EHEC). NSP4 enterotoxin of rotavirus — first viral enterotoxin described; mediates calcium influx & chloride secretion. Always give zinc supplementation with ORS in children <5 yr — reduces duration, severity, & future episodes; WHO recommendation. Breastfeeding protects against rotavirus — secretory IgA & lactadherin inhibit viral attachment. Avoid antimotility agents (loperamide) in young children — risk of toxic megacolon, respiratory depression (FDA contraindicated <2 yr).

Introduction

Influenza virus — family Orthomyxoviridae — undergoes two types of antigenic variation that allow it to evade host immunity & cause recurrent epidemics & pandemics: antigenic drift & antigenic shift.

Two Antigenic Variants of Influenza Virus

1. Antigenic Drift — Minor Variation (Point Mutations)

  • Mechanism:
    • Point mutations in genes encoding surface antigens haemagglutinin (HA) & neuraminidase (NA).
    • Due to error-prone RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (no proofreading) — mutation rate ~1 in 10,000 nucleotides per replication.
    • Single amino acid changes alter antigenic sites.
    • Selection pressure from host antibodies selects for escape mutants.
  • Frequency — continuous; ongoing every flu season.
  • Magnitude — minor (<1% amino acid change per year).
  • Clinical consequence:
    • Causes annual seasonal epidemics.
    • Reduced vaccine effectiveness — reason annual flu vaccine update needed.
    • Reinfection possible throughout life — partial immunity from prior exposure is incomplete.
  • Strains affected — all types (A, B, C); influenza B undergoes only drift (no shift).
  • Example — H3N2 A/Hong Kong/4801/2014 → A/Singapore/INFIMH-16-0019/2016 (drifted variant of same H3N2).

2. Antigenic Shift — Major Variation (Gene Reassortment)

  • Mechanism:
    • Gene reassortment in cells co-infected with two different influenza A strains (human + animal — avian, swine).
    • Influenza A genome has 8 segmented RNA strands — when two strains infect same cell, segments can re assort into new combinations.
    • Result — novel HA &/or NA subtype to which humans have no prior immunity.
  • Frequency — rare; only occasionally (every 10–40 years).
  • Magnitude — major (new HA or NA subtype — e.g., H1 → H2, H2 → H3).
  • Clinical consequence:
    • Causes pandemics — global spread due to lack of population immunity.
    • Higher mortality than seasonal flu.
    • Vaccine needs complete reformulation based on new strain.
  • Strains affected — influenza A only (B & C infect humans only — no animal reservoir for reassortment).
  • Animal reservoirs:
    • Birds (especially aquatic birds — ducks, geese, shorebirds) — natural reservoir of all 16 HA & 9 NA subtypes.
    • Pigs — "mixing vessel" — susceptible to both avian & human strains → reassortment.
  • Historical pandemics:
    • 1918 — Spanish flu (H1N1) — 50–100 million deaths; avian origin; young adults most affected.
    • 1957 — Asian flu (H2N2) — replaced H1N1; 1–2 million deaths.
    • 1968 — Hong Kong flu (H3N2) — replaced H2N2; 1 million deaths.
    • 1977 — Russian flu (H1N1) — re-emergence of H1N1 (laboratory strain?); co-circulated with H3N2 since.
    • 2009 — Swine flu (H1N1pdm09) — quadruple reassortant (swine + avian + human genes); ~280,000 deaths globally.

Comparison: Drift vs Shift

Feature Antigenic Drift Antigenic Shift
MechanismPoint mutations in HA/NA genesGene reassortment between strains
FrequencyContinuous; every seasonRare; every 10–40 years
MagnitudeMinor — small antigenic changesMajor — new HA/NA subtype
Virus types affectedA, B, CA only (B & C have no animal reservoir)
Clinical effectSeasonal epidemics; annual vaccine updatePandemics; novel vaccine
Population immunityPartial — cross-protection someNone — pandemic potential
ExampleAnnual H3N2 drift variants1918 H1N1; 1957 H2N2; 1968 H3N2; 2009 H1N1pdm

Surface Antigens

  • Haemagglutinin (HA):
    • 16 subtypes in birds (H1–H16); H1, H2, H3 common in humans.
    • Binds sialic acid receptors on host cells (α2,6 in human upper respiratory tract; α2,3 in birds & human lower respiratory tract).
    • Mediates viral entry & fusion.
    • Major target of neutralising antibodies.
  • Neuraminidase (NA):
    • 9 subtypes (N1–N9); N1 & N2 common in humans.
    • Cleaves sialic acid → releases new virions from infected cells → spreads infection.
    • Target of antiviral drugs — oseltamivir, zanamivir (NA inhibitors).

Influenza Types

Type Hosts Antigenic variation Severity
AHumans, birds, pigs, horses, whales, sealsDrift + ShiftMost severe; pandemics
BHumans onlyDrift only (no shift)Moderate; epidemics; no pandemics; two lineages — Victoria & Yamagata
CHumans, pigsDrift onlyMild; sporadic; not in vaccine
DCattle, pigs (no human disease)——

Vaccine

  • Trivalent — H1N1, H3N2, B/Victoria (or B/Yamagata).
  • Quadrivalent — adds second B lineage.
  • Updated annually by WHO based on global surveillance (Northern & Southern hemisphere strains).
  • Types — inactivated (IM); live attenuated (intranasal — LAIV); high-dose for elderly; adjuvanted; cell-based.

Clinical Pearl

Antigenic drift causes annual seasonal epidemics — minor mutations in HA & NA selected by antibody pressure; reason flu vaccine must be updated every year. Antigenic shift causes pandemics — gene reassortment between human & animal strains (especially in pigs — "mixing vessel") creates novel HA/NA combination to which humans have no immunity; reason pandemic preparedness is critical. Only influenza A undergoes shift — B & C have no animal reservoir. The 1918 Spanish flu (H1N1) killed 50–100 million — more than WWI; avian origin without reassortment (entire avian virus adapted to humans). The 2009 swine flu (H1N1pdm09) was a quadruple reassortant — North American swine, North American avian, human, Eurasian swine genes; replaced seasonal H1N1; now circulates as seasonal H1N1. Avian influenza H5N1 & H7N9 — zoonotic (bird-to-human); high mortality (60% for H5N1) but no sustained human-to-human transmission yet; pandemic potential if they acquire human-transmissible mutations. Annual flu vaccine — best protection; updated based on WHO global surveillance; quadrivalent preferred (covers both B lineages); effectiveness varies (30–60%) due to drift & strain mismatch. Antivirals — oseltamivir, zanamivir (NA inhibitors) — reduce severity & duration if started within 48 h; adamantanes (amantadine, rimantadine) — no longer recommended (resistance in H1N1 & H3N2). India — annual seasonal flu vaccine recommended for high-risk groups (elderly, chronic illness, pregnancy, healthcare workers); H1N1pdm09 (swine flu) outbreaks common.

Introduction

Zoonoses are diseases transmitted from animals to humans. Bacterial zoonoses are common in India due to close human-animal contact (agriculture, livestock, slaughterhouse, veterinary). Here are two important ones.

Two Zoonotic Bacterial Diseases

1. Brucellosis (Brucella spp.)

  • Causative organism:
    • Brucella abortus — cattle; most common worldwide.
    • Brucella melitensis — sheep & goats; most virulent; most common in India, Mediterranean, Middle East.
    • Brucella suis — pigs.
    • Brucella canis — dogs.
  • Gram-negative, intracellular coccobacillus; aerobic; non-motile; non-spore-forming.
  • Transmission:
    • Ingestion of unpasteurised dairy — most common (raw milk, cheese, butter from infected animals).
    • Direct contact with infected animal tissues — farmers, veterinarians, slaughterhouse workers, hunters; through skin abrasions; placenta/aborted foetus highly infectious.
    • Inhalation of aerosols — laboratory workers; slaughterhouse.
    • NOT person-to-person (except rare transfusion, organ transplant, sexual).
  • Incubation — 1–3 weeks (range 5 days to months).
  • Clinical features:
    • Insidious onset — fever (undulant — rises in evening, falls in morning), chills, malaise, fatigue, headache, myalgia, anorexia, weight loss; sweats (characteristic — malodorous, "mouldy hay" smell).
    • osteoarticular — arthritis (sacroiliitis, spondylitis), osteomyelitis; most common focal complication.
    • Genitourinary — epididymo-orchitis (unilateral); abortion in pregnant women & animals.
    • Hepatosplenomegaly; lymphadenopathy.
    • Endocarditis (rare; caused by B. melitensis; life-threatening).
    • Neurobrucellosis — meningitis, encephalitis, depression.
    • Chronic brucellosis — persists >1 year; fatigue, low-grade fever.
  • Diagnosis:
    • Blood culture — gold standard; Castaneda method (biphasic — solid + liquid); BACTEC; positive in 50–70%; incubate 4–6 weeks (slow growing); BSL-3 required (laboratory-acquired infection risk).
    • Serology:
      • Rose Bengal test — rapid screening; agglutination.
      • Standard Agglutination Test (SAT) — quantitative; titre ≥1:160 significant; gold standard serology; cross-reacts with Vibrio cholerae, Yersinia enterocolitica O9, Francisella tularensis, E. coli O157.
      • 2-Mercaptoethanol (2-ME) test — detects IgG (eliminates IgM); indicates active infection.
      • ELISA — IgM, IgG; sensitive.
      • Coombs test — for blocking antibodies in chronic brucellosis.
    • PCR — rapid; species-specific; IS711, bcsp31; blood, tissue.
    • Bone marrow culture — higher yield than blood.
    • CBG — leucopenia, relative lymphocytosis, thrombocytopenia.
    • LFT — mild elevation.
  • Treatment:
    • Adults — Doxycycline 100 mg BD + Rifampicin 600 mg OD × 6 weeks; OR Doxycycline 100 mg BD × 6 weeks + Streptomycin 1 g IM daily × 2–3 weeks (preferred for spondylitis/endocarditis).
    • Children <8 yr — Cotrimoxazole + Rifampicin × 6 weeks.
    • Pregnancy — Rifampicin 900 mg OD × 6 weeks; or cotrimoxazole (avoid 3rd trimester — kernicterus).
    • Endocarditis, neurobrucellosis — triple therapy (doxycycline + rifampicin + cotrimoxazole or aminoglycoside) × 3–6 months.
    • Relapse rate 5–15%.
  • Prevention:
    • Pasteurisation of milk & milk products.
    • Vaccinate cattle (B. abortus RB51) & sheep/goats (B. melitensis Rev-1).
    • Slaughter of infected animals; quarantine.
    • Protective clothing for farmers, veterinarians, slaughterhouse workers.
    • Laboratory biosafety BSL-3.
    • No human vaccine widely available.

2. Leptospirosis (Leptospira interrogans)

  • Causative organism:
    • Leptospira interrogans — spirochete; thin (0.1 µm × 6–20 µm), tightly coiled, hook-ended; actively motile.
    • >250 serovars; grouped into ~24 serogroups.
    • Common serovars in India — icterohaemorrhagiae (rats — severe Weil disease), autumnalis, australis, canicola (dogs), pomona (pigs/cattle), grippotyphosa, hebdomadis, bataviae.
  • Reservoir:
    • Rodents (rats — most important) — chronic renal carrier; shed in urine.
    • Cattle, pigs, dogs, horses, wild animals.
  • Transmission:
    • Direct contact of skin (especially abraded) or mucosa with water/soil contaminated with animal urine.
    • Occupational — farmers (rice paddies, sugarcane), sewage workers, abattoir workers, veterinarians, miners, fish farmers, military.
    • Recreational — swimming, rafting, kayaking in contaminated water.
    • Heavy rainfall & flooding — common outbreak setting (monsoon in India).
  • Incubation — 5–14 days (range 2–30 days).
  • Clinical features:
    • Biphasic illness:
      1. Leptospiraemic phase (3–7 days) — abrupt onset fever, chills, headache (severe, retro-orbital), myalgia (calf — characteristic), conjunctival suffusion (red eyes, no exudate — pathognomonic), abdominal pain, vomiting, rash; symptoms resolve temporarily.
      2. Immune phase (4–30 days) — fever returns; meningitis (aseptic); uveitis; rash; organ involvement (immune-mediated).
    • Mild form (anicteric) — most common; self-limiting; flu-like.
    • Severe form (Weil disease — icteric) — 5–10%; jaundice (hepatocellular), AKI (tubulointerstitial nephritis), pulmonary haemorrhage (life-threatening), myocarditis, multi-organ failure; mortality 10–50%.
    • Pulmonary haemorrhage — leading cause of death in severe leptospirosis; ARDS-like.
  • Diagnosis:
    • Culture — blood, CSF (first 7–10 days); urine (after 1–2 weeks); on EMJH (Ellinghausen-McCullough-Johnson-Harris) medium or Fletcher, Korthof; slow — 1–6 weeks; BSL-2.
    • Dark-field microscopy — urine, CSF; low sensitivity.
    • Serology:
      • MAT (Microscopic Agglutination Test) — gold standard; titre ≥1:800 (or 4-fold rise) significant; detects serovar-specific antibodies; live antigen; complex; reference labs only.
      • IgM ELISA — screening; sensitivity 80–90%; detects recent infection.
      • Leptadip slide agglutination — rapid; bedside.
      • Lateral flow assay — point-of-care.
    • PCR — blood, urine, CSF; early; detects DNA; serovar-specific.
    • Other tests:
      • CBG — leucocytosis, thrombocytopenia; ESR high.
      • LFT — bilirubin high (predominantly direct); AST/ALT mildly elevated (hepatocellular); AKI (raised urea, creatinine); CK elevated (myositis).
      • Urinalysis — proteinuria, haematuria, pyuria, casts.
      • Chest X-ray — pulmonary infiltrates, haemorrhage.
      • CSF — aseptic meningitis (lymphocytic pleocytosis, raised protein, normal glucose).
  • Treatment:
    • Mild — Doxycycline 100 mg BD × 7 days; OR Amoxicillin 500 mg TID × 7 days; OR Azithromycin 500 mg OD × 3 days.
    • Severe (Weil disease) — IV Penicillin G 1.5 MU 6-hourly × 7 days; OR IV Ceftriaxone 1–2 g OD × 7 days; OR IV Doxycycline + Ceftriaxone.
    • Children <8 yr — Azithromycin, Penicillin, Ceftriaxone.
    • Pregnancy — Penicillin, Ceftriaxone.
    • Supportive — IV fluids, dialysis, mechanical ventilation, blood transfusion.
    • Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction — possible with penicillin (less common than in syphilis).
    • Prophylaxis — Doxycycline 200 mg weekly for high-risk exposure.
  • Prevention:
    • Avoid contact with contaminated water — wear protective clothing, boots, gloves.
    • Rodent control.
    • Drainage of standing water; sanitation.
    • Vaccinate domestic animals (dogs, cattle).
    • Chemoprophylaxis — Doxycycline 200 mg weekly for high-risk (military, farmers, after floods).
    • Human vaccine (China, Cuba, France) — limited use.

Relapsing feverBorrelia recurrentis (louse); B. duttoni (tick)Humans (louse); rodents (tick)

CampylobacteriosisC. jejuniPoultry, cattle
ListeriosisListeria monocytogenesCattle, sheep, goats
Cat scratch diseaseBartonella henselaeCats
Rickettsial diseases (scrub typhus, murine typhus, Indian tick typhus)Orientia tsutsugamushi, Rickettsia typhi, R. conoriiRodents; mites, fleas, ticks

Clinical Pearl

Brucellosis & leptospirosis are two of the most common bacterial zoonoses in India — both often undiagnosed or misdiagnosed as typhoid/malaria due to non-specific febrile presentation. Always ask about occupational & animal exposure — farmer, slaughterhouse worker, veterinarian; consumption of unpasteurised milk/cheese (brucellosis); exposure to floodwater, rice paddies, sugarcane fields, recreational swimming (leptospirosis); rat infestation (both). Brucellosis — undulant fever, sweating (malodorous), arthralgia, epididymo-orchitis, hepatosplenomegaly, sacroiliitis; blood culture (positive in 50–70%; slow — 4–6 weeks; BSL-3); SAT ≥1:160 (serology); treatment — doxycycline + rifampicin × 6 weeks. Leptospirosis — biphasic fever, severe myalgia (calf), conjunctival suffusion (red eye, no exudate — pathognomonic); Weil disease (severe — jaundice, AKI, pulmonary haemorrhage); diagnosis — MAT (gold standard) ≥1:800, IgM ELISA (screening), PCR; treatment — doxycycline (mild) or IV penicillin/ceftriaxone (severe); chemoprophylaxis with doxycycline 200 mg weekly for high-risk (military, farmers after floods). Always consider leptospirosis in any febrile patient with exposure to floodwater or animal urine — common in India's monsoon season; Mumbai, Gujarat, Kerala, Andaman outbreaks reported. Pulmonary haemorrhage is the leading cause of death in severe leptospirosis — watch for cough, haemoptysis, dyspnoea; chest X-ray shows bilateral infiltrates; needs ICU & mechanical ventilation.
