Introduction

Angina pectoris is the clinical syndrome of transient chest pain or discomfort due to myocardial ischaemia (imbalance between myocardial oxygen supply and demand). Three main types — stable (chronic stable) angina, unstable angina, variant (Prinzmetal/vasospastic) angina. Treatment aims to restore the supply-demand balance — reduce demand (heart rate, contractility, wall stress) and/or increase supply (coronary vasodilation).

Classification of Drugs Used in Angina Pectoris (5 marks)

A. Organic Nitrates

  • Short-acting — Nitroglycerin (glyceryl trinitrate, GTN) — sublingual tablet, spray; onset 1–3 min; duration 20–30 min.
  • Long-acting:
    • Isosorbide dinitrate (ISDN) — sublingual, oral; duration 4–6 h.
    • Isosorbide mononitrate (ISMN) — oral; duration 6–8 h.
    • Nitroglycerin transdermal patch, ointment — duration 8–14 h.
    • Erythrityl tetranitrate, pentaerythritol tetranitrate (rarely used).
    • Amyl nitrite (inhalant — historically for cyanide poisoning).

B. β-Adrenergic Blockers (β-Blockers)

  • Cardioselective (β1-selective) — Atenolol, Metoprolol, Bisoprolol, Nebivolol (also NO-mediated vasodilation), Acebutolol, Betaxolol, Esmolol (ultra-short-acting — IV).
  • Non-selective (β1 + β2) — Propranolol, Timolol, Nadolol, Sotalol (also class III antiarrhythmic).
  • Non-selective with α1-blockade — Carvedilol, Labetalol.

C. Calcium Channel Blockers (CCBs)

  • Dihydropyridines (DHP) — predominantly vasodilators:
    • Short-acting — Nifedipine (avoid short-acting capsule — reflex tachycardia, hypotension).
    • Long-acting — Amlodipine, Felodipine, Nicardipine, Lercanidipine, Nitrendipine, Clevidipine (IV).
  • Non-dihydropyridines (Non-DHP) — predominantly cardiac depressants:
    • Phenylalkylamine — Verapamil.
    • Benzothiazepine — Diltiazem.

D. Antiplatelet & Antithrombotic Drugs

  • Aspirin — COX-1 inhibitor; ↓platelet aggregation.
  • Clopidogrel, Prasugrel, Ticagrelor — P2Y12 ADP receptor antagonists.
  • Heparin, LMWH (enoxaparin), Fondaparinux — anticoagulants (acute coronary syndromes).
  • Abciximab, Eptifibatide, Tirofiban — GP IIb/IIIa antagonists (PCI).
  • Rivaroxaban, Apixaban — factor Xa inhibitors (recent ACS trials).

E. Lipid-Lowering Drugs

  • Statins — Atorvastatin, Rosuvastatin, Simvastatin, Pravastatin; HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors; plaque stabilisation; anti-inflammatory.
  • Ezetimibe — cholesterol absorption inhibitor.
  • PCSK9 inhibitors — Evolocumab, Alirocumab (familial hypercholesterolaemia, statin intolerance).
  • Bempedoic acid — ATP citrate lyase inhibitor.
  • Fibrates, Niacin, Omega-3 fatty acids — adjuncts.

F. Other Antianginal Drugs

  • Ranolazine — inhibits late sodium current (late INa) → ↓ Ca²⁺ overload → ↓ myocardial wall stress & oxygen demand; does not affect HR or BP; used for chronic stable angina refractory to standard therapy.
  • Ivabradine — selective inhibitor of If (funny channel) in SA node → ↓ heart rate without affecting contractility or BP; used for chronic stable angina in sinus rhythm with HR >70 bpm.
  • Nicorandil — nitrate + K-ATP channel opener; dual mechanism; vasodilator; used for stable angina.
  • Trimetazidine — inhibits fatty acid oxidation (3-ketoacyl-CoA thiolase) → shifts to glucose oxidation → ↓ oxygen demand; metabolic modulator.
  • Molsidomine — NO donor (like nitrates).
  • ACE inhibitors / ARBs — reduce CV events; protect endothelium; especially in diabetes, LV dysfunction, hypertension.

G. Combination Therapy

  • β-blocker + DHP-CCB (amlodipine) — synergistic; β-blocker counters reflex tachycardia from DHP.
  • β-blocker + long-acting nitrate.
  • Nitrate + CCB (avoid non-DHP + β-blocker — bradycardia, AV block).
  • Antiplatelet + statin + ACEI — for secondary prevention.

Mechanism of Action of Nitrates (5 marks)

1. Pharmacokinetics

  • Nitroglycerin (GTN):
    • Sublingual — onset 1–3 min; peak 4–8 min; duration 20–30 min; bioavailability <5% oral (extensive first-pass); sublingual bypasses liver.
    • IV — for unstable angina, acute MI, acute heart failure, hypertensive emergency; titratable.
    • Transdermal patch, ointment — sustained release; 8–14 h duration; patch-off period (12 h) to prevent tolerance.
    • Metabolism — by mitochondrial aldehyde dehydrogenase-2 (ALDH2) in liver, blood vessel walls; inactive metabolites (glyceryl dinitrate, mononitrate, glycerol).
  • Isosorbide dinitrate (ISDN):
    • Sublingual — onset 2–5 min; duration 1–2 h.
    • Oral — onset 20–40 min; duration 4–6 h.
    • Hepatic metabolism to active ISMN (5-ISMN & 2-ISMN).
  • Isosorbide mononitrate (ISMN):
    • Oral — 100% bioavailability (no first-pass); duration 6–8 h.
    • Slow-release formulation — once daily; patch-off period (≥8 h) to prevent tolerance.

2. Mechanism of Action

  1. Prodrug activation:
    • Organic nitrates are prodrugs; require enzymatic bioactivation to release nitric oxide (NO).
    • ALDH2 (mitochondrial aldehyde dehydrogenase-2) — main enzyme for nitroglycerin; converts GTN to 1,2-glyceryl dinitrate + nitrite → NO.
    • Other enzymes — cytochrome P450 reductase, xanthine oxidoreductase, glutathione-S-transferase.
    • Released NO is identical to endogenous endothelium-derived relaxing factor (EDRF) — discovered by Furchgott, Ignarro, Murad (Nobel Prize 1998).
  2. NO-mediated vasodilation:
    1. NO diffuses from endothelial cell (or from nitrate metabolism in vascular smooth muscle) to adjacent vascular smooth muscle cell.
    2. NO activates soluble guanylyl cyclase (sGC) → converts GTP → cyclic GMP (cGMP).
    3. cGMP activates protein kinase G (PKG).
    4. PKG phosphorylates multiple targets:
      • Phospholamban → ↑ Ca²⁺-ATPase (SERCA) → ↑ Ca²⁺ reuptake into sarcoplasmic reticulum → ↓ cytosolic Ca²⁺.
      • Myosin light chain phosphatase → dephosphorylates myosin light chain → relaxation.
      • K⁺ channels → hyperpolarisation → closes voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels → ↓ Ca²⁺ influx.
      • IP3 receptor → ↓ Ca²⁺ release.
    5. ↓ Intracellular Ca²⁺ → smooth muscle relaxation → vasodilation.
  3. Vascular selectivity:
    • Low doses — preferential venodilation (capacitance veins) → ↓ venous return (preload) → ↓ ventricular end-diastolic volume & wall stress → ↓ myocardial oxygen demand.
    • Higher doses — arteriolar dilation (resistance arteries) → ↓ peripheral resistance → ↓ afterload → ↓ myocardial work.
    • Coronary arteries:
      • Dilates large epicardial coronary arteries (conductance vessels) — improves blood flow to ischaemic subendocardium; redistributes flow.
      • Dilates collateral coronary vessels → improves perfusion of ischaemic areas.
      • Relieves coronary vasospasm (Prinzmetal angina).
      • Little effect on arterioles (<100 µm) — prevents "coronary steal" syndrome.
    • Platelets — NO + cGMP → ↓ platelet aggregation; may reduce thrombosis in unstable angina.

3. Haemodynamic Effects

  • Venodilation → ↓ preload (ventricular end-diastolic pressure & volume) → ↓ myocardial wall stress → ↓ oxygen demand.
  • Arteriolar dilation → ↓ afterload (systemic vascular resistance) → ↓ cardiac work → ↓ oxygen demand.
  • Coronary dilation → ↑ coronary blood flow; relief of spasm; redistribution to ischaemic subendocardium.
  • Reflex tachycardia — ↓ BP triggers baroreceptor reflex → ↑ sympathetic outflow → ↑ HR & contractility → may offset oxygen-sparing effect (combine with β-blocker).
  • Pulmonary vasodilation — ↓ pulmonary vascular resistance; useful in pulmonary oedema.
  • Reduced platelet aggregation — anti-thrombotic effect.

4. Therapeutic Uses

  • Acute anginal attack — sublingual GTN (1 tablet or spray under tongue; repeat every 5 min × 3 doses; if no relief, call emergency — possible MI).
  • Prophylaxis of stable angina — long-acting nitrates (ISMN, GTN patch) with patch-off period to prevent tolerance; β-blocker; CCB; aspirin; statin.
  • Variant (Prinzmetal) angina — nitrates + CCBs (especially DHP); avoid β-blockers (may worsen spasm via unopposed α).
  • Unstable angina / NSTEMI — IV nitroglycerin; antiplatelet (aspirin + clopidogrel/ticagrelor); anticoagulant (heparin/LMWH); statin; β-blocker; coronary angiography ± PCI.
  • Acute MI — IV nitroglycerin (if BP allows); aspirin; clopidogrel; heparin; β-blocker; ACEI; statin; primary PCI or thrombolysis.
  • Acute left ventricular failure / pulmonary oedema — IV/sublingual GTN; venodilation reduces preload; afterload reduction improves cardiac output.
  • Hypertensive emergency — IV nitroprusside (arterial + venous vasodilation); IV nitroglycerin (especially if cardiac ischaemia).
  • Chronic heart failure — ISDN + hydralazine (especially in African-Americans — A-HeFT trial with fixed-dose Bidil).
  • Anal fissure — topical GTN 0.2–0.4% ointment (relieves internal anal sphincter spasm).
  • Cyanide poisoning — sodium nitrite + sodium thiosulfate; amyl nitrite (forms methaemoglobin which binds cyanide).
  • Esophageal spasm, biliary colic — sublingual GTN may relieve smooth muscle spasm.

5. Adverse Effects

  • Vasodilatory:
    • Headache (most common; ~50%) — meningeal vasodilation; ameliorates with continued use; treat with paracetamol.
    • Flushing, dizziness, postural hypotension, syncope.
    • Reflex tachycardia — may worsen angina; combine with β-blocker.
  • Methaemoglobinaemia — high doses or prolonged use; nitrites oxidise Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ in haemoglobin; ↓ oxygen-carrying capacity; treat with methylene blue 1–2 mg/kg IV.
  • Tolerance (nitrate tolerance) — develops with continuous therapy (>24 h); due to:
    • Depletion of sulphydryl (-SH) groups (required for ALDH2-mediated NO release) — "thiol hypothesis".
    • ↑ ALDH2 inactivation by oxidative stress.
    • ↑ Superoxide production → ↑ NO degradation (uncoupling of eNOS).
    • Neurohormonal activation — RAAS, sympathetic activation.
    • Plasma volume expansion.
  • Prevention — nitrate-free interval (≥8–12 h daily); eccentric dosing (e.g., ISMN at 8 AM & 2 PM — nitrate-free overnight); intermittent transdermal patch (12 h on, 12 h off).
  • Withdrawal / rebound — abrupt cessation of long-term nitrate therapy → rebound vasoconstriction, angina, MI; taper gradually.
  • Alcohol interaction — severe hypotension; avoid concurrent use.
  • Sildenafil (PDE5 inhibitor) interaction — contraindicated; both ↑ cGMP → severe, life-threatening hypotension; at least 24 h gap (48 h for tadalafil).
  • Increased intracranial pressure — vasodilation; avoid in raised ICP, recent head injury.
  • Increased intraocular pressure — historical concern (open-angle glaucoma); modern evidence suggests safe.
  • Contact dermatitis — transdermal patch.
  • Sodium nitroprusside — cyanide & thiocyanate toxicity (with prolonged use >48 h or renal impairment); monitor thiocyanate levels; treat with sodium thiosulfate + hydroxocobalamin.

6. Contraindications

  • Hypotension (SBP <90 mmHg).
  • Severe aortic stenosis, hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM) — ↓ preload worsens outflow obstruction.
  • Right ventricular infarction — ↓ preload worsens RV failure.
  • Recent PDE5 inhibitor use (sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil) — within 24–48 h.
  • Severe anaemia (methaemoglobinaemia risk).
  • Raised intracranial pressure (head injury, haemorrhage).
  • Hypersensitivity to nitrates.
  • Constrictive pericarditis, cardiac tamponade.

Comparison of Antianginal Drug Classes

Class Mechanism Effect on HR Effect on BP Use
NitratesNO → ↑cGMP → vasodilation (venous > arterial)↑ (reflex)↓Acute angina, prophylaxis, ACS, HF
β-blockers↓ β1 → ↓ HR, contractility, renin↓↓Stable angina (first-line), post-MI, HTN, HF
DHP-CCBBlock L-type Ca²⁺ → arteriolar dilation↑ (reflex)↓Angina, HTN; avoid β-blocker + non-DHP CCB
Non-DHP-CCB (verapamil, diltiazem)Block L-type Ca²⁺ → ↓ HR, contractility, AV conduction↓↓Variant angina, stable angina (if β-blocker contraindicated), AF
Ranolazine↓ Late INa → ↓ Ca²⁺ overload00Refractory stable angina
IvabradineBlock If → ↓ SA node HR↓0Stable angina in sinus rhythm HR >70; HF

Clinical Pearl

Nitrates remain first-line for acute angina relief — sublingual GTN tablet or spray under tongue; relief within 1–3 min; if no relief after 3 doses 5 min apart, call emergency — possible MI. Mechanism — nitrate → NO → activates soluble guanylyl cyclase → ↑cGMP → ↓intracellular Ca²⁺ → smooth muscle relaxation → vasodilation. Low dose = venodilation (↓preload); high dose = arteriolar dilation (↓afterload); combined effect reduces myocardial oxygen demand. Nitrate tolerance develops with continuous therapy — prevent with nitrate-free interval ≥8–12 h daily (eccentric dosing; patch-off overnight). Always combine nitrates with β-blocker — β-blocker counters reflex tachycardia from nitrates & provides additional anti-ischaemic effect; avoid β-blocker + non-DHP CCB (verapamil/diltiazem) — bradycardia, AV block. NEVER combine nitrates with PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil) — both ↑cGMP → life-threatening hypotension; 24 h gap (48 h for tadalafil). Avoid β-blockers in variant (Prinzmetal) angina — unopposed α-mediated vasoconstriction worsens spasm; use nitrates + CCBs. For secondary prevention — aspirin (or clopidogrel), statin (target LDL <70 mg/dL), ACEI/ARB (especially if diabetes, LV dysfunction), β-blocker, lifestyle (smoking cessation, exercise, Mediterranean diet). Ranolazine & ivabradine — newer agents for refractory stable angina; ranolazine doesn't affect HR/BP (metabolic modulator); ivabradine selectively lowers HR (If channel blocker) — useful in sinus rhythm with HR >70. Revascularisation — PCI (stent) or CABG for refractory angina, left main disease, multivessel disease, diabetes with multivessel disease (CABG preferred — FREEDOM trial).

Introduction

Adrenergic transmission refers to the synthesis, storage, release, action, and termination of the neurotransmitter noradrenaline (norepinephrine) at sympathetic postganglionic nerve terminals (and adrenaline from adrenal medulla). Understanding this process is essential for pharmacology of sympathomimetics, sympatholytics, and many cardiovascular drugs.

Steps of Adrenergic Transmission (6 marks)

Step 1 — Synthesis of Noradrenaline

Occurs in the neuronal cytoplasm; catalysed by three enzymes acting sequentially:

  1. Tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) — rate-limiting step; converts L-tyrosine → L-DOPA (3,4-dihydroxyphenylalanine); requires tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4), Fe²⁺, O₂; feedback-inhibited by noradrenaline (end-product inhibition).
  2. DOPA decarboxylase (aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase, AADC) — converts L-DOPA → dopamine; requires pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6).
  3. Dopamine β-hydroxylase (DβH) — converts dopamine → noradrenaline; requires ascorbic acid (vitamin C), Cu²⁺, O₂; located in vesicle (after dopamine enters vesicle).
  4. In adrenal medulla, additional enzyme phenylethanolamine-N-methyltransferase (PNMT) — converts noradrenaline → adrenaline; requires S-adenosylmethionine (SAM); located in cytoplasm (adrenaline then re-enters vesicle).

Step 2 — Storage in Vesicles

  • Dopamine (cytoplasmic) is taken up into synaptic vesicles (dense-core granules) via vesicular monoamine transporter (VMAT2) — H⁺-ATPase-driven, exchange H⁺ for monoamine; blocked by reserpine & tetrabenazine.
  • Inside vesicle, DβH converts dopamine → noradrenaline.
  • Noradrenaline stored with ATP (4:1 molar ratio), chromogranin A, DβH, enkephalins; forms dense core.
  • Vesicular storage protects noradrenaline from degradation by MAO (mitochondrial).

Step 3 — Release

  • Action potential arrives at varicosity → opens voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels (N-type, P/Q-type) → Ca²⁺ influx.
  • ↑ Ca²⁺ triggers vesicle docking (SNARE complex — synaptobrevin, SNAP-25, syntaxin) & fusion with plasma membrane.
  • Exocytosis — noradrenaline + ATP + DβH + chromogranin released into synaptic cleft.
  • Modulation of release:
    • α2-presynaptic autoinhibitory receptors — noradrenaline binds α2 on its own neuron → ↓ Ca²⁺ influx → ↓ further release (negative feedback); blocked by α2 antagonists (yohimbine, phentolamine) → ↑ release.
    • β2-presynaptic facilitatory receptors — adrenaline enhances release (positive feedback).
    • Presynaptic receptors for other transmitters:
      • M2 muscarinic (acetylcholine) — inhibits release.
      • H2 histamine, A2 adenosine, PGE2, GABA-B, opioids, somatostatin — inhibit.
      • Angiotensin II (AT1), 5-HT2 — facilitate.

Step 4 — Receptor Action

Noradrenaline binds to adrenergic receptors on postsynaptic (and presynaptic) cells:

  • α1 (Gq) — vasoconstriction (skin, splanchnic), mydriasis, piloerection, ejaculation, bladder neck contraction, GI sphincter contraction; IP3/DAG/PKC → ↑ intracellular Ca²⁺.
  • α2 (Gi) — presynaptic inhibition of noradrenaline release; platelet aggregation; insulin inhibition; ↓ cAMP.
  • β1 (Gs) — ↑ heart rate (SA node), ↑ contractility (atria, ventricles), ↑ AV conduction, ↑ renin release (kidney); ↑ cAMP → PKA.
  • β2 (Gs) — bronchodilation, vasodilation (skeletal muscle), uterine relaxation (tocolysis), glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis, ↑ insulin release, mast cell stabilisation.
  • β3 (Gs) — lipolysis (adipose); thermogenesis; bladder detrusor relaxation (mirabegron).

Step 5 — Termination of Action

Two mechanisms:

  1. Neuronal reuptake (Uptake-1) — primary mechanism (~80%); noradrenaline taken back into nerve terminal via norepinephrine transporter (NET, uptake-1) — Na⁺/Cl⁻-dependent, high affinity, saturable; also takes up adrenaline, dopamine, tyramine, amphetamine, metaraminol. Then re-stored in vesicles (via VMAT2) or degraded by MAO.
  2. Extraneuronal uptake (Uptake-2) — non-neuronal; into effector cells (smooth muscle, glial, liver) via extraneuronal monoamine transporter (EMT, uptake-2) — low affinity, high capacity; adrenaline, isoprenaline preferred; followed by degradation by COMT.
  3. Diffusion — small amount enters systemic circulation; reaches liver (COMT, MAO).

Step 6 — Metabolism

Two enzymes degrade catecholamines:

  • Monoamine oxidase (MAO):
    • Mitochondrial; located in neurons (MAO-A), glial cells, liver, GI tract.
    • MAO-A — deaminates noradrenaline, adrenaline, serotonin (5-HT); inhibited by moclobemide (selective MAO-A inhibitor).
    • MAO-B — deaminates dopamine, phenylethylamine; inhibited by selegiline, rasagiline (Parkinson's disease).
    • Converts noradrenaline → 3,4-dihydroxymandelic acid (DOMA) → vanillylmandelic acid (VMA).
  • Catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT):
    • Cytosolic; located in synaptic cleft, effector cells, liver, kidney; not in neurons.
    • Catalyses O-methylation of catecholamines; requires Mg²⁺, S-adenosylmethionine (SAM).
    • Converts noradrenaline → normetanephrine; adrenaline → metanephrine; dopamine → 3-methoxytyramine.
    • Inhibited by entacapone, tolcapone (Parkinson's disease — prolong L-DOPA action).
  • Final metabolites:
    • Noradrenaline → 3-methoxy-4-hydroxymandelic acid (VMA — vanillylmandelic acid) — main urinary metabolite.
    • Adrenaline → metanephrine → VMA.
    • Dopamine → homovanillic acid (HVA).
  • Clinical use — VMA (24-hour urine) & plasma/urinary metanephrines for diagnosis of phaeochromocytoma; HVA for neuroblastoma.

Drugs Acting Through Modification of Adrenergic Transmission (9 marks)

A. Drugs Affecting Synthesis

  • α-Methyl-p-tyrosine (metyrosine) — inhibits tyrosine hydroxylase (rate-limiting step); ↓ synthesis of catecholamines; used for phaeochromocytoma (pre-operative), refractory hypertension.
  • Carbidopa, benserazide — peripheral DOPA decarboxylase inhibitors; do not cross BBB; combined with levodopa in Parkinson's disease — ↑ brain delivery of L-DOPA, ↓ peripheral side effects (nausea, arrhythmia).
  • α-Methyldopa — false neurotransmitter precursor; converted to α-methyl-noradrenaline (less potent vasoconstrictor than noradrenaline) → replaces noradrenaline in vesicles → released → acts on central α2 receptors (in medulla) → ↓ sympathetic outflow → antihypertensive; used in pregnancy-induced hypertension.
  • Disulfiram — inhibits DβH (also aldehyde dehydrogenase) → ↓ noradrenaline synthesis; historical (not used clinically for this purpose).

B. Drugs Affecting Storage

  • Reserpine — irreversible inhibitor of VMAT2 → noradrenaline leaks into cytoplasm → degraded by MAO → depletion of vesicular noradrenaline; antihypertensive (rarely used now; side effects — severe depression, parkinsonism, peptic ulcer, diarrhoea).
  • Tetrabenazine — reversible VMAT2 inhibitor; depletes central monoamines (dopamine > noradrenaline > serotonin); used for Huntington's chorea, tardive dyskinesia.
  • 6-Hydroxydopamine (6-OHDA) — neurotoxin; taken up by noradrenergic neurons → destroys them; experimental.

C. Drugs Affecting Release

  • Indirectly acting sympathomimetics — taken up by NET (uptake-1) into neuron → displace noradrenaline from vesicles → noradrenaline released into synaptic cleft → acts on receptors:
    • Amphetamine, methamphetamine — CNS stimulants (release dopamine & noradrenaline); ADHD, narcolepsy; abuse potential.
    • Ephedrine, pseudoephedrine — mixed action (direct + indirect); nasal decongestant; ephedrine for hypotension (anaesthesia).
    • Phenylpropanolamine — nasal decongestant; withdrawn (haemorrhagic stroke risk).
    • Tyramine — in fermented foods (cheese, wine, beer); normally metabolised by MAO in gut & liver; in patients on MAO inhibitors → reaches sympathetic nerve terminals → displaces noradrenaline → hypertensive crisis ("cheese reaction").
    • Metaraminol — indirect + direct α-agonist; shock.
  • α2-Agonists (centrally acting):
    • Clonidine — central α2 agonist (brainstem) → ↓ sympathetic outflow → ↓ BP, HR; also ↓ renal renin; antihypertensive; ADHD (patch), opioid/alcohol withdrawal, severe pain.
    • α-Methyldopa — prodrug; converted to α-methylnoradrenaline → central α2 agonist; antihypertensive; pregnancy.
    • Guanfacine, guanabenz — α2A-selective; ADHD (guanfacine); hypertension.
    • Dexmedetomidine — α2A-selective; IV sedative in ICU; analgesia; anxiolysis; minimal respiratory depression.
    • Tizanidine — α2 agonist; centrally acting skeletal muscle relaxant (spasticity, multiple sclerosis).
    • Brimonidine, apraclonidine — α2 agonist; glaucoma (↓ aqueous humour production); brimonidine also reduces redness.
  • α2-Antagonists:
    • Yohimbine, rauwolscine — α2 antagonist; ↑ noradrenaline release; experimental; used for psychogenic erectile dysfunction; anxiety.
    • Mirtazapine — α2 antagonist (also 5-HT2/5-HT3 antagonist); antidepressant; ↑ noradrenaline & serotonin release.
  • Bretylium — blocks noradrenaline release (taken up by NET, accumulates in neuron, blocks Ca²⁺-dependent release); class III antiarrhythmic (historical — VT/VF).
  • Guanethidine — taken up by NET → displaces noradrenaline → depletes stores → blocks release; antihypertensive (historical; rarely used).
  • Botulinum toxin — blocks SNARE complex → prevents exocytosis; used for cervical dystonia, spasticity, wrinkles, migraine, hyperhidrosis, strabismus; (cholinergic junctions more affected than adrenergic).

D. Drugs Affecting Reuptake (NET Inhibitors)

  • Cocaine — blocks NET (and DAT, SERT) → ↑ noradrenaline, dopamine, serotonin in synapse → CNS stimulation, euphoria, vasoconstriction, hypertension; local anaesthetic (topical); high abuse potential.
  • Tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs) — amitriptyline, imipramine, nortriptyline, desipramine — inhibit NET & SERT → ↑ noradrenaline & serotonin; antidepressant, neuropathic pain, migraine prophylaxis, enuresis.
  • Atomoxetine — selective NET inhibitor; ADHD (non-stimulant).
  • Reboxetine — selective NRI; antidepressant (Europe).
  • Viloxazine — NRI; ADHD.
  • SNRIs — venlafaxine, duloxetine, desvenlafaxine, milnacipran, levomilnacipran — inhibit SERT & NET; depression, anxiety, neuropathic pain, fibromyalgia.
  • Nortriptyline, desipramine — more NRI than SRI.

E. Drugs Affecting Metabolism

  • MAO inhibitors (MAOIs):
    • Non-selective (MAO-A + B) — phenelzine, tranylcypromine, isocarboxazid; antidepressants; risk of cheese reaction (tyramine); hypertensive crisis with SSRIs, meperidine ("serotonin syndrome").
    • MAO-A selective (RIMA) — moclobemide; antidepressant; less risk of cheese reaction.
    • MAO-B selective — selegiline (L-deprenyl), rasagiline; Parkinson's disease (↓ dopamine degradation; enhances L-DOPA effect); low risk of cheese reaction at low doses; selegiline at high doses loses selectivity.
    • Linezolid — antibiotic; weak non-selective MAOI; risk of serotonin syndrome with SSRIs.
    • Methylene blue — MAOI; risk with SSRIs.
    • Procarbazine — anticancer; weak MAOI.
  • COMT inhibitors:
    • Entacapone — peripheral COMT inhibitor; combined with L-DOPA/carbidopa (Stalevo) → ↑ L-DOPA bioavailability & duration; Parkinson's disease.
    • Tolcapone — central + peripheral COMT inhibitor; more effective; risk of hepatotoxicity (reserved for refractory cases; monitor LFT).
    • Nitecapone, opicapone — newer.

F. Direct Adrenergic Receptor Agonists & Antagonists (Brief)

  • α1-agonists — phenylephrine, methoxamine (nasal decongestant, mydriatic, shock).
  • α2-agonists — clonidine, methyldopa, dexmedetomidine, brimonidine (see above).
  • β1-agonists — dobutamine (cardiogenic shock, cardiac stress testing).
  • β2-agonists — salbutamol, terbutaline, salmeterol, formoterol (asthma, COPD, tocolysis).
  • Non-selective β — isoprenaline (bradycardia, AV block); adrenaline (anaphylaxis, cardiac arrest).
  • Dopamine receptor agonists — dopamine (shock, heart failure — D1 renal vasodilation); fenoldopam (hypertensive emergency).
  • α1-antagonists — prazosin, terazosin, doxazosin (hypertension, BPH); tamsulosin, silodosin (uroselective — BPH).
  • α1 + α2 antagonists — phenoxybenzamine (irreversible — phaeochromocytoma); phentolamine (reversible).
  • β-blockers — propranolol (non-selective); atenolol, metoprolol (β1); carvedilol, labetalol (α1 + β); nebivolol (β1 + NO release).

Clinical Pearl

The rate-limiting step in noradrenaline synthesis is tyrosine hydroxylase — inhibited by α-methyl-p-tyrosine (metyrosine) for phaeochromocytoma preparation. Reserpine depletes vesicular noradrenaline by blocking VMAT2 — historical antihypertensive; causes severe depression (avoid in patients with mood disorder). Indirectly acting sympathomimetics (amphetamines, tyramine, ephedrine) are taken up by NET (uptake-1) and displace noradrenaline from vesicles — produce sympathomimetic effects without directly binding receptors; their action is blocked by uptake-1 inhibitors (cocaine, TCAs) and abolished by reserpine (depleted stores). Cheese reaction — tyramine in fermented foods (cheese, wine) normally degraded by gut MAO; in patients on MAO-A inhibitors, tyramine reaches systemic circulation → displaces noradrenaline → hypertensive crisis; advise dietary restriction. NEVER combine MAOIs with SSRIs, SNRIs, meperidine, tramadol, dextromethorphan, linezolid — serotonin syndrome (hyperthermia, tremor, hyperreflexia, seizures, death). Cocaine blocks NET (and DAT, SERT) — ↑ noradrenaline at adrenergic synapses → vasoconstriction, hypertension, arrhythmia; avoid β-blockers alone in cocaine intoxication (unopposed α → worsening vasoconstriction); use benzodiazepine + nitrate + α-blocker. Phaeochromocytoma workup — plasma/urinary metanephrines (most sensitive); 24-h urinary VMA (historical); pre-operative preparation with α-blocker (phenoxybenzamine) before β-blocker; α-methyl-tyrosine for severe cases; avoid β-blocker alone (unopposed α → hypertensive crisis). Levodopa + carbidopa in Parkinson's disease — carbidopa is peripheral DOPA decarboxylase inhibitor (doesn't cross BBB) → ↑ brain delivery of L-DOPA → ↓ peripheral side effects (nausea, arrhythmia); add entacapone (COMT inhibitor) → further prolong L-DOPA action.

Definition

Anticoagulants are drugs that prevent or reduce the coagulation (clotting) of blood — used in prevention & treatment of thromboembolic disorders (DVT, PE, atrial fibrillation, mechanical heart valves, ACS).

Classification of Anticoagulants (3 marks)

A. Parenteral Anticoagulants

  1. Indirect thrombin inhibitors (acting via antithrombin):
    • Heparin (Unfractionated Heparin, UFH) — IV/SC; inhibits thrombin (IIa) & factor Xa via antithrombin (AT).
    • Low Molecular Weight Heparin (LMWH) — enoxaparin, dalteparin, tinzaparin; SC; preferentially inhibit factor Xa > thrombin.
    • Fondaparinux — synthetic pentasaccharide; selective factor Xa inhibitor via antithrombin; SC.
    • Idraparinux, idrabiotaparinux — long-acting pentasaccharides (investigational).
  2. Direct thrombin inhibitors (do not require antithrombin):
    • Lepirudin, desirudin — recombinant hirudin (from leech); IV/SC; for heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT).
    • Bivalirudin — hirudin analogue; IV; PCI, HIT.
    • Argatroban — small molecule; IV; HIT.

B. Oral Anticoagulants

  1. Vitamin K Antagonists (Coumarins):
    • Warfarin — most common; racemic mixture.
    • A cenocoumarol — shorter half-life; used in Europe, India.
    • Phenprocoumon — longer half-life; Europe.
    • Dicoumarol, ethyl biscoumacetate — historical.
  2. Direct Oral Anticoagulants (DOACs / NOACs / Target-Specific Oral Anticoagulants):
    • Direct thrombin (IIa) inhibitor — Dabigatran (Pradaxa).
    • Direct factor Xa inhibitors:
      • Rivaroxaban (Xarelto).
      • Apixaban (Eliquis).
      • Edoxaban (Lixiana, Savaysa).
      • Betrixaban (Bevyxxa) — withdrawn.

C. Other Anticoagulants

  • Defibrotide — purified polydeoxyribonucleotide; modulates endothelial function; hepatic veno-occlusive disease (VOD) post-HSCT.
  • Antithrombin concentrate — for AT deficiency; heparin resistance.
  • Protein C concentrate — purpura fulminans (homozygous protein C deficiency).
  • Thrombomodulin (recombinant soluble) — sepsis-associated DIC (historical).
  • Sulodexide — glycosaminoglycan; diabetic nephropathy (investigational).

Heparin (5 marks)

Source & Chemistry

  • Naturally occurring glycosaminoglycan (mucopolysaccharide); extracted from porcine intestinal mucosa or bovine lung.
  • Mixture of sulphated polysaccharides; MW 3,000–30,000 Da (average 15,000).
  • Strongly negatively charged (sulphate groups) — basis for neutralisation by protamine sulphate (positively charged).

Mechanism of Action

  1. Heparin binds to antithrombin III (AT) (endogenous serine protease inhibitor) via a specific pentasaccharide sequence.
  2. Binding induces conformational change in AT → exposes active site → accelerates AT-mediated inhibition of clotting factors (1000-fold).
  3. Inactivates thrombin (IIa), factor Xa, IXa, XIa, XIIa, kallikrein.
  4. Unfractionated heparin inhibits both thrombin & factor Xa equally (1:1 ratio).
  5. LMWH (<6500 Da) — preferentially inhibits factor Xa (ratio ~3–4:1) — cannot simultaneously bind thrombin & AT (short chain).
  6. Fondaparinux — pure pentasaccharide; exclusively inhibits factor Xa.

Pharmacokinetics

  • Not absorbed orally (large, charged molecule); given IV or SC.
  • Onset — IV immediate; SC 1–2 h.
  • Half-life — 1–2 h (dose-dependent; longer at high doses); 60–90 min after IV bolus.
  • Metabolism — hepatic (heparinase) & reticuloendothelial; partial renal excretion.
  • Does not cross placenta (large molecule) — safe in pregnancy.
  • Monitoring — aPTT (activated partial thromboplastin time); target 1.5–2.5× control. LMWH does not require routine monitoring (predictable pharmacokinetics); monitor anti-Xa level in pregnancy, renal impairment, obesity, children.
  • Antidote — protamine sulphate 1 mg neutralises 100 U heparin (given IV slowly; risk of hypotension, anaphylaxis).

Therapeutic Uses

  • Venous thromboembolism (VTE) — DVT & PE — acute & long-term.
  • Acute coronary syndrome (ACS) — unstable angina, NSTEMI, STEMI (with antiplatelets).
  • PCI (percutaneous coronary intervention) — UFH or bivalirudin.
  • Atrial fibrillation — cardioversion (if not on warfarin/DOAC); bridging therapy.
  • Mechanical heart valves — perioperative bridging.
  • Cardiopulmonary bypass, haemodialysis, extracorporeal circuits — anticoagulation.
  • Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) — selected cases (with bleeding).
  • Pregnancy — LMWH for VTE prophylaxis/treatment, mechanical heart valves, antiphospholipid syndrome (APS).
  • Heparin flushes — IV catheter patency.

Adverse Effects

  • Bleeding — most common; dose-dependent; monitor aPTT; reverse with protamine.
  • Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT):
    • Immune-mediated (IgG antibody against heparin-platelet factor 4 [PF4] complex).
    • Type I — mild, non-immune, early (days 1–4), platelet count >100,000; not clinically significant.
    • Type II — severe, immune-mediated, 5–14 days after exposure (or sooner if previous exposure); platelet count <100,000 (or 50% drop); paradoxical thrombosis (arterial & venous) — limb gangrene, stroke, PE; STOP heparin immediately; switch to direct thrombin inhibitor (argatroban, bivalirudin) or fondaparinux; never re-expose to heparin.
    • Diagnosis — clinical (4T score) + laboratory (PF4 ELISA, serotonin release assay [SRA]).
    • LMWH has lower risk than UFH but still contraindicated once HIT develops.
  • Osteoporosis — long-term use (>1 month); ↓ bone formation, ↑ bone resorption; vertebral fractures; mechanism — osteoclast activation, ↓ osteocalcin.
  • Hypoaldosteronism & hyperkalaemia — heparin inhibits aldosterone synthesis; rare but significant in renal impairment, diabetes.
  • Hypersensitivity reactions — urticaria, anaphylaxis, bronchospasm (bovine source higher risk).
  • Skin necrosis — rare; at injection sites; may precede HIT.
  • Withdrawal rebound — possible thrombosis after abrupt cessation; taper.
  • Elevated liver transaminases — common, benign.
  • Priapism — rare.

Contraindications

  • Active bleeding (GI, intracranial, etc.).
  • Severe bleeding diathesis (haemophilia, thrombocytopenia <50,000).
  • Recent neurosurgery, ophthalmic surgery, intracranial haemorrhage.
  • Severe uncontrolled hypertension.
  • Bacterial endocarditis (risk of mycotic aneurysm rupture).
  • HIT (current or past).
  • Known hypersensitivity (porcine or bovine).

Warfarin (5 marks)

Source & Chemistry

  • 4-Hydroxycoumarin derivative; synthetic; racemic mixture of R- & S-enantiomers (S more potent).
  • Discovered as cause of haemorrhagic disease in cattle (sweet clover disease — dicoumarol from spoiled sweet clover; Link, 1940s); warfarin developed as rat poison (1948); first used clinically in 1954.
  • Oral; highly protein-bound (99%); small volume of distribution.

Mechanism of Action

  1. Inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKORC1) — enzyme that recycles oxidised vitamin K (vitamin K 2,3-epoxide) back to active reduced form (hydroquinone, KH2).
  2. ↓ Active vitamin K → ↓ γ-carboxylation of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors.
  3. Vitamin K-dependent clotting factors — II (prothrombin), VII, IX, X; also protein C & protein S (endogenous anticoagulants).
  4. γ-carboxylation (by γ-glutamyl carboxylase) adds carboxyl groups to glutamic acid residues → γ-carboxyglutamic acid (GLA) → enables calcium binding → anchors factors to phospholipid surfaces → active clotting.
  5. Without γ-carboxylation, factors are dysfunctional (PIVKA — Proteins Induced by Vitamin K Antagonism).
  6. Onset of action — slow (8–12 h for factor VII; 2–7 days for full anticoagulation) — due to long half-life of existing carboxylated factors (II: 60 h, X: 24–48 h, VII: 6 h, IX: 24 h).
  7. Protein C has shortest half-life (8 h) — its levels fall first → transient procoagulant state → skin necrosis in deficient patients.

Pharmacokinetics

  • Rapid & complete oral absorption; bioavailability ~100%.
  • 99% bound to plasma albumin; small Vd (~0.14 L/kg).
  • Hepatic metabolism — CYP2C9 (S-warfarin, more potent); CYP1A2, CYP3A4 (R-warfarin).
  • Half-life — 36–42 h; long duration of action.
  • Crosses placenta — teratogenic (contraindicated in pregnancy).
  • Monitoring — PT (Prothrombin Time) / INR (International Normalised Ratio).
    • Target INR — 2.0–3.0 for most indications (DVT, PE, AF, mechanical bioprosthetic valve); 2.5–3.5 for mechanical mitral valve, recurrent VTE on warfarin, antiphospholipid syndrome.
    • Initial dose — 5 mg/day (2.5 mg if elderly, liver disease, malnourished); adjust based on INR at 3, 7, 14 days, then monthly.
  • Antidote — vitamin K1 (phytonadione) (oral, SC, IV — slow); FFP (fresh frozen plasma); PCC (prothrombin complex concentrate — four-factor preferred); recombinant factor VIIa (refractory).

Therapeutic Uses

  • VTE (DVT & PE) — treatment & secondary prevention — 3–6 months (provoked) or lifelong (unprovoked, recurrent, cancer, thrombophilia).
  • Atrial fibrillation — stroke prevention (CHA2DS2-VASc score ≥2 in men, ≥3 in women).
  • Mechanical heart valves — lifelong; mitral valve target INR 3.0 (range 2.5–3.5); aortic valve 2.5 (range 2.0–3.0).
  • Bioprosthetic valves — 3–6 months after implantation (then aspirin).
  • Antiphospholipid syndrome — lifelong; INR 2.5–3.5.
  • LV thrombus, mural thrombus post-MI — 3–6 months.
  • Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis — 3–12 months.
  • Peripheral arterial disease — selected cases (with antiplatelet).

Adverse Effects

  • Bleeding — most common; dose-dependent; risk increases with INR >4, age, concomitant antiplatelet/NSAID, comorbidities; reverse with vitamin K, FFP, PCC based on severity & INR.
  • Skin necrosis:
    • Rare (~0.01–0.1%); occurs 3–10 days after starting warfarin.
    • Due to depletion of protein C (shortest half-life — 8 h) before procoagulant factors (II, X) fall → transient procoagulant state → microvascular thrombosis in skin (breasts, buttocks, thighs, penis).
    • Higher risk in protein C deficiency (congenital or acquired).
    • Prevention — "bridge" with heparin (UFH/LMWH) until INR therapeutic for 2 days; start warfarin at low dose (2.5–5 mg); check protein C level if family history.
    • Treatment — stop warfarin; give vitamin K; heparin; FFP/PCC; protein C concentrate if deficient.
  • Teratogenicity:
    • Contraindicated in pregnancy (crosses placenta).
    • 1st trimester — embryopathy (nasal hypoplasia, stippled epiphyses, limb hypoplasia, ocular abnormalities); "warfarin embryopathy" — risk 5–10% if exposed weeks 6–12.
    • 2nd & 3rd trimester — foetal bleeding, CNS abnormalities (Dandy-Walker malformation, optic atrophy), miscarriage, stillbirth.
    • Use LMWH in pregnancy; switch back to warfarin postpartum (safe in breastfeeding).
  • Purple toe syndrome — rare; cholesterol microembolisation; painful purple toes; stop warfarin.
  • Hair loss, rash, fever, GI upset — uncommon.
  • Hepatotoxicity — rare; cholestatic.
  • Tracheal calcification, osteoporosis — long-term; rare.

Drug Interactions

Warfarin has the most drug interactions of any medication — due to high protein binding, narrow therapeutic index, hepatic metabolism, gut flora effects.

  • Enhanced anticoagulation (↑ INR, bleeding risk):
    • CYP2C9 inhibitors — amiodarone, fluconazole, metronidazole, miconazole, sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim, fluvoxamine, phenytoin (variable).
    • CYP3A4 inhibitors — macrolides (erythromycin, clarithromycin), azole antifungals, protease inhibitors, grapefruit juice.
    • Displacement from albumin — NSAIDs (also antiplatelet effect), sulfonamides, chloral hydrate.
    • Decreased vitamin K absorption — antibiotics (kill gut flora that synthesise vitamin K2); cholestyramine, orlistat, mineral oil.
    • ↑ Catabolism of clotting factors — thyroid hormones.
    • Additive bleeding risk — antiplatelets (aspirin, clopidogrel), NSAIDs, SSRIs.
    • Alcohol — acutely inhibits metabolism (↑ INR); chronically induces enzymes (↓ INR).
  • Reduced anticoagulation (↓ INR, thrombosis risk):
    • CYP inducers — rifampin, phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital, griseofulvin, St John's wort, nevirapine.
    • ↑ Vitamin K intake — green leafy vegetables, supplements, enteral feeds.
    • Reduced absorption — cholestyramine, sucralfate, antacids.
    • Genetic — VKORC1 polymorphisms (require lower dose); CYP2C9 polymorphisms (slow metabolism, lower dose).

Direct Oral Anticoagulants (DOACs) (2 marks)

Drug Target Half-life Antidote
DabigatranDirect thrombin (IIa)12–17 hIdarucizumab (monoclonal antibody)
RivaroxabanFactor Xa5–13 hAndexanet alfa (decoy factor Xa)
ApixabanFactor Xa8–15 hAndexanet alfa
EdoxabanFactor Xa10–14 hAndexanet alfa

Advantages over warfarin

  • Predictable pharmacokinetics — no routine monitoring (no INR).
  • Rapid onset (2–4 h) — no heparin bridging.
  • Short half-life — quick offset.
  • Few drug interactions (CYP3A4/P-gp).
  • No dietary vitamin K restriction.
  • Lower intracranial haemorrhage risk than warfarin (in AF trials).

Disadvantages

  • Renal excretion — dose adjustment in CKD; avoid in severe renal impairment (CrCl <30 for dabigatran, <15 for rivaroxaban/apixaban).
  • Cost — expensive vs warfarin.
  • No routine monitoring — compliance concern.
  • Antidotes expensive & not always available.
  • Higher GI bleeding risk than warfarin (especially dabigatran, rivaroxaban).
  • Not recommended in pregnancy, mechanical heart valves (RE-ALIGN trial — dabigatran worse than warfarin).
  • Antiphospholipid syndrome with triple positivity — warfarin preferred.

Clinical Pearl

Heparin & warfarin have different mechanisms — heparin potentiates antithrombin (immediate); warfarin inhibits vitamin K recycling (slow onset, days). Always bridge with heparin when starting warfarin — 5–7 days overlap until INR therapeutic for 2 consecutive days, then stop heparin. Warfarin skin necrosis — occurs in first week; due to protein C depletion (shortest half-life) before procoagulant factors fall → transient procoagulant state; higher risk in protein C deficiency; prevent with heparin bridging & low starting dose. HIT (heparin-induced thrombocytopenia) type II — paradoxical thrombosis 5–14 days after heparin; platelet count drops >50%; STOP all heparin immediately; switch to argatroban or bivalirudin (direct thrombin inhibitors); never re-expose to heparin/LMWH. Warfarin is teratogenic — avoid in pregnancy; use LMWH (does not cross placenta). Always check INR before surgery/procedure — stop warfarin 5 days before; bridge with LMWH if high thrombotic risk (mechanical valve, recent VTE, AF with high CHA2DS2-VASc). DOACs are replacing warfarin for most indications (AF, VTE) — no monitoring, no dietary restriction, fewer interactions, lower intracranial bleed. However, warfarin remains preferred for — mechanical heart valves, severe renal impairment, antiphospholipid syndrome (triple positive), pregnancy (LMWH preferred actually), patients with poor adherence (warfarin's long half-life is forgiving). Reversal — warfarin: vitamin K + FFP or PCC (4-factor preferred); heparin: protamine; dabigatran: idarucizumab; rivaroxaban/apixaban: andexanet alfa; all: supportive care, activated charcoal if recent ingestion. India — warfarin widely used (low cost); DOACs increasingly available but expensive; generic apixaban launched 2023 — improving affordability.

Clinical Approach to the Unconscious Patient — Suspected Poisoning

The 35-year-old male brought unconscious to the emergency requires a systematic ABCDE approach with simultaneous history taking, examination, investigations, and empirical treatment. Common causes of unconsciousness in a young adult include poisoning (organophosphorus, opioid, benzodiazepine, alcohol, carbon monoxide, barbiturate, tricyclic antidepressant), head trauma, metabolic (hypoglycaemia, DKA, hepatic encephalopathy), CNS infection, post-ictal state, and stroke.

Step 1 — Initial Assessment & Resuscitation (ABCDE) (3 marks)

  1. Airway (A) — assess patency; clear secretions, vomitus; head tilt-chin lift or jaw thrust (if cervical spine injury suspected); oropharyngeal/nasopharyngeal airway; endotracheal intubation if GCS <8, absent gag reflex, or unable to maintain airway.
  2. Breathing (B) — assess rate, depth, pattern, chest movement, SpO₂; oxygen 100% via mask (15 L/min with non-rebreather mask); bag-mask ventilation if apnoeic; mechanical ventilation if respiratory failure; check for cyanosis, needle decompression if tension pneumothorax.
  3. Circulation (C) — assess pulse, BP, heart rate, capillary refill, skin temperature; IV access (2 large-bore cannulae); fluid bolus (normal saline 20 mL/kg) if hypotensive; ECG monitoring; treat arrhythmias; check blood glucose (hypoglycaemia — give 50 mL 50% dextrose IV after taking blood sample); vasopressors (noradrenaline) if refractory shock.
  4. Disability (D) — GCS (Glasgow Coma Scale); pupil size & reactivity (pinpoint — opioid, organophosphorus; dilated — TCA, atropine, antihistamine); check for focal neurological deficits, meningismus, trauma signs; blood glucose; AVPU.
  5. Exposure (E) — fully expose patient; look for evidence of poisoning (injection marks, pill bottles, suicide note, chemical smell — garlic [organophosphorus, arsenic], bitter almond [cyanide], rotten eggs [H2S]); check skin for tracks, burns, petechiae; rectal temperature.

Step 2 — Rapid History (from relatives, bystanders, paramedics) (1 mark)

  • What was the patient doing before collapse? — work (agriculture — organophosphorus), home, social.
  • Any chemicals/medications found nearby? — empty bottles, blister packs, syringes.
  • Time of exposure — determines decontamination strategy.
  • Route of exposure — ingestion, inhalation, injection, dermal.
  • Past medical history — depression, diabetes, epilepsy, cardiac disease, addiction.
  • Current medications — especially insulin, oral hypoglycaemics, opioids, TCAs, lithium.
  • Occupational exposure — farmer (OPC), factory worker, painter.
  • Recent stressors — financial, relationship, exam.
  • Witnessed seizure, trauma, fever before collapse.

Step 3 — Examination — Look for Toxidromes (3 marks)

  • Bedside:

    • Pulse oximetry — CO poisoning may have normal SpO₂ (use CO-oximetry).
    • ABG — metabolic acidosis (methanol, ethylene glycol, salicylates, TCAs); respiratory acidosis (opioids, sedatives).
  • Laboratory:
    • CBG — leucocytosis; anaemia; thrombocytopenia.
    • Electrolytes, urea, creatinine — renal failure; anion gap (methanol, ethylene glycol).
    • LFT — hepatic failure (paracetamol, mushroom poisoning).
    • CK — rhabdomyolysis (prolonged immobilisation, NMS, serotonin syndrome, statins).
    • Coagulation — DIC; warfarin overdose.
    • Plasma cholinesterase & RBC acetylcholinesterase — organophosphorus poisoning.
    • Drug levels — paracetamol (4-hour level — Rumack-Matthew nomogram), salicylate, lithium, digoxin, iron, methanol (osmolal gap), ethylene glycol (osmolal gap + crystals in urine), theophylline, valproate, phenytoin, carbamazepine.
    • Urine drug screen — opioids, amphetamines, cocaine, cannabis, benzodiazepines, barbiturates.
  • Imaging:
    • Chest X-ray — aspiration pneumonia, pulmonary oedema (opioids, salicylates), chemical pneumonitis (hydrocarbons).
    • CT head — exclude intracranial haemorrhage, mass, trauma; especially if focal signs or no improvement.

Step 5 — General Management of Poisoning (4 marks)

A. Decontamination

  • Activated charcoal (single dose):
    • 1 g/kg (adults 50–100 g) within 1 h of ingestion; adsorbs drugs in gut.
    • Effective for most oral poisons except — alcohols, hydrocarbons, metals (iron, lithium, potassium), strong acids/alkalis, cyanide.
    • Contraindicated — unprotected airway (aspiration risk), corrosive ingestion, ileus, GI obstruction.
  • Gastric lavage:
    • Rarely used now — only if life-threatening ingestion within 1 h & airway protected.
    • Contraindicated — corrosives, hydrocarbons (aspiration risk), unknown time of ingestion.
  • Whole bowel irrigation — polyethylene glycol electrolyte solution; for sustained-release drugs, iron, lithium, packets of illicit drugs (body packers).
  • Syrup of ipecac — no longer recommended.
  • Skin decontamination — remove clothes; wash with soap & water (organophosphorus); staff protection.
  • Eye decontamination — copious saline irrigation for 15–30 min.

  • ICU admission for — coma (GCS <8), respiratory failure, cardiac instability, seizures, severe metabolic derangement, need for antidote infusion.
  • Continuous monitoring — ECG, BP, SpO₂, urine output, neurology.
  • Treat complications — aspiration pneumonia (antibiotics), pressure sores (turning), DVT prophylaxis (LMWH — if no bleeding), rhabdomyolysis (IV fluids, alkalinise urine), renal failure (haemodialysis), hepatic failure (NAC for paracetamol, supportive).
  • Psychiatric evaluation — once conscious; rule out suicidal intent; admit under Mental Healthcare Act if necessary.
  • Forensic / medico-legal documentation — preserve samples (blood, urine, gastric contents) for forensic analysis; police intimation if unnatural cause suspected.
  • Discharge planning — psychiatric follow-up; family counselling; poison prevention education.

Always check blood glucose first in any unconscious patient — hypoglycaemia is the most easily reversible cause and missed diagnosis can be devastating. Empirical "coma cocktail" — naloxone (opioid), dextrose (hypoglycaemia), thiamine (alcoholic — Wernicke's encephalopathy). Pupil examination is the single most useful bedside sign — pinpoint (opioid, organophosphorus); dilated (anticholinergic, TCA, sympathomimetic); normal (sedative-hypnotic). India — common poisonings — organophosphorus (farmers), aluminium phosphide (fumigant — "rice tablet"; fatal — no antidote; magnesium sulphate may help), oleander seeds, snake bite, benzodiazepines, alcohol, paracetamol, pesticides (endosulfan, paraquat). Prevention — restrict access to pesticides; safe storage; community education; mental health support; pesticide regulation.

Introduction

Acute myocardial infarction (AMI) is myocardial necrosis due to prolonged ischaemia, usually from coronary artery thrombosis over an atherosclerotic plaque. ST-elevation MI (STEMI) requires immediate reperfusion; non-ST-elevation MI (NSTEMI) requires antithrombotic therapy and risk-stratified invasive strategy. Goal — restore coronary patency, reduce myocardial oxygen demand, prevent complications, improve survival.

Phases of Treatment

  1. Pre-hospital — aspirin 300 mg chewed; nitroglycerin sublingual if BP allows; oxygen if hypoxic; morphine for pain; immediate transfer to PCI-capable hospital.
  2. Immediate (reperfusion) — primary PCI (preferred) or fibrinolysis (if PCI not available within 120 min).
  3. Antiplatelet & anticoagulant therapy.
  4. Adjunctive therapy — β-blocker, ACEI/ARB, statin.
  5. Secondary prevention & long-term.

Pharmacotherapy

1. Reperfusion Therapy

  • Primary PCI (percutaneous coronary intervention):
    • Preferred if performed within 90 min of first medical contact (door-to-balloon time).
    • Stenting (drug-eluting stent preferred); aspiration thrombectomy; GP IIb/IIIa inhibitor (abciximab, eptifibatide, tirofiban) during PCI.
  • Fibrinolytic therapy (thrombolysis):
    • If PCI unavailable within 120 min; door-to-needle time <30 min.
    • Streptokinase — 1.5 million U IV over 60 min (historical; cheapest; antigenic — single use; allergic reactions; hypotension).
    • Alteplase (rt-PA) — 15 mg IV bolus, then 0.75 mg/kg over 30 min (max 50 mg), then 0.5 mg/kg over 60 min (max 35 mg); total max 100 mg.
    • Reteplase (r-PA) — 10 U IV over 2 min × 2 doses, 30 min apart.
    • Tenecteplase (TNK-t-PA) — single bolus 0.5 mg/kg (max 50 mg); preferred — easy, weight-based, fewer non-cerebral bleeds.
    • Contraindications — active bleeding, recent stroke, intracranial haemorrhage, intracranial neoplasm, severe hypertension (>180/110), recent surgery, aortic dissection, pregnancy.

2. Antiplatelet Therapy

  • Aspirin:
    • Loading dose — 300 mg chewed (non-enteric-coated) ASAP; then 75–100 mg daily lifelong.
    • Irreversibly acetylates COX-1 in platelets → ↓ thromboxane A2 → ↓ platelet aggregation.
    • Reduces mortality by ~25% in AMI.
  • P2Y12 ADP receptor antagonists:
    • Ticagrelor — 180 mg loading then 90 mg BD; reversible; faster onset; preferred with aspirin (PLATO trial — reduced mortality vs clopidogrel); contraindicated in history of intracranial haemorrhage; dyspnoea side effect.
    • Prasugrel — 60 mg loading then 10 mg daily; irreversible; more potent than clopidogrel; avoid in age >75, weight <60 kg, history of stroke/TIA (bleeding risk); used in PCI.
    • Clopidogrel — 600 mg loading (PCI) or 300 mg (fibrinolysis) then 75 mg daily; irreversible; prodrug (CYP2C19) — variable response; genetic polymorphism; cheapest.
    • Duration — DAPT (dual antiplatelet therapy) for 12 months post-STEMI (with drug-eluting stent); then aspirin lifelong; ticagrelor 60 mg BD monotherapy or with aspirin beyond 1 year in high-risk (PEGASUS trial).
  • GP IIb/IIIa antagonists — abciximab, eptifibatide, tirofiban; during PCI for thrombus burden; less used with newer P2Y12 inhibitors.

3. Anticoagulant Therapy

  • Unfractionated heparin (UFH) — 60 IU/kg bolus (max 4000 IU), then 12 IU/kg/h infusion (target aPTT 1.5–2× control); used during PCI & with fibrinolytics (alteplase, reteplase, tenecteplase).
  • Enoxaparin (LMWH) — 1 mg/kg SC every 12 h; preferred with fibrinolytics in patients <75 yr (for >75 yr — 0.75 mg/kg every 12 h; renal adjustment if CrCl <30); ExTRACT-TIMI 25 trial.
  • Fondaparinux — 2.5 mg IV then SC daily; preferred in conservative strategy (OASIS-6 trial); not for PCI (catheter thrombosis risk).
  • Bivalirudin — direct thrombin inhibitor; used in primary PCI (reduces bleeding vs heparin + GP IIb/IIIa; HORIZONS-AMI trial).
  • Duration — until hospital discharge or PCI completion; longer if LV thrombus, AF, mechanical valve.

4. Adjunctive Anti-ischaemic & Cardioprotective Therapy

  • β-Blockers:
    • Started within 24 h if no contraindication (heart failure, hypotension, bradycardia, AV block, severe asthma).
    • Metoprolol, atenolol, bisoprolol, carvedilol; oral.
    • IV esmolol if tachyarrhythmia, hypertension, ongoing ischaemia.
    • Reduces mortality, reinfarction, arrhythmias; long-term for secondary prevention.
  • ACE inhibitors / ARBs:
    • Started within 24 h if no contraindication (hypotension, bilateral renal artery stenosis, pregnancy, hyperkalaemia, angioedema history).
    • Especially beneficial in anterior MI, LV dysfunction (EF <40%), heart failure, diabetes, hypertension.
    • Ramipril, lisinopril, enalapril, perindopril; valsartan, losartan, telmisartan if ACEI intolerant.
    • Reduces mortality, remodelling, heart failure.
    • ARNI (sacubitril/valsartan) in post-MI HFrEF (PARADISE-MI trial — emerging).
  • Statins:
    • High-intensity — atorvastatin 80 mg daily or rosuvastatin 20–40 mg daily; started within 24 h; continued lifelong.
    • Target LDL <70 mg/dL (or <55 mg/dL in very high-risk per ESC 2019).
    • Plaque stabilisation; anti-inflammatory; ↓ mortality.
    • Add ezetimibe or PCSK9 inhibitor (evolocumab, alirocumab) if target not met.
  • Nitrates:
    • Sublingual GTN for ongoing chest pain; IV nitroglycerin for persistent pain, hypertension, acute LV failure.
    • Avoid in hypotension (SBP <90), RV infarction, recent PDE5 inhibitor.
    • No mortality benefit; symptom relief.
  • Morphine:
    • 5–10 mg IV for pain, anxiety, pulmonary oedema; reduces sympathetic drive & preload.
    • Caution — may delay antiplatelet absorption (↓ ticagrelor/clopidogrel levels); use judiciously.
  • Oxygen — only if SpO₂ <90% or respiratory distress; routine O₂ may worsen outcome in normoxic patients (AVOID trial).
  • Electrolytes — maintain K⁺ >4.0, Mg²⁺ >2.0; reduce arrhythmias.

5. Secondary Prevention (Lifelong)

  • Aspirin (lifelong) + P2Y12 inhibitor (12 months — longer if high thrombotic risk).
  • β-blocker (lifelong — especially if LV dysfunction).
  • ACEI/ARB (lifelong — especially if LV dysfunction, diabetes, hypertension).
  • High-intensity statin (lifelong); target LDL <70 mg/dL.
  • Aldosterone antagonist (eplerenone 25–50 mg daily) if LV EF ≤40% & heart failure or diabetes (EPHESUS trial).
  • Lifestyle — smoking cessation; Mediterranean diet; exercise; cardiac rehabilitation; weight management; diabetes control; BP control.
  • Vaccination — annual influenza; pneumococcal.
  • Treat comorbidities — hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidaemia, obesity, OSA.

Complications & Their Treatment

  • Arrhythmias — VT/VF (defibrillation; amiodarone; lidocaine); AF (anticoagulate; rate control with β-blocker; cardiovert if unstable); bradycardia/AV block (atropine; temporary pacemaker).
  • Acute heart failure — IV furosemide; nitrates; oxygen; NIV; inotropes (dobutamine, milrinone) if hypotensive; mechanical support (IABP, Impella, ECMO).
  • Cardiogenic shock — early revascularisation; inotropes; vasopressors; mechanical circulatory support (IABP, Impella, ECMO).
  • Mechanical complications (papillary muscle rupture, VSD, free wall rupture) — surgical repair.
  • LV thrombus — anticoagulation (warfarin or DOAC) 3–6 months.
  • Pericarditis (Dressler) — aspirin high dose; NSAIDs; corticosteroids if refractory.

Clinical Pearl

Time is muscle — every minute of delay in reperfusion results in additional myocardial necrosis; door-to-balloon time <90 min for primary PCI; door-to-needle time <30 min for fibrinolysis. Aspirin + P2Y12 inhibitor (ticagrelor preferred) + anticoagulant (heparin/enoxaparin/bivalirudin) + statin + β-blocker + ACEI form the pharmacological backbone of AMI management. Ticagrelor + aspirin is preferred DAPT in STEMI/NSTEMI (PLATO trial — reduced all-cause mortality vs clopidogrel); but higher dyspnoea, bleeding risk. Prasugrel — more potent; avoid in age >75, weight <60 kg, history of stroke/TIA. Primary PCI is superior to fibrinolysis if performed within 90 min; fibrinolysis if PCI unavailable within 120 min; tenecteplase single bolus preferred (easiest). Always check contraindications to fibrinolysis — active bleeding, recent stroke, intracranial surgery/neoplasm, severe hypertension, aortic dissection. High-intensity statin within 24 h — atorvastatin 80 mg daily; target LDL <70 mg/dL; add ezetimibe or PCSK9 inhibitor if not achieved. β-blocker within 24 h if no contraindication — reduces mortality; avoid in acute heart failure, hypotension, bradycardia, severe asthma. ACEI within 24 h — especially anterior MI, LV dysfunction, diabetes; reduces remodelling & mortality. Eplerenone — if LV EF ≤40% + heart failure or diabetes (EPHESUS trial). Cardiac rehabilitation — exercise, education, psychological support, secondary prevention; reduces mortality by 20–30%. India — STEMI mortality high; access to PCI limited in rural areas; fibrinolysis (streptokinase — cheap) still widely used; AMI registry & systems of care (hub-and-spoke model) improving outcomes.

Introduction

Drug antagonism is the phenomenon where the combined effect of two drugs is less than the sum of their individual effects (i.e., one drug reduces or blocks the effect of another). It is the opposite of synergism (potentiation/additive). Antagonism is exploited therapeutically (antidotes, treatment of overdose) and is also an important source of adverse drug interactions.

Types of Drug Antagonism

1. Pharmaceutical Antagonism (Incompatibility)

  • Definition — two drugs react chemically or physically before administration or in the body, resulting in inactivation or precipitation.
  • Mechanism:
    • Chemical reaction — acid + base neutralisation; chelation; oxidation-reduction.
    • Physical — precipitation; adsorption; pH changes.
  • Examples:
    • Protamine sulphate + heparin — positively charged protamine binds negatively charged heparin → neutralises anticoagulant effect (used as heparin antidote).
    • Chelating agents + heavy metals — EDTA, dimercaprol (BAL), penicillamine, succimer (DMSA), deferoxamine bind & remove lead, mercury, arsenic, iron.
    • Activated charcoal + drugs — adsorbs drugs in gut; prevents absorption (used in poisoning).
    • Tetracyclines + calcium/magnesium/iron/aluminium antacids or dairy — chelation; ↓ tetracycline absorption.
    • Fluoroquinolones + antacids — chelation; ↓ absorption.
    • Penicillin + aminoglycosides (in same IV line) — penicillin binds aminoglycosides → inactivation.
    • Phenytoin + dextrose infusion — phenytoin precipitates in dextrose; give in normal saline.
    • Sulphadiazine silver + enzymes — inactivation.

2. Pharmacokinetic Antagonism

One drug reduces the effective concentration of another at the site of action by altering its absorption, distribution, metabolism, or excretion.

  • Absorption:
    • Antacids (pH change) ↓ ketoconazole, itraconazole, atazanavir absorption.
    • Cholestyramine, colestipol bind bile acids & drugs (warfarin, thyroxine, digoxin) in gut.
    • Activated charcoal (poisoning).
    • Metoclopramide speeds gastric emptying (↑ rate but variable extent); anticholinergics slow it.
    • Iron + tea (tannins) — ↓ absorption.
  • Distribution:
    • Displacement from plasma protein binding — warfarin displaced by NSAIDs, sulfonamides, chloral hydrate → transient ↑ free warfarin → ↑ anticoagulation.
    • Usually clinically significant only for highly bound drugs with narrow therapeutic index.
  • Metabolism (most important clinically):
    • Enzyme induction — rifampin, phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital, griseofulvin, St John's wort, alcohol (chronic), smoking → ↑ CYP450 → ↓ effect of warfarin, OCPs, theophylline, cyclosporine, HIV protease inhibitors, corticosteroids.
    • Enzyme inhibition — macrolides (erythromycin, clarithromycin), azole antifungals (ketoconazole, fluconazole, itraconazole), cimetidine, fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin), amiodarone, diltiazem, verapamil, grapefruit juice, SSRIs (fluoxetine, fluvoxamine), metronidazole, sulfonamides, protease inhibitors → ↓ metabolism → ↑ effect of warfarin, theophylline, phenytoin, carbamazepine, cyclosporine, tacrolimus, statins (simvastatin, atorvastatin), benzodiazepines.
  • Excretion:
    • Altered renal tubular secretion — probenecid inhibits OAT (organic anion transporter) → ↓ penicillin excretion → ↑ penicillin levels (historical use — syphilis, gonorrhoea); also ↓ excretion of methotrexate, NSAIDs, furosemide.
    • Urinary pH alteration — sodium bicarbonate alkalinises urine → ↑ excretion of weak acids (salicylates, phenobarbital); ammonium chloride acidifies urine → ↑ excretion of weak bases (amphetamine, phencyclidine).
    • Lithium + NSAIDs/thiazides — ↓ lithium excretion → toxicity.
    • Digoxin + verapamil/quinidine/amiodarone — ↓ digoxin clearance (P-gp inhibition) → toxicity.

3. Pharmacodynamic Antagonism

Both drugs act at the same or different receptors/physiological systems but produce opposite physiological effects.

  • Competitive (surmountable) antagonism:
    • Antagonist binds reversibly to the same receptor as agonist; can be overcome by increasing agonist concentration (rightward shift of dose-response curve, no change in Emax).
    • Examples:
      • Acetylcholine (muscarinic) vs atropine — atropine is competitive muscarinic antagonist (organophosphorus poisoning antidote).
      • Histamine (H1) vs antihistamines — cetirizine, fexofenadine, chlorpheniramine.
      • Adrenaline (β) vs propranolol — β-blocker.
      • Morphine (μ) vs naloxone — opioid antagonist (opioid overdose).
      • Angiotensin II (AT1) vs losartan — ARB.
      • Benzodiazepine vs flumazenil — antidote.
      • Suxamethonium vs neostigmine — neuromuscular blockade reversal.
      • Salbutamol (β2) vs propranolol — propranolol blocks bronchodilator effect → bronchospasm in asthmatics.
  • Non-competitive (insurmountable) antagonism:
    • Antagonist binds irreversibly (covalent bond) or to a different (allosteric) site; cannot be overcome by increasing agonist concentration (↓ Emax, may or may not shift curve rightward).
    • Examples:
      • Phenoxybenzamine (irreversible α-blocker) vs adrenaline — phaeochromocytoma preparation.
      • Aspirin (irreversible COX inhibitor) vs thromboxane — antiplatelet effect lasts 7–10 days (platelet lifespan).
      • Omeprazole (irreversible H⁺/K⁺-ATPase inhibitor) vs gastric acid.
      • MAO inhibitors vs tyramine — cheese reaction.
      • Sulfonylureas vs diazoxide — insulin vs hyperglycaemia.
      • Ketamine (NMDA channel blocker) — use-dependent non-competitive.
  • Physiological (functional) antagonism:
    • Two drugs act at different receptors or systems to produce opposite physiological effects; cancels out.
    • Examples:
      • Histamine vs adrenaline — histamine lowers BP (vasodilation); adrenaline raises BP (vasoconstriction); adrenaline used in anaphylaxis (physiological antagonist of histamine).
      • Insulin vs glucagon/catecholamines/glucocorticoids — insulin lowers blood glucose; others raise it.
      • Acetylcholine (muscarinic) vs adrenaline (β1) — ACh slows heart; adrenaline speeds it.
      • Glucagon vs propranolol — glucagon increases heart rate via different receptor; used in β-blocker overdose.
      • Levodopa vs antipsychotics — dopamine vs dopamine antagonism; worsen Parkinson's.
  • Chemical antagonism:
    • One drug binds directly to another (not receptor) & inactivates it.
    • Examples:
      • Protamine + heparin — neutralisation (also pharmaceutical).
      • Dimercaprol (BAL) + heavy metals — chelation.
      • Deferoxamine + iron — chelation.
      • Digoxin-specific Fab antibody (DigiFab) + digoxin — binds and removes digoxin.
      • Idarucizumab + dabigatran — monoclonal antibody binds dabigatran.
      • Andexanet alfa + rivaroxaban/apixaban — decoy factor Xa.
  • Allosteric antagonism:
    • Antagonist binds to a different site on the receptor, causing conformational change that reduces agonist affinity or efficacy.
    • Examples:
      • Picrotoxin vs GABA-A — blocks chloride channel (different site from GABA).
      • Naloxone at very high doses — may have allosteric effects.

Quantitative Aspects — Dose-Response Curves

  • Competitive antagonist — produces parallel rightward shift of agonist dose-response curve; Emax unchanged; can be overcome by ↑ agonist dose.
  • Non-competitive antagonist — ↓ Emax (maximum response reduced); may or may not shift curve; cannot be overcome by ↑ agonist dose.
  • pA₂ — negative logarithm of the molar concentration of antagonist that requires doubling of agonist concentration to produce the same response as before; measure of antagonist potency (Schild plot).

Clinical Significance

  • Therapeutic uses — antidotes (naloxone for opioids, flumazenil for benzodiazepines, atropine + pralidoxime for organophosphates, protamine for heparin, vitamin K for warfarin, idarucizumab for dabigatran, digoxin Fab for digoxin); treatment of overdose (charcoal for many poisons); reversing adverse effects.
  • Adverse drug interactions — reduce therapeutic effect of essential drugs (warfarin + rifampin → ↓ anticoagulation → thrombosis; OCPs + rifampin → contraceptive failure; theophylline + phenytoin → ↓ theophylline → asthma exacerbation).
  • Contraindications — β-blockers in asthma (block β2 bronchodilator effect of adrenaline); prostaglandin synthesis inhibitors in pregnancy (maintain ductus arteriosus patency — indomethacin closes PDA).
  • Combination therapy — sometimes desired (antihypertensive combination — ACEI + thiazide, ACEI + CCB; antibiotics — β-lactam + aminoglycoside synergy).

Clinical Pearl

Distinguish competitive from non-competitive antagonism by dose-response curve — competitive produces parallel rightward shift (Emax unchanged, overcome by ↑ agonist); non-competitive reduces Emax (cannot be overcome). Aspirin is a non-competitive irreversible COX inhibitor — antiplatelet effect lasts 7–10 days (platelet lifespan); must stop 7 days before surgery. Phenoxybenzamine is the only irreversible α-blocker — used pre-operatively for phaeochromocytoma; effect lasts days until new α-receptors synthesised. Always check for pharmacokinetic interactions when adding or stopping drugs — rifampin (potent enzyme inducer) reduces warfarin, OCP, tacrolimus, HIV PIs, levothyroxine; macrolides + statins ↑ rhabdomyolysis risk; grapefruit juice ↑ statin, CCB, cyclosporine levels (intestinal CYP3A4 inhibition). Naloxone is the prototypical competitive antagonist — opioid overdose; titrate to respiratory rate, not full consciousness (avoid withdrawal); short half-life (1 h) — may need infusion for long-acting opioids (methadone, fentanyl, tramadol). Flumazenil — benzodiazepine antagonist; risk of seizures in chronic users or TCA co-ingestion; use cautiously. Drug antagonism forms the basis of many antidotes — atropine + pralidoxime (OPC), naloxone (opioid), flumazenil (benzodiazepine), protamine (heparin), vitamin K (warfarin), idarucizumab (dabigatran), andexanet alfa (rivaroxaban/apixaban), digoxin Fab (digoxin), fomepizole (methanol/ethylene glycol), hydroxocobalamin (cyanide), methylene blue (methaemoglobinaemia), N-acetylcysteine (paracetamol — restores glutathione).

Introduction

Skeletal muscle relaxants are drugs that reduce skeletal muscle tone & spasm. Two broad categories:

  • Neuromuscular blockers — act at NMJ; produce paralysis (used in anaesthesia, intubation); e.g., succinylcholine, vecuronium.
  • Spasmolytics (centrally & peripherally acting) — reduce muscle spasm without paralysis; used for spasticity, muscle spasms, anxiety.

Centrally Acting Skeletal Muscle Relaxants

Act on the CNS (brainstem, spinal cord) to reduce muscle tone by enhancing inhibitory neurotransmission (GABA, glycine) or inhibiting excitatory pathways.

Classification

  1. Mephenesin group — Mephenesin, Chlorphenesin, Methocarbamol, Chlorzoxazone (older; mostly replaced).
  2. Benzodiazepines — Diazepam, Lorazepam (GABA-A positive modulators).
  3. α2-Adrenergic agonists — Tizanidine, Clonidine, Dexmedetomidine.
  4. GABA-B agonists — Baclofen.
  5. Other central — Cyclobenzaprine (TCA-like structure), Eperisone, Thiocolchicoside.

Individual Drugs

1. Diazepam (Benzodiazepine)

  • Mechanism — binds to benzodiazepine site on GABA-A receptor → ↑ frequency of Cl⁻ channel opening → ↑ inhibitory neurotransmission → ↓ muscle tone & spinal reflexes; also anxiolytic, sedative, anticonvulsant.
  • Uses — muscle spasm (acute); anxiety; alcohol withdrawal; status epilepticus; spasticity (cerebral palsy, MS); tetanus.
  • Dose — 2–10 mg PO TID; 5–10 mg IV (status epilepticus, spasm).
  • Adverse effects — sedation, drowsiness, dependence, tolerance, hypotension (IV), respiratory depression (IV).

2. Baclofen (GABA-B Agonist)

  • Mechanism — agonist at GABA-B receptor (Gi/Go-coupled) → ↓ Ca²⁺ influx & ↑ K⁺ efflux → ↓ release of excitatory transmitters (glutamate, aspartate) in spinal cord & brain → ↓ muscle tone & spasticity.
  • Uses:
    • Spasticity (spinal origin — multiple sclerosis, spinal cord injury; cerebral origin — cerebral palsy, stroke less effective).
    • Intrathecal baclofen — severe spasticity unresponsive to oral; programmable pump.
    • Trigeminal neuralgia (adjunct).
    • Alcohol withdrawal (off-label).
    • Gastroesophageal reflux (lower esophageal sphincter relaxation).
  • Dose — 5 mg PO TID, titrate to 20 mg TID/QID (max 80 mg/day); intrathecal 50–2000 µg/day.
  • Adverse effects — sedation, drowsiness, confusion, dizziness, weakness, ataxia, hypotonia; abrupt withdrawal → seizures, hallucinations, hyperthermia; intrathecal — overdose → respiratory depression, coma (antidote — physostigmine, supportive).

3. Tizanidine (α2-Adrenergic Agonist)

  • Mechanism — α2-adrenergic agonist (central) → ↑ presynaptic inhibition of motor neuron excitability → ↓ spasticity; less hypotension than clonidine (more selective α2A at spinal cord).
  • Uses:
    • Spasticity (multiple sclerosis, spinal cord injury, stroke; less effective than baclofen for severe).
    • Muscle spasm (acute).
    • Headache (tension, migraine — off-label).
  • Dose — 2–4 mg PO every 6–8 h (max 36 mg/day).
  • Adverse effects — sedation, drowsiness, dizziness, hypotension, dry mouth, weakness; hepatotoxicity (rare — monitor LFT); hallucinations; bradycardia.
  • Drug interactions — CYP1A2 inhibitors (ciprofloxacin, fluvoxamine) ↑ tizanidine levels → severe hypotension; contraindicated.

4. Cyclobenzaprine (TCA-Like)

  • Mechanism — structurally related to tricyclic antidepressants; acts at brainstem & spinal cord → ↓ somatic motor activity; anticholinergic; serotonin/norepinephrine effects.
  • Uses — acute muscle spasm (2–3 weeks); fibromyalgia (off-label); not for spasticity (chronic CNS disorders).
  • Dose — 5–10 mg PO TID (max 30 mg/day); extended-release 15–30 mg daily.
  • Adverse effects — sedation, anticholinergic (dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention, constipation), confusion (elderly); arrhythmias; avoid in elderly, cardiac disease, glaucoma, BPH.

5. Methocarbamol

  • Mechanism — central action (sedation); no direct action on muscle; GABA-A effects.
  • Uses — acute muscle spasm; tetanus; IV for severe spasm.
  • Dose — 1.5 g PO QID initially, then 1 g QID; IV 1–3 g (max 4.5 g/day first day).
  • Adverse effects — sedation, dizziness, hypotension (IV), bradycardia, brown/black discoloration of urine (harmless); avoid IV in renal disease (may precipitate).

6. Chlorzoxazone

  • Mechanism — acts on spinal cord & subcortical brain → ↓ muscle tone.
  • Uses — acute muscle spasm.
  • Dose — 250–500 mg PO TID/QID.
  • Adverse effects — sedation, dizziness, GI upset; hepatotoxicity (rare — boxed warning).

7. Thiocolchicoside

  • Mechanism — GABA-A & glycine receptor antagonist (paradoxically — thought to act centrally as muscle relaxant); anti-inflammatory.
  • Uses — muscle spasm (acute); orthopaedic, rheumatological.
  • Dose — 4–8 mg PO BD; IM 4 mg every 12 h.
  • Adverse effects — sedation, GI upset; seizures (avoid in epilepsy).

8. Eperisone

  • Mechanism — central & peripheral; ↓ γ-motor neuron activity; vasodilator; no sedation.
  • Uses — muscle spasm in cervical spondylosis, shoulder periarthritis, low back pain.
  • Dose — 50 mg PO TID.
  • Adverse effects — dizziness, GI upset; minimal sedation.

9. Other Centrally Acting

  • Orphenadrine — anticholinergic + NMDA antagonist; Parkinsonism & muscle spasm.
  • Carisoprodol — GABA-A effects; metabolised to meprobamate (dependence potential); abuse risk; withdrawn in many countries.
  • Metaxalone — mechanism unclear; sedation.
  • Chlormezanone — withdrawn (severe skin reactions).

Comparison

Drug Mechanism Main use Key adverse effect
DiazepamGABA-A +Acute spasm, anxiety, status epilepticusSedation, dependence
BaclofenGABA-B agonistSpasticity (spinal > cerebral)Sedation; withdrawal seizures
Tizanidineα2 agonistSpasticity (MS, spinal injury)Hypotension; LFT; interactions
CyclobenzaprineTCA-likeAcute muscle spasmAnticholinergic; arrhythmia
MethocarbamolCentral sedativeAcute spasm, tetanusSedation; urine discolouration
ChlorzoxazoneCentralAcute spasmHepatotoxicity
ThiocolchicosideGABA-A/glycine antagonistAcute spasm (orthopaedic)Seizures
EperisoneCentral + vasodilatorCervical/lumbar painMinimal sedation

Clinical Uses

  • Acute muscle spasm — musculoskeletal injury, strain, sprain; short course (1–2 weeks) — cyclobenzaprine, methocarbamol, chlorzoxazone, diazepam, thiocolchicoside.
  • Spasticity (chronic CNS disorders):
    • Spinal origin (MS, spinal cord injury) — baclofen (oral or intrathecal), tizanidine.
    • Cerebral origin (cerebral palsy, stroke, traumatic brain injury) — less responsive; baclofen, diazepam, tizanidine; botulinum toxin for focal.
  • Tetanus — IV diazepam, methocarbamol; severe cases — vecuronium + mechanical ventilation.
  • Stiff-person syndrome — diazepam, baclofen, IVIG.
  • Neuroleptic malignant syndrome — dantrolene (peripherally acting); bromocriptine (dopamine agonist).
  • Malignant hyperthermia — dantrolene (only drug; ryanodine receptor antagonist).

Adverse Effects (Common to All Centrally Acting)

  • Sedation, drowsiness, dizziness, lightheadedness.
  • Weakness, ataxia, incoordination.
  • Cognitive impairment, confusion (especially elderly).
  • Paradoxical excitement (children, elderly).
  • Dependence, tolerance (benzodiazepines, carisoprodol).
  • Hypotension (tizanidine, IV methocarbamol).
  • Anticholinergic (cyclobenzaprine).
  • Hepatotoxicity (chlorzoxazone, tizanidine).
  • Withdrawal — abrupt cessation of baclofen → seizures, hallucinations; taper gradually.

Clinical Pearl

Centrally acting muscle relaxants are sedatives — not truly muscle-specific; they reduce muscle tone by generalised CNS depression. For acute muscle spasm (orthopaedic injury) — cyclobenzaprine, methocarbamol, thiocolchicoside; short course (1–2 weeks); combine with NSAIDs & physical therapy. For chronic spasticity (MS, spinal cord injury, cerebral palsy) — baclofen (oral or intrathecal) is drug of choice for spinal spasticity; tizanidine for cerebral & spinal; diazepam for severe. Intrathecal baclofen pump — for severe spasticity unresponsive to oral; programmable; highly effective; risk of overdose (respiratory depression) & withdrawal (seizures, fever, rhabdomyolysis). Tizanidine — avoid with CYP1A2 inhibitors (ciprofloxacin, fluvoxamine) → severe hypotension; check LFT; less hypotension than clonidine. Cyclobenzaprine — structurally TCA; avoid in elderly, cardiac disease, glaucoma, BPH (anticholinergic); short-term only. Always taper baclofen — abrupt withdrawal causes seizures, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis (life-threatening). Botulinum toxin — for focal spasticity (cerebral palsy, stroke, dystonia); local injection; lasts 3 months; preferred for focal over generalised spasticity. Dantrolene — peripherally acting (ryanodine receptor antagonist); only drug for malignant hyperthermia & NMS; acts directly on skeletal muscle (no sedation). India — common centrally acting SMRs — thiocolchicoside, eperisone, diazepam, baclofen, tizanidine; many available as OTC (concern about irrational use); prefer short course + NSAID combination.
