q2_0_2_8:
Introduction

HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors (statins) are the most effective lipid-lowering drugs; cornerstone of cardiovascular disease prevention. They inhibit the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis, reducing hepatic cholesterol & upregulating LDL receptors.

Classification

  • Natural / Fungal-derived:
    • Lovastatin — first statin (from Aspergillus terreus); US 1987.
    • Simvastatin — semi-synthetic from lovastatin; prodrug.
    • Pravastatin — derived from Penicillium; hydrophilic; non-enzymatic metabolism.
  • Synthetic:
    • Fluvastatin — first fully synthetic.
    • Atorvastatin — most potent; most widely used.
    • Rosuvastatin — most potent; longest half-life.
    • Pitavastatin — newer; minimal CYP metabolism.
  • By potency (cholesterol-lowering):
    • Low intensity — fluvastatin, pravastatin, simvastatin (20–40 mg).
    • Moderate intensity — atorvastatin 10–20 mg, rosuvastatin 5–10 mg, simvastatin 40 mg.
    • High intensity — atorvastatin 40–80 mg, rosuvastatin 20–40 mg.

Mechanism of Action

  1. Inhibition of HMG-CoA reductase — rate-limiting enzyme in cholesterol biosynthesis (catalyses HMG-CoA → mevalonate).
  2. Statins are structural analogues of HMG-CoA — compete for active site; ~10,000× more affinity than natural substrate.
  3. ↓ Hepatic cholesterol synthesis → hepatocytes sense low cholesterol → upregulate LDL receptor (LDLR) expression on cell surface (SREBP2 transcription factor pathway).
  4. ↑ LDLR → ↑ uptake of LDL & VLDL remnants from circulation → ↓ plasma LDL-C.
  5. ↓ Production of VLDL — reduced cholesterol for VLDL assembly.
  6. Pleiotropic effects (beyond LDL lowering):
    • ↓ Inflammation (↓ CRP; ↓ TNF-α, IL-6, MMPs).
    • ↑ Endothelial nitric oxide (NO) synthase → vasodilation.
    • ↓ Oxidative stress; ↓ oxidised LDL.
    • Plaque stabilisation — ↓ lipid content, ↓ macrophage activity, ↑ collagen.
    • ↓ Thrombosis — ↓ tissue factor, ↓ platelet aggregation.
    • Immunomodulatory — ↓ MHC-II expression.
    • ↓ Bone turnover — may reduce osteoporosis (controversial).
    • Anti-cancer (cell cycle arrest, apoptosis — investigational).

Pharmacokinetics

  • Oral; absorbed in small intestine; first-pass metabolism (liver).
  • Most are lipophilic (lovastatin, simvastatin, atorvastatin, fluvastatin) — cross cell membranes, BBB; more muscle toxicity.
  • Pravastatin & rosuvastatin — hydrophilic; hepatic uptake transporters (OATP1B1); less muscle toxicity; less CNS effects.
  • Metabolism — simvastatin, lovastatin, atorvastatin (CYP3A4); fluvastatin (CYP2C9); rosuvastatin, pitavastatin (minimal CYP — renal & hepatic).
  • Half-life — atorvastatin 14 h (active metabolites longer); rosuvastatin 19 h (longest); simvastatin 2–3 h; pravastatin 1.8 h; fluvastatin 1.2 h.
  • Once-daily dosing (evening preferred for short half-life — cholesterol synthesis peaks at night); atorvastatin & rosuvastatin any time.
  • Excretion — hepatic (bile, faeces); renal (pravastatin, rosuvastatin).

Lipid-Lowering Effects

Lipid Effect
LDL-C↓ 30–60% (dose-dependent; high-intensity statin lowers ≥50%)
Triglycerides↓ 10–30% (more if baseline high)
HDL-C↑ 5–10% (modest)
VLDL↓
Lp(a)No significant effect (may ↑ slightly); PCSK9 inhibitors ↓ Lp(a)

Therapeutic Uses

  1. Primary prevention — asymptomatic patients at increased CV risk; ASCVD risk ≥7.5% (ACC/AHA) or ≥10% (older); diabetes age 40–75; LDL ≥190 mg/dL.
  2. Secondary prevention — established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) — post-MI, stroke/TIA, peripheral arterial disease, revascularisation; all patients regardless of LDL.
  3. Acute coronary syndrome (ACS) — high-intensity statin started within 24 h; atorvastatin 80 mg daily; reduces recurrent events & mortality.
  4. Hypercholesterolaemia — familial (heterozygous FH); statin first-line; combination with ezetimibe, PCSK9 inhibitor, bempedoic acid.
  5. Homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia — high-dose statin + ezetimibe + PCSK9 inhibitor + lomitapide + apheresis.
  6. Stroke prevention — SPARCL trial (atorvastatin 80 mg reduced recurrent stroke in patients with prior TIA/stroke).
  7. Aortic aneurysm — may slow growth (controversial).
  8. Pre-operative statin — before major vascular surgery; reduces perioperative cardiac events.
  9. Chronic kidney disease — 4D, AURORA trials; reduced CV events in non-dialysis CKD; SHARP (simvastatin + ezetimibe) in CKD; less benefit on dialysis.
  10. Heart failure — CORONA, GISSI-HF trials; no clear benefit in established HF; statins not routinely recommended.
  11. Other emerging uses — sepsis, ARDS, cancer prevention, Alzheimer's disease, osteoporosis — investigational; routine use not recommended.

Guidelines — When to Start & Targets

FH without ASCVDHigh<55 mg/dL AND ≥50% reduction

Diabetes without risk factors (age <40 or >10 yr duration)Moderate<70 mg/dL
Very high risk (no ASCVD)High<55 mg/dL
High risk (SCORE ≥5%)Moderate<70 mg/dL
Moderate risk (SCORE 1–5%)Moderate<100 mg/dL
Low riskLifestyle; statin if LDL >190 mg/dL<116 mg/dL

Adverse Effects

  • Muscle-related (most common):
    • Myopathy — muscle pain, weakness; CK >10× ULN; risk 5–10%.
    • Myalgia — muscle pain without CK elevation; ~5–10%.
    • Myositis — muscle inflammation with CK elevation.
    • Rhabdomyolysis — severe; CK >10× ULN + myoglobinuria + AKI; rare (1/10,000); more with high doses, drug interactions (CYP3A4 inhibitors — macrolides, azoles, protease inhibitors, cyclosporine, gemfibrozil), hypothyroidism, vitamin D deficiency, elderly, female, low body weight, renal/hepatic impairment, genetic (SLCO1B1 polymorphism).
    • Treatment — stop statin; hydration; monitor CK, renal function; switch to different statin or low dose; coenzyme Q10 (controversial); ezetimibe/PCSK9 inhibitor alternative.
  • Hepatic:
    • Transaminase elevation — 1–3%; usually transient; dose-dependent; check LFT at baseline, 3 months, then annually; stop if ALT >3× ULN.
    • Frank hepatitis — rare; usually reversible on stopping.
    • Does NOT cause liver failure (rare reports — controversial).
  • Diabetes mellitus:
    • ↑ Risk of new-onset diabetes — ~1 in 255 patients treated for 4 years; more with high-intensity statins, prediabetes, metabolic syndrome.
    • Benefit (CV risk reduction) far outweighs risk; do not stop statin.
  • Neurological:
    • Memory loss, confusion — FDA warning (controversial; evidence conflicting); reversible.
    • Peripheral neuropathy — rare; controversial.
  • GI — nausea, diarrhoea, constipation, abdominal pain.
  • Renal:
    • Proteinuria — rosuvastatin high dose (transient; not progressive); rarely significant.
    • Acute kidney injury — rare; from rhabdomyolysis.
  • Reproductive — contraindicated in pregnancy (teratogenic in animals); avoid in lactation.
  • Skin — rash, photosensitivity.
  • Haemorrhagic stroke — SPARCL trial showed small ↑ risk of haemorrhagic stroke with high-dose atorvastatin; benefit (ischaemic stroke reduction) far outweighs.
  • Other — sleep disturbance, headache, fatigue.

Drug Interactions

  • CYP3A4 inhibitors (simvastatin, lovastatin, atorvastatin):
    • Macrolides — erythromycin, clarithromycin (NOT azithromycin).
    • Azole antifungals — ketoconazole, itraconazole, fluconazole, voriconazole.
    • Protease inhibitors (HIV) — ritonavir, saquinavir.
    • Calcium channel blockers — diltiazem, verapamil (especially with simvastatin — dose limit 10–20 mg).
    • Amiodarone — simvastatin dose limit 20 mg.
    • Grapefruit juice — >1 L/day.
    • Cyclosporine — avoid with most statins; pravastatin, rosuvastatin less affected.
    • Danazol, gemfibrozil.
  • Fibrates — gemfibrozil significantly ↑ statin myopathy risk (avoid); fenofibrate safer.
  • Warfarin — ↑ INR (displacement; CYP); monitor.
  • Oral contraceptives — ↑ ethinylestradiol & norethisterone levels.
  • Digoxin — ↑ digoxin levels (atorvastatin, simvastatin — P-gp).
  • Colchicine — ↑ myopathy risk.
  • SLCO1B1 polymorphism — ↑ simvastatin myopathy risk; pharmacogenomic testing.

Monitoring

  • Lipid profile — baseline, 4–12 weeks after starting/dose change, then annually.
  • LFT — baseline, 3 months, then annually (more often if symptoms).
  • CK — baseline if risk factors; if muscle symptoms develop; not routine.
  • Renal function — baseline; if rhabdomyolysis.
  • HbA1c — monitor for new-onset diabetes (especially prediabetes).
  • Thyroid function — exclude hypothyroidism if myopathy (statin unmasking).

Combination Therapy

  • Ezetimibe — cholesterol absorption inhibitor; ↓ LDL additional 15–25%; first add-on if LDL target not met.
  • PCSK9 inhibitors — evolocumab, alirocumab (subcutaneous mAbs); ↓ LDL additional 50–60%; for FH, statin intolerance, very high-risk; FOURIER, ODYSSEY trials reduced CV events.
  • Bempedoic acid — ATP citrate lyase inhibitor; oral; ↓ LDL 15–20%; for statin intolerance.
  • Fibrates — fenofibrate (safe with statins); for hypertriglyceridaemia.
  • Niacin — AIM-HIGH, HPS2-THRIVE trials — no added benefit with statin; avoid.
  • Omega-3 fatty acids — icosapent ethyl (Vascepa) — REDUCE-IT trial reduced CV events in hypertriglyceridaemia on statin.
  • Inclisiran — siRNA targeting PCSK9; twice-yearly SC injection; ↓ LDL ~50%; for FH, statin intolerance.

Clinical Pearl

Statins are the most evidence-based cardiovascular drugs — reduce CV events & mortality in primary & secondary prevention. High-intensity statin (atorvastatin 40–80 mg or rosuvastatin 20–40 mg) — reduces LDL ≥50%; preferred for established ASCVD, ACS, FH, diabetes with high risk. Start statin in ACS within 24 h — atorvastatin 80 mg daily; reduces recurrent MI & mortality. LDL target — <55 mg/dL (1.4 mmol/L) for very high-risk (ESC 2019); <70 for high-risk; >50% reduction from baseline. Muscle symptoms are most common side effect — myalgia (5–10%); myopathy; rhabdomyolysis (rare, 1/10,000); check CK if symptoms; stop if CK >10× ULN; switch to hydrophilic statin (pravastatin, rosuvastatin) or low dose; check TSH (hypothyroidism unmasking); vitamin D; SLCO1B1 polymorphism (simvastatin). Avoid CYP3A4 inhibitors with simvastatin/lovastatin/atorvastatin — macrolides, azoles, protease inhibitors, grapefruit, diltiazem, amiodarone (dose limits); use pravastatin, rosuvastatin, pitavastatin (minimal CYP). Small ↑ risk of new-onset diabetes — benefit >> risk; do not stop statin. Contraindicated in pregnancy — teratogenic; use bile acid sequestrants in pregnancy. Combination therapy if LDL target not met — add ezetimibe (↓15–25%); then PCSK9 inhibitor (evolocumab, alirocumab — ↓50–60%; SC every 2 weeks); inclisiran (siRNA, twice yearly); bempedoic acid (oral, for statin intolerance). India — statins widely available & affordable (generic atorvastatin, rosuvastatin); underprescribed in eligible patients; high-intensity statin use low; physician & patient education needed about benefit:risk ratio.

Definition

Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (PSVT) — sudden onset/offset regular narrow-complex tachycardia (150–250 bpm) from re-entry circuit involving AV node or accessory pathway.

Management

1. Vagal Maneuvers (First-Line)

  • Carotid sinus massage (unilateral; contraindicated in carotid bruit, TIA, stroke).
  • Valsalva manoeuvre (modified — passive leg elevation).
  • Cold water immersion of face (diving reflex).

2. Pharmacological — Acute Termination

  • Adenosine — drug of choice; 6 mg rapid IV bolus (followed by saline flush); if no response in 1–2 min → 12 mg → 12 mg; transient AV block; extremely short half-life (10 sec); warn patient about flushing, chest tightness, dyspnoea; contraindicated in asthma (bronchospasm), 2nd/3rd degree AV block, sick sinus syndrome; avoid with dipyridamole (potentiates).
  • Verapamil — 5 mg IV over 2 min (repeat 5 mg after 10 min if needed); alternative if adenosine contraindicated; avoid in LV dysfunction, WPW with AF.
  • Diltiazem — 0.25 mg/kg IV; alternative.
  • β-blocker — Esmolol 500 µg/kg loading then 50 µg/kg/min; or metoprolol 5 mg IV.
  • Digoxin — 0.5 mg IV (if HF); slow onset.
  • Amiodarone — 150 mg IV (refractory).

3. Synchronised Cardioversion

  • If haemodynamically unstable (hypotension, chest pain, altered sensorium, heart failure) — 50–100 J synchronised DC shock.

4. Long-Term Prevention

  • Catheter ablation — curative; first-line for recurrent PSVT; success 95%+.
  • β-blockers, verapamil, diltiazem — for patients not suitable for ablation.
  • Flecainide, propafenone — “pill in pocket” approach.

Clinical Pearl

Adenosine is drug of choice for acute PSVT termination — rapid IV bolus (6 mg → 12 mg → 12 mg); extremely short half-life (10 sec); must be given fast with saline flush; warn about transient flushing, chest tightness, sense of doom. Always try vagal manoeuvres first — Valsalva (modified with leg elevation most effective), carotid sinus massage (check for bruit first). Synchronised cardioversion if unstable. Catheter ablation is curative — first-line for recurrent PSVT; 95%+ success; minimal complications. Avoid verapamil in WPW with AF — may accelerate accessory pathway → VF.

Mechanism

Topical β-blockers reduce intraocular pressure (IOP) by decreasing aqueous humour production in the ciliary body — block β2 receptors on non-pigmented ciliary epithelium → ↓ cAMP → ↓ active secretion of aqueous humour (~20–30% reduction in IOP).

Drugs

  • Timolol — non-selective (β1 + β2); 0.25% or 0.5%, 1 drop BD; most commonly used; cheapest.
  • Betaxolol — β1-selective; safer in asthma/COPD; 0.25% or 0.5%, BD.
  • Levobunolol — non-selective; once daily; long duration.
  • Carteolol — non-selective with ISA; less effect on lipids.
  • Metipranolol — non-selective.

Advantages

  • Effective IOP reduction (20–30%).
  • No pupillary effect (no mydriasis/miosis).
  • No accommodation changes.
  • Once or twice daily dosing.
  • Cheap (especially timolol).
  • Local side effects minimal.

Adverse Effects

  • Systemic absorption — significant (nasolacrimal drainage → GI absorption); may cause bradycardia, bronchospasm (especially non-selective — timolol), hypotension, fatigue, depression, masked hypoglycaemia.
  • Local — stinging, dry eyes, allergic conjunctivitis, punctate keratitis.

Contraindications

  • Asthma, severe COPD (bronchospasm — non-selective).
  • 2nd/3rd degree AV block, sinus bradycardia, sick sinus syndrome.
  • Severe heart failure.
  • Hypotension.

Clinical Pearl

Timolol is most commonly used topical β-blocker for glaucoma — cheap, effective, well-tolerated. Systemic absorption is significant — topical timolol can cause bronchospasm in asthmatics and bradycardia; always use nasolacrimal occlusion (press inner canthus for 1–2 min after instillation) to reduce systemic absorption. Betaxolol (β1-selective) is safer in asthma/COPD — but less potent than non-selective. Fixed-dose combinations — timolol + dorzolamide (Cosopt), timolol + latanoprost (Xalacom), timolol + brimonidine (Combigan) — improved adherence & additive IOP reduction. First-line for open-angle glaucoma — prostaglandin analogues (latanoprost) increasingly preferred (once daily, more potent, fewer systemic effects); β-blockers remain widely used (especially in India — affordable).

Introduction

Anticholinergics (muscarinic antagonists) reduce GI smooth muscle spasm & secretions by blocking M3 receptors on smooth muscle & secretory glands.

Classification

1. Quaternary Ammonium Compounds (Poor GI Absorption — Gut-Specific)

  • Dicyclomine — antispasmodic; for IBS, colic, dysmenorrhoea.
  • Hyoscine butylbromide (Buscopan) — antispasmodic; IV/IM for renal/biliary colic; rapid onset.
  • Oxyphenonium, mepenzolate, pipenzolate, clidinium — older antispasmodics.
  • Pirenzepine — M1-selective; reduces gastric acid (historical; replaced by PPIs).
  • Propantheline — antisecretory + antispasmodic.

2. Tertiary Amines (Cross BBB — More CNS Effects)

  • Atropine — non-selective; systemic effects.
  • Hyoscine (scopolamine) — antiemetic (motion sickness — transdermal patch).
  • Dicyclomine (also listed above; partial CNS penetration).

Mechanism

  • Block M3 receptors on GI smooth muscle → ↓ contraction → relief of spasm/colic.
  • Block M3 on secretory glands → ↓ gastric acid, saliva, sweat, respiratory secretions.
  • Block M1 on enteric nervous system → ↓ peristalsis.

Therapeutic Uses

  • Antispasmodic — IBS, diverticular disease, renal colic, biliary colic, dysmenorrhoea, post-operative spasm.
  • Antisecretory — reduce GI secretions (historical; replaced by PPIs/H2 blockers); reduce respiratory secretions (pre-anaesthesia — atropine, glycopyrrolate).
  • Pre-anaesthetic medication — atropine, glycopyrrolate (↓ secretions, ↓ vagal reflexes).
  • Peptic ulcer (historical — pirenzepine, propantheline; replaced by PPIs).
  • Motion sickness — hyoscine (scopolamine) transdermal patch.
  • Organophosphorus poisoning — atropine (antidote; blocks excess ACh at muscarinic receptors).

Adverse Effects (Atropinic Side Effects)

  • Dry mouth, blurred vision, photophobia (mydriasis, cycloplegia), urinary retention, constipation, tachycardia, flushed skin, hyperthermia (anhydrosis), confusion (elderly — delirium).
  • Mnemonic: "Dry as a bone, red as a beet, blind as a bat, hot as a hare, mad as a hatter."

Contraindications

  • Glaucoma (angle-closure — mydriasis worsens); BPH (urinary retention); GI obstruction; paralytic ileus; tachyarrhythmias; myasthenia gravis.

Clinical Pearl

Hyoscine butylbromide (Buscopan) IV/IM is drug of choice for acute renal & biliary colic — rapid onset; spasm relief; less CNS effects (quaternary — doesn't cross BBB). Dicyclomine — oral; for IBS, dysmenorrhoea; mild antispasmodic. Quaternary compounds preferred over tertiary — less CNS effects (don't cross BBB); gut-specific action. Avoid in elderly — confusion, urinary retention, constipation ("anticholinergic burden"); Beers criteria. Glycopyrrolate preferred over atropine as pre-anaesthetic — less CNS effects; longer duration; used for ↓ secretions & ↓ vagal reflexes. Atropine — drug of choice for organophosphorus poisoning (titrate to atropinisation — dry mouth, HR >80, pupils dilated, clear chest).
q2_0_2_12:
Introduction

Inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) are the cornerstone of chronic asthma management — anti-inflammatory; reduce airway hyperresponsiveness, eosinophils, mast cells, cytokines; prevent exacerbations & airway remodelling.

Drugs

  • Beclomethasone dipropionate — oldest; 50–400 µg BD; QVAR (extra-fine particle — better lung deposition).
  • Budesonide — 200–800 µg BD; Turbohaler; can be used in pregnancy (safety data best).
  • Fluticasone propionate — 100–500 µg BD; Accuhaler/Diskus; potent; negligible oral bioavailability.
  • Fluticasone furoate — newer; longer-acting; once daily with vilanterol.
  • Ciclesonide — prodrug; activated in lung; minimal local side effects; once daily.
  • Mometasone furoate — 200–400 µg; once daily; Twisthaler.
  • Triamcinolone — older; less used.

Mechanism of Action

  1. Bind cytoplasmic glucocorticoid receptor → translocates to nucleus → ↑ anti-inflammatory genes (transactivation — lipocortin-1, IL-10, IκB); ↓ pro-inflammatory genes (transrepression — TNF-α, IL-1, IL-4, IL-5, IL-6, COX-2, iNOS, adhesion molecules).
  2. ↓ Eosinophil recruitment & survival; ↓ mast cells; ↓ T cell activation (Th2).
  3. ↓ Airway oedema, mucus secretion; ↑ β2-receptor expression (upregulation — enhances bronchodilator response).
  4. ↓ Airway hyperresponsiveness; prevent remodelling (subepithelial fibrosis, smooth muscle hypertrophy).

Therapeutic Uses

  • Asthma — first-line controller for all persistent asthma (step 2+); reduces exacerbations, hospitalisations, mortality.
  • COPD — for severe COPD (FEV1 <50%) with frequent exacerbations; GOLD D; combination with LABA.
  • Eosinophilic oesophagitis — topical swallowed fluticasone or budesonide.
  • Allergic rhinitis — intranasal corticosteroids (fluticasone, mometasone, budesonide).

Stepwise Approach (GINA)

  • Step 1 — SABA PRN (or low-dose ICS-formoterol PRN — newer GINA recommendation).
  • Step 2 — Low-dose ICS daily + SABA PRN.
  • Step 3 — Low-dose ICS + LABA (or medium-dose ICS).
  • Step 4 — Medium-dose ICS + LABA.
  • Step 5 — High-dose ICS + LABA ± biologic (omalizumab, mepolizumab, dupilumab).

Adverse Effects

  • Local — oral candidiasis (thrush — rinse mouth after use); hoarseness/dysphonia (myopathy of vocal cord muscles); throat irritation; cough.
  • Systemic (dose-dependent; less than oral steroids) — adrenal suppression (high doses); growth retardation in children (1–2 cm final height — small; not clinically significant); osteoporosis; cataracts; glaucoma; skin thinning; easy bruising; hyperglycaemia.

Reducing Side Effects

  • Use lowest effective dose; spacer device (improves lung deposition, reduces oropharyngeal deposition); rinse mouth after use; good inhaler technique.
  • Use ICS with low oral bioavailability (fluticasone, mometasone, ciclesonide).
  • Once-daily formulations improve adherence.

Clinical Pearl

ICS are the most effective controller therapy for persistent asthma — anti-inflammatory; reduces exacerbations, hospitalisations, mortality; first-line for all persistent asthma (GINA step 2+). Always rinse mouth after use — prevents oral candidiasis (thrush) & dysphonia. Use spacer device — improves drug delivery to lungs, reduces oropharyngeal deposition & side effects. ICS + LABA combination inhalers — fluticasone + salmeterol (Seretide); budesonide + formoterol (Symbicort — also used as MART — maintenance & reliever therapy); improves adherence & outcomes. Budesonide is preferred in pregnancy — most safety data. SMART (Symbicort Maintenance and Reliever Therapy) — budesonide-formoterol as both maintenance & reliever — reduces exacerbations vs fixed-dose + SABA. Systemic side effects minimal at low-moderate doses — adrenal suppression, growth retardation only at very high chronic doses; don't withhold ICS from children due to growth concerns — uncontrolled asthma is worse. India — ICS underutilised; SABA overused; cost & education barriers; increasing availability of generic budesonide & fluticasone improving access.

Introduction

Dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) — aspirin + P2Y12 inhibitor — is the cornerstone of ACS management; prevents stent thrombosis & recurrent ischaemic events.

Aspirin

  • Mechanism — irreversibly acetylates COX-1 → blocks thromboxane A2 (TXA2) synthesis in platelets → ↓ platelet aggregation; effect lasts platelet lifespan (7–10 days).
  • Dose in ACS — 300 mg chewed immediately (non-enteric-coated); then 75–100 mg daily lifelong.
  • Reduces mortality ~25% in ACS.

Clopidogrel

  • Mechanism — prodrug; CYP2C19-mediated activation; irreversibly blocks P2Y12 ADP receptor on platelets → ↓ ADP-mediated platelet aggregation; effect lasts platelet lifespan.
  • Dose in ACS — 300–600 mg loading; then 75 mg daily for 12 months (STEMI with fibrinolysis — 300 mg load if <75 yr; 75 mg without loading if ≥75 yr).
  • CYP2C19 polymorphism — poor metabolisers (15% Asians) → ↓ active metabolite → ↓ antiplatelet effect → ↑ stent thrombosis; consider prasugrel or ticagrelor.

Newer P2Y12 Inhibitors

  • Ticagrelor — 180 mg loading then 90 mg BD; reversible; faster onset; not prodrug; PLATO trial — reduced mortality vs clopidogrel; preferred in ACS (with aspirin); dyspnoea side effect; avoid in history of intracranial haemorrhage.
  • Prasugrel — 60 mg loading then 10 mg daily; irreversible; more potent; avoid in age >75, weight <60 kg, history of stroke/TIA (bleeding risk); used in primary PCI.

DAPT Duration

  • STEMI/NSTEMI — 12 months (with drug-eluting stent); then aspirin lifelong.
  • Ticagrelor 60 mg BD beyond 1 year — PEGASUS trial; for high-risk patients.

Clinical Pearl

Aspirin 300 mg chewed immediately + P2Y12 inhibitor (ticagrelor preferred) is first-line for all ACS. Ticagrelor reduced mortality vs clopidogrel in PLATO trial — preferred unless contraindicated (intracranial haemorrhage). Prasugrel — more potent; avoid in elderly (>75), low weight (<60 kg), stroke/TIA history. Clopidogrel — cheapest; CYP2C19 polymorphism in Asians (15%) → poor response → consider ticagrelor/prasugrel. DAPT for 12 months post-STEMI (with DES); then aspirin lifelong. Bleeding risk assessment — PRECISE-DAPT, ARC-HBR scores; balance ischaemic vs bleeding risk. PPI co-prescription — omeprazole/pantoprazole reduces GI bleeding (controversial — CYP2C19 interaction with clopidogrel; pantoprazole preferred).
q2_0_3_0:
Role of Atropine in Organophosphate Poisoning

Organophosphates inhibit acetylcholinesterase → ↑ acetylcholine at muscarinic & nicotinic receptors → SLUDGE-BB (salivation, lacrimation, urination, defecation, GI cramps, emesis, bradycardia, bronchospasm) + fasciculations, seizures, coma.

Atropine — competitive muscarinic antagonist; blocks excess ACh at muscarinic receptors → reverses bradycardia, bronchospasm, secretions, GI hypermotility. Does NOT reverse nicotinic effects (fasciculations, muscle weakness) — that requires pralidoxime (2-PAM).

Dose — 1.2–2 mg IV bolus; double every 5 min until "atropinisation" achieved (dry skin, HR >80, SBP >80, clear chest, pupils dilated); then infusion 10–20% of total loading dose per hour; titrate to maintain atropinisation for 24–48 h.

Clinical Pearl — Titrate to atropinisation (dry mouth, HR >80, clear chest); NOT to pupil size; continue infusion for days (lipid-soluble OP redistribution); always combine with pralidoxime (reverses nicotinic effects; reactivates AChE if given early — within 24–48 h).
q2_0_3_1:
Pharmacological Basis of Low-Dose Aspirin as Antiplatelet

Aspirin — irreversible acetylation of COX-1 in platelets → blocks thromboxane A2 (TXA2) synthesis → ↓ platelet aggregation for platelet lifespan (7–10 days).

Why low dose (75–150 mg)?

  • Platelets have no nucleus → cannot synthesise new COX-1 → irreversible inhibition lasts for platelet lifespan (7–10 days).
  • Endothelial cells (which produce prostacyclin — PGI2, antiplatelet) HAVE nucleus → can regenerate COX → recover within hours.
  • Low dose (75 mg) — selectively inhibits platelet COX-1 (TXA2) with minimal effect on endothelial COX-2 (PGI2) — preserves antithrombotic prostacyclin.
  • High dose (>300 mg) — inhibits both TXA2 & PGI2 — negates antithrombotic benefit.
  • Once daily dosing sufficient — new platelets produced daily (~10% turnover) but low dose maintains inhibition of TXA2.

Uses — secondary prevention (post-MI, stroke, PAD); primary prevention (controversial — ASCVD risk ≥7.5% per ACC/AHA; bleeding risk must be considered); pregnancy — anti-phospholipid syndrome.

Clinical Pearl — Low-dose aspirin (75 mg) selectively inhibits platelet TXA2 while sparing endothelial PGI2 (antithrombotic) — "selective antiplatelet effect". Higher doses may paradoxically reduce antithrombotic benefit by also inhibiting PGI2.
q2_0_3_2:
Pharmacological Basis of Theophylline in Asthma

Theophylline — methylxanthine bronchodilator; less commonly used now (narrow therapeutic index; replaced by ICS + LABA).

Mechanism:

  1. Phosphodiesterase (PDE) inhibition — ↓ cAMP & cGMP breakdown → ↑ intracellular cAMP → ↓ intracellular Ca²⁺ → bronchial smooth muscle relaxation (bronchodilation).
  2. Adenosine receptor antagonism — adenosine causes bronchoconstriction in asthmatics; theophylline blocks A1 & A2 receptors → bronchodilation; also responsible for CNS stimulation & cardiac effects.
  3. Anti-inflammatory — ↑ histone deacetylase (HDAC) activity → ↓ inflammatory gene transcription; ↓ eosinophils & cytokines (similar to low-dose corticosteroid effect).
  4. ↑ Diaphragmatic contractility — improves respiratory muscle function.

Therapeutic range — 10–20 µg/mL; narrow therapeutic index; monitor levels; toxicity — arrhythmias, seizures (no warning; can be fatal), nausea, headache. Drug interactions — CYP1A2 & CYP3A4 metabolism; ↑ levels with erythromycin, ciprofloxacin, cimetidine, oral contraceptives; ↓ levels with rifampicin, phenytoin, smoking, barbiturates.

Clinical Pearl — Theophylline is now 3rd/4th-line for asthma (behind ICS, LABA, LTRA); used in severe persistent asthma or when ICS/LABA unavailable. Always monitor serum levels — 10–20 µg/mL; seizures can occur without warning at levels >25 µg/mL and are often fatal. Avoid in cardiac disease, seizure disorder, peptic ulcer.
q2_0_3_3:
Why Folinic Acid Preferred Over Folic Acid for Methotrexate Toxicity

Methotrexate — inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) → ↓ tetrahydrofolate (THF) → ↓ DNA synthesis (↓ thymidylate, ↓ purines) → stops rapidly dividing cells (cancer, psoriasis, RA).

Folic acid — must be reduced by DHFR to THF before it can function; if DHFR is inhibited by methotrexate, folic acid CANNOT be converted to active form → useless.

Folinic acid (leucovorin, 5-formyl-THF) — already reduced (bypasses DHFR); directly provides THF → restores DNA synthesis → rescues normal cells from methotrexate toxicity.

Uses:

  • Methotrexate rescue — after high-dose methotrexate (cancer); leucovorin given 24 h later to rescue normal cells.
  • Methotrexate overdose — accidental or intentional.
  • Trimethoprim/pyrimethamine toxicity — also DHFR inhibitors.
  • Colorectal cancer — 5-FU + leucovorin (enhances 5-FU binding to thymidylate synthase).

Clinical Pearl — Folinic acid (leucovorin) bypasses the blocked DHFR enzyme; folic acid requires DHFR (blocked by MTX) → useless. Never give leucovorin with methotrexate for cancer treatment — rescues tumour cells too! Only give after MTX has had time to act (rescue 24 h later).
q2_0_3_4:
Why Loading Doses Required for Drugs Like Digoxin

Loading dose — initial higher dose to rapidly achieve therapeutic plasma concentration; needed when:

  1. Long half-life — drug takes too long to reach steady state by regular dosing alone (digoxin t½ 36 h; takes 5 half-lives = 7 days to reach steady state); loading achieves therapeutic level in hours.
  2. Large volume of distribution (Vd) — drug distributes widely in tissues (digoxin Vd ~500 L; binds to Na-K-ATPase in muscle); large loading dose needed to saturate tissue binding & achieve therapeutic plasma level.
  3. Urgent therapeutic need — e.g., digoxin for acute AF rate control; phenytoin for status epilepticus; amiodarone for VT.

Formula — Loading dose = (Vd × Target plasma concentration) / Bioavailability

For digoxin — Vd 7 L/kg; target 1.5 ng/mL; loading dose = 7 × 1.5 × 70 kg = 735 µg (give as 0.5 mg + 0.25 mg × 2 at 6 h intervals).

Other drugs needing loading — amiodarone (Vd 60 L/kg; t½ 50 days), phenytoin (status epilepticus), procainamide, digoxin, voriconazole, chloroquine.

Clinical Pearl — Loading dose is needed when drug has long half-life & urgent effect needed; without loading, takes 5 half-lives (3.3 × t½) to reach 90% steady state — too slow for digoxin (7 days), amiodarone (250 days!).
q2_0_3_5:
Methods for Prolongation of Drug Action

  1. Sustained/Extended release formulations — matrix tablets, coated beads, osmotic pumps (e.g., nifedipine GITS, metoprolol succinate ER); slow release over 12–24 h; once-daily dosing.
  2. Transdermal patches — nitroglycerin, fentanyl, oestrogen, clonidine, rivastigmine, rotigotine; sustained release through skin over 24–72 h.
  3. Depot injections — IM/SC; oily vehicle or microspheres; haloperidol decanoate, fluphenazine decanoate, medroxyprogesterone acetate (Depo-Provera), risperidone microspheres, paliperidone palmitate, olanzapine pamoate; weekly to monthly dosing.
  4. Prodrugs — inactive form converted to active in body slowly; enalapril → enalaprilat; valacyclovir → acyclovir; tenofovir disoproxil → tenofovir.
  5. Chemical modification — add bulky group; esterification (benzathine penicillin — IM; duration 3–4 weeks); procaine penicillin (12–24 h).
  6. Bioerodible implants — subcutaneous; sustained release; contraceptive implants (etonogestrel — 3 years; levonorgestrel — 5 years).
  7. Liposomal formulations — liposomal amphotericin B, liposomal doxorubicin; sustained release; reduced toxicity.
  8. Pegylation — attach PEG (polyethylene glycol); pegylated interferon (t½ 80 h vs 8 h standard); pegfilgrastim (once per cycle vs daily filgrastim); pegvisomant.
  9. Protein binding — highly protein-bound drugs have longer duration (warfarin 99% bound).
  10. Active metabolites — diazepam → nordiazepam (t½ 100 h); extended duration.

Clinical Pearl — Prolongation of drug action improves adherence (less frequent dosing), reduces side effects (smoother plasma levels), and enables outpatient treatment of chronic diseases (antipsychotic depots, contraceptive implants, transdermal patches).
q2_0_3_6:
Mucolytics

Mucolytics — drugs that break down or reduce viscosity of mucus; used for productive cough with thick secretions (COPD, bronchiectasis, cystic fibrosis).

Classification

  1. N-acetylcysteine (NAC) — breaks disulphide bonds in mucus glycoproteins → ↓ viscosity; direct; also antioxidant (↑ glutathione); used in COPD, CF, paracetamol overdose (antidote — restores glutathione).
  2. Carbocisteine — breaks disulphide bonds; also ↓ mucus secretion; oral; for COPD, chronic bronchitis.
  3. Erdosteine — prodrug; breaks disulphide bonds; also antibacterial (↑ ciliary function); for acute exacerbation of COPD.
  4. Bromhexine — breaks mucus polymers; also ↑ ciliary activity; metabolised to ambroxol.
  5. Ambroxol — active metabolite of bromhexine; ↑ surfactant production; ↓ mucus viscosity; anaesthetic effect (lozenge for sore throat).
  6. Dornase alfa (recombinant human DNase) — breaks down DNA in pus (from neutrophils) → ↓ viscosity; inhaled; for cystic fibrosis; NOT for COPD.
  7. Hypertonic saline (7%) — osmotic; draws water into mucus → ↓ viscosity; inhaled; for CF; also for bronchiectasis.

Uses

  • COPD exacerbation — carbocisteine, erdosteine, NAC.
  • Cystic fibrosis — dornase alfa, hypertonic saline, NAC.
  • Bronchiectasis — NAC, hypertonic saline.
  • Paracetamol overdose — IV NAC (antidote; restores hepatic glutathione).

Clinical Pearl — N-acetylcysteine is the most versatile mucolytic — breaks mucus disulphide bonds AND is antidote for paracetamol overdose (restores glutathione). Dornase alfa (rhDNase) — specific for cystic fibrosis (breaks DNA in purulent sputum); NOT effective in COPD (mucus is DNA-poor). Steam inhalation & oral hydration — cheapest & safest mucolytics; ↑ water content of mucus → ↓ viscosity.
q2_0_3_7:
Pharmacological Basis of Prazosin in BPH

Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) — enlarged prostate → compression of urethra → urinary symptoms (frequency, urgency, hesitancy, weak stream, incomplete emptying, nocturia).

Prazosin — selective α1-adrenergic receptor antagonist; blocks α1 receptors on:

  1. Prostate capsule, bladder neck, & urethral smooth muscle (α1A predominant) → relaxation → ↓ dynamic component of obstruction → improved urine flow, reduced symptoms.
  2. Peripheral vascular smooth muscle (α1B) → vasodilation → ↓ blood pressure (may be beneficial if coexisting hypertension; may cause postural hypotension).

Rationale: Prostatic & bladder neck smooth muscle tone is mediated by sympathetic α1-adrenergic receptors; blocking these receptors relaxes the prostate & bladder neck → relieves the "dynamic" component of BPH obstruction (as opposed to the "static" component — enlarged gland tissue, addressed by 5α-reductase inhibitors like finasteride).

Other α1-blockers for BPH — tamsulosin (uroselective — α1A; less hypotension; preferred), silodosin (α1A highly selective), doxazosin, terazosin, alfuzosin.

Clinical Pearl — Tamsulosin (uroselective α1A) is preferred for BPH — less postural hypotension than prazosin/doxazosin (less α1B effect on vascular smooth muscle). α1-blockers address the dynamic component (muscle tone); 5α-reductase inhibitors (finasteride, dutasteride) address the static component (gland size); combination for severe BPH. First-dose hypotension "first-dose effect" — start low (prazosin 0.5 mg), give at bedtime; especially in elderly. IFIS (Intraoperative Floppy Iris Syndrome) — tamsulosin causes iris instability during cataract surgery; inform ophthalmologist.
q2_0_3_8:
Pharmacological Basis of Adrenaline in Anaphylactic Shock

Anaphylaxis — Type I (IgE-mediated) hypersensitivity → massive mast cell & basophil degranulation → histamine, leukotrienes, prostaglandins, PAF → vasodilation (↓ BP, shock), bronchospasm, ↑ vascular permeability (oedema, laryngeal obstruction), urticaria, GI cramps.

Adrenaline (epinephrine) — physiological antagonist of histamine (acts at DIFFERENT receptors to produce OPPOSITE effects):

  • α1 (vasoconstriction) — reverses vasodilation & hypotension; ↓ mucosal oedema (laryngeal, bronchial) → relieves upper airway obstruction.
  • β1 (cardiac) — ↑ heart rate, contractility → ↑ cardiac output → ↑ BP; counteracts bradycardia.
  • β2 (bronchodilation) — relaxes bronchial smooth muscle → reverses bronchospasm; ↓ mast cell mediator release (stabilises mast cells); ↑ cAMP in mast cells → ↓ degranulation.
  • β2 (metabolic) — ↑ glucose; ↓ allergy mediator release.

Why adrenaline (not other drugs)? — Only adrenaline acts on ALL relevant receptors (α1 + β1 + β2) simultaneously; antihistamines only block H1 (slow onset; incomplete); corticosteroids take hours to act; β2-agonists only bronchodilate (no vascular effect). Adrenaline is "all-in-one" — vasoconstrictor + bronchodilator + mast cell stabiliser + cardiac stimulant.

Dose — 0.5 mg (0.5 mL of 1:1000) IM into anterolateral thigh; repeat every 5 min if no response; IV 50–100 µg (1 mL of 1:10,000) if cardiac arrest or profound shock.

Clinical Pearl — Adrenaline is the ONLY life-saving drug in anaphylaxis — give IM 0.5 mg into anterolateral thigh ASAP; do NOT delay for IV access; repeat every 5 min; antihistamines, steroids, fluids, oxygen are adjuncts — NOT substitutes for adrenaline. Always prescribe EpiPen (epinephrine autoinjector) for patients with history of anaphylaxis. IV adrenaline only if cardiac arrest or profound shock — risk of arrhythmia if given too rapidly.
q2_0_3_9:
Drug for Reversal of Competitive Neuromuscular Blockade

Neostigmine — acetylcholinesterase inhibitor — is the drug of choice for reversal of competitive (non-depolarising) neuromuscular blockade (e.g., vecuronium, rocuronium, atracurium).

Mechanism:

  1. Inhibits acetylcholinesterase → ↑ acetylcholine at NMJ.
  2. Excess ACh competes with non-depolarising NMBA for nicotinic (N2) receptors → displaces NMBA → restores neuromuscular transmission.

Co-administered with atropine or glycopyrrolate — neostigmine also increases ACh at muscarinic receptors → bradycardia, bronchospasm, salivation, GI hypermotility; anticholinergic prevents these.

Dose — neostigmine 0.04–0.07 mg/kg IV + glycopyrrolate 0.01 mg/kg IV (or atropine 0.02 mg/kg).

Limitations:

  • Cannot reverse deep block effectively (TOF count 0–1) — wait for spontaneous recovery first.
  • Cannot reverse depolarising block (succinylcholine) — actually prolongs it.
  • Side effects — bradycardia (without atropine), nausea, bronchospasm.

Newer alternative — Sugammadex — modified γ-cyclodextrin; encapsulates rocuronium/vecuronium (forms inactive complex) → direct removal; does NOT require AChE inhibition; no muscarinic side effects; can reverse deep block immediately; dose 2–4 mg/kg IV; expensive.

Clinical Pearl — Neostigmine + glycopyrrolate is standard reversal; sugammadex is revolutionary — encapsulates rocuronium directly; reverses even deep block immediately; no muscarinic side effects; expensive but game-changer for "cannot intubate, cannot ventilate" situations (rocuronium → immediate reversal with sugammadex 16 mg/kg). Always confirm adequate reversal — train-of-four (TOF) ratio ≥0.9; clinical criteria — sustained head lift >5 sec, grip strength, vital capacity.
q2_0_3_10:
Drug Therapy of Acute Congestive Glaucoma (Angle-Closure)

Acute angle-closure glaucoma — sudden closure of iridocorneal angle → blocked aqueous outflow → rapidly ↑ IOP (50–80 mmHg) → severe eye pain, headache, blurred vision, halos, nausea/vomiting, fixed mid-dilated pupil, corneal oedema. Ophthalmic emergency — vision loss within hours.

Immediate Medical Therapy

  1. Topical β-blocker — Timolol 0.5%, 1 drop; ↓ aqueous humour production.
  2. Topical α2-agonist — Brimonidine 0.15%, 1 drop; ↓ aqueous production & ↑ uveoscleral outflow.
  3. Systemic carbonic anhydrase inhibitor — Acetazolamide 500 mg IV or PO; ↓ aqueous humour production; most effective systemic agent.
  4. Topical steroid — Prednisolone acetate 1%, 1 drop QID; ↓ inflammation.
  5. Hyperosmotic agent — Mannitol 20% 1–2 g/kg IV over 45 min OR glycerol 1–1.5 g/kg PO; draws fluid from eye → ↓ IOP; for very high IOP.
  6. Analgesia & antiemetic — for comfort.
  7. Pilocarpine 1–2% — miotic; constricts pupil → opens angle; NOT effective while IOP >40 mmHg (iris sphincter ischaemic); give AFTER IOP reduced (e.g., after 1 h of above therapy).

Definitive Treatment

  • Laser peripheral iridotomy (LPI) — creates hole in peripheral iris → bypasses pupillary block → equalises pressure between posterior & anterior chambers → opens angle; definitive; performed after IOP controlled & cornea clears (24–48 h).
  • Surgical iridectomy — if laser not possible.
  • Prophylactic LPI in fellow eye — prevent attack (50% risk in 5 years).

Clinical Pearl — Acute angle-closure glaucoma is an ophthalmic emergency — reduce IOP within hours to prevent permanent optic nerve damage. Immediate: timolol + brimonidine + acetazolamide IV + mannitol if severe; pilocarpine AFTER IOP <40 (ischaemic sphincter won't respond). Definitive: laser peripheral iridotomy (creates alternative aqueous outflow pathway). Always treat fellow eye prophylactically — narrow angles are bilateral; 50% risk of attack in fellow eye within 5 years. Avoid mydriatics/anticholinergics in patients with narrow angles — precipitate attack.
q2_0_3_11:
Effects of Atropine on Eyes & Uses/Contraindications

Effects on Eye

  • Mydriasis (pupil dilation) — blocks M3 on iris sphincter → unopposed α1 (dilator) → dilation.
  • Cycloplegia (paralysis of accommodation) — blocks M3 on ciliary muscle → cannot contract for near vision → blurred near vision.
  • ↑ Intraocular pressure — in angle-closure glaucoma (dilated iris blocks trabecular meshwork → ↑ IOP); no effect or minimal in open-angle.
  • Photophobia — due to mydriasis.

Therapeutic Uses (Ophthalmological)

  • Refraction testing in children — cycloplegic refraction (atropine 1%, homatropine 2%, cyclopentolate 1%); paralyse accommodation for accurate measurement.
  • Treatment of uveitis/iritis — cycloplegia prevents synechiae (adhesions between iris & lens); rests ciliary muscle (relieves pain).
  • Amblyopia (lazy eye) — atropine 1% in good eye → forces child to use amblyopic eye ("penalisation").
  • Mydriasis for fundoscopy — tropicamide (short-acting; preferred), phenylephrine (α1; no cycloplegia).

Systemic Uses (Related)

  • Organophosphorus poisoning antidote (muscarinic antagonist).
  • Pre-anaesthetic medication (↓ secretions, ↓ vagal reflexes).
  • Bradycardia, AV block (↑ HR).
  • Antispasmodic (GI, biliary, renal colic).

Contraindications for Ophthalmic Use

  • Angle-closure glaucoma — mydriasis precipitates acute attack; ↑ IOP.
  • Known hypersensitivity.
  • Children with Down syndrome, cerebral palsy — ↑ sensitivity (paradoxical reaction; hyperthermia).
  • Elderly with BPH — urinary retention (systemic absorption).
  • Tachycardia — systemic absorption → ↑ HR.

Clinical Pearl — Atropine is longest-acting mydriatic/cycloplegic (7–14 days); tropicamide is preferred for fundoscopy (short duration — 3–6 h; no cycloplegia); cyclopentolate for refraction in children (onset 30 min; duration 24 h); atropine for uveitis & amblyopia (long-acting; preferred for sustained cycloplegia). NEVER use atropine/mydriatics in angle-closure glaucoma — dilated iris blocks trabecular meshwork → acute attack → blindness.
q2_0_3_12:
Why Cisatracurium Preferred for Liver/Kidney Disease

Cisatracurium — non-depolarising neuromuscular blocker (benzylisoquinolinium); stereoisomer of atracurium.

Organ-independent elimination — Hofmann elimination:

  • Cisatracurium is degraded by Hofmann elimination — spontaneous non-enzymatic degradation at physiological pH & temperature → cleaved into laudanosine & monoquaternary acrylate.
  • Does NOT require liver, kidney, or plasma cholinesterase for elimination.
  • Independent of organ function → safe in hepatic & renal failure.
  • Also some non-specific ester hydrolysis (independent of plasma cholinesterase).

Advantages in liver/kidney disease:

  • No accumulation in renal failure (unlike vecuronium, rocuronium — hepatic/renal excretion).
  • No accumulation in hepatic failure (unlike vecuronium, rocuronium — hepatic metabolism).
  • Predictable recovery regardless of organ function.
  • No histamine release (unlike atracurium — less hypotension, bronchospasm).
  • Less laudanosine than atracurium (laudanosine — CNS excitation, seizures in high doses; less concern with cisatracurium).

Comparison with other NMBAs in organ failure:

  • Vacuronium — hepatic metabolism + renal excretion → accumulates in both liver & kidney disease.
  • Rocuronium — hepatic excretion → accumulates in liver disease; sugammadex reversal is renal-cleared (problematic in CKD).
  • Atracurium — Hofmann elimination (organ-independent) but histamine release → hypotension, bronchospasm.
  • Cisatracurium — Hofmann elimination + no histamine release → safest for organ failure & haemodynamically unstable patients.

Clinical Pearl — Cisatracurium is the NMBA of choice for ICU patients with hepatic or renal failure — Hofmann elimination (pH & temperature-dependent non-enzymatic degradation) makes it organ-independent; no accumulation; no histamine release (unlike atracurium). Also preferred in haemodynamically unstable patients — no cardiovascular effects. ICU sedation/paralysis — cisatracurium infusion for ARDS, severe asthma, elevated ICP. Laudanosine (metabolite) — CNS excitation; theoretical seizure risk with very high doses or prolonged infusion; less than atracurium.
q2_0_3_13:
Why Sacubitril/Valsartan Preferred Over ACEI in Chronic Heart Failure

Sacubitril/valsartan (Entresto) — ARNI (Angiotensin Receptor-Neprilysin Inhibitor) — combination of:

  • Valsartan — ARB; blocks AT1 receptor → ↓ angiotensin II effects (vasoconstriction, aldosterone, remodelling).
  • Sacubitril — prodrug; converted to sacubitrilat (active); inhibits neprilysin — enzyme that degrades natriuretic peptides (ANP, BNP, CNP) → ↑ natriuretic peptides → vasodilation, natriuresis, diuresis, ↓ fibrosis, ↓ remodelling.

Why preferred over ACE inhibitor?

  1. PARI GMENT-HF trial (2014) — sacubitril/valsartan reduced CV mortality & HF hospitalisation by 20% vs enalapril in HFrEF; stopped early due to benefit.
  2. Dual mechanism — blocks RAAS (valsartan) AND enhances natriuretic peptide system (sacubitril) → more comprehensive neurohormonal modulation than ACEI alone.
  3. ↑ Natriuretic peptides → vasodilation, natriuresis, ↓ fibrosis, ↓ hypertrophy — additional benefit beyond RAAS blockade.
  4. Less cough & angioedema than ACEI — ARB (not ACEI) → no bradykinin potentiation (less cough, angioedema).
  5. Superior outcomes — reduced all-cause mortality, CV mortality, HF hospitalisation; improved symptoms & quality of life.

Indications:

  • HFrEF (EF ≤40%) — NYHA II–IV; replaces ACEI/ARB as first-line (ESC 2016 guidelines).
  • Post-MI with LV dysfunction (PARADISE-MI trial — emerging).

Cautions:

  • Do NOT combine with ACEI (↑ angioedema risk) — washout 36 h after stopping ACEI before starting ARNI.
  • Do NOT use in pregnancy (teratogenic — ARB component).
  • Do NOT use in hereditary angioedema.
  • Caution in severe renal impairment, hyperkalaemia.

Clinical Pearl — PARADIGM-HF trial showed sacubitril/valsartan reduced mortality 20% vs enalapril — first drug in decades to show superiority over ACEI in HFrEF. Replace ACEI/ARB with ARNI in symptomatic HFrEF (NYHA II–IV, EF ≤40%). 36-hour washout from ACEI before starting ARNI (risk of angioedema if combined). Monitor K⁺, renal function — may cause hyperkalaemia & AKI (like ACEI/ARB). Start low (24/26 mg or 49/51 mg BD), titrate to target (97/103 mg BD).
q2_0_3_14:
Why Thiazides Preferred Over Loop Diuretics in Recurrent Calcium Stones

Idiopathic hypercalciuria — most common metabolic abnormality in calcium stone formers; ↑ urinary calcium → calcium oxalate/phosphate stone formation.

Thiazide diuretics — reduce urinary calcium excretion (paradoxical effect):

  1. Block Na-Cl cotransporter in DCT → ↓ intracellular Na → ↑ Na-Ca exchange on basolateral membrane → ↑ Ca²⁺ reabsorption (paracellular) → ↓ urinary Ca²⁺.
  2. ↑ Ca²⁺ reabsorption in DCT → ↓ urinary calcium → ↓ calcium oxalate supersaturation → ↓ stone formation.

Loop diuretics — INCREASE urinary calcium (opposite effect):

  • Block NKCC2 in TAL → ↓ positive lumen potential → ↓ paracellular Ca²⁺ & Mg²⁺ reabsorption → ↑ urinary Ca²⁺ → ↑ stone risk.
  • Used for hypercalcaemia (with IV saline) — opposite of thiazide.

Therefore — thiazides are preferred (↓ urinary Ca²⁺ → ↓ stones); loop diuretics are contraindicated (↑ urinary Ca²⁺ → ↑ stones).

Clinical use:

  • Hydrochlorothiazide 25–50 mg/day OR chlorthalidone 25 mg/day OR indapamide 2.5 mg/day.
  • Indicated for recurrent calcium stones with hypercalciuria.
  • Also ↓ new stone formation in normocalciuric stone formers.
  • Monitor K⁺ (hypokalaemia → ↓ citrate excretion → ↑ stone risk; supplement K⁺ or use K-sparing diuretic).
  • Monitor Na⁺ (↓ Na intake → ↓ urinary Ca²⁺).

Clinical Pearl — Thiazides reduce urinary calcium (↑ reabsorption in DCT) → reduce calcium stone formation; loop diuretics increase urinary calcium → promote stones. Always check 24-hour urinary calcium in recurrent stone formers; thiazide indicated if hypercalciuria (>4 mg/kg/day in men, >3.5 in women). Combine with K⁺ supplementation or amiloride — hypokalaemia ↓ citrate excretion → ↑ stone risk (citrate is stone inhibitor). Also advise ↑ fluid intake (>2 L/day), ↓ dietary sodium, normal dietary calcium, ↓ animal protein, ↓ oxalate foods.
q2_0_3_15:
Phenoxybenzamine in Pheochromocytoma Surgery

Phenoxybenzamine — irreversible alpha-blocker (alpha1+alpha2); given pre-operatively (7-14 days) and intra-operatively during pheochromocytoma surgery. Rationale: (1) Blocks alpha1 receptors → vasodilation → controls BP, expands contracted blood volume; (2) Must give alpha-blocker BEFORE beta-blocker — if beta-blocker first, unopposed alpha → hypertensive crisis; (3) Irreversible blockade preferred over competitive (phentolamine) — cannot be overcome by massive catecholamine release during tumour manipulation; (4) Intra-operative: prevents hypertensive crisis during tumour handling; after tumour removal, sudden catecholamine drop → hypotension (prepare with fluids, vasopressors). Clinical Pearl: Start phenoxybenzamine 10 mg BD, titrate to 20-40 mg TID/QID, 7-14 days pre-op; add beta-blocker only after alpha-blockade established (day 3-4); goal: BP <140/90 seated with orthostatic drop but SBP >90; expand volume with IV saline.
q2_0_3_16:
Neostigmine Preferred Over Physostigmine in Myasthenia Gravis

Neostigmine preferred because: (1) Quaternary ammonium compound — does NOT cross BBB (charged molecule) → no CNS side effects; acts selectively at peripheral NMJ; (2) Physostigmine — tertiary amine; crosses BBB → CNS effects (confusion, seizures, bradycardia, excessive salivation, bronchoconstriction); (3) Neostigmine — more selective for NMJ; available oral (15-30 mg TID) and IM/IV; (4) Pyridostigmine (Mestinon) actually preferred over neostigmine for chronic MG (longer duration, less muscarinic side effects; 60 mg TID-QID). Clinical Pearl: Pyridostigmine is drug of choice for MG; neostigmine IV for myasthenic crisis; physostigmine is NOT used for MG (crosses BBB — CNS toxicity); physostigmine is used for anticholinergic poisoning (reverses CNS anticholinergic effects).
q2_0_3_17:
Why Folic Acid Added When Treating B12 Deficiency

B12 deficiency causes megaloblastic anaemia by impairing folate utilization ("folate trap" — B12 is cofactor for methionine synthase which regenerates THF from N5-methyl-THF). When B12 is given, folate utilization resumes → folate stores may be depleted → concurrent folic acid prevents folate deficiency. Some patients have combined B12 + folate deficiency. CRITICAL CAUTION: Never give folic acid ALONE in B12 deficiency — folic acid will correct anaemia (bypasses folate trap) but will NOT prevent/reverse neurological damage (subacute combined degeneration, peripheral neuropathy, cognitive decline). Only B12 prevents neurological complications. Always give B12 first (or simultaneously). Clinical Pearl: Always check B12 before treating megaloblastic anaemia with folic acid; folic acid alone corrects anaemia but allows irreversible neurological damage to progress. Treat with B12 IM hydroxocobalamin 1000 µg on alternate days × 2 weeks; add folic acid 5 mg/day only if folate deficiency confirmed.
q2_0_3_18:
Adrenaline as Physiological Antagonist to Histamine in Anaphylaxis

Adrenaline is a PHYSIOLOGICAL antagonist — acts at DIFFERENT receptors (adrenoceptors, NOT histamine receptors) to produce OPPOSITE effects: alpha1 → vasoconstriction (reverses histamine vasodilation → ↑ BP, ↓ oedema); beta1 → ↑ cardiac output (reverses hypotension); beta2 → bronchodilation (reverses bronchospasm) + ↓ mast cell degranulation (↑ cAMP). Why not antihistamines? — H1 antihistamines are SLOW (30-60 min), don't block H2 effects, don't reverse bronchospasm/hypotension effectively. Why not steroids? — take 4-6 h to act; useful for preventing biphasic reaction but NOT acute. Clinical Pearl: Adrenaline is the ONLY drug that reverses ALL manifestations of anaphylaxis simultaneously; IM 0.5 mg into anterolateral thigh ASAP; repeat every 5 min; antihistamines & steroids are ADJUNCTS, not substitutes.
q2_0_3_19:
Why Dantrolene Used in Malignant Hyperthermia

Malignant hyperthermia (MH) — RYR1 mutation; triggered by volatile anaesthetics & succinylcholine → uncontrolled Ca2+ release from sarcoplasmic reticulum → sustained muscle contraction → hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalaemia, acidosis. Dantrolene — blocks ryanodine receptor (RyR1) on sarcoplasmic reticulum → ↓ Ca2+ release → muscle relaxation. Only drug that directly blocks the pathophysiological mechanism; all other muscle relaxants act at NMJ or CNS — ineffective. Dose: 2.5 mg/kg IV rapid bolus; repeat every 5 min (max 10 mg/kg). Also used for NMS, severe serotonin syndrome. Clinical Pearl: Dantrolene is the ONLY specific antidote for MH; give IV 2.5 mg/kg immediately when MH suspected (↑ ETCO2, tachycardia, rigidity, hyperthermia after anaesthesia); also stop triggering agent, hyperventilate with 100% O2, cool patient, treat hyperkalaemia/acidosis. MH cart should be available in every OT.
q2_0_3_20:
Why Alpha Blocker Before Beta Blocker in Pheochromocytoma

If beta-blocker given FIRST without alpha-blockade: beta2 blockade removes vasodilatory effect of adrenaline on skeletal muscle blood vessels → alpha1-mediated vasoconstriction is UNOPPOSED → massive vasoconstriction → hypertensive crisis, stroke, MI, death. If alpha-blocker given FIRST: alpha1 blockade → vasodilation → controls hypertension; then beta-blocker can be added to control tachycardia. Sequence: alpha-blocker (phenoxybenzamine 7-14 days pre-op) → beta-blocker (propranolol day 3-4 after alpha-blockade). Clinical Pearl: ALWAYS alpha before beta in pheochromocytoma; beta-blocker alone → unopposed alpha → hypertensive crisis.
q2_0_3_21:
Why Novel Drug Delivery Systems Preferred Over Conventional

Advantages: (1) Controlled/sustained release → maintains therapeutic levels, avoids peaks/troughs, ↓ side effects, ↓ dosing frequency, ↑ adherence; (2) Targeted delivery → ↑ efficacy, ↓ systemic toxicity (liposomal doxorubicin — less cardiotoxicity; antibody-drug conjugates); (3) Improved bioavailability — protects from degradation; (4) Reduced dosing frequency — once daily to yearly (depot antipsychotics, contraceptive implants, zoledronic acid yearly); (5) Patient compliance — better adherence; (6) Reduced side effects — lower peak levels; (7) Protection of drug from acid, first-pass metabolism, enzymatic degradation; (8) Site-specific delivery — colon (IBD), brain (BBB bypass), intracellular (gene therapy, mRNA vaccines). Examples: transdermal patches, liposomes, nanoparticles, implants, PEGylated proteins, mRNA COVID vaccines. Clinical Pearl: NDDS transform pharmacotherapy — sustained release (adherence), targeted delivery (less toxicity), protection (bioavailability). mRNA COVID vaccines (lipid nanoparticles) demonstrated NDDS at population scale.
q2_0_3_22:
Why Selective Beta Blockers Preferred Over Non-Selective

Selective beta1-blockers preferred because: (1) Bronchospasm — non-selective block beta2 → bronchospasm in asthma/COPD; selective beta1 spare beta2 → safer; (2) Metabolic — non-selective mask hypoglycaemia symptoms & impair recovery; selective less effect; safer in diabetics; (3) Peripheral vascular — non-selective block beta2 vasodilation → cold extremities, Raynaud's, claudication; selective less effect; (4) Lipid profile — non-selective ↑ triglycerides, ↓ HDL more; selective less; carvedilol/nebivolol neutral; (5) Exercise tolerance — non-selective reduce more. Selectivity is dose-dependent — lost at high doses. Clinical Pearl: Beta1-selective (atenolol, metoprolol, bisoprolol, nebivolol) preferred in HTN with asthma/COPD, diabetes, PAD, elderly. Nebivolol — most selective + NO-mediated vasodilation. Carvedilol (alpha1+beta) — preferred in diabetes & HF.
q2_1_0_0:
Classification of Opioid Analgesics & Morphine

Classification

Natural: Morphine, Codeine, Papaverine, Noscapine. Semisynthetic: Heroin, Hydrocodone, Oxycodone, Hydromorphone, Buprenorphine. Synthetic: Pethidine, Fentanyl, Methadone, Tramadol, Tapentadol, Dextropropoxyphene. Antagonists: Naloxone, Naltrexone. Mixed: Pentazocine, Butorphanol, Nalbuphine.

Pharmacological Actions of Morphine

CNS: Analgesia (mu & kappa receptors); sedation; euphoria; respiratory depression (↓ CO2 response); miosis (no tolerance); nausea/vomiting (CTZ). GI: Constipation (↑ sphincter tone, ↓ peristalsis); biliary spasm. CV: Vasodilation (histamine); hypotension; bradycardia; ↑ ICP. GU: Urinary retention; ↑ ADH. Skin: Flushing, pruritus (histamine).

Therapeutic Uses

Moderate-severe pain (post-op, MI, cancer, trauma); acute pulmonary oedema (venodilation, anxiolysis); anaesthesia adjunct (fentanyl); cough (codeine); diarrhoea (loperamide); opioid substitution (methadone, buprenorphine).

Adverse Effects

Respiratory depression (most dangerous); constipation (universal, no tolerance); nausea; sedation; pruritus; urinary retention; tolerance (to analgesia, euphoria, respiratory depression — NOT constipation/miosis); dependence (physical withdrawal + psychological craving). Overdose triad: coma + pinpoint pupils + respiratory depression → naloxone 0.4-2 mg IV/IM.

Contraindications

Respiratory depression, severe asthma/COPD; raised ICP; intestinal obstruction; biliary colic (use pethidine); head injury; MAOI therapy (serotonin syndrome — pethidine, tramadol).

Clinical Pearl

WHO analgesic ladder: Step 1 (non-opioid ± adjuvant) → Step 2 (weak opioid ± non-opioid ± adjuvant) → Step 3 (strong opioid ± non-opioid ± adjuvant). Always co-prescribe laxative with opioids — constipation universal. Naloxone is antidote for overdose. Fentanyl — transdermal for chronic cancer pain; 100× more potent than morphine. Methadone — opioid substitution; long-acting. Buprenorphine — partial agonist; ceiling on respiratory depression. India — opioid access severely restricted (NDPS Act); morphine consumption among lowest globally despite high cancer burden.
q2_1_0_1:
Anti-tubercular Drugs

Classification

First-line: Isoniazid (H), Rifampicin (R), Pyrazinamide (Z), Ethambutol (E). Second-line injectable: Amikacin, Kanamycin, Capreomycin, Streptomycin. Fluoroquinolones: Levofloxacin, Moxifloxacin. Group D1: Ethionamide, Cycloserine, Linezolid, Clofazimine. Group D2: Bedaquiline, Delamanid.

First-Line Mechanism, Uses, Adverse Effects

Isoniazid (H): Inhibits mycolic acid synthesis (inhA); bactericidal; penetrates CSF. Uses: all TB, latent TB. ADR: peripheral neuropathy (give pyridoxine B6 10-25 mg/day); hepatotoxicity; drug-induced lupus. Acetylated by NAT2 (slow vs fast acetylators).

Rifampicin (R): Inhibits DNA-dependent RNA polymerase (rpoB); bactericidal; sterilising action (kills dormant bacilli). Uses: all TB, leprosy, meningococcal prophylaxis. ADR: hepatotoxicity; orange urine/sweat/tears; flu-like syndrome; potent CYP inducer (↓ warfarin, OCPs, steroids, PIs, ketoconazole, digoxin, ciclosporin).

Pyrazinamide (Z): Converted to pyrazinoic acid; disrupts membrane energy; bactericidal in acidic environment (macrophages); sterilising. Uses: intensive phase only (2 months). ADR: hepatotoxicity (most hepatotoxic); hyperuricaemia (gout); arthralgia.

Ethambutol (E): Inhibits arabinosyl transferase (embB); bacteriostatic; prevents resistance. Uses: intensive phase. ADR: optic neuritis (↓ visual acuity, red-green colour blindness; monitor vision monthly; reversible if caught early); hyperuricaemia.

NTEP Regimen

Drug-sensitive TB: HRZE × 2 months intensive + HRE × 4 months continuation = 6 months. MDR-TB: BPaL (Bedaquiline + Pretomanid + Linezolid) × 6 months.

Clinical Pearl

Always give pyridoxine (B6) with isoniazid (prevents neuropathy). Monitor LFT (H+R+Z hepatotoxicity). Monitor vision with ethambutol. Rifampicin — potent CYP inducer (check ALL medications). Orange urine normal. MDR-TB — BPaL regimen (6 months) revolutionary. India NTEP — free diagnosis & treatment; daily therapy; CBNAAT for diagnosis & rifampicin resistance.
q2_1_0_2:
Classification of Anti-epileptic Drugs

Classification by Mechanism

Na+ channel blockers (use-dependent): Phenytoin, Carbamazepine, Lamotrigine, Oxcarbazepine, Eslicarbazepine, Lacosamide, Rufinamide, Topiramate, Zonisamide, Valproate.

Calcium channel blockers: Ethosuximide (T-type, absence seizures); Gabapentin, Pregabalin (alpha-2-delta subunit); Verapamil (investigational for cluster headache).

GABA enhancers: Benzodiazepines (Diazepam, Lorazepam, Clonazepam, Clobazam); Barbiturates (Phenobarbital, Primidone); Vigabatrin (irreversible GABA-T inhibitor); Tiagabine (GAT-1 inhibitor).

Glutamate antagonists: Perampanel (AMPA antagonist); Felbamate (NMDA antagonist — restricted use, aplastic anaemia risk).

SV2A ligands: Levetiracetam, Brivaracetam.

Broad-spectrum: Valproate, Lamotrigine, Topiramate, Levetiracetam, Zonisamide, Felbamate, Rufinamide.

Narrow-spectrum (focal): Phenytoin, Carbamazepine, Oxcarbazepine, Gabapentin, Pregabalin, Lacosamide, Eslicarbazepine.

Phenytoin — Mechanism, Uses, Adverse Effects

Mechanism: Use-dependent blockade of voltage-gated Na+ channels → ↓ sustained high-frequency repetitive firing → ↓ seizure spread. Zero-order kinetics (saturation at therapeutic doses; small dose changes → large level changes).

Uses: Focal (partial) seizures; generalized tonic-clonic; status epilepticus (IV fosphenytoin); trigeminal neuralgia; cardiac arrhythmias (class Ib antiarrhythmic).

Adverse effects: Gum hypertrophy (↑ collagen synthesis — dental hygiene); hirsutism; coarse facial features; acne; osteomalacia (↑ vitamin D metabolism — CYP inducer); megaloblastic anaemia (↓ folate absorption); neuropathy; nystagmus, ataxia, confusion (dose-related CNS toxicity); zero-order kinetics → narrow therapeutic index (10-20 µg/mL); drug interactions (CYP inducer — ↓ OCPs, warfarin, corticosteroids, cyclosporine, doxycycline, theophylline; CYP inhibitors ↑ phenytoin — isoniazid, sulphonamides, chloramphenicol, cimetidine, fluconazole, amiodarone, diltiazem, fluoxetine, omeprazole). Contraindications: absence seizures (may worsen), pregnancy (teratogenic — fetal hydantoin syndrome: cleft lip/palate, cardiac defects, nail/digit hypoplasia, growth retardation).

Clinical Pearl

Phenytoin has zero-order (saturable) kinetics — small dose increases cause disproportionately large plasma level increases → toxicity. Always monitor levels (10-20 µg/mL). Gum hypertrophy — encourage dental hygiene. CYP inducer — many drug interactions. Teratogenic — avoid in pregnancy (use levetiracetam, lamotrigine). Newer AEDs preferred: levetiracetam (no interactions, no hepatic metabolism, broad-spectrum), lamotrigine (mood stabilizer too, broad-spectrum), topiramate (migraine prophylaxis, weight loss).
q2_1_0_3:
Hormonal Contraceptives

Types

Combined oral contraceptives (COCs): Estrogen (ethinylestradiol) + Progestin (levonorgestrel, norethisterone, drospirenone, desogestrel). Progestin-only pills (POPs/mini-pills): Levonorgestrel, norethisterone, desogestrel. Injectable: DMPA (Depo-Provera) — every 3 months. Implants: Etonogestrel (Implanon NXT — 3 years), Levonorgestrel (Jadelle — 5 years). Transdermal patch: Norelgestromin/ethinylestradiol (Xulane — weekly). Vaginal ring: Etonogestrel/ethinylestradiol (NuvaRing — monthly). Emergency contraception: Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg within 72h; ulipristal acetate 30 mg within 120h; copper IUD within 5 days. IUD: Levonorgestrel IUD (Mirena — 5-8 years); Copper IUD (ParaGard — 10 years).

Mechanism

COCs: (1) Suppress ovulation (↓ FSH, ↓ LH surge → no follicular development, no ovulation); (2) Thicken cervical mucus (↓ sperm penetration); (3) Thin endometrium (↓ implantation); (4) Alter tubal motility. POPs: mainly (2) and (3); ovulation suppression variable (more with desogestrel). DMPA: reliably suppresses ovulation.

Adverse Effects

Estrogen-related: Nausea, breast tenderness, fluid retention, headache, thrombosis (DVT, PE, stroke, MI — ↑ with smoking >35 yr); hypertension; melasma. Progestin-related: Weight gain, mood changes, acne (androgenic progestins — levonorgestrel; less with drospirenone — antiandrogenic); irregular bleeding/amenorrhoea. Serious: VTE (estrogen dose-dependent; 3-5× baseline risk; drospirenone slightly higher risk); stroke/MI (especially smokers >35); breast cancer (slight ↑ risk; disappears 10 years after stopping); cervical cancer (↑ with HPV); liver adenoma (rare).

Contraindications

Absolute: pregnancy; breastfeeding <6 weeks postpartum; smoking >15 cigarettes/day & age >35; hypertension (SBP >160 or DBP >100); VTE/PE (current or history); ischaemic heart disease; stroke; complicated valvular heart disease; migraine with aura (any age); breast cancer (current); liver disease (cirrhosis, hepatitis, tumour); diabetes with vascular complications; SLE with antiphospholipid; major surgery with prolonged immobilisation.

Non-contraceptive Benefits

↓ Ovarian cancer (50% ↓); ↓ endometrial cancer (50% ↓); ↓ colorectal cancer; regular cycles; ↓ dysmenorrhoea; ↓ menstrual blood loss; ↓ acne (with antiandrogenic progestins); ↓ premenstrual syndrome; treatment of endometriosis, PCOS, menorrhagia.

Clinical Pearl

WHO MEC (Medical Eligibility Criteria) guides contraceptive choice. Smokers >35 must NOT use estrogen-containing contraceptives — ↑ stroke/MI risk. POPs/DMPA/IUD safe in smokers, hypertension, migraine with aura (no estrogen). Drospirenone (antiandrogenic) — improves acne, hirsutism; but ↑ VTE risk. LNG-IUD (Mirena) — also treats menorrhagia, endometriosis, endometrial protection in estrogen therapy; 5-8 year duration. Emergency contraception — levonorgestrel 1.5 mg within 72h (most effective if taken ASAP); copper IUD within 5 days (most effective emergency contraception). India — family planning programme: free contraceptives (COCs, POPs, DMPA, condoms, IUDs); sterilization (tubectomy/vasectomy) — most common method; increasing use of IUDs & implants.
q2_1_0_4:
Drug Therapy of P. vivax Malaria

Treatment of P. vivax Malaria (NTEP/WHO Guidelines)

1. Chloroquine-sensitive P. vivax (most of India):

  • Chloroquine: 10 mg/kg on day 1 (600 mg base), then 10 mg/kg on day 2 (600 mg), then 5 mg/kg on day 3 (300 mg) — total 25 mg/kg over 3 days.
  • Primaquine: 0.25 mg/kg daily × 14 days (15 mg/day adult) — radical cure (kills hypnozoites in liver to prevent relapse). MUST check G6PD before giving primaquine.

2. Chloroquine-resistant P. vivax (northeast India, Indonesia, PNG):

  • ACT: Artemether-lumefantrine OR artesunate + sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine × 3 days.
  • Plus Primaquine 0.25-0.5 mg/kg daily × 14 days.

3. Severe P. vivax malaria:

  • IV Artesunate: 2.4 mg/kg IV at 0, 12, 24 h, then daily until oral tolerated → ACT × 3 days + primaquine × 14 days.

Chloroquine — Mechanism, Adverse Effects

Mechanism: Concentrates in parasite food vacuole; inhibits haem polymerase → toxic haem accumulates → parasite death. Also raises vacuolar pH → inhibits protein degradation.

Adverse effects: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea; headache; pruritus (especially dark-skinned — tolbutamide-responsive); skin rash; photosensitivity; bluish-black pigmentation; retinopathy (bull's eye maculopathy — with chronic high doses >5 years; hydroxychloroquine less toxic); ototoxicity; QT prolongation; hypoglycaemia; neuropsychiatric (rare — psychosis, seizures). Contraindications: psoriasis (may exacerbate); epilepsy; retinopathy; G6PD deficiency (haemolysis — relative).

Primaquine — Adverse Effects

Haemolysis in G6PD deficiency (screen before giving!); methaemoglobinaemia; abdominal cramps; nausea; headache; pruritus. Contraindicated in pregnancy (haemolysis in G6PD-deficient fetus).

Clinical Pearl

Always check G6PD before primaquine — haemolysis in G6PD deficiency can be fatal. Primaquine is essential for P. vivax radical cure — kills hypnozoites (dormant liver forms) that cause relapse; without primaquine, P. vivax relapses in 20-60% within months. 14-day course is standard (some use 7 days in SE Asia; 14 days in India). Tafenoquine — single-dose 8-aminoquinoline (300 mg) — radical cure in one dose; also requires G6PD screening; FDA-approved 2018. India — P. vivax accounts for ~50% of malaria cases; chloroquine still effective in most areas; chloroquine-resistant in northeast (use ACT). India NTEP/NVBDCP: free diagnosis (RDT/microscopy) & treatment; ASHA workers for community-level management.
q2_1_0_5:
Drugs for Diabetes Mellitus

Classification

Insulin: Rapid-acting (lispro, aspart, glulisine); Short-acting (regular); Intermediate (NPH/isophane); Long-acting (glargine, detemir, degludec); Premixed.

Oral hypoglycemic agents (OHAs):

  • Biguanides: Metformin — ↓ hepatic gluconeogenesis; ↑ insulin sensitivity; first-line for T2DM.
  • Sulfonylureas: Glimepiride, Gliclazide, Glipizide, Glibenclamide — ↑ insulin secretion (close KATP channel on beta cell).
  • DPP-4 inhibitors (gliptins): Sitagliptin, Vildagliptin, Linagliptin, Saxagliptin, Alogliptin — ↑ GLP-1 (incretin effect).
  • SGLT2 inhibitors (gliflozins): Dapagliflozin, Empagliflozin, Canagliflozin, Ertugliflozin — ↓ renal glucose reabsorption → glucosuria.
  • GLP-1 receptor agonists: Exenatide, Liraglutide, Dulaglutide, Semaglutide, Tirzepatide (GIP/GLP-1 dual) — ↑ insulin, ↓ glucagon, ↓ gastric emptying, ↓ appetite.
  • Thiazolidinediones (glitazones): Pioglitazone, Rosiglitizone — ↑ insulin sensitivity (PPAR-gamma).
  • Alpha-glucosidase inhibitors: Acarbose, Miglitol, Voglibose — ↓ carbohydrate digestion/absorption.
  • Meglitinides (glinides): Repaglinide, Nateglinide — ↑ insulin secretion (short-acting).
  • Bile acid sequestrants: Colesevelam — ↓ bile acid reabsorption; modest glucose lowering.
  • Dopamine D2 agonist: Bromocriptine QR — ↓ hepatic gluconeogenesis.

Mechanism of Metformin

Activates AMPK (AMP-activated protein kinase) → ↓ hepatic gluconeogenesis (main effect); ↑ insulin sensitivity in muscle (↑ glucose uptake); ↓ intestinal glucose absorption; ↓ fatty acid oxidation; does NOT stimulate insulin secretion → no hypoglycaemia; no weight gain (may cause weight loss).

Adverse Effects of Metformin

GI (nausea, diarrhoea, abdominal discomfort — dose-related, start low, take with food, extended-release formulation); vitamin B12 deficiency (long-term — ↓ absorption); lactic acidosis (rare but fatal — accumulate in renal failure; contraindicated if eGFR <30; hold before contrast, surgery, severe illness); metallic taste.

Therapeutic Uses of Metformin

T2DM first-line (all patients unless contraindicated); pre-diabetes (IFG/IGT — high-risk); PCOS (insulin resistance); non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD); weight management (adjunct).

Contraindications of Metformin

eGFR <30 mL/min; acute kidney injury; severe hepatic disease; acute heart failure; hypoxia/shock/sepsis; before IV contrast (hold 48h); alcoholism; pregnancy (historically — now used in GDM if needed; insulin preferred).

Clinical Pearl

Metformin is first-line for all T2DM (unless contraindicated) — reduces CV events, mortality (UKPDS trial); no hypoglycaemia; weight neutral/loss; cheap. SGLT2 inhibitors — revolutionary — reduce HF hospitalisation, CV mortality (EMPA-REG, CANVAS), slow CKD progression (DAPA-CKD); now first-line add-on for T2DM with HF/CKD. GLP-1 agonists — reduce CV events, weight loss (5-15%); semaglutide 2.4 mg weekly approved for obesity (Wegovy). Tirzepatide (dual GIP/GLP-1) — most effective (HbA1c ↓2-3%, weight loss 15-20%). Insulin — T1DM (essential); T2DM when OHAs fail or severe hyperglycaemia. India — diabetes capital (~77 million); metformin widely available & cheap; SGLT2 & GLP-1 increasingly used but cost barrier; lifestyle modification essential.
q2_1_0_6:
Oral Hypoglycemic Agents — Sulfonylureas

Classification

First-generation (rarely used): Tolbutamide, Chlorpropamide, Glibenclamide (glyburide). Second-generation: Glipizide, Gliclazide, Glimepiride (most commonly used).

Mechanism of Action

Bind to SUR1 subunit of KATP channel on pancreatic beta-cell membrane → close KATP channel → membrane depolarisation → opens voltage-gated Ca2+ channel → Ca2+ influx → insulin granule exocytosis → ↑ insulin secretion. Requires functioning beta cells (ineffective in T1DM).

Pharmacokinetics

Oral; well absorbed; hepatic metabolism; renal excretion (glibenclamide has active metabolites — caution in CKD); glimepiride — longest duration (24h, once daily); gliclazide — modified release once daily.

Therapeutic Uses

T2DM — second-line after metformin (if metformin contraindicated or inadequate); especially if insulin deficiency predominant (lean T2DM); cheap; rapid onset.

Adverse Effects

Hypoglycaemia — most common & most important; especially in elderly, renal impairment, irregular meals, alcohol; glibenclamide highest risk (avoid in elderly & CKD); glimepiride lower risk. Weight gain — 1-2 kg (insulinotropic effect). Hyponatraemia (SIADH — especially chlorpropamide). Cardiovascular safety — controversial (older concerns about KATP channel blockade in heart; UGDP trial — tolbutamide ↑ CV mortality; modern evidence — glimepiride neutral). Photosensitivity, rash. Hepatotoxicity (rare). Disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol (chlorpropamide).

Contraindications

T1DM; diabetic ketoacidosis; pregnancy (crosses placenta — neonatal hypoglycaemia; use insulin); severe renal/hepatic impairment; sulfa allergy (cross-reactivity — low but caution); elderly (hypoglycaemia risk — avoid glibenclamide).

Drug Interactions

↑ Effect (hypoglycaemia): NSAIDs, sulfonamides, warfarin, fluconazole, miconazole, clarithromycin, cimetidine, alcohol, MAOIs, beta-blockers (also mask hypoglycaemia symptoms). ↓ Effect (hyperglycaemia): corticosteroids, thiazides, phenytoin, sympathomimetics, OCPs, niacin.

Clinical Pearl

Hypoglycaemia is the most important adverse effect — especially in elderly, CKD, irregular meals; always educate patient about symptoms & carry glucose. Glibenclamide (glyburide) has highest hypoglycaemia risk — avoid in elderly & CKD; use glimepiride (lower risk, once daily) or gliclazide MR instead. Second-line after metformin — if insulin deficiency predominant; cheap; rapid onset. Masking of hypoglycaemia by beta-blockers — tremor, palpitations masked (except sweating); educate diabetic patients. India — sulfonylureas widely used & cheap; glimepiride most common; often combined with metformin (FDC). Newer drugs (SGLT2, GLP-1) preferred for patients with CV/CKD/HF.

Classification of Antiretroviral Drugs

Classification by Mechanism

1. NRTIs (Nucleoside/Nucleotide Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitors): Tenofovir (TDF), Tenofovir alafenamide (TAF), Lamivudine (3TC), Emtricitabine (FTC), Abacavir (ABC), Zidovudine (AZT), Stavudine (d4T), Didanosine (ddI) — competitive inhibitors of RT; chain terminators (lack 3'-OH).

2. NNRTIs (Non-Nucleoside RT Inhibitors): Efavirenz (EFV), Nevirapine (NVP), Rilpivirine (RPV), Doravirine (DOR), Etravirine (ETR) — non-competitive binding to RT → conformational change → inactivation.

3. PIs (Protease Inhibitors): Atazanavir (ATV), Darunavir (DRV), Lopinavir/ritonavir (LPV/r), Saquinavir, Fosamprenavir — inhibit HIV protease → immature, non-infectious virions.

4. INSTIs (Integrase Strand Transfer Inhibitors): Dolutegravir (DTG), Bictegravir (BIC), Raltegravir (RAL), Elvitegravir (EVG) — inhibit HIV integrase → prevent viral DNA integration into host genome. Preferred first-line (DTG, BIC).

5. Entry/Attachment Inhibitors: Maraviroc (CCR5 antagonist — requires tropism testing); Enfuvirtide (fusion inhibitor — gp41; SC injection); Ibalizumab (CD4 monoclonal; post-attachment); Fostemsavir (gp120 attachment inhibitor).

6. Capsid inhibitor: Lenacapavir (twice-yearly SC injection — revolutionary long-acting).

Mechanism of Three Drugs

Tenofovir (NRTI): Phosphorylated to tenofovir diphosphate → competes with dATP for RT → incorporated into growing DNA chain → chain termination (no 3'-OH for next nucleotide).

Dolutegravir (INSTI): Binds to active site of HIV integrase → blocks strand transfer (ST) reaction → prevents integration of viral DNA into host chromosome → no proviral DNA formation → no viral replication.

Darunavir (PI): Mimics natural substrate of HIV protease → binds to active site (aspartyl protease) → prevents cleavage of gag-pol polyprotein → produces immature, non-infectious virions. Boosted with ritonavir (CYP3A4 inhibitor) → ↑ darunavir levels.

First-Line ART (WHO 2021)

TLD: Tenofovir (TDF) + Lamivudine (3TC) + Dolutegravir (DTG) — single tablet, once daily. Preferred globally. India's NACP uses TLD as first-line.

Clinical Pearl

INSTIs (especially DTG) are now preferred first-line — high barrier to resistance, well-tolerated, once daily, fewer interactions than PIs/EFV. TLD regimen (TDF+3TC+DTG) is WHO & India NACP first-line. Long-acting injectable ART — cabotegravir + rilpivirine monthly/bimonthly IM (FDA-approved 2021); lenacapavir (twice-yearly SC — revolutionary for adherence). PrEP — TDF/FTC daily or on-demand (2-1-1); long-acting cabotegravir every 2 months (approved 2021). India — NACP provides free ART; TLD first-line; viral load monitoring; ~2.4 million people on ART.
