Adverse Effects & Contraindications of Corticosteroids

Adverse Effects

CNS: Psychiatric disturbance (euphoria, insomnia, anxiety, depression, psychosis, mania); pseudotumour cerebri (benign intracranial hypertension).

Musculoskeletal: Osteoporosis (↓ osteoblast, ↑ osteoclast; vertebral fractures; give calcium + vitamin D + bisphosphonate); myopathy (proximal muscle weakness; especially fluoro steroids); avascular necrosis (femoral head).

GI: Peptic ulcer (↑ acid, ↓ mucus; especially with NSAIDs); pancreatitis; GI bleeding/perforation.

Endocrine: Cushingoid features (moon face, buffalo hump, central obesity, striae, acne, hirsutism); hyperglycaemia/diabetes (↑ gluconeogenesis, ↓ insulin sensitivity); HPA suppression (↓ ACTH → adrenal atrophy; abrupt withdrawal → adrenal crisis); menstrual irregularities; growth retardation (children).

Immune: Immunosuppression (↑ infections — bacterial, viral, fungal, reactivation of TB, herpes, hepatitis B); ↓ wound healing; mask signs of infection.

CV: Hypertension (Na & water retention); dyslipidemia; atherosclerosis.

Skin: Thinning, atrophy, striae, telangiectasia, easy bruising, poor wound healing, acne, hirsutism, hyperpigmentation.

Ocular: Cataract (posterior subcapsular); glaucoma (↑ IOP); increased infection risk.

Metabolic: Hyperglycaemia; hypokalaemia; hypernatraemia; fluid retention; weight gain; negative nitrogen/calcium balance.

Contraindications

Active infection (TB, fungal, bacterial, viral — unless life-saving with concurrent antimicrobial); peptic ulcer; osteoporosis; diabetes mellitus; hypertension; heart failure; renal failure; psychiatric illness; glaucoma/cataract; pregnancy (relative — not absolutely contraindicated but use cautiously); live vaccines (immunosuppression).

Clinical Pearl

Always use lowest effective dose for shortest duration. Never stop abruptly — taper gradually (HPA suppression → adrenal crisis on withdrawal). Give in morning (mimics physiological cortisol rhythm; ↓ HPA suppression). Alternate-day dosing — reduces HPA suppression & growth retardation in children. Co-prescribe: calcium + vitamin D (osteoporosis); bisphosphonate (long-term >3 months); PPI (if concurrent NSAID); potassium supplement (if hypokalaemia). Double the dose during stress (illness, surgery — "stress dose steroids"). Always consider steroid-sparing agents (azathioprine, methotrexate, mycophenolate, biologics) for chronic conditions. Inhaler/oral rinse after ICS — prevents oral candidiasis.
q2_1_1_2:
Treatment of Diarrhoea

Principles

(1) Rehydration (most important — saves lives); (2) Nutritional support; (3) Symptomatic treatment; (4) Specific antimicrobial (selected cases); (5) Zinc supplementation (children).

1. Rehydration

ORS (Oral Rehydration Solution) — WHO formula: Na 75, K 20, Cl 65, citrate 10, glucose 75 mmol/L; osmolarity 245 mOsm/L (hypo-osmolar — better absorption, less stool output). For mild-moderate dehydration. IV fluids (Ringer's lactate) — for severe dehydration, shock, vomiting.

2. Zinc Supplementation

20 mg/day × 10-14 days (children <5 yr); reduces duration, severity, & future episodes; WHO recommended.

3. Symptomatic Treatment

Antimotility: Loperamide 4 mg loading then 2 mg after each loose stool (max 16 mg/day); avoid in children <2 yr, infectious/bloody diarrhoea, C. difficile. Bismuth subsalicylate: antisecretory + antimicrobial; traveller's diarrhoea.

4. Specific Antimicrobials (Selected Cases)

  • Acute watery diarrhoea (viral): no antibiotics; self-limited.
  • Invasive (bloody/mucoid): Shigella — ciprofloxacin/azithromycin; Campylobacter — azithromycin; Salmonella (non-typhoidal) — only if severe/septicaemia; EHEC O157:H7 — avoid antibiotics (↑ HUS risk).
  • Cholera: doxycycline 300 mg single dose; azithromycin.
  • Traveller's diarrhoea: ciprofloxacin/azithromycin/rifaximin × 1-3 days.
  • C. difficile: oral vancomycin/fidaxomicin; stop offending antibiotic.
  • Giardia: metronidazole/tinidazole.
  • Amoebic dysentery: metronidazole/tinidazole + luminal amoebicide (paromomycin/diloxanide).

5. Probiotics

Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG, Saccharomyces boulardii — reduce duration of acute infectious diarrhoea by ~1 day; especially antibiotic-associated.

6. Diet

Continue feeding (do not starve); BRAT diet (banana, rice, apple sauce, toast) — mild; avoid lactose (transient lactase deficiency), high-sugar/fat foods; breastfeed (continue in infants).

Clinical Pearl

ORS is the single most important intervention — saves millions of lives globally. Avoid antimotility agents in children <2 yr and in bloody/infectious diarrhoea (toxic megacolon risk). Always give zinc to children — reduces duration & future episodes. India — diarrhoea is leading cause of child mortality; ORS + zinc widely available through NTEP/Ayushman Bharat; irrational antibiotic use common; antimicrobial stewardship needed. Rota virus vaccine in UIP (2016) — reduces rotavirus diarrhoea mortality by ~50%.

Complications of General & Spinal Anaesthesia

General Anaesthesia Complications

Immediate (intra-operative): Hypotension; hypertension; arrhythmias; bronchospasm; laryngospasm; hypoxia; hypercapnia; awareness under anaesthesia; malignant hyperthermia (RyR1 mutation; dantrolene); anaphylaxis (neuromuscular blockers, latex, antibiotics); aspiration pneumonitis (Mendelson syndrome); airway trauma (teeth, lips, vocal cords); endobronchial intubation; oesophageal intubation; equipment failure.

Post-operative: PONV (post-operative nausea & vomiting — most common; 5-HT3 antagonist + dexamethasone + droperidol); shivering (meperidine/clonidine); emergence delirium (especially children; propofol, sevoflurane); delayed emergence (residual anaesthesia, hypothermia, hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, stroke); sore throat (intubation); hoarseness; corneal abrasion; pressure injuries; nerve injuries (positioning); urinary retention; DVT/PE (prophylaxis); atelectasis; pneumonia; cognitive dysfunction (POCD — elderly; delirium).

Spinal Anaesthesia Complications

Common/Immediate: Hypotension (sympathetic block — most common; treat with fluids + vasopressors — ephedrine, phenylephrine); bradycardia (high block → vagal unopposed; atropine); nausea/vomising (hypotension or vagal); urinary retention (S2-S4 block — catheterize).

Less common: High/total spinal block (respiratory arrest, unconsciousness — ventilate, vasopressors); subdural block (patchy, slow onset); intravascular injection (systemic toxicity — CNS & CV); post-dural puncture headache (PDPH — CSF leak; onset 24-48h; worse upright, better lying; treatment — hydration, caffeine, NSAIDs, epidural blood patch); backache; transient neurological symptoms (TNS — pain in buttocks/thighs; resolves in days; more with lidocaine).

Rare/Serious: Spinal epidural/subdural haematoma (bleeding disorder/anticoagulants; surgical emergency); abscess (infection; surgical drainage); meningitis/arachnoiditis (infection/chemical); anterior spinal artery syndrome (hypotension + atherosclerosis); cauda equina syndrome (neurological injury); adhesive arachnoiditis (chronic); permanent neurological damage.

Contraindications to spinal: Patient refusal; coagulopathy (INR >1.4, platelets <75,000, on anticoagulants); infection at injection site; sepsis; raised ICP; severe aortic/mitral stenosis; severe hypovolaemia; fixed cardiac output states.

Clinical Pearl

Hypotension is the most common complication of spinal anaesthesia — sympathetic blockade (T4-T6 for abdominal surgery); treat with IV fluids + vasopressors (ephedrine 5-10 mg IV — alpha+beta; phenylephrine 50-100 µg IV — pure alpha1). PDPH — characteristic postural headache (worse sitting/standing, better lying); treat conservatively first (hydration, caffeine, NSAIDs); if persistent >24-48h → epidural blood patch (autologous blood injected into epidural space — seals CSF leak; 70-90% success). Avoid spinal in coagulopathy/anticoagulation — risk of epidural haematoma (surgical emergency → paralysis if not decompressed within 8h). Malignant hyperthermia — stop triggering agent; dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg IV; hyperventilate 100% O2; cool; treat hyperkalaemia.
q2_1_1_4:
ACT (Artemisinin-based Combination Therapy) in Malaria

Definition

ACT — combination of an artemisinin derivative (rapid acting, reduces parasite biomass quickly) + a longer-acting partner drug (eliminates remaining parasites; prevents resistance).

Rationale

  1. Synergy — artemisinin rapidly kills 10^4-10^5 parasites per cycle (within 48h); partner drug eliminates remaining parasites.
  2. Prevent resistance — two drugs with different mechanisms → ↓ probability of simultaneous resistance mutation.
  3. Shorter course — 3 days (vs 7 days monotherapy).
  4. ↓ Gametocyte carriage — artemisinin reduces gametocytes → ↓ transmission.
  5. WHO recommends ACT as first-line for uncomplicated falciparum malaria globally.

WHO-Approved ACTs

  • Artemether + lumefantrine (Coartem) — most widely used; 6 doses over 3 days.
  • Artesunate + amodiaquine.
  • Artesunate + mefloquine.
  • Artesunate + sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine.
  • Dihydroartemisinin + piperaquine.

Mechanism of Artemisinin

Artemisinin contains endoperoxide bridge → cleaved by haem iron (from digested haemoglobin) → generates free radicals → alkylates parasite proteins & lipids → parasite death. Selective for parasite (which digests haemoglobin) vs host cells.

Clinical Pearl

ACT is WHO first-line for uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria — 3-day course; reduces treatment failure, gametocyte carriage, transmission. Artemether-lumefantrine (Coartem) — most widely used; take with fatty food (↑ absorption). For severe malaria — IV artesunate (not ACT) → 2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12, 24h; switch to ACT when oral tolerated. India NVBDCP: ACT ( artesunate + sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine) for P. falciparum; chloroquine for P. vivax (chloroquine-sensitive in most of India). Artemisinin resistance — emerging in Greater Mekong subregion (Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar, Vietnam, Thailand); delayed parasite clearance; threatens global malaria control; K13 gene mutations; ACTs still effective in Africa & India.
q2_1_1_5:
Chloramphenicol

Mechanism

Binds to 50S ribosomal subunit (overlapping peptidyl transferase centre) → inhibits peptidyl transferase → blocks peptide bond formation → inhibits protein synthesis (bacteriostatic). Same site as macrolides & clindamycin (competitive antagonism — do not combine).

Spectrum

Broad-spectrum — Gram-positive (S. pneumoniae, S. pyogenes, S. aureus, enterococci); Gram-negative (H. influenzae, N. meningitidis, N. gonorrhoeae, Salmonella typhi, Shigella, E. coli, Klebsiella, Proteus, Bacteroides, Vibrio, Yersinia pestis); anaerobes; rickettsiae; spirochaetes; Chlamydia. Inactive against: Pseudomonas, Proteus (some), mycobacteria, fungi, protozoa (except Rickettsia).

Therapeutic Uses (Limited Due to Toxicity)

  • Topical — eye drops/ointment (0.5%) for bacterial conjunctivitis; ear drops for otitis externa. Still commonly used topically in India.
  • Systemic (reserved for serious infections when alternatives unavailable): Typhoid fever (MDR — but ceftriaxone/azithromycin preferred); rickettsial infections (scrub typhus — doxycycline preferred); meningitis (H. influenzae — third-generation cephalosporin preferred); plague; anaerobic infections; VRE (vancomycin-resistant enterococcus).
  • Historical — drug of choice for typhoid fever before resistance developed.

Adverse Effects

Bone marrow suppression: (1) Dose-related reversible — ↓ RBC, WBC, platelets (common; dose-related; monitor CBC); (2) Aplastic anaemia (idiosyncratic, irreversible, fatal; 1 in 25,000-40,000; not dose-related; may occur weeks-months after stopping; mechanism — toxic metabolite nitroso-chloramphenicol damages stem cells).

Grey baby syndrome — neonates (especially premature); inability to conjugate (glucuronidation) & excrete chloramphenicol → accumulation → grey skin, hypothermia, cyanosis, hypotonia, cardiovascular collapse, death; contraindicated in neonates.

Other — optic neuritis (long-term); allergic reactions; GI disturbance; disulfiram-like reaction; inhibition of CYP450 (↑ warfarin, phenytoin, tolbutamide, phenobarbital).

Clinical Pearl

Aplastic anaemia is the most feared complication — irreversible, often fatal; idiosyncratic (not dose-related); can occur weeks after stopping; restricted use globally — replaced by safer alternatives (cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones). Grey baby syndrome — neonates lack glucuronyl transferase → drug accumulates → cardiovascular collapse; never give to neonates. India — topical chloramphenicol still widely used (eye drops for conjunctivitis); systemic use rare (reserved for MDR typhoid, rickettsial if doxycycline unavailable). Do NOT combine with macrolides or clindamycin — competitive antagonism at 50S ribosome.
q2_1_1_6:
Rifampicin

Mechanism

Inhibits DNA-dependent RNA polymerase (beta-subunit — rpoB gene) → blocks RNA synthesis → bacterial death. Bactericidal. Sterilising action — kills slow-growing & dormant bacilli (unlike isoniazid which kills rapidly multiplying bacilli). Essential for short-course TB therapy (6 months vs 18 months without R).

Spectrum

Mycobacterium tuberculosis (most potent anti-TB drug); M. leprae; Gram-positive (S. aureus including MRSA, S. pneumoniae, enterococci); Gram-negative (N. meningitidis, H. influenzae); Chlamydia; Rickettsia.

Pharmacokinetics

Oral (well absorbed); food ↓ absorption (take on empty stomach); widely distributed (CSF, caseous tissue, macrophages, bone); hepatic metabolism (deacetylation → active metabolite); enterohepatic circulation; excreted in bile, urine, saliva, sweat, tears (orange-red discolouration — normal); half-life 3-5h (shortens with chronic use — autoinduction of CYP).

Therapeutic Uses

  • Tuberculosis — first-line; all categories; essential for 6-month short-course.
  • Leprosy — MB-MDT (monthly rifampicin + daily dapsone + clofazimine).
  • Meningococcal prophylaxis — 600 mg BD × 2 days (close contacts of meningococcal meningitis).
  • Haemophilus influenzae type b prophylaxis — 600 mg daily × 4 days (unvaccinated household contacts <4 yr).
  • Staphylococcal infections — adjunct in prosthetic valve endocarditis, osteomyelitis (with vancomycin); MRSA decolonization.
  • Brucellosis — doxycycline + rifampicin × 6 weeks (alternative to streptomycin).
  • Q fever (Coxiella) — doxycycline + rifampicin/hydroxychloroquine (chronic).

Adverse Effects

  • Hepatotoxicity — dose-related; ↑ with isoniazid + pyrazinamide; monitor LFT (baseline & monthly); stop if ALT >3× ULN with symptoms.
  • Orange-red discolouration — urine, sweat, tears, sputum, stool; stains contact lenses; harmless but alarming — reassure patient.
  • Flu-like syndrome — intermittent dosing (fever, chills, myalgia, rash; switch to daily or reduce dose).
  • Thrombocytopenia — intermittent dosing (immune-mediated).
  • Interstitial nephritis — rare.
  • Gastrointestinal — nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea.
  • Potent CYP3A4 inducer — ↓ levels of MANY drugs: warfarin (↑ INR monitoring), OCPs (use barrier), corticosteroids, cyclosporine, tacrolimus, protease inhibitors (avoid with most PIs — check compatibility), ketoconazole/itraconazole, digoxin, theophylline, phenytoin, propafenone, verapamil, diltiazem, valproate, levothyroxine, haloperidol, methadone, dabigatran, DOACs. Always check ALL medications when starting rifampicin.

Contraindications

Jaundice; severe hepatic dysfunction; hypersensitivity; pregnancy (relative — animal teratogen but used if essential; leprosy — monthly dose considered safe); concurrent use with most protease inhibitors (PIs).

Clinical Pearl

Rifampicin is the most important anti-TB drug — sterilising action; essential for 6-month therapy. Always check drug interactions — potent CYP3A4 inducer; ↓ levels of warfarin, OCPs, steroids, PIs, ciclosporin, many others. Orange urine is normal — reassure patient; warn about contact lenses. Monitor LFT — hepatotoxicity (especially with H+Z). Give on empty stomach (food ↓ absorption). India NTEP: rifampicin 450 mg (<50 kg) or 600 mg (≥50 kg) daily in intensive & continuation phases; fixed-dose combination (HRZE) for adherence.
q2_1_1_7:
Antiseptics and Disinfectants

Definitions

Antiseptic — chemical applied to LIVING tissue (skin, mucous membranes, wounds) to inhibit/kill microorganisms. Disinfectant — chemical applied to INANIMATE objects (surfaces, instruments) to kill microorganisms (not necessarily spores). Sterilant — destroys ALL microbial life including spores.

Classification by Mechanism

  1. Alcohols — Ethanol (70%), Isopropanol (70%); denature proteins, dissolve lipids; rapid (30 sec); no sporicidal; flammable; skin antisepsis, hand hygiene, small instruments.
  2. Halogens:
    • Chlorine compounds — Sodium hypochlorite (0.5-1% for surfaces; 5,000 ppm for blood spills); chloramine; chlorine dioxide; broad-spectrum; inactivated by organic matter; corrosive; water disinfection, surfaces, blood spills.
    • Iodophores — Povidone-iodine (Betadine; 7.5-10%); slow release of iodine; broad-spectrum; skin antisepsis (pre-op scrub, wound care); mucosal (oral, vaginal); inactivated by blood/pus; avoid in neonates (thyroid), iodine allergy.
  3. Phenolics — Phenol, cresol, Lysol, hexachlorophene, chlorhexidine; disrupt cell wall; Chlorhexidine (2% & 4%) — broad-spectrum, persistent (6h), low toxicity; skin antisepsis, oral rinse, hand wash; avoid in neonates (brain toxicity — kernicterus), middle ear (ototoxic).
  4. Quaternary ammonium compounds (QACs) — Benzalkonium chloride, cetrimide; cationic surfactants; disrupt membrane; Gram-positive > Gram-negative; inactivated by soap, anions; skin, instruments, surfaces.
  5. Aldehydes:
    • Glutaraldehyde 2% (Cidex) — high-level disinfectant; sporicidal (10h); sterilises endoscopes, instruments; irritant vapour; 20-45 min HLD.
    • Formaldehyde — 37% formalin (10% = 4% formaldehyde); gas/fumigation; histopathology fixation; carcinogen; irritant.
    • Ortho-phthalaldehyde (OPA) 0.55% — replacement for glutaraldehyde; faster (12 min HLD); less irritant; stains skin/proteins.
  6. Oxidising agents — Hydrogen peroxide (3-6%); peracetic acid (0.2%); ozone; release free radicals; broad-spectrum; sporicidal; environmentally friendly (decompose to water/oxygen).
  7. Heavy metals — Silver nitrate (1% eye drops — historical for neonatal conjunctivitis prophylaxis; Crede prophylaxis); silver sulfadiazine (burns); mercurials (obsolete — toxicity); copper (water purification).
  8. Dyes — Gentian violet (antifungal); acriflavine/proflavine (wounds); eosin; methylene blue.
  9. Gases — Ethylene oxide (EtO; sterilises heat-sensitive items; carcinogen; requires aeration); formaldehyde gas; ozone; hydrogen peroxide vapour/plasma (Sterrad).

Spaulding Classification

Critical (enter sterile tissue) → sterilisation. Semi-critical (contact mucosa) → high-level disinfection. Non-critical (contact intact skin) → intermediate/low-level disinfection.

Clinical Pearl

Alcohol-based handrub (60-80% ethanol/isopropanol) — WHO gold standard for hand hygiene; 20-30 sec; most effective intervention against HAI. Chlorhexidine-alcohol (2% CHG + 70% alcohol) — preferred pre-operative skin prep (persistent activity, broad-spectrum). Povidone-iodine — alternative (especially iodine allergy to CHG; mucosal surfaces). Glutaraldehyde 2% (Cidex) — HLD for endoscopes (20-45 min); discard after 14 days; check MRC strips. Sodium hypochlorite — blood spills (5,000 ppm = 1:10 dilution of 5.25% bleach); surfaces. Ethylene oxide — sterilises heat-sensitive items (catheters, endoscopes); carcinogen; requires aeration 8-12h. India — irrational use of antiseptics/disinfectants common; always follow manufacturer's instructions for contact time, dilution, reuse life; monitor with chemical & biological indicators.
q2_1_1_8:
Albendazole

Mechanism

Binds to beta-tubulin of parasite (selective — much higher affinity than mammalian tubulin) → inhibits microtubule polymerisation → disrupts microtubule-dependent glucose uptake → ↓ glycogen stores → ↓ ATP production → parasite death (energy starvation). Also inhibits fumarate reductase (parasite-specific enzyme in anaerobic metabolism).

Spectrum

Nematodes (roundworms): Ascaris lumbricoides, hookworm (Necator, Ancylostoma), Enterobius (pinworm), Trichuris (whipworm), Strongyloides (less effective — ivermectin preferred), Toxocara (visceral larva migrans), Cutaneous larva migrans, Trichinella.

Cestodes (tapeworms): Taenia solium (neurocysticercosis — drug of choice), Taenia saginata, Hymenolepis nana, Echinococcus (hydatid disease — prolonged course).

Trematodes: Less effective; praziquantel preferred for most flukes.

Others: Giardia lamblia (alternative to metronidazole); Microsporidium; Capillaria.

Pharmacokinetics

Oral; poor absorption (<5%) — take with fatty food (↑ absorption 5×); hepatic metabolism to active sulfoxide metabolite; widely distributed (CSF, hydatid cysts); half-life 8-12h; excreted in bile & urine.

Therapeutic Uses & Doses

  • Intestinal nematodes (Ascaris, hookworm, Enterobius, Trichuris): 400 mg single dose (adults & children >2 yr); repeat after 2-3 weeks for Enterobius.
  • Neurocysticercosis: 15 mg/kg/day (max 1200 mg/day) in 2 divided doses × 7-14 days (with corticosteroids & anticonvulsants).
  • Hydatid disease (Echinococcus): 10-15 mg/kg/day × 1-6 months (pre & post-surgical; or PAIR procedure).
  • Cutaneous larva migrans: 400 mg daily × 3-7 days.
  • Toxocariasis (visceral larva migrans): 400 mg BD × 5 days.
  • Giardiasis: 400 mg daily × 5 days (alternative to metronidazole).
  • Capillariasis: 400 mg daily × 10 days.
  • Mass drug administration (MDA): School-based deworming — 400 mg single dose every 6-12 months for STH control in endemic areas.

Adverse Effects

Generally well-tolerated at single-dose (intestinal helminths): GI (nausea, abdominal pain, diarrhoea); headache; dizziness; transient ↑ liver enzymes. High doses/prolonged (cysticercosis, hydatid): hepatotoxicity; alopecia; bone marrow suppression (↓ WBC, platelets — monitor CBC); rash; fever; neurological deterioration in neurocysticercosis (inflammatory reaction to dying parasites — always give corticosteroids before & during albendazole).

Contraindications

Pregnancy (teratogenic in animals — avoid especially 1st trimester); ocular cysticercosis (blindness from inflammatory reaction — surgical removal); spinal cord cysticercosis (risk of paralysis — surgical). Caution: hepatic impairment; renal impairment; monitor LFT & CBC during prolonged therapy.

Clinical Pearl

Albendazole is the drug of choice for neurocysticercosis — 15 mg/kg/day × 7-14 days; always give corticosteroids (dexamethasone) before & during therapy to prevent inflammatory reaction to dying cysticerci (oedema → raised ICP → seizures, encephalitis). Avoid in ocular/spinal cysticercosis — inflammation can cause irreversible blindness/paralysis; surgical removal preferred. Take with fatty food — ↑ absorption 5× (poorly absorbed otherwise). Single-dose 400 mg for intestinal helminths — safe, effective, cheap; ideal for mass drug administration (school deworming). India — school-based deworming programme (National Deworming Day — albendazole 400 mg single dose to all children 1-19 years, twice yearly). Mebendazole — alternative (100 mg BD × 3 days or 500 mg single dose); less systemic absorption; preferred for intestinal worms where systemic effect not needed.

q0_0_0_0:
Definition

Neoplasia ("new growth") is an abnormal mass of tissue, the growth of which exceeds and is uncoordinated with that of the normal tissues, and persists in the same excessive manner after cessation of the stimuli that evoked the change — Willis' definition, still the gold standard for viva recall.

Contrasting Features — Benign vs Malignant

FeatureBenignMalignant
DifferentiationWell differentiated; resembles parent tissuePoorly differentiated; anaplastic
Growth rateSlow, mitoses rare & normalRapid, mitoses frequent & atypical
Local invasionCapsulated, pushes tissues asideInfiltrative, destroys adjacent structures
MetastasisAbsentPresent (the hallmark of malignancy)
Nuclear featuresBland, uniform chromatinHyperchromatic, pleomorphic, prominent nucleoli
Clinical courseLocal pressure effects; usually curable by excisionRecurrence, cachexia, death if untreated

Routes of Spread of tumour & their mechanism

1. Local / Direct Invasion

  • Progressive infiltration, permeation and destruction of surrounding tissue — easiest route, occurs first.
  • Tumour cells lose E-cadherin (cell–cell adhesion), secrete proteases (MMP-2, MMP-9), and migrate through degraded ECM.
  • Clinical e.g. — carcinoma rectum invading bladder / prostate.

2. Lymphatic Spread

  • Most common route for carcinomas. Tumour emboli enter lymphatics → regional nodes (sentinel node first).
  • Mechanism: tumour cells express chemokine receptor CCR7 which binds CCL21 on lymphatic endothelium.
  • Examples — carcinoma breast → axillary nodes; carcinoma stomach → Virchow's node (Troisier's sign).

3. Haematogenous Spread

  • Typical of sarcomas, but also seen with carcinomas (renal cell, hepatocellular, follicular thyroid, choriocarcinoma).
  • Tumour cells invade thin-walled venules; emboli lodge in the first capillary bed encountered — liver (GIT), lungs (systemic), vertebral veins (Batson's plexus, no valves → pelvic tumours to spine).

4. Transcoelomic / Seeding

  • Spread across body cavities — most characteristically the peritoneum.
  • Krukenberg tumour — bilateral ovarian metastasis from gastric / colon signet-ring carcinoma.
  • Pseudomyxoma peritonei — mucinous carcinoma of appendix seeding peritoneum.

5. Implantation / Iatrogenic

  • Tumour cells deposited along needle tract or surgical scar — e.g. seeding after laparoscopic biopsy of mesothelioma.
flowchart TD A[Primary Tumour Cell] -->|Loss of E-cadherin| B[Detachment] B -->|MMP-2 / MMP-9| C[ECM Degradation] C --> D{Route of spread} D -->|Direct| E[Local Invasion] D -->|Lymphatic CCR7-CCL21| F[Regional Lymph Node] D -->|Venule invasion| G[Haematogenous - Liver / Lung / Bone] D -->|Body cavity| H[Transcoelomic Seeding] D -->|Instrument / needle| I[Implantation] E & F & G & H & I --> J[Secondary Deposit / Metastasis]

Clinical Pearls

  • "Carcinomas love lymphatics, sarcomas love blood." Exception: renal cell, hepatocellular, follicular thyroid carcinomas prefer blood.
  • Sentinel lymph node biopsy (using methylene blue / Tc-99) is the standard of care in breast cancer & melanoma staging.
  • Batson's vertebral venous plexus explains why prostate cancer metastasises to lumbar spine without pulmonary involvement.

Definition

Thrombosis is the formation of a solid mass (thrombus) from the constituents of the flowing blood, within the vascular tree, during life. Mass formed after death = post-mortem clot; formed outside vasculature = haematoma. The distinction matters legally and diagnostically.

Virchow's Triad — the Etiopathogenesis

Every cause of thrombosis eventually acts through one (or more) of Virchow's three pillars. Memorise the triad first — the rest follows.

PillarMechanismClinical Examples
1. Endothelial injuryLoss of anti-thrombotic (NO, PGI2, thrombomodulin, heparan sulfate); exposes subendothelial collagen & vWFAtherosclerosis, hypertension, hyperhomocysteinaemia, smoking, radiation, indwelling catheters
2. Stasis / TurbulenceDisrupts laminar flow → platelets contact endothelium; inhibits dilution of clotting factors; reduces clearance of activated factors by liverBed rest, immobilisation, prolonged travel, CHF, AFib, varicose veins, post-op
3. Hypercoagulability↑ procoagulants or ↓ anticoagulantsPrimary: Factor V Leiden, Prothrombin G20210A, AT-III / Protein C/S deficiency. Secondary: malignancy (Trousseau), pregnancy, OCPs, nephrotic syndrome, APS
flowchart LR A[Virchow Triad] --> B1[Endothelial Injury] A --> B2[Stasis / Turbulence] A --> B3[Hypercoagulability] B1 --> C[Platelet adhesion
via vWF - GP Ib] C --> D[Platelet activation
release ADP, TXA2] D --> E[Platelet aggregation
fibrinogen - GP IIb/IIIa] B3 --> F[Coagulation cascade
Tissue Factor → Extrinsic → Common] F --> G[Thrombin generation] G --> H[Fibrin polymerisation] E & H --> I[THROMBUS]

Morphology

Arterial (White) Thrombus

  • Formed in high-flow system — predominantly platelets + fibrin, pale, firm.
  • Lines of Zahn — alternating pale platelet layers and dark RBC layers (only seen in post-mortem clots in heart, but pathognomonic of true thrombus).
  • Usually mural (attached to wall) at sites of endothelial injury — e.g. over atherosclerotic plaque.

Venous (Red) Thrombus

  • Formed in slow-flow system — predominantly RBCs enmeshed in fibrin, dark red, gelatinous.
  • No lines of Zahn typically. Almost always occlusive; propagates toward the heart.
  • Classic location: deep veins of leg (DVT).

Special morphologies

  • Mural thrombus — attached to wall of heart / aorta, non-occlusive (post-MI, aneurysm).
  • Valvular vegetations — infective (large, friable, destroy valve) vs non-bacterial thrombotic (marantic, sterile, in malignancy).
  • Microthrombi — DIC, TTP/HUS; widespread capillary hyaline thrombi.

Consequences — by site

  • Coronary artery → MI; carotid / cerebral → ischaemic stroke; mesenteric → bowel infarction.
  • DVT → leg swelling, pain (Homan's sign — unreliable now); main danger = pulmonary embolism.
  • Portal vein → portal hypertension; hepatic vein → Budd-Chiari.
  • Disseminated (DIC) → consumptive coagulopathy → bleeding + microvascular thrombosis.

Fate of Thrombus

  1. Resolution — complete lysis by plasmin (best outcome).
  2. Propagation — enlarges proximally (danger of embolisation).
  3. Organisation — ingrowth of granulation tissue; may recanalise → restore some flow.
  4. Embolisation — detached fragment travels downstream (PE, stroke, limb ischaemia).

Clinical pearl

Trousseau's syndrome — migratory superficial thrombophlebitis in occult visceral malignancy (classically pancreatic carcinoma). One of the few bedside signs that should prompt an aggressive hunt for cancer.

Clinical Differentiation — Benign vs Malignant

Clinical FeatureBenignMalignant
OnsetSlow, often incidentalProgressive, symptomatic
MarginsWell-defined, mobile, encapsulatedIrregular, fixed to surrounding tissue
PainRare (unless compressing nerve)Often present (nerve infiltration, capsule stretching)
Systemic symptomsNone; weight preservedWeight loss, anorexia, cachexia, fatigue (TNF-α, IL-6)
VesselsWell-formed, not friableNeovascular, leaky, tortuous — bleed easily
Recurrence after excisionRareFrequent

Histological Differentiation

HistologyBenignMalignant
PleomorphismMild / absentMarked — variation in size/shape
N:C ratioNormal (1:4 to 1:6)Increased (1:1)
HyperchromatismMildMarked (↑ chromatin)
NucleolusInconspicuousProminent, may be multiple
MitosesRare, normalNumerous, atypical (tripolar, ring forms)
NecrosisAbsentCommon (comedo necrosis in DCIS)
CapsulePresent, true capsuleAbsent; infiltrative margin

Routes of Metastasis — with Examples

  • Lymphatic — carcinomas (breast → axillary nodes; lung → hilar & mediastinal nodes).
  • Haematogenous — sarcomas & select carcinomas (renal cell → renal vein → IVC → lungs; follicular thyroid → bone; hepatocellular → portal & hepatic veins).
  • Transcoelomic — ovarian Krukenberg (from stomach); pseudomyxoma peritonei (appendix).
  • CSF / Subarachnoid — medulloblastoma drop metastases to spinal cord.
  • Iatrogenic implantation — needle-tract seeding (mesothelioma, HCC).

Molecular Mechanism of Invasion & Metastasis

Metastasis is an inefficient, multi-step cascade — most circulating tumour cells die; only ~0.01% seed a successful colony. Each step must succeed.

flowchart TD A[Primary tumour
loosening] -->|↓ E-cadherin| B[Detachment] B -->|MMP-2, MMP-9, Cathepsin| C[ECM degradation
Basement membrane] C -->|Autocrine chemotaxis| D[Locomotion
Pseudopodia] D --> E[Intravasation
through venule wall] E --> F[Circulating Tumour Cells
coated with platelets] F -->|Arrest on capillary bed| G[Adhesion to endothelium
via CD44, selectins] G --> H[Extravasation
into parenchyma] H --> I[Pre-metastatic niche
VEGF, CXCL12] I --> J[Colonisation & Angiogenesis
dormant or proliferative] J -->|Success| K[Clinical Metastasis] J -->|Failure| L[Apoptosis / Dormancy]

Key molecular players

  • E-cadherin loss — hallmark of epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT); cells dissociate.
  • MMPs (matrix metalloproteinases) — cleave collagen IV of basement membrane; inhibited by TIMPs.
  • Integrins (α3β1, αvβ3) — transmit motility signals, bind ECM components.
  • VEGF — drives tumour angiogenesis (Folkman's hypothesis — tumour cannot grow beyond 1–2 mm² without blood supply).
  • CXCR4–CXCL12 axis — explains organ-specific homing (e.g. breast cancer → bone, liver, lung, brain).
  • "Seed and Soil" hypothesis (Paget, 1889) — metastasis occurs only when compatible seed lands on hospitable soil (organ microenvironment).

Clinical Pearl

Not every malignant tumour metastasises — basal cell carcinoma of skin is locally invasive but virtually never metastasises, while small cell lung carcinoma has often disseminated at presentation. This biological behaviour guides treatment intensity.

Definition

Amyloidosis is a heterogeneous group of disorders characterised by extracellular deposition of insoluble, fibrillar β-pleated sheet proteinaceous material — amyloid — that exhibits:

  • Congophilia — stains pink with Congo red; shows apple-green birefringence under polarised light (gold standard for diagnosis).
  • Fibrillar appearance on EM (7.5–10 nm, non-branching).
  • β-pleated sheet conformation confirmed by X-ray diffraction & infra-red spectroscopy.

Composition of Amyloid

  • Fibril protein (90%) — varies by type (AL, AA, ATTR etc.).
  • P-component (~5%) — glycoprotein, derived from serum amyloid P (SAP); protects fibrils from proteolysis.
  • Glycosaminoglycans — heparan sulfate.

Classification (Modern — Biochemical)

TypePrecursor ProteinClinical Setting
AL (Primary)Immunoglobulin light chains (λ > κ)Plasma cell dyscrasia — multiple myeloma, MGUS, B-cell lymphoma
AA (Secondary)Serum amyloid A (acute-phase reactant)Chronic inflammation — TB, rheumatoid arthritis, IBD, bronchiectasis, familial Mediterranean fever
ATTR (Hereditary / Familial)Transthyretin (TTR)Familial amyloid polyneuropathy; wild-type (senile cardiac) ATTR
Aβ2Mβ2-microglobulinLong-term haemodialysis — carpal tunnel, arthropathy
AβAmyloid β peptide (A4)Alzheimer disease, Down syndrome (after age 40)
EndocrineProcalcitonin / calcitonin, ANPMedullary carcinoma thyroid, type 2 diabetes, atria of elderly
flowchart TD A[Chronic Inflammation / Plasma cell dyscrasia / Mutant TTR] --> B[Precursor protein] B --> C[Proteolytic cleavage / Misfolding] C --> D[β-pleated sheet fibril] D --> E[Aggregation with P-component & GAGs] E --> F[Extracellular amyloid deposit] F --> G[Tissue architectural disruption] F --> H[Vascular infiltration → ischaemia] G & H --> I[Organ dysfunction]

Morphology

Gross

  • Affected organs appear enlarged, pale, waxy, firm ("lardaceous" / "bacon-like" appearance).
  • Cut surface shows homogeneous, translucent, grey-pink material.
  • Liver, spleen, kidney classically enlarged.

Microscopy (H&E)

  • Extracellular, amorphous, eosinophilic (pink) hyaline material in:
  • Vessels — walls of small arteries & arterioles (universal early site).
  • Spleen — two patterns: sago (follicular, tapioca-like) or lardaceous (diffuse red pulp).
  • Liver — begins in space of Disse, extends into sinusoids, compresses hepatocytes.
  • Kidney — glomerular mesangium & capillary walls; classically nephrotic syndrome.

Special Stains

  • Congo red → pink (light), apple-green birefringence (polarised) — diagnostic.
  • Thioflavin T → yellow-green fluorescence.
  • Crystal violet → metachromatic rose-pink.
  • Immunohistochemistry with anti-λ, anti-κ, anti-AA — to type the amyloid.

Clinical Features (by organ)

  • Renal — proteinuria → nephrotic syndrome → progressive renal failure (commonest cause of death).
  • Cardiac — restrictive cardiomyopathy, arrhythmias, heart failure (common in AL & senile ATTR).
  • GI — macroglossia (classic AL sign), hepatosplenomegaly, malabsorption, pseudo-obstruction.
  • Neuro — peripheral & autonomic neuropathy (ATTR, AL); carpal tunnel (Aβ2M, ATTR).
  • Mucocutaneous — periorbital purpura ("raccoon eyes", pathognomonic of AL), easy bruising (factor X binds amyloid).

Diagnosis

  1. Biopsy of involved organ (renal, cardiac, liver) — gold standard.
  2. Subcutaneous fat aspiration / rectal biopsy — less invasive; ~80% sensitivity in systemic disease.
  3. Congo red staining + polarised microscopy — confirmatory.
  4. Mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) — modern gold standard for typing after laser microdissection.
  5. SAP scintigraphy — maps organ distribution (less useful in cardiac).
  6. Work-up for underlying cause — serum/urine immunofixation electrophoresis (M-band in AL), serum free light chain assay, marrow biopsy; CRP/ESR for AA; TTR gene sequencing for hereditary ATTR.

Complications

  • End-stage renal disease requiring dialysis/transplant.
  • Restrictive cardiomyopathy, sudden cardiac death (arrhythmia).
  • Hepatic failure, malnutrition (GI infiltration).
  • Death — untreated systemic AL amyloidosis: median survival 6–15 months from diagnosis.

Clinical Pearl

Suspect amyloidosis in any patient with nephrotic syndrome + non-diabetic restrictive cardiomyopathy + macroglossia. The triad of "proteinuria, periorbital purpura, and a raised M-band" is a near-pathognomonic bedside presentation of AL amyloidosis.
q0_0_0_4:
Probable Diagnosis

Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) — a chronic, multisystem, autoimmune connective tissue disease characterised by production of autoantibodies against nuclear antigens (ANA), immune complex deposition, and a relapsing–remitting course predominantly affecting women of childbearing age (F:M = 9:1).

Etiology — Multifactorial

  • Genetic — HLA-DR2, HLA-DR3; C1q, C2, C4 deficiency ( homozygous deficiency → 90% lifetime risk of lupus-like illness); twin concordance ~25% monozygotic vs 2% dizygotic.
  • Hormonal — female predominance; oestrogen enhances B-cell autoimmunity; flares in pregnancy & with OCPs.
  • Environmental triggers:
    • UV light — induces keratinocyte apoptosis → exposure of nuclear antigens.
    • Drugs — procainamide, hydralazine, isoniazid, anti-TNF → drug-induced lupus (anti-histone +).
    • Infections — EBV seroprevalence near 100% in paediatric SLE.
  • Immune dysregulation — defective clearance of apoptotic bodies, polyclonal B-cell activation, T-helper bias.

Pathogenesis

flowchart TD A[Genetic susceptibility + Trigger e.g. UV] --> B[Defective clearance of apoptotic bodies] B --> C[Accumulation of nuclear material] C --> D[Activation of autoreactive B & T cells] D --> E[Autoantibody production
ANA, anti-dsDNA, anti-Sm, anti-phospholipid] E --> F[Immune complex formation] F --> G[Circulating immune complexes] G --> H[Deposition in tissues
glomeruli, skin, serosa, vessels] H --> I[Complement activation
C3a, C5a, MAC] I --> J[Inflammation, tissue damage] J --> K[Clinical lesions — glomerulonephritis, malar rash, serositis, vasculitis] F --> L[Type II hypersensitivity
cytopenias - haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia]

Key pathogenetic triad: (1) autoantibodies, (2) immune complexes, (3) complement activation & tissue inflammation.

Gross Pathology

  • Skin — erythematous, slightly raised malar (butterfly) rash sparing nasolabial fold; discoid lesions with scarring & follicular plugging.
  • Kidney — may be normal sized or slightly enlarged; "flea-bitten" appearance if petechial haemorrhages; class IV has the most dramatic changes.
  • Serosal surfaces — fibrinous or serous effusions (pleuritis, pericarditis).
  • Spleen — moderate splenomegaly; "onion-skin" arteriolar thickening (pathognomonic on microscopy).
  • Heart — Libman-Sacks verrucous vegetations on both sides of valves (especially mitral).
  • Joints — deforming but non-erosive Jaccoud arthropathy.

Microscopy

Skin (Lupus Band Test)

  • Basement membrane — vacuolar degeneration of basal keratinocytes; epidermal atrophy.
  • Dermo-epidermal junction — granular deposit of IgG, IgM, C3 by immunofluorescence (positive lupus band test in lesional AND sun-exposed non-lesional skin of SLE).

Kidney — Lupus Nephritis (ISN/RPS Classification)

ClassPatternHistology
IMinimal mesangialNormal LM; immune deposits by IF/EM only
IIMesangial proliferativeMesangial hypercellularity & deposits
IIIFocal proliferative<50% glomeruli; segmental endocapillary proliferation, karyorrhexis (fibrinoid necrosis), "wire-loop" lesions
IVDiffuse proliferative (worst, commonest severe)≥50% glomeruli; wire-loop, hyaline thrombi, crescents; "full-house" IF
VMembranousDiffuse thickening; subepithelial deposits → nephrotic syndrome
VIAdvanced sclerosing≥90% global glomerulosclerosis

Other Micro Findings

  • "Onion-skin" splenic arterioles — concentric periarterial fibrosis; virtually pathognomonic of SLE.
  • Libman-Sacks endocarditis — verrucae of fibrin, platelets, immune complexes on both sides of valve leaflets (distinguishes from rheumatic and infective endocarditis).
  • Hyaline thrombi in small vessels — occasionally with TMA picture.
  • Non-erosive synovitis — joints affected but cartilage preserved.

Clinical Pearl — Diagnostic Criteria

Use the SLICC 2012 or EULAR/ACR 2019 criteria — ≥4 criteria (including ≥1 clinical & ≥1 immunological) with a score ≥10 yields ~93% sensitivity & specificity. ANA is the entry criterion. Anti-dsDNA & anti-Sm are highly specific; anti-dsDNA titres also track disease activity & nephritis.
q0_0_0_5:
Probable Diagnosis

Septic shock — a subset of distributive shock caused by a dysregulated host response to infection, presenting with circulatory, cellular & metabolic abnormalities and persisting hypotension requiring vasopressors despite adequate fluid resuscitation, with associated organ dysfunction (Sepsis-3 definition, JAMA 2016).

Etiology

  • Commonest organisms — Gram-negative bacilli (E. coli, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas) and Gram-positive cocci (S. aureus, S. pneumoniae, Enterococci) are now nearly equal in incidence.
  • Fungal sepsis (Candida) — increasing in ICU & immunocompromised.
  • Sources — genitourinary, respiratory, GI/biliary, skin/soft tissue, indwelling catheters, post-operative wounds.
  • Risk factors — extremes of age, immunosuppression, diabetes, malignancy, malnutrition, burns, invasive devices, asplenia.

Pathogenesis — The "Cytokine Storm"

flowchart TD A[Infection / Microbial products
LPS, PGN, CpG DNA] --> B[PRR recognition
TLR4, TLR2, NLRs] B --> C[Activation of monocytes/macrophages & endothelium] C --> D[Massive cytokine release
TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6, IL-8, IFN-γ] D --> E1[↑ NOS → NO overproduction] D --> E2[↑ iNOS in vessels → vasodilation] D --> E3[Endothelial activation & injury
↑ adhesion molecules, glycocalyx shedding] D --> E4[Complement & coagulation activation] E1 & E2 --> F[Systemic vasodilation
↓ SVR, refractory hypotension] E3 --> G[Capillary leak → tissue oedema] E4 --> H[Microvascular thrombosis → DIC] F & G & H --> I[Maldistribution of blood flow
regional hypoperfusion] I --> J[Cellular hypoxia & mitochondrial dysfunction] J --> K[Multi-Organ Dysfunction Syndrome - MODS]

The fundamental lesion is not pump failure (like cardiogenic shock) but a maldistribution of blood flow with capillary leak, microthrombi and mitochondrial dysfunction — so patients often have a high cardiac output ("warm shock") initially before cardiovascular collapse.

Phases — Warm vs Cold Shock

  • Early (Warm) shock — vasodilated, flushed, warm peripheries, bounding pulse, widened pulse pressure, oliguria, altered mental state. Often missed at bedside.
  • Late (Cold) shock — vasoconstriction kicks in secondarily; cold clammy skin, weak thready pulse, narrow pulse pressure, multi-organ failure. Mortality rises steeply.

Gross Pathology

  • Non-specific — organs congested, oedematous.
  • Lungs — heavy, congested, haemorrhagic; ARDS picture with hyaline membranes.
  • Adrenals — bilateral haemorrhagic necrosis in Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome (meningococcaemia).
  • GIT — patchy haemorrhagic necrosis (gut is the "motor of multi-organ failure").
  • Spleen — may be enlarged (septic spleen) in subacute sepsis.
  • Kidneys — acute tubular necrosis (gross: pale, swollen kidneys with muddy brown casts).

Microscopy

  • Microvascular thrombi — widespread capillary fibrin-platelet thrombi (DIC).
  • Acute tubular necrosis — kidney tubular epithelial necrosis, muddy brown casts.
  • Diffuse alveolar damage (DAD) — lungs show hyaline membranes, type II pneumocyte hyperplasia.
  • Hepatic — centrilobular necrosis (zone 3) due to hypotension; cholestasis.
  • Adrenal — haemorrhage & necrosis (Waterhouse-Friderichsen).
  • Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation — microthrombi in many organs; depletion of platelets & clotting factors.

Organ Dysfunction Markers (qSOFA at Bedside)

  • Respiratory rate ≥ 22/min
  • Altered mentation (GCS < 15)
  • Systolic BP ≤ 100 mmHg
  • ≥2 of 3 → high risk of poor outcome; prompts sepsis work-up.

Clinical Pearl

"Surviving Sepsis Campaign Hour-1 Bundle": within 1 hour of recognition — measure lactate, obtain blood cultures, administer broad-spectrum antibiotics, begin 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate ≥4, start vasopressors if hypotensive during/after fluids. Early antibiotics (every hour delay = ~7–8% rise in mortality) is the single most modifiable factor.
q0_0_0_6:
Setting the Scene

A patient on ventilator with devastating brain injury has been certified brain-stem dead. The physician now has three interlocking duties — medical (confirm death & maintain physiology for donation), legal (follow Transplantation of Human Organs Act, 1994), and ethical (autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, justice). Counselling the family for organ donation is woven through all three.

1. Medical Responsibilities

  • Diagnose brain-stem death using laid-down apnoea & brain-stem reflex testing — performed by a panel of four physicians (in India, per THOA 1994 & amendments): administrator-in-charge, a neurologist/neurosurgeon, the treating physician, and an independent registered medical practitioner. Two evaluations 6 hours apart are required; the second is legally the time of death.
  • Maintain donor physiology — ventilatory support, normotension, normothermia (core >35°C), euglycaemia, urine output >1 mL/kg/h. Manage diabetes insipidus (DDAVP), correct electrolyte disturbances (hypernatraemia common).
  • Avoid harm — discontinue futile interventions if family declines donation; continue dignified end-of-life care.
  • Document meticulously — time, findings, panel signatures; chain of custody if organ retrieval planned.

2. Legal Responsibilities (India — THOA 1994, amended 2011 & 2014)

  • Brain-stem death is legally recognised as death in India (THOA amended 2011, Section 2(d)). The patient is dead — there is no ethical conflict in withdrawing the ventilator after certification.
  • Informed consent for organ retrieval must be obtained from the next of kin in writing on Form 8 (or equivalent state form). Consent must be voluntary, free of coercion, and specific to organs/tissues.
  • Required consent hierarchy: spouse, then adult son/daughter, then parents, then sibling, then other legal guardian.
  • Organ trafficking is a cognisable, non-bailable offence — punishable up to 10 years + fine. Doctors must never act as brokers between recipient and donor families (transplant coordinator, an independent functionary, is mandatory under THOA Rules 2014).
  • Mandatory death certificate — issue in standard format, mention brain-stem death as cause where applicable.
  • Confidentiality — donor and recipient identities are kept confidential from each other.
  • Mandatory reporting to NOTTO/ROTTO/SOTTO registries for transparency.

3. Ethical Responsibilities

  • Autonomy — respect the prior wishes of the deceased (donor card, family-aware directives) and of the family now.
  • Beneficence — transplantation can save up to 8 lives (kidneys ×2, liver, heart, lungs ×2, pancreas, small bowel) and enhance many more via tissues (cornea, skin, bone, heart valves). Frame donation as a positive legacy.
  • Non-maleficence — do not hasten death to retrieve organs; the Dead Donor Rule is inviolable — retrieval must not begin before death certification.
  • Justice — fair allocation via NOTTO waitlist on objective criteria (blood group, HLA match, urgency, waiting time, age) — never wealth, social status, or influence.
  • Cultural & religious sensitivity — many families have concerns about bodily integrity in afterlife; approach with humility, not persuasion.

4. Counselling the Family for Organ Donation — A Step-by-Step Approach

flowchart TD A[Breaking bad news - SPIKES protocol] --> B[Allow grief reaction - silence, time, tissues] B --> C[Confirm understanding of brain-stem death
avoid jargon; 'death of brain, heart still beating on machine'] C --> D{Family accepts concept of death?} D -->|No - denial| E[Re-explain, offer spiritual counsellor, second opinion] D -->|Yes| F[Introduce option of organ donation
separate from death declaration - decouple] F --> G[Use plain language - 'gift of life', save up to 8 lives] G --> H[Address fears - body disfigurement, religious objection, cost] H --> I[Transplant coordinator joins
- explains procedure, paperwork, NOTTO registry] I --> J{Family decision} J -->|Consent| K[Sign Form 8; activate retrieval team] J -->|Decline| L[Respect decision; continue dignified end-of-life care; no coercion]

Practical counselling principles

  • "Decoupling" — first communicate death clearly and let it sink in. Only after the family accepts the reality of death, raise the topic of donation. Combining the two is emotionally confusing and reduces consent rates.
  • SPIKES protocol for breaking bad news: Setting, Perception (ask what they understand), Invitation (how much detail they want), Knowledge (give the news in small chunks), Emotions (acknowledge), Strategy & Summary.
  • Use the transplant coordinator — a trained, neutral professional — for the actual donation conversation. Doctors tend to be perceived as "rushing"; coordinators improve consent rates by ~30%.
  • Address common fears directly: "Will the body be disfigured?" (No — surgical incisions are closed like any operation; can view body afterwards); "Will it cost us?" (No — all costs borne by retrieval hospital/recipient); "Is my religion against it?" (No major religion opposes organ donation; many actively endorse it).
  • Document consent clearly, including which specific organs are consented — family may consent to corneas only and decline solid organs; respect that.
  • Offer bereavement support follow-up; share outcome (which recipient received which organ) after a few weeks if family wishes — this often helps grieving.

5. Common Pitfalls & Medico-legal Risks

  • Certifying brain-stem death without full panel or incomplete documentation — invalid in court.
  • Approaching family for donation before they have accepted death — perceived as pressure, reduces consent and risks complaint.
  • Conflict of interest — a member of the transplant team cannot be on the brain-stem death certification panel.
  • Continuing ventilator after refusal of donation without a clear plan — "futile care" communication breakdown causes medico-legal disputes.

Clinical Pearl

India has an organ donation rate of only ~0.34 per million population (vs 30+ in Spain). The single largest modifiable factor is early, trained, decoupled counselling by a transplant coordinator. As the certifying physician, your job is to diagnose death correctly, document it meticulously, and introduce the conversation gently — not to persuade. Persuasion is a fine line that can quickly become coercion.

Overview

Urinalysis is one of the oldest, cheapest, and most informative bedside investigations — a "liquid biopsy" of the kidney & urinary tract. A complete examination has three components: Physical, Chemical, and Microscopic.

1. Physical Examination

ParameterNormalAbnormal — Clinical Significance
Volume600–2000 mL/day↑ Polyuria (DM, DI, CKD); ↓ Oliguria (<400 mL/day), Anuria (<100 mL/day)
ColourPale yellow / amber (urochrome)Red — haematuria, beeturia, porphyria, rifampicin; Brown — old blood, bilirubin; Smoky — glomerulonephritis; Milky — chyluria, pyuria
Appearance / TurbidityClearCloudy — phosphates (alkaline), urates (acid), pyuria, chyluria; Frothy — proteinuria
OdourAromaticPungent — ammonia (UTI); Fruity — ketones (DKA); Mousy — phenylketonuria; Maple syrup — maple syrup urine disease
Specific gravity1.003–1.030↑ Dehydration, glycosuria, contrast; ↓ DI, over-hydration; Fixed 1.010 — chronic renal disease (isosthenuria)
pH4.5–8.0 (avg ~6, acidic)↑ Alkaline — UTI with urea-splitting organisms (Proteus), RTA type 1, vomiting; ↓ Acidic — DKA, lactic acidosis, fever, diarrhoea

2. Chemical Examination

Modern dipsticks (e.g. Combur, Multistix) use dry chemistry pads read visually or by automated reader.

  • pH — double indicator (methyl red / bromothymol blue).
  • Specific gravity — ionic strength indicator (bromothymol blue).
  • Protein — tetrabromophenol blue dye-binding; detects mainly albumin (false negative for Bence-Jones proteins → use sulphosalicylic acid test / protein electrophoresis).
  • Glucose — glucose oxidase-peroxidase (GOD-POD); specific for glucose only. False + with peroxide cleaners; false − with high dose vitamin C.
  • Ketones — sodium nitroprusside reaction with acetoacetate (not β-hydroxybutyrate).
  • Blood / Haemoglobin — peroxidase-like activity of Hb / myoglobin lyses chromogen; intact RBCs produce speckled pattern; lysed RBCs / myoglobin produce uniform colour.
  • Bilirubin — diazo reaction (2,4-dichloroaniline); absent in normal urine.
  • Urobilinogen — Ehrlich aldehyde reaction; normally present in traces; absent in complete biliary obstruction; raised in haemolysis & hepatocellular dysfunction.
  • Nitrite — Greiss reaction; positive with nitrate-reducing bacteria (E. coli, Klebsiella, Proteus) — needs urine to dwell ≥4 h in bladder; first morning sample most useful.
  • Leucocyte esterase — detects esterases from lysed WBCs; sensitive for pyuria.

3. Microscopic Examination

Performed on freshly voided, midstream, centrifuged urine (10 mL at 1500 rpm × 5 min), examined under low & high power. Findings are reported per high-power field (HPF).

Cells

  • RBCs — >3 RBC/HPF = haematuria. Dysmorphic RBCs & RBC casts → glomerular bleeding; Isomorphic RBCs → urological cause (stones, tumour, infection).
  • WBCs — >5 WBC/HPF = pyuria. Sterile pyuria — TB, Chlamydia, gonococcus, stones, interstitial nephritis, partially treated UTI.
  • Epithelial cells — squamous (contamination); transitional (catheterised, catheter-induced); renal tubular (ATN, acute interstitial nephritis, acute tubular injury).
  • Oval fat bodies — lipid-laden renal tubular cells; "Maltese cross" appearance under polarised light — nephrotic syndrome.

Casts (formed in distal & collecting tubules; matrix = Tamm-Horsfall protein)

  • Hyaline — clear, colourless; normal after exercise, dehydration; nonspecific.
  • Granular — degenerated tubular cells; "muddy brown" coarse granular casts → acute tubular necrosis.
  • RBC casts — pathognomonic of glomerulonephritis (e.g. post-streptococcal, IgA nephropathy).
  • WBC casts — acute pyelonephritis, acute interstitial nephritis.
  • Broad waxy casts — formed in dilated tubules of chronically diseased kidney; chronic renal failure.
  • Fatty casts — nephrotic syndrome.

Crystals

  • Calcium oxalate (envelope / "envelope" appearance) — acidic urine; ethylene glycol poisoning shows envelope & needle forms.
  • Uric acid (rhomboid / "whetstone") — acidic urine; gout, tumour lysis.
  • Triple phosphate ("coffin-lid") — alkaline urine; Proteus UTI (struvite stones).
  • Cystine (hexagonal, benzene ring) — cystinuria.
  • Sulphonamide, radiographic contrast — drug-induced crystals with acute kidney injury.

Organisms

  • Bacteria (rods / cocci) — UTI; confirm with culture & sensitivity.
  • Trichomonas vaginalis, yeast (Candida), Schistosoma haematobium ova — depending on geography.
flowchart LR A[Fresh MSU sample] --> B[Physical - colour / clarity / SG / pH] A --> C[Chemical - dipstick 10 parameters] A --> D[Centrifuge 5 min 1500 rpm] D --> E[Sediment microscopy - cells / casts / crystals / organisms] B & C & E --> F[Correlate with clinical picture] F --> G[Diagnosis]

Clinical Pearl

The combination "dipstick protein + dysmorphic RBCs + RBC casts" is the bedside fingerprint of glomerular disease and warrants urgent nephrology referral & renal biopsy. Conversely, dipstick blood with isomorphic RBCs and no proteinuria points to a urological cause — investigate with imaging/cystoscopy, not biopsy.

Overview

Neutrophils are the first responders of acute inflammation. Their journey from the bloodstream into the tissue is described by a 5-step paradigm — each step governed by specific adhesion molecules and chemokines. Failure of any step produces immunodeficiency (e.g. leucocyte adhesion deficiency type 1 due to CD18 deficiency → recurrent infections without pus).

flowchart TD A[Margination] --> B[Rolling] B --> C[Adhesion / Firm arrest] C --> D[Transmigration / Diapedesis] D --> E[Chemotaxis] E --> F[Phagocytosis at site]

Step 1 — Margination

  • In normal laminar flow, RBCs occupy the axial (central) stream and WBCs are pushed to the periphery — the "plasma skimming" effect.
  • With inflammation, vasodilation slows blood flow & increases viscosity → neutrophils settle against the endothelium (margination).

Step 2 — Rolling (Loose, Transient Adhesion)

  • Selectin family mediates weak, reversible binding — bond breaks & re-forms, so leucocytes "roll" along the endothelium.
  • E-selectin (endothelium; induced by TNF-α & IL-1 within 2 hours).
  • P-selectin (preformed in Weibel-Palade bodies; mobilised to surface within minutes by histamine & thrombin).
  • L-selectin (on neutrophil surface).
  • Ligands — sialyl-Lewis X on leucocytes; PSGL-1 (P-selectin glycoprotein ligand-1).

Step 3 — Adhesion / Firm Arrest

  • Chemokines (IL-8, C5a, LTB4) activate neutrophils and trigger conformational change in integrins on the leucocyte surface → high-affinity binding.
  • β2 integrins (CD18) — LFA-1 (CD11a/CD18), Mac-1 (CD11b/CD18) on the neutrophil.
  • Ligands on endothelium — ICAM-1 (inducible by TNF-α, IL-1) and ICAM-2.
  • This step is the tightest — once integrins bind ICAM-1, the neutrophil stops rolling and flattens.

Step 4 — Transmigration / Diapedesis

  • Neutrophils crawl to intercellular junctions and squeeze between endothelial cells.
  • Mediated by PECAM-1 (CD31) — homophilic binding between endothelial & leucocyte CD31.
  • Other molecules — VE-cadherin, CD99, JAM (junctional adhesion molecules).
  • The neutrophil then crosses the basement membrane by secreting collagenases (MMP-8, MMP-9) & elastase.

Step 5 — Chemotaxis

  • Directed migration along a chemical gradient toward the site of injury.
  • Exogenous chemotaxins — bacterial products (N-formyl peptides like fMet-Leu-Phe).
  • Endogenous chemotaxins — C5a, LTB4, IL-8, fibrinopeptides, platelet-activating factor (PAF).
  • Receptors — G-protein coupled receptors; ligand binding triggers actin polymerisation at the leading edge (pseudopod formation).

Step 6 — Phagocytosis (after arrival)

  • Recognition & attachment — enhanced by opsonins (IgG, C3b); binds FcγR & CR1/CR3.
  • Engulfment — pseudopods encircle the particle → phagosome → phagolysosome.
  • Killing — two mechanisms:
    • Oxygen-dependent — NADPH oxidase (respiratory burst) → superoxide → H₂O₂ → via MPO + Cl⁻ → hypochlorous acid (bleach). Defect = chronic granulomatous disease.
    • Oxygen-independent — lysozyme, lactoferrin, defensins, proteases, low pH.

Clinical Correlations — When the Cascade Fails

  • LAD-1 — CD18 deficiency; neutrophils can't bind ICAM-1 → no pus formation despite high neutrophil count; delayed umbilical stump separation.
  • LAD-2 — fucose transporter defect (Sialyl-Lewis X absent) → mentally retarded child with recurrent infections.
  • Chronic Granulomatous Disease — NADPH oxidase defect → recurrent catalase-positive infections (S. aureus, Aspergillus, Serratia); diagnostic NBT/DHR test.
  • Chédiak-Higashi syndrome — giant lysosomal granules; defective chemotaxis & degranulation; partial albinism.
  • Hyper-IgE (Job) syndrome — impaired chemotaxis → cold staphylococcal abscesses, retained primary teeth, eczema, high IgE.

Clinical Pearl

Glucocorticoids reduce ICAM-1 expression on endothelium — explaining both their anti-inflammatory benefit and their propensity to impair bacterial clearance. This is also why a patient on steroids may show a paucity of pus at an infection site even with florid sepsis — clinical signs are masked, and a high index of suspicion is required.

Overview

Chemical mediators of inflammation are released from cells (mast cells, platelets, neutrophils, macrophages, endothelium) and from plasma (kinin, complement, coagulation/fibrinolytic systems). Here we focus on the cell-derived mediators — the viva expects you to list, classify, and indicate actions.

Functional Summary (for viva recall)

  • Vasodilation — histamine, PGE2, PGI2, NO, PAF.
  • ↑ Vascular Permeability — histamine, bradykinin (plasma), PAF, LTC4/D4/E4, substance P.
  • Pain — bradykinin, PGE2 (sensitises nociceptors), substance P.
  • Fever — PGE2 (acts on hypothalamus), IL-1, TNF-α, IL-6 (acute-phase pyrogens).
  • Chemotaxis — LTB4, C5a, IL-8, bacterial f-Met peptides, PAF.
  • Tissue damage — ROS, lysosomal proteases (elastase, collagenase), NO.

Clinical Pearl — Drug Targets

  • NSAIDs block COX-1 & COX-2 → ↓ PGs & thromboxanes. COX-2 selective (celecoxib) spares gastric protection (PGE2) but ↑ thrombotic risk (loss of PGI2 leaving TXA2 unopposed).
  • Corticosteroids induce lipocortin-1 → ↓ phospholipase A2 → ↓ both PGs & LTs. Comprehensive anti-inflammatory action.
  • Leukotriene-receptor antagonists (montelukast, zafirlukast) block LTD4 receptor — useful in asthma, especially aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease.
  • Anti-IgE (omalizumab) & anti-IL-5 (mepolizumab) target upstream signalling in severe asthma.
  • Anti-TNF biologics (infliximab, adalimumab, etanercept) — TNF-α blockade in rheumatoid arthritis, IBD, psoriasis, ankylosing spondylitis.
